stem: Unless otherwise authorized, which situation requires Automatic Dependent Surveillance-Broadcast (ADS-B)?
options: Landing at an airport with an operating control tower.
Overflying Class C airspace below 10,000 feet MSL.
Flying under the shelf of Class C airspace.
explanation: ADS-B Out is required above the ceiling and within the lateral boundaries of Class B or Class C airspace up to 10,000 feet MSL, so overflying Class C below 10,000 feet requires it. Flying under a Class C shelf does not require ADS-B unless you are also inside a Class B Mode C veil or another required area, which is the trap. Landing at a towered airport in Class D airspace does not by itself require ADS-B.

stem: The correct method of stating 5,500 feet MSL to ATC is
options: FIVE POINT FIVE.
FIFTY-FIVE HUNDRED FEET MSL.
FIVE THOUSAND FIVE HUNDRED.
explanation: Altitudes below 18,000 feet MSL are stated by separate digits for thousands plus the hundreds, so 5,500 is spoken as FIVE THOUSAND FIVE HUNDRED. Pilots should not add MSL or say FIFTY FIVE HUNDRED. FIVE POINT FIVE could be heard as a frequency or a decimal value.

stem: Each person who holds a pilot certificate or a medical certificate shall present it for inspection upon the request of any
options: authorized representative of the Department of Transportation.
person in a position of authority.
local law enforcement officer.
explanation: A pilot must present the pilot certificate, medical certificate and photo identification on request of the Administrator, an authorized NTSB representative, any federal, state or local law enforcement officer, or an authorized TSA representative. Of the choices, a local law enforcement officer is listed in the rule. A person in a position of authority is too vague. The Department of Transportation is not named in the rule, although the FAA itself sits within DOT, which makes option A tempting.

stem: When warm, moist, stable air flows upslope, it
options: produces stratus type clouds.
causes showers and thunderstorms.
develops convective turbulence.
explanation: Stable air that is forced up a slope cools to saturation and forms stratus type clouds and fog, with smooth air. Showers, thunderstorms and convective turbulence come from unstable air. The trap is tying any lifting to thunderstorms; stability decides the cloud type.

stem: When there is a temperature inversion, you would expect to experience
options: clouds with extensive vertical development above an inversion aloft.
good visibility in the lower levels of the atmosphere and poor visibility above an inversion aloft.
an increase in temperature as altitude increases.
explanation: An inversion is a layer in which temperature increases with altitude, the reverse of the normal lapse rate. It makes air stable and traps haze, smoke and fog beneath it, so visibility is poor below the inversion and good above it. Option B reverses that, and an inversion suppresses vertical cloud development rather than causing it.

stem: Eye movements during daytime collision avoidance scanning should
options: not exceed 10 degrees and view each sector at least 1 second.
be 30 degrees and view each sector at least 3 seconds.
use peripheral vision by scanning small sectors and utilizing off-center viewing.
explanation: For daytime scanning, the AIM recommends short, regularly spaced eye movements that bring successive areas into the central field of vision, with each movement not exceeding 10 degrees and each area viewed for at least 1 second. Off center viewing is the technique for night vision, which is the trap here.

stem: The wind at 5,000 feet AGL is southwesterly while the surface wind is southerly. This difference in direction is primarily due to
options: stronger pressure gradient at higher altitudes.
friction between the wind and the surface.
stronger Coriolis force at the surface.
explanation: Surface friction slows the wind near the ground, which weakens the Coriolis force so the wind turns toward low pressure and crosses isobars at an angle. Aloft, without friction, the wind flows nearly parallel to the isobars. That is why the surface wind is backed (southerly) relative to the southwesterly wind at 5,000 feet. Coriolis force is weaker at the surface, not stronger, which is the trap.

stem: In what flight condition are torque effects more pronounced in a single-engine airplane?
options: Low airspeed, high power, high angle of attack.
Low airspeed, low power, low angle of attack.
High airspeed, high power, high angle of attack.
explanation: Torque, P factor, slipstream and gyroscopic effects are strongest with high power at low airspeed and a high angle of attack, as in a full power climb or takeoff. At low airspeed the control surfaces are also less effective at countering them. High airspeed lets the rudder and the airplane's design offset the left turning tendencies, so option C is the trap.

stem: Your cousin wants you to take him flying. You must have made at least three takeoffs and three landings in your aircraft within the preceding
options: 90 days.
60 days.
30 days.
explanation: To carry passengers you must have made at least three takeoffs and three landings within the preceding 90 days in an aircraft of the same category, class and, if a type rating is required, type. At night those landings must be to a full stop between one hour after sunset and one hour before sunrise. The 30 and 60 day options are not currency periods in part 61.

stem: You plan to phone a weather briefing facility for preflight weather information. You should
options: provide the number of occupants on board.
identify yourself as a pilot.
begin with your route of flight.
explanation: Start a briefing request by identifying yourself as a pilot, so the briefer gives you an aviation briefing rather than general information. Then give the type of flight, aircraft, departure, route, destination, altitude and timing. Route is part of the request, but stating you are a pilot comes first; the number of occupants is flight plan information, not briefing information.

stem: If Receiver Autonomous Integrity Monitoring (RAIM) capability is lost in-flight,
options: the pilot may still rely on GPS derived altitude for vertical information.
the pilot has no assurance of the accuracy of the GPS position.
GPS position is reliable provided at least 3 GPS satellites are available.
explanation: RAIM checks GPS integrity by comparing ranges from several satellites. Without it the receiver cannot detect a bad satellite signal, so the pilot has no assurance the position is accurate. Three satellites give only a two dimensional fix and cannot provide RAIM, and GPS altitude is less accurate than lateral position, so neither wrong option helps.

stem: (Refer to FAA-CT-8080-2H, Figure 78.) What are the basic VFR weather minima required to takeoff from the Onawa, IA (K36) airport during the day?
options: 3 statute miles visibility, 500 feet below the clouds, 1,000 feet above the clouds, and 2,000 feet horizontally from the clouds.
0 statute miles, clear of clouds.
1 statute mile, clear of clouds.
explanation: Onawa (K36) has no dashed Class D or Class E surface area line, and no magenta vignette, so the airspace at the surface is Class G and Class E begins at 1,200 feet AGL. Day VFR in Class G at or below 1,200 feet AGL requires 1 statute mile visibility and clear of clouds. Option A gives the controlled airspace minimums, and zero visibility is never a VFR takeoff minimum.

stem: From the cockpit, this marking confirms the aircraft to be
options: on a taxiway, about to enter runway zone.
on a runway, about to clear.
near an instrument approach clearance zone.
explanation: The runway holding position marking has two solid yellow lines on the taxiway side and two dashed yellow lines on the runway side. Approaching from the dashed side, as the arrow shows, means you are on the runway and about to clear it. You are clear once the whole airplane has crossed the solid lines. The trap is option A, which describes approaching from the solid side.

stem: This sign confirms your position on
options: runway 22.
routing to runway 22.
taxiway 22.
explanation: A black sign with a yellow inscription and yellow border is a location sign. A number on a location sign identifies the runway you are on, so this sign confirms you are on runway 22. A taxiway location sign shows a letter, and a sign giving the route to a runway is a yellow direction or destination sign with black lettering and an arrow, which is the trap.

stem: A pilot experiencing the effects of hyperventilation should be able to restore the proper carbon dioxide level in the body by
options: slowing the breathing rate, breathing into a paper bag, or talking aloud.
breathing spontaneously and deeply or gaining mental control of the situation.
increasing the breathing rate in order to increase lung ventilation.
explanation: Hyperventilation is breathing too fast or too deeply, which drives too much carbon dioxide out of the body. Slowing the breathing rate, breathing into a paper bag, or talking aloud lets carbon dioxide build back up. Breathing faster or more deeply makes the condition worse, which is the trap in both wrong options.

stem: When making routine transponder code changes, pilots should avoid inadvertent selection of which code?
explanation: Code 7500 signals unlawful interference (a hijacking). When changing codes, avoid passing through 7500, 7600 and 7700, since even a momentary selection can set off alarms on ATC displays. 7000 and 7200 are ordinary codes that carry no special meaning in the United States.

stem: The Aeronautical Information Manual (AIM) specifically encourages pilots to turn on their landing lights when operating below 10,000 feet, day or night, and especially when operating
options: in Class B airspace.
in conditions of reduced visibility.
within 15 miles of a towered airport.
explanation: The AIM encourages landing lights on below 10,000 feet, day or night, especially within 10 miles of any airport, in conditions of reduced visibility, and where flocks of birds may be expected. Reduced visibility is the condition listed in the options. The 15 miles of a towered airport option is the trap; the AIM figure is 10 miles of any airport.

stem: (Refer to FAA-CT-8080-2H, Figure 8.) What is the effect of a temperature increase from 35 to 50°F on the density altitude if the pressure altitude remains at 3,000 feet MSL?
options: 1,000-foot increase.
1,100-foot decrease.
1,300-foot increase.
explanation: On Figure 8, follow the 3,000 foot pressure altitude line. At 35 degrees F it reads about 2,100 feet density altitude, and at 50 degrees F, just warmer than the 48 degree standard temperature for 3,000 feet, it reads about 3,100 feet. That is an increase of roughly 1,000 feet. As a cross check, 15 degrees F is about 8 degrees C, and at roughly 120 feet per degree C that is about 1,000 feet. A rise in temperature always raises density altitude, so the decrease option is wrong in principle, and 1,300 feet overstates the change.

stem: The radius of the procedural outer area of Class C airspace is normally
options: 10 NM.
20 NM.
30 NM.
explanation: Class C airspace normally has an outer area with a 20 NM radius from the primary airport, where approach provides sequencing and separation to participating aircraft. The 10 NM figure is the radius of the outer shelf of the Class C itself, the most common trap. Thirty miles is the Mode C veil around Class B primary airports.

stem: How far will an aircraft travel in 7.5 minutes with a ground speed of 114 knots?
explanation: Distance = ground speed x time: 114 knots x 7.5 / 60 hours = 114 x 0.125 = 14.25 NM. 15.00 NM is what you get if you round the speed to 2 NM per minute (120 knots), a common shortcut slip.

stem: When executing an emergency approach to land in a single-engine airplane, it is important to maintain a constant glide speed because variations in glide speed will
options: increase the chances of shock cooling the engine.
assure the proper descent angle is maintained until entering the flare.
nullify all attempts at accuracy in judgment of gliding distance and landing spot.
explanation: Holding a constant best glide speed gives a predictable glide angle, which lets you judge whether you can reach the chosen landing spot. Each change in airspeed changes the glide path and ruins that judgment. Shock cooling is a real concern for engines but has nothing to do with the accuracy of a forced landing approach.

stem: Deviation error of the magnetic compass is caused by
options: a northerly turning error.
certain metals and electrical systems within the aircraft.
the difference in location of true north and magnetic north.
explanation: Deviation is compass error caused by magnetic fields from metal parts and electrical equipment in the airplane, and it is recorded on the compass correction card. The angle between true north and magnetic north is variation, which is the trap. Northerly turning error is a separate dip related error.

stem: Which statement relates to Bernoulli's principle?
options: For every action there is an equal and opposite reaction.
An additional upward force is generated as the lower surface of the airfoil deflects air downward.
Air traveling faster over the curved upper surface of an airfoil causes lower pressure on the top surface.
explanation: Bernoulli's principle says that as the velocity of a fluid increases its pressure decreases, so faster air over the curved upper surface of the wing produces lower pressure on top. Option A is Newton's third law and option B describes the downwash effect, also Newtonian. Both contribute to lift but neither is Bernoulli's principle.

stem: ATC advises, "traffic 12 o'clock." This advisory is relative to your
options: true course.
ground track.
magnetic heading.
explanation: Radar traffic advisories use the clock system based on the airplane's ground track as the radar sees it, since ATC cannot see your heading. If you are holding a wind correction angle, the traffic may appear off the nose rather than where the clock position says. Magnetic heading is the trap, because pilots naturally think in terms of where the nose points.

stem: While on a VFR cross country and not in contact with ATC, what frequency would you use in the event of an emergency?
explanation: 121.5 MHz is the VHF emergency frequency, monitored by many ATC facilities, Flight Service and military facilities. If you are not already talking to ATC, it is the quickest way to reach help. 122.5 is a Flight Service frequency used at some locations and 128.725 is just a working frequency, so neither is the guaranteed emergency channel.

stem: (Refer to FAA-CT-8080-2H, Figure 20, area 1.) The NALF Fentress (NFE) Airport is in what type of airspace?
options: Class C.
Class E.
Class G.
explanation: In Figure 20, NALF Fentress (NFE) is surrounded by a dashed magenta line, which marks a Class E surface area. It lies south of the solid magenta Norfolk Class C boundary, not within it. The trap is Class C because Norfolk's Class C is close by; a dashed blue line would have meant Class D.

stem: If an aircraft is equipped with a fixed-pitch propeller and a float-type carburetor, the first indication of carburetor ice would most likely be
options: a drop in oil temperature and cylinder head temperature.
engine roughness.
loss of RPM.
explanation: With a fixed pitch propeller, carburetor ice restricts the airflow to the engine and the first sign is a loss of RPM. Roughness usually follows as the ice builds, so engine roughness is the tempting but later symptom. Oil and cylinder head temperatures are not reliable early indicators of carburetor ice.

stem: A pilot and two passengers landed on a 2,100 foot east-west gravel strip with an elevation of 1,800 feet. The temperature is warmer than expected and after computing the density altitude it is determined the takeoff distance over a 50 foot obstacle is 1,980 feet. The airplane is 75 pounds under gross weight. What would be the best choice?
options: Taking off into the headwind will give the extra climb-out time needed.
Try a takeoff without the passengers to make sure the climb is adequate.
Wait until the temperature decreases, and recalculate the takeoff performance.
explanation: Needing 1,980 feet on a 2,100 foot strip leaves a margin of only about 6 percent, and a gravel surface typically lengthens the takeoff further. Waiting for cooler air lowers the density altitude and restores performance, after which you recalculate before deciding. Option A is the trap: the runway runs east and west, so a usable headwind is not assured, and hoping for extra climb is not a plan. A trial takeoff without passengers is still a test flight with an inadequate margin.

stem: (Refer to FAA-CT-8080-2H, Figure 64.) Which marking indicates a vehicle lane?
options: A.
C.
E.
explanation: Vehicle roadway markings are white solid lines marking the road edges with a dashed white center line, or zipper style edge lines in some places, as shown at C in Figure 64. They define a path for ground vehicles crossing areas also used by aircraft. E is a yellow taxiway marking, not a road, which makes it the trap for anyone who keys on the dashed line.

stem: (Refer to FAA-CT-8080-2H, Figure 52.) When approaching Lincoln Municipal from the west at noon for the purpose of landing, initial communications should be with
options: Lincoln Approach Control on 124.0 MHz.
Minneapolis Center on 128.75 MHz.
Lincoln Tower on 118.5 MHz.
explanation: Lincoln is UTC minus 6 (minus 5 in daylight time), so noon local is 1800Z or 1700Z, inside the Class C service hours of 1130 to 0600Z. Approach control must be contacted before entering Class C, and arrivals in the 180 to 359 degree sector use 124.0; approaching from the west puts you in that sector. Calling the tower first is the trap, because approach hands you off to the tower only once you are sequenced in close to the airport.

stem: (Refer to FAA-CT-8080-2H, Figure 52.) Where is Loup City Municipal located in relation to the city?
options: Northeast approximately 3 miles.
Northwest approximately 1 mile.
East approximately 7 miles.
explanation: The Loup City Muni entry reads 1 NW, meaning the airport is about 1 nautical mile northwest of the city it is named for. The trap is reversing the direction: the code gives the airport's position from the city, not the city's position from the airport.

stem: (Refer to FAA-CT-8080-2H, Figure 25, area 5.) The navigation facility at Dallas-Ft. Worth International (DFW) is a
options: VOR.
VORTAC.
VOR/DME.
explanation: The DFW navaid symbol in Figure 25 is a hexagon with a dot in the center enclosed in a square, which is the chart symbol for a VOR/DME. A plain VOR is the hexagon alone, and a VORTAC has small solid blocks on three of the hexagon's sides. Mistaking the square for the VORTAC tabs is the common trap.

stem: (Refer to FAA-CT-8080-2H, Figure 52.) What is the recommended communications procedure for landing at Lincoln Municipal during the hours when the tower is not in operation?
options: Monitor airport traffic and announce your position and intentions on 118.5 MHz.
Contact UNICOM on 122.95 MHz for traffic advisories.
Monitor ATIS for airport conditions, then announce your position on 122.95 MHz.
explanation: Figure 52 lists CTAF 118.5 for Lincoln, which is also the tower frequency. When the tower is closed, pilots self announce position and intentions on the CTAF, so you monitor and broadcast on 118.5. The trap is UNICOM 122.95, which provides airport services, not traffic advisories, and ATIS is on 118.05, not 122.95.

stem: (Refer to FAA-CT-8080-2H, Figure 26, area 2.) The day VFR visibility and cloud clearance requirements to operate over the town of Cooperstown, after departing and climbing out of the Cooperstown Airport at or below 700 feet AGL are
options: 1 mile and clear of clouds.
1 mile and 1,000 feet above, 500 feet below, and 2,000 feet horizontally from clouds.
3 miles and clear of clouds.
explanation: Cooperstown airport lies inside a magenta vignette, so Class E airspace begins at 700 feet AGL and the airspace from the surface up to 700 feet AGL is Class G. Day VFR in Class G at or below 1,200 feet AGL requires 1 statute mile visibility and clear of clouds. The trap is the 500 below, 1,000 above, 2,000 horizontal cloud clearance, which applies in Class G only above 1,200 feet AGL. Three miles and clear of clouds is the Class B minimum, which does not apply over Cooperstown.

stem: When the course deviation indicator (CDI) needle is centered using a VOR test signal (VOT), the omnibearing selector (OBS) and the TO/FROM indicator should read
options: 180° FROM, only if the pilot is due north of the VOT.
0° TO or 180° FROM, regardless of the pilot's position from the VOT.
0° FROM or 180° TO, regardless of the pilot's position from the VOT.
explanation: A VOT broadcasts the 360 degree radial in every direction, so a correctly working receiver centers the CDI with 0 degrees and FROM, or 180 degrees and TO, wherever the airplane is. The allowable error for a VOT check is plus or minus 4 degrees. The trap is reversing TO and FROM: 0 TO or 180 FROM describes the opposite case.

stem: The term 'angle of attack' is defined as the angle between the
options: chord line of the wing and the relative wind.
airplane's longitudinal axis and that of the air striking the airfoil.
airplane's center line and the relative wind.
explanation: Angle of attack is the angle between the wing's chord line and the relative wind. It is not measured from the longitudinal axis or the fuselage centerline; the angle between the longitudinal axis and the chord line is the angle of incidence. Confusing angle of attack with pitch attitude is the core trap here.

stem: (Refer to FAA-CT-8080-2H, Figure 35.) Determine the approximate manifold pressure setting with 2,450 RPM to achieve 65 percent maximum continuous power at 6,500 feet with a temperature of 36°F higher than standard.
options: 19.8 inches Hg.
20.8 inches Hg.
21.0 inches Hg.
explanation: 36 degrees F above standard is ISA +20 degrees C, the right hand block of Figure 35. At 2,450 RPM the manifold pressure is 21.0 inches at 6,000 feet and 20.8 inches at 8,000 feet, so at 6,500 feet it is 21.0 minus one quarter of 0.2, about 20.95, or approximately 21.0 inches. The trap is 20.8, which is the 8,000 foot value; 19.8 comes from the ISA minus 20 degrees column.

stem: (Refer to FAA-CT-8080-2H, Figure 38.) Determine the total distance required to land over a 50-foot obstacle. Pressure altitude: 5,000 ft Headwind: 8 kts Temperature: 41°F Runway: Hard surface
options: 837 feet.
956 feet.
1,076 feet.
explanation: At 5,000 feet and 41 degrees F the total distance to clear a 50 foot obstacle is 1,195 feet. Note 1 reduces distances 10 percent for each 4 knots of headwind, so 8 knots gives 20 percent: 1,195 x 0.80 = 956 feet. 1,076 feet applies only a 10 percent reduction, and 837 feet takes off 30 percent. The runway is hard surface, so the grass correction does not apply.

stem: (Refer to FAA-CT-8080-2H, Figure 38.) Determine the approximate landing ground roll distance. Pressure altitude: 5,000 ft Headwind: Calm Temperature: 101°F
options: 445 feet.
545 feet.
495 feet.
explanation: The table gives a ground roll of 495 feet at 5,000 feet and 41 degrees F, which is the standard temperature column for that altitude. 101 degrees F is 60 degrees above standard, so note 2 adds 10 percent: 495 x 1.10 = about 545 feet. The trap is 495 feet, which skips the temperature correction, and 445 feet is the sea level value.

stem: Who has final authority to accept or decline any land and hold short (LAHSO) clearance?
options: Pilot in command.
Air Traffic Controller.
Second in command.
explanation: The pilot in command has final authority to accept or decline any land and hold short clearance. The pilot should decline when the available landing distance, wind or runway condition makes holding short unsafe. The controller issues the clearance but cannot make the pilot accept it, which is the trap.

stem: (Refer to FAA-CT-8080-2H, Figure 47.) While on final approach to a runway equipped with a standard 2-bar VASI, the lights appear as shown by illustration D. This means that the aircraft is
options: above the glide path.
below the glide path.
on the glide path.
explanation: On a two bar VASI, red over red (illustration D) means the airplane is below the glide path. Red over white means on the glide path, and white over white means above it. A handy memory aid is red over white, you are all right; red over red, you are dead.

stem: (Refer to FAA-CT-8080-2H, Figure 48.) The portion of the runway identified by the letter A may be used for
options: landing.
taxiing and takeoff.
taxiing and landing.
explanation: In Figure 48, area A has white arrows pointing toward the runway number, which marks a displaced threshold. Pavement behind a displaced threshold may be used for taxiing, the takeoff run, and the landing rollout from the opposite direction, but not for touching down. The trap is taxiing and landing: landing here means touching down short of the threshold, which is not allowed.

stem: What does the red line on an airspeed indicator represent?
options: Maneuvering speed.
Turbulent or rough-air speed.
Never-exceed speed.
explanation: The red radial line on the airspeed indicator marks VNE, the never exceed speed, beyond which structural damage or flutter can occur. Maneuvering speed is not marked on the airspeed indicator at all. Rough air operations belong below the yellow arc, so the turbulent air speed option is the trap.

stem: With regard to carburetor ice, float-type carburetor systems in comparison to fuel injection systems are generally considered to be
options: more susceptible to icing.
equally susceptible to icing.
less susceptible to icing.
explanation: A float type carburetor cools the incoming air sharply through fuel vaporization and the pressure drop in the venturi, so ice can form even in warm, humid air. Fuel injection sprays fuel near the intake valves and has no venturi, so it is far less susceptible to induction icing. The trap is assuming the two systems are equally exposed because both draw in moist air.

stem: What is one purpose of wing flaps?
options: To enable the pilot to make steeper approaches to a landing without increasing the airspeed.
To relieve the pilot of maintaining continuous pressure on the controls.
To decrease wing area to vary the lift.
explanation: Flaps increase both lift and drag, so the airplane can descend at a steeper angle without picking up airspeed, which makes obstacle clearance and short field approaches easier. Relieving control pressure is the job of trim, the tempting wrong answer. Most flaps on light airplanes increase wing camber and some increase wing area; they do not decrease it.

stem: Unless otherwise authorized, if flying a transponder equipped aircraft, a pilot should squawk which VFR code?
explanation: Code 1200 is the standard VFR code when no other code has been assigned. Code 7600 means lost communications and 7700 means emergency, so squawking either during routine flight would trigger an unnecessary response from ATC.

stem: What action should a pilot take when operating under VFR in a Military Operations Area (MOA)?
options: Obtain a clearance from the controlling agency prior to entering the MOA.
Operate only on the airways that transverse the MOA.
Exercise extreme caution when military activity is being conducted.
explanation: A Military Operations Area separates military training from IFR traffic, but VFR pilots may fly through without a clearance. Pilots should exercise extreme caution while the MOA is active and can contact the controlling agency or Flight Service for activity status. Needing a clearance is the trap: that applies to restricted areas, not MOAs.

stem: (Refer to FAA-CT-8080-2H, Figures 32 and 33.) Which action can adjust the airplane's weight to maximum gross weight and the CG within limits for takeoff? Front seat occupants: 425 lb Rear seat occupants: 300 lb Fuel, main tanks: 44 gal
options: Drain 12 gallons of fuel.
Drain 9 gallons of fuel.
Transfer 12 gallons of fuel from the main tanks to the auxiliary tanks.
explanation: Takeoff weight is 2,015 empty + 425 front + 300 rear + 264 fuel (44 gal x 6) = 3,004 lb, which is 54 lb over the 2,950 lb maximum. 54 lb / 6 lb per gal = 9 gallons to drain. Check the moment: 1,554 + 361.3 (425 x 85 / 100) + 363 (300 x 121 / 100) + 158 (35 gal) = about 2,436, which is inside the 2,422 to 2,499 moment limits for 2,950 lb. Draining 12 gallons also ends inside limits but leaves the airplane below maximum gross weight, and transferring fuel to the auxiliary tanks does not reduce weight at all.

stem: The mature stage of a thunderstorm begins with
options: formation of the anvil top.
the start of precipitation.
continuous downdrafts.
explanation: A thunderstorm enters the mature stage when precipitation begins falling from the cloud base, because falling rain drags air down and starts the downdraft alongside the updraft. The anvil forms during the mature stage and is not its starting point. Downdrafts that predominate throughout the cell mark the dissipating stage, which is the most common mix up.

stem: (Refer to FAA-CT-8080-2H, Figure 17.) What wind is forecast for STL at 12,000 feet?
options: 230° true at 56 knots.
230° true at 39 knots.
230° magnetic at 56 knots.
explanation: In Figure 17 the STL entry in the 12000 column is 2339-04: the first two digits are direction in tens of degrees (230), the next two are speed in knots (39), and minus 4 is the temperature in degrees C. Winds aloft forecasts are referenced to true north. The 56 knots trap comes from reading the 18000 column (2356-16), and magnetic is wrong because only surface winds given by a tower or ATIS are magnetic.
ref: Aviation Weather Handbook (FAA-H-8083-28), Winds and Temperatures Aloft Forecast

stem: Why is frost considered hazardous to flight?
options: Frost changes the basic aerodynamic shape of the airfoils, thereby increasing lift.
Frost slows the airflow over the airfoils, thereby increasing control effectiveness.
Frost spoils the smooth flow of air over the wings, thereby decreasing lifting capability.
explanation: Even a thin layer of frost roughens the wing surface and disrupts the smooth airflow over it. That reduces the lift the wing can produce and raises the stall speed, so the airplane may need a longer takeoff run or be unable to climb out of ground effect. The other options get the effect backward: frost decreases lift and control effectiveness, it never increases them.

stem: When speaking to a flight service weather briefer, you should state
options: the pilot in command's full name and address.
a summary of your qualifications.
whether the flight is VFR or IFR.
explanation: When you request a briefing, give the briefer the facts needed to tailor it: that you are a pilot, whether the flight is VFR or IFR, aircraft number or your name, aircraft type, departure point, route, destination, altitude and estimated time of departure. Whether the flight is VFR or IFR changes what the briefer emphasizes, so it is part of the request. Your address and a summary of qualifications are not needed.

stem: A 100-hour inspection was due at 3302.5 hours. The 100-hour inspection was actually done at 3309.5 hours. When is the next 100-hour inspection due?
options: 3312.5 hours.
3395.5 hours.
3402.5 hours.
explanation: The 100 hour limit may be exceeded by up to 10 hours to reach a place where the inspection can be done, but the excess counts against the next interval. The next inspection is therefore due 100 hours after it was originally due: 3302.5 + 100 = 3402.5 hours. The trap is 3395.5, which deducts the 7 hour overrun from that due time; 3312.5 simply adds the 10 hour allowance to the old due time.

stem: Pre-takeoff briefing of passengers about the use of seat belts for a flight is the responsibility of
options: all passengers.
the pilot in command.
the right seat pilot.
explanation: The pilot in command must ensure each person on board is briefed on how to fasten and unfasten the seat belt and, if installed, the shoulder harness. Passengers must comply, but the briefing duty rests on the pilot in command. There is no regulatory role for a right seat pilot in this briefing.

stem: Two-way radio communication must be established with the Air Traffic Control facility having jurisdiction over the area prior to entering which class airspace?
options: Class C.
Class E.
Class G.
explanation: Before entering Class C airspace a pilot must establish two way radio communication with the ATC facility providing service there. Class E and Class G have no such entry requirement for VFR aircraft. Class E is the tempting choice because it is controlled airspace, but controlled does not mean a radio call is required for VFR traffic.

stem: During operations outside controlled airspace at altitudes of more than 1,200 feet AGL, but less than 10,000 feet MSL, the minimum distance below clouds requirement for VFR flight at night is
options: 500 feet.
1,000 feet.
1,500 feet.
explanation: At night in Class G airspace above 1,200 feet AGL and below 10,000 feet MSL, the cloud clearances are 500 feet below, 1,000 feet above and 2,000 feet horizontally, with 3 miles visibility. So the distance below clouds is 500 feet. The 1,000 foot value is the clearance above clouds, and 1,500 feet is not a VFR cloud clearance at all.

stem: Unless otherwise authorized, two-way radio communications with Air Traffic Control are required for landings or takeoffs at all towered airports
options: regardless of weather conditions.
only when weather conditions are less than VFR.
within Class D airspace only when weather conditions are less than VFR.
explanation: Unless ATC authorizes otherwise, two way radio communication with the tower is required to operate to, from or on any airport with an operating control tower, whatever the weather. The requirement is about the tower being open, not about VFR versus IFR conditions. Both wrong options tie the rule to weather, which is the trap.

stem: During operations outside controlled airspace at altitudes of more than 1,200 feet AGL, but less than 10,000 feet MSL, the minimum flight visibility for day VFR flight is
options: 1 mile.
3 miles.
5 miles.
explanation: In Class G airspace more than 1,200 feet AGL but below 10,000 feet MSL, day VFR requires 1 statute mile flight visibility with 500 feet below, 1,000 feet above and 2,000 feet horizontally from clouds. At night the same altitude band needs 3 miles, which is the most tempting wrong answer. Five miles applies only at or above 10,000 feet MSL.

stem: A flashing white light signal from the control tower to a taxiing aircraft is an indication to
options: taxi at a faster speed.
taxi only on taxiways and not cross runways.
return to the starting point on the airport.
explanation: A flashing white light from the tower means return to the starting point on the airport, and it applies only to aircraft on the ground. There is no light signal that means taxi faster or stay off runways. Flashing white has no meaning to an aircraft in flight, which is why it is easy to forget.

stem: With respect to the certification of airmen, which are categories of aircraft?
options: Gyroplane, helicopter, airship, free balloon.
Airplane, rotorcraft, glider, lighter-than-air.
Single-engine land and sea, multiengine land and sea.
explanation: For airman certification, category is the broad grouping of aircraft: airplane, rotorcraft, glider, lighter than air, and also powered lift, powered parachute and weight shift control. Gyroplane, helicopter, airship and free balloon are classes within the rotorcraft and lighter than air categories. Single engine land and sea and multiengine land and sea are classes of the airplane category, which is the usual trap.

stem: Maintenance records show the last transponder inspection was performed on September 1, 2014. The next inspection will be due no later than
options: September 30, 2015.
September 1, 2016.
September 30, 2016.
explanation: A transponder must have been tested and inspected within the preceding 24 calendar months. Calendar months run to the last day of the month, so an inspection on September 1, 2014 stays good through September 30, 2016. The trap is September 1, 2016, which treats the interval as exact days instead of calendar months; September 30, 2015 uses the 12 month interval that applies to annual inspections.

stem: Under 14 CFR 61.31, a high performance airplane is one with an engine of
options: 200 horsepower or more.
more than 200 horsepower.
more than 180 horsepower and a controllable pitch propeller.
explanation: A high performance airplane has an engine of more than 200 horsepower, and acting as pilot in command of one requires a one time endorsement under 61.31(f). The common trap is "200 or more": an airplane with exactly 200 horsepower is not high performance. Propeller type has nothing to do with the definition.

stem: A private pilot holds a complex endorsement and has flown only a 200 horsepower retractable gear airplane. The pilot now wants to act as pilot in command of a fixed gear airplane with a 230 horsepower engine and a constant speed propeller. What is required?
options: Nothing further, because the complex endorsement already covers a controllable pitch propeller.
A complex endorsement for the new airplane, because it has a controllable pitch propeller.
Ground and flight training from an authorized instructor and a one time high performance endorsement.
explanation: The new airplane has more than 200 horsepower, so it is high performance and needs the 61.31(f) endorsement. The earlier airplane had exactly 200 horsepower, which does not count. The complex endorsement is a separate endorsement and does not cover high performance, and the new airplane is not complex anyway because its gear is fixed.

stem: For the purpose of the 61.31 endorsement, a complex airplane is one that has
options: retractable landing gear, flaps, and a controllable pitch propeller (or a FADEC engine control in place of the controllable propeller).
an engine of more than 200 horsepower and retractable landing gear.
any two of the following: retractable landing gear, flaps, or a controllable pitch propeller.
explanation: Part 1 defines a complex airplane as one with all three items: retractable gear, flaps, and a controllable pitch propeller, with a FADEC counting in place of the controllable propeller. Horsepower is the high performance test, not the complex test. Having only two of the three items does not make an airplane complex.

stem: A newly certificated private pilot with an airplane single engine land rating wants to act as pilot in command of a tailwheel airplane. Under 61.31(i), the pilot needs
options: a tailwheel class rating added by a practical test with an examiner.
flight training in a tailwheel airplane and a one time logbook endorsement from an authorized instructor.
at least 10 solo takeoffs and full stop landings in a tailwheel airplane.
explanation: Tailwheel operations require flight training and a one time endorsement from an authorized instructor, not a new rating. There is no tailwheel class; the class is still single engine land. No specific number of solo landings is set by the rule.

stem: The high altitude endorsement of 61.31(g) is required to act as pilot in command of
options: any airplane flown above 18,000 feet MSL.
any airplane that requires supplemental oxygen for the planned flight.
a pressurized airplane with a service ceiling or maximum operating altitude, whichever is lower, above 25,000 feet MSL.
explanation: The high altitude endorsement applies to pressurized aircraft whose service ceiling or maximum operating altitude, whichever is lower, is above 25,000 feet MSL. The 18,000 foot figure is the base of Class A airspace, not the trigger for this endorsement. Oxygen use under 91.211 does not by itself require any endorsement.

stem: A private pilot rents an airplane and flies three friends to a lake for lunch. Fuel, oil, the rental fee, and landing fees total $320. Under 61.113(c), what is the least the pilot may pay?
options: Nothing, if the friends volunteer to cover the full cost.
explanation: A private pilot may not pay less than the pro rata share of the operating expenses. Four occupants share the cost, so $320 divided by 4 is $80. Letting the passengers pay everything is compensation to the pilot, which is the classic trap.

stem: Under 91.105, each required flight crewmember must keep the shoulder harness fastened, if one is installed,
options: at all times while the aircraft is in flight.
during takeoff and landing, unless it would prevent the crewmember from performing required duties.
only when flying in turbulence or at night.
explanation: 91.105 requires required crewmembers to stay at their stations with safety belts fastened during takeoff, landing, and en route, and to keep shoulder harnesses fastened during takeoff and landing unless the harness would keep them from performing required duties. There is no rule requiring the harness for the whole flight. Turbulence and night are good practice reasons, not regulatory triggers.

stem: A private pilot works as a sales manager and flies a company airplane alone to visit customers. The company pays her salary and the airplane costs. Is this permitted?
options: Yes, because the flight is only incidental to her business and no passengers or property are carried for compensation or hire.
No, because a private pilot may never receive any compensation connected to a flight.
Yes, but only after she logs at least 200 hours of flight time.
explanation: 61.113(b) allows a private pilot to act as pilot in command for compensation in connection with a business when the flight is only incidental to that business and no passengers or property are carried for compensation or hire. The 200 hour figure belongs to the aircraft salesman exception in 61.113(f) and does not apply here.

stem: A private pilot wants to act as pilot in command on a charitable sightseeing flight conducted under 91.146, where passengers make a donation to the sponsoring nonprofit. What minimum flight time must the pilot have?
options: 200 hours.
250 hours.
500 hours.
explanation: 61.113(d) allows a private pilot to fly a charitable, nonprofit, or community event flight only if the requirements of 91.146 are met, and 91.146 requires a private pilot in command to have at least 500 hours of flight time. The flights must also be day VFR, nonstop, and within 25 statute miles of the departure airport. 250 hours is the commercial certificate minimum, a tempting but wrong number.

stem: A student pilot is on a solo flight during the day. Under 61.89, the student may not act as pilot in command when the flight or surface visibility is less than
options: 1 statute mile.
3 statute miles.
5 statute miles.
explanation: 61.89 bars a student pilot from acting as pilot in command with less than 3 statute miles visibility during daylight hours or less than 5 statute miles at night. Choosing 5 confuses the night value with the day value. 1 mile is the Class G day minimum for other pilots and does not apply to student solo flight.

stem: When acting as pilot in command, a private pilot who holds a third class medical certificate must have in physical possession or readily accessible in the aircraft the pilot certificate, the medical certificate, and
options: the pilot logbook showing a current flight review.
a government issued photo identification, such as a driver's license or passport.
a copy of the most recent FAA knowledge test report.
explanation: 61.3(a) requires the pilot certificate, a photo identification acceptable to the FAA, and the medical certificate (or the BasicMed driver's license). A logbook must be carried only by a student pilot on a solo cross country, so that is the trap. A private pilot must still be able to present the logbook on request, but need not carry it.

stem: A private pilot moves to a new permanent mailing address. To keep exercising pilot privileges, the pilot must notify the FAA Airman Certification Branch in writing within
options: 30 days after moving.
60 days after moving.
10 days after moving.
explanation: Under 61.60, a pilot who changes permanent mailing address may not exercise certificate privileges after 30 days from the move unless the FAA has been notified in writing. The 60 day value belongs to reporting a motor vehicle action under 61.15. 10 days is the NTSB accident report deadline.

stem: Which flight time is a private pilot required to log?
options: All flight time, including every flight as pilot in command.
Only cross country and night flight time.
Only the time used to meet the requirements for a certificate, rating, flight review, or recent flight experience.
explanation: 61.51(a) requires logging only the training and aeronautical experience used to meet the requirements for a certificate, rating, or flight review, and the recent flight experience requirements. Most pilots log everything, but the rule does not require it. Cross country and night time must be logged only when it is used for one of those purposes.

stem: A private pilot with an airplane single engine land rating, but no tailwheel endorsement, flies a tailwheel airplane during dual instruction and is the sole manipulator of the controls. May the private pilot log this time as pilot in command?
options: No, because the pilot cannot act as pilot in command without the tailwheel endorsement.
No, because only the instructor may log pilot in command time on a dual flight.
Yes, because the pilot is the sole manipulator of the controls of an aircraft for which the pilot is rated.
explanation: Logging pilot in command time under 61.51(e)(1)(i) depends on ratings (category, class, and type if required), not on endorsements. A tailwheel airplane is still airplane single engine land, so the pilot is rated for it and may log the time while the instructor acts as pilot in command. The trap mixes up acting as pilot in command, which does need the endorsement, with logging it. The instructor may also log pilot in command time.

stem: A private pilot completed a flight review on June 14, 2024. Without another review or a qualifying practical test, the pilot may act as pilot in command through
explanation: The flight review is valid for 24 calendar months, which run to the end of the month. June 2024 plus 24 calendar months ends on June 30, 2026. Picking June 14 forgets the calendar month rule, and June 30, 2025 uses 12 months instead of 24.

stem: What is the minimum training content of a flight review under 61.56?
options: 1 hour of flight training and 1 hour of ground training.
2 hours of flight training, with no ground training required.
1 hour of flight training and a passing score on an FAA knowledge test.
explanation: A flight review is at least 1 hour of flight training and 1 hour of ground training. It must include a review of the general operating and flight rules of part 91 and the maneuvers the instructor considers necessary. No knowledge test is involved, and the review ends with a logbook endorsement, not a pass or fail grade.

stem: A private pilot's flight review was due by the end of March 2026. In February 2026 the pilot passed the practical test for an instrument rating. When is the next flight review due?
options: By the end of March 2026, because a practical test does not replace a flight review.
By the end of February 2028.
By the end of March 2028.
explanation: Under 61.56(d), passing a practical test for a certificate, rating, or operating privilege takes the place of a flight review. The new 24 calendar month period starts from the month of the practical test, February 2026, so it ends February 29, 2028. Counting from the old due month gives March 2028, which is one month too late.

stem: A private pilot discovers the last flight review was 25 calendar months ago. Which flight may the pilot conduct?
options: A solo flight, as long as no passengers are carried.
A flight with an authorized instructor to accomplish the flight review.
A flight with passengers, provided three takeoffs and landings were made in the last 90 days.
explanation: Without a current flight review a pilot may not act as pilot in command of any flight, solo or with passengers. The pilot can still fly with an authorized instructor, who can give the flight review. Passenger currency under 61.57 does not substitute for the flight review.

stem: A private pilot made three takeoffs and landings in a Cessna 172 seven weeks ago and has not flown since. Today the pilot wants to carry passengers during the day in a Piper Cherokee, which is also a single engine land airplane. Does the pilot meet 61.57(a)?
options: Yes, because the landings were made in the same category and class within the preceding 90 days.
No, because the landings must have been made in the same make and model.
No, because passenger currency requires landings within the preceding 30 days.
explanation: 61.57(a) requires three takeoffs and landings within the preceding 90 days in the same category and class, and type only if a type rating is required. Seven weeks is within 90 days, and both airplanes are airplane single engine land. Make and model do not matter for currency, although a rental checkout or insurance may require more.

stem: To carry passengers in a tailwheel airplane, the three takeoffs and landings required within the preceding 90 days must be
options: touch and go landings in any single engine airplane.
full stop landings in any single engine land airplane.
full stop landings in a tailwheel airplane.
explanation: 61.57(a) requires the landings for tailwheel passenger currency to be made to a full stop in a tailwheel airplane. Landings in a tricycle gear airplane do not count even though the category and class are the same. Touch and go landings do not satisfy the tailwheel requirement.

stem: Official sunset is 1820 local time. A private pilot makes three takeoffs and full stop landings between 1835 and 1910 in the same category and class. Do these landings satisfy the night passenger currency requirement of 61.57(b)?
options: Yes, because all three were made after sunset.
Yes, because they were full stop landings in the same category and class.
No, because none were made during the period beginning 1 hour after sunset.
explanation: Night currency landings must be made during the period from 1 hour after sunset to 1 hour before sunrise. With sunset at 1820 that period starts at 1920, and all of these landings were finished by 1910. Being after sunset is enough to require position lights, but not enough for night currency.

stem: To impress friends, a private pilot makes repeated low passes and steep turns over a crowded beach, while staying just above the altitude minimums of 91.119 and never exceeding 60 degrees of bank. Which is true?
options: No rule is broken, because the altitude minimums were met.
The pilot can be cited under 91.13 for operating in a careless or reckless manner that endangers the life or property of another.
Only 91.303 could apply, and only if the maneuvers were aerobatic.
explanation: 91.13 prohibits operating an aircraft in a careless or reckless manner so as to endanger the life or property of another, and it applies even when no specific altitude or maneuver rule is broken. The FAA often charges it along with other violations. The scenario also shows the macho hazardous attitude, whose antidote is "taking chances is foolish."

stem: For logging night flight time, night is the period
options: from sunset to sunrise.
from 1 hour after sunset to 1 hour before sunrise.
from the end of evening civil twilight to the beginning of morning civil twilight.
explanation: Part 1 defines night as the time between the end of evening civil twilight and the beginning of morning civil twilight, and that definition governs logging night time. Sunset to sunrise is the position light period under 91.209. The 1 hour after sunset period is used only for night passenger currency under 61.57(b).

stem: A private pilot made three landings 80 days ago in calm wind but has not landed in a significant crosswind in over a year. Today the forecast calls for a 15 knot direct crosswind, and two friends are waiting to fly. What is the best decision?
options: Fly, because meeting 61.57 shows the pilot is proficient for the conditions.
Recognize that legal currency is not proficiency, and either fly with an instructor first or wait for conditions within personal minimums.
Fly, but leave one friend behind to reduce weight and improve crosswind control.
explanation: 61.57 sets the legal minimum to carry passengers, not a measure of skill in demanding conditions. A rusty pilot facing a strong crosswind with passengers and social pressure should get refresher training or wait. Reducing weight does nothing for crosswind technique, so that option only looks like risk management.

stem: A private pilot's last takeoffs and landings were 95 days ago. What must the pilot do before carrying passengers?
options: Make the three takeoffs and landings with the passengers aboard on the first flight of the day.
Complete a flight review, which also resets passenger currency.
Make three takeoffs and landings as sole manipulator of the controls in the same category and class, either solo or with an instructor.
explanation: Passenger currency must be regained before any passenger is carried, so the pilot flies the three takeoffs and landings solo or with an instructor. Making them with passengers aboard is exactly what 61.57 forbids. A flight review is a separate requirement and does not reset passenger currency unless the required landings are made during it.

stem: A pilot born on May 3, 1988 receives a third class medical certificate on August 10, 2026. For private pilot privileges, the certificate is valid through
options: August 31, 2028.
August 31, 2031.
explanation: Duration depends on the pilot's age on the date of the examination. The pilot was 38, so the certificate lasts 60 calendar months: August 2026 plus 60 months ends August 31, 2031. Turning 40 during that period does not shorten it, which is the trap in the other two answers.

stem: A 45 year old pilot receives a first class medical certificate on January 15, 2026. Until when may the pilot use it for commercial pilot privileges?
options: January 31, 2027.
January 31, 2028.
explanation: For commercial privileges a first or second class certificate lasts 12 calendar months regardless of age, so it ends January 31, 2027. July 31, 2026 is the 6 month first class period for airline transport privileges at age 40 or older. January 31, 2028 is how long it remains good for private pilot privileges at this age.

stem: A 52 year old private pilot passes a third class medical examination on March 3, 2026. The certificate allows private pilot privileges through
options: March 3, 2028.
explanation: A pilot 40 or older at the exam gets 24 calendar months for private privileges, ending on the last day of the 24th month: March 31, 2028. Medical durations run to the end of the month, so March 3 is wrong. 60 months applies only to pilots under 40 at the exam.

stem: A private pilot holds a current medical certificate but has started a prescription medication that causes drowsiness. Under 61.53, the pilot
options: may fly, because the medical certificate remains valid until it expires.
may not act as pilot in command or as a required crewmember while taking a medication that makes the pilot unable to meet the medical certificate requirements.
may fly only with another certificated pilot aboard.
explanation: 61.53 is the self grounding rule: a pilot may not act as pilot in command while knowing of a medical deficiency, or while taking medication or treatment that would keep the pilot from meeting the medical standards. A valid certificate does not override this. Having another pilot aboard does not make an impaired pilot legal.

stem: Under BasicMed, how often must the pilot complete the medical education course and the comprehensive medical examination?
options: Course within the preceding 24 calendar months; exam within the preceding 48 calendar months.
Course within the preceding 48 calendar months; exam within the preceding 24 calendar months.
Course within the preceding 12 calendar months; exam within the preceding 60 calendar months.
explanation: BasicMed requires the online medical education course every 24 calendar months and an exam by a state licensed physician every 48 calendar months. The second option swaps the two intervals, which is the common mixup. 60 months is the under 40 third class medical duration, not a BasicMed number.

stem: Which is a limitation on a private pilot acting as pilot in command under BasicMed?
options: The flight must be conducted in day VFR conditions.
The flight may not be conducted under IFR.
The airplane may not be flown at an indicated airspeed above 250 knots.
explanation: Under 61.113(i), BasicMed flights may not exceed 250 knots indicated or go above 18,000 feet MSL, and must stay inside the United States unless the other country allows it. Night and IFR flight are both allowed if the pilot is otherwise rated and current. The aircraft occupant and weight limits also apply.

stem: A private pilot's last FAA medical certificate, a third class, expired in 2015. It was never suspended or revoked, and no later application was denied. Can the pilot fly under BasicMed?
options: No, because the last medical certificate expired more than 10 years ago.
Yes, after completing the BasicMed course and comprehensive medical exam, because the pilot held a medical certificate after July 14, 2006.
No, because BasicMed requires a medical certificate that is currently valid.
explanation: BasicMed requires that the pilot held an FAA medical certificate at some time after July 14, 2006. The most recent one may be expired, but it may not have been suspended or revoked, and the most recent application may not have been denied. There is no limit on how long ago it expired.

stem: When acting as pilot in command under BasicMed, what must the pilot have in physical possession or readily accessible in the aircraft, along with the pilot certificate and photo identification?
options: A valid U.S. driver's license.
The original signed comprehensive medical examination checklist.
An expired FAA medical certificate showing it was never revoked.
explanation: A BasicMed pilot uses a valid U.S. driver's license in place of the medical certificate under 61.3. The signed examination checklist and the course completion certificate must be kept with the pilot's logbook under 61.113(i)(3), but they do not have to be carried. The old medical certificate is not a required document.

stem: A private pilot's driver's license is suspended after an arrest for driving under the influence. Under 61.15, the pilot must send a written report of this motor vehicle action to the FAA within
options: 30 days.
60 days.
90 days.
explanation: 61.15 requires a written report to the FAA within 60 days of each motor vehicle action, such as a conviction or a license suspension or revocation tied to alcohol or drugs. Two such actions within 3 years are grounds to deny, suspend, or revoke a certificate. The 30 day value is the change of address rule.

stem: A student pilot who has never held an FAA medical certificate wants to make a first solo flight in an airplane using BasicMed. Is this allowed?
options: Yes, if the student completes the BasicMed course and a physician's exam.
Yes, because student pilots need no medical qualification for solo flight in an airplane.
No, because BasicMed requires having held an FAA medical certificate at some time after July 14, 2006.
explanation: BasicMed is available only to a pilot who has held a part 67 medical certificate at some time after July 14, 2006. A student who has never held one cannot use BasicMed and would normally obtain a third class medical certificate before soloing. Option B fails because the no medical exceptions of 61.23(b) cover glider and balloon operations, not airplanes.

stem: For a flight entirely within the United States, which item from the traditional ARROW list is NOT required to be on board a U.S. registered airplane?
options: The radio station license.
The weight and balance data.
The registration certificate.
explanation: ARROW stands for Airworthiness certificate, Registration certificate, Radio station license, Operating limitations, and Weight and balance. The radio station license is needed only for flights outside the United States. The registration certificate is required on board by 91.203, and weight and balance information is part of the approved flight manual material that 91.9 requires for most airplanes.

stem: Under 91.203, the airworthiness certificate must be
options: kept with the aircraft maintenance records in a binder in the cabin.
carried by the pilot in command along with the pilot certificate.
displayed at the cabin or cockpit entrance so that it is legible to passengers or crew.
explanation: 91.203(b) requires the airworthiness certificate to be displayed at the cabin or cockpit entrance where passengers or crew can read it. Keeping it folded in a binder does not meet the display requirement. Maintenance records do not need to be on board at all.

stem: An airplane's last annual inspection was signed off on May 20, 2025. The next annual inspection is due no later than
explanation: An annual inspection must have been done within the preceding 12 calendar months. May 2025 plus 12 calendar months ends at the end of May 2026. The exact anniversary date is the classic trap, because calendar months always run to the end of the month.

stem: An airplane's annual inspection expired last month. The owner wants to fly it to a maintenance shop at a nearby airport to have the inspection done. What is required?
options: Nothing, provided the flight takes less than 10 hours.
A logbook entry by the pilot stating that the airplane is safe to fly.
A special flight permit.
explanation: An airplane with an expired annual is not airworthy, so it needs a special flight permit to be ferried to a place where the inspection can be done. The 10 hour allowance applies only to the 100 hour inspection, never to the annual. A pilot has no authority to approve an unairworthy airplane for flight.

stem: An airplane used for flight instruction for hire was due for its 100 hour inspection at 1,450.0 hours time in service. The flight to the maintenance shop ran over, and the inspection was completed at 1,456.0 hours. The next 100 hour inspection is due at
explanation: The 100 hour limit may be exceeded by up to 10 hours only to reach a place where the inspection can be done, and the extra time counts against the next interval. The next one is due 100 hours after the original due point: 1,450.0 plus 100 equals 1,550.0. Counting from the actual inspection time gives 1,556.0, which gives away hours the rule does not allow.

stem: In which situation must the airplane have had an annual or 100 hour inspection within the preceding 100 hours of time in service?
options: A flight instructor gives paid instruction in an airplane owned by the student.
A flight school provides its own airplane for paid flight instruction.
A private pilot shares fuel costs with two friends in her own airplane.
explanation: 91.409(b) applies to aircraft carrying any person other than a crewmember for hire, and to aircraft provided by the person giving flight instruction for hire. When the student supplies the airplane, the instructor is not providing it, so no 100 hour inspection is needed. Pro rata cost sharing is not carriage for hire.

stem: An airplane used for flight instruction for hire received a 100 hour inspection at 2,140 hours time in service and then an annual inspection at 2,190 hours. The next 100 hour inspection is due at
options: 2,240 hours.
2,290 hours.
2,250 hours, including the 10 hour allowance.
explanation: 91.409(b) accepts either an annual or a 100 hour inspection within the preceding 100 hours, so the annual at 2,190 resets the count. The next one is due at 2,190 plus 100, or 2,290 hours. 2,240 forgets that the annual counts, and the 10 hour allowance is only for reaching a place to do the inspection.

stem: Who may perform an annual inspection and approve the airplane for return to service?
options: Any certificated mechanic with airframe and powerplant ratings.
A certificated mechanic with airframe and powerplant ratings who also holds an Inspection Authorization.
The owner, if the owner holds at least a private pilot certificate.
explanation: An annual inspection requires a mechanic holding an Inspection Authorization, or an appropriately rated repair station or the manufacturer. An A&P mechanic without an Inspection Authorization may do a 100 hour inspection but not an annual, which is the classic trap. A pilot owner may do only preventive maintenance.

stem: Who is primarily responsible for maintaining an airplane in an airworthy condition, including compliance with applicable airworthiness directives?
options: The mechanic who signed off the last annual inspection.
The pilot in command of each flight.
The owner or operator.
explanation: 91.403 makes the owner or operator primarily responsible for maintaining the aircraft in airworthy condition, including AD compliance. The pilot in command must determine under 91.7 that the airplane is in condition for safe flight, which is why that option tempts. A mechanic is responsible only for the work that mechanic performs.

stem: In cruise, a pilot sees engine oil streaking across the windshield and the leak is getting worse. Under 91.7, the pilot in command
options: may continue to the destination as long as oil pressure stays in the green arc.
must discontinue the flight, because an unairworthy mechanical condition has occurred.
must notify the nearest NTSB office immediately before taking any other action.
explanation: 91.7 makes the pilot in command responsible for determining that the aircraft is in condition for safe flight and requires discontinuing the flight when an unairworthy mechanical, electrical, or structural condition occurs. A growing oil leak is exactly that, so the pilot should land at a suitable airport. Waiting for the oil pressure to drop is how engine failures happen. An oil leak is not an NTSB immediate notification item.

stem: How does a Special Airworthiness Information Bulletin (SAIB) differ from an airworthiness directive?
options: An SAIB gives advisory information and recommendations, while compliance with an AD is mandatory.
An SAIB is an emergency AD that must be complied with before the next flight.
An SAIB applies only to experimental aircraft, while ADs apply to standard category aircraft.
explanation: An SAIB alerts owners and mechanics to a safety issue that does not meet the threshold for an AD, and its recommendations are not mandatory. An emergency AD is still an AD and is mandatory, so it should not be confused with an SAIB. Compliance with an AD is required for every operation, private or for hire. SAIBs are not limited to experimental aircraft.

stem: An airworthiness directive requires a repetitive inspection every 50 hours of time in service. Under 91.417, the airplane's maintenance records must show
options: the current status of the AD, including the method of compliance and the time when the next action is required.
only the date of the first inspection, since later inspections are routine.
nothing, if the inspection is done during a 100 hour inspection.
explanation: 91.417 requires records of the current status of applicable ADs, including the method of compliance, the AD number and revision date, and for a recurring AD the time and date when the next action is due. A one time entry would not show when the next inspection is due. Doing the work during another inspection does not remove the record requirement.

stem: Which task may a certificated private pilot perform as preventive maintenance on an airplane the pilot owns, provided it is not operated under part 121, 129, or 135?
options: Replacing a magneto and timing it to the engine.
Repairing a cracked exhaust stack by welding.
Replacing, cleaning, or setting the gap of spark plugs.
explanation: Spark plug replacement, cleaning, and gap setting are on the preventive maintenance list in part 43 Appendix A, which a pilot may do on an aircraft the pilot owns or operates. Magneto timing and welding are maintenance or repairs that need a certificated mechanic. The rule covers simple, minor jobs that do not involve complex assembly.

stem: After a private pilot replaces a worn main wheel tire on the airplane he owns, what documentation is required?
options: A maintenance record entry describing the work, with the date, the pilot's name, signature, certificate number, and kind of certificate.
None, because preventive maintenance by the owner does not need to be recorded.
An inspection and return to service signature by an A&P mechanic before the next flight.
explanation: Preventive maintenance must be recorded under 43.9: a description of the work, the completion date, the name of the person who did it, and, for return to service, that person's signature, certificate number, and kind of certificate. The pilot who did the work approves it for return to service, so no mechanic signature is required. Skipping the entry is the common mistake.

stem: Which instrument is required by 91.205 for day VFR flight in a single engine airplane with an air cooled engine?
options: Attitude indicator.
Oil temperature gauge.
Vertical speed indicator.
explanation: 91.205(b) requires an oil temperature gauge for each air cooled engine, along with the airspeed indicator, altimeter, magnetic compass, tachometer, oil pressure gauge, and fuel gauges. Gyroscopic instruments such as the attitude indicator are required for IFR under 91.205(d), not for VFR. The vertical speed indicator is not required for either.

stem: A private pilot plans a night VFR flight, not for hire, in an airplane equipped for day VFR. Which additional item does 91.205(c) require?
options: An electric landing light.
An attitude indicator.
Approved position lights.
explanation: Night VFR adds approved position lights, an anticollision light system, an adequate source of electrical energy, and a spare set of fuses (or three of each kind) to the day VFR list. A landing light is required only when the airplane is operated for hire, which is the classic trap. An attitude indicator is an IFR item.

stem: Under 91.209, an aircraft in flight must display lighted position lights during the period from
options: sunset to sunrise.
the end of evening civil twilight to the beginning of morning civil twilight.
1 hour after sunset to 1 hour before sunrise.
explanation: Position lights are required from sunset to sunrise. The civil twilight period is the Part 1 definition of night used for logging and for night equipment, and the 1 hour after sunset period is for night passenger currency. Keeping the three periods apart is a favorite test topic.

stem: Before a day VFR flight in an airplane with no approved MEL, the pilot finds the left fuel quantity gauge inoperative. The left tank has been visually confirmed full. May the pilot depart?
options: Yes, because the tank was visually checked and the quantity is known.
Yes, after the gauge is placarded inoperative and the flight is logged.
No, because 91.205 requires a fuel gauge for each tank, so the item cannot be deferred under 91.213(d).
explanation: 91.213(d) allows flight with inoperative equipment only if the item is not required by the type certification, the equipment list or KOEL, 91.205 or any other rule, or an AD. 91.205(b) requires a fuel quantity gauge for each tank, so this gauge must be repaired, or a special flight permit obtained. A visual check does not change what the regulation requires.

stem: Before a day VFR flight in an airplane with no approved MEL, the pilot finds the second navigation radio inoperative. It is not on the equipment list or KOEL, not required by 91.205 or any other rule, and not required by an AD. What must happen before flight?
options: Nothing, because the radio is not required equipment.
It must be removed or deactivated and placarded inoperative, and a pilot or mechanic must determine that it is not a hazard.
A special flight permit must be obtained from the FAA.
explanation: Passing the four questions of 91.213(d)(2) is only half the job. The item must also be removed (with the cockpit control placarded and the maintenance recorded) or deactivated and placarded "Inoperative", and an appropriately rated pilot or a certificated maintenance person must decide that it is not a hazard. A special flight permit is needed only when the airplane is not airworthy.

stem: To operate an airplane with inoperative equipment under an approved minimum equipment list (MEL), which FAA document must be carried in the aircraft?
options: The manufacturer's master MEL, which applies to every airplane of that model.
A letter of authorization issued by the FAA, which together with the approved MEL constitutes a supplemental type certificate for the aircraft.
A Kinds of Operations Equipment List signed by an FAA inspector.
explanation: Under 91.213(a), the approved MEL and the letter of authorization from the FAA together count as a supplemental type certificate, and the letter must be carried in the aircraft. A master MEL is the generic starting point that an operator tailors and gets approved; it cannot be used by itself. A KOEL is a different document that does not authorize deferring items.

stem: A Kinds of Operations Equipment List (KOEL), when the manufacturer provides one in the airplane flight manual, shows
options: which equipment must work for each kind of operation, such as day VFR, night VFR, IFR, or flight into known icing.
the inspection intervals for each installed instrument.
the items that may be inoperative under an approved MEL.
explanation: A KOEL, usually in the limitations section, lists the equipment required for each kind of operation the airplane is approved for. Under 91.213(d)(2)(ii), an item marked required on the KOEL for the planned operation cannot be deferred. The MEL, not the KOEL, is the document that lists items that may be inoperative.

stem: Under 91.207, when must ELT batteries be replaced, or recharged if rechargeable?
options: Every 12 calendar months, at the ELT inspection.
After the transmitter has been used for more than 1 cumulative hour, or when 50 percent of the battery's useful life has expired.
After the transmitter has been used for more than 2 cumulative hours, or when 75 percent of the battery's useful life has expired.
explanation: 91.207(c) requires battery replacement or recharge after more than 1 cumulative hour of use or when 50 percent of the useful life, as set by the manufacturer, has expired. The new expiration date goes on the outside of the transmitter and in the maintenance record. The 12 calendar month figure is the ELT inspection interval, not the battery rule.

stem: The ELT has been removed from an airplane for repair. Under 91.207, the airplane may be operated without it
options: for up to 10 days, provided the pilot carries a personal locator beacon.
for up to 90 days after removal, with the removal recorded in the aircraft records and a placard reading "ELT not installed" in view of the pilot.
only under a special flight permit.
explanation: 91.207(f)(10) allows operation for up to 90 days after the ELT is removed for inspection, repair, modification, or replacement. The aircraft records must show the removal date, the ELT details, and the reason, and a placard reading "ELT not installed" must be visible to the pilot. A personal locator beacon is not a legal substitute.

stem: Which operation is exempt from the requirement to have an ELT installed?
options: Any flight that stays within 25 nautical miles of the departure airport.
Day VFR cross country flights in an airplane equipped with ADS-B Out.
Training flights conducted entirely within a 50 nautical mile radius of the departure airport.
explanation: 91.207(f) exempts training operations conducted entirely within a 50 nautical mile radius of the airport where the local flight began, along with a few others such as aircraft built to carry only one person. There is no general 25 mile exemption. ADS-B Out does not replace an ELT.

stem: On March 3, 2027, a pilot plans a VFR flight into Class C airspace. The maintenance records show the transponder was last tested and inspected under 91.413 on February 9, 2025. Which is correct?
options: The inspection expired at the end of February 2027, so the transponder may not be used and the pilot should not enter Class C airspace unless ATC authorizes a deviation.
The inspection is still current because it is valid for 24 months plus a 30 day grace period.
The inspection does not matter, because transponder checks are required only for IFR flight.
explanation: 91.413 requires a transponder test and inspection within the preceding 24 calendar months. February 2025 plus 24 calendar months ends February 28, 2027, so on March 3 the transponder may not be used, and Class C requires one under 91.215. There is no grace period. The IFR only test is the altimeter and static system check of 91.411, which is the trap.

stem: The altimeter, static system, and altitude reporting tests of 91.411, required every 24 calendar months, apply to
options: operation in controlled airspace under IFR.
all flights in Class B, C, and D airspace.
night VFR flights that carry passengers.
explanation: 91.411 applies only to airplanes operated in controlled airspace under IFR. A VFR only airplane does not need this test. The transponder test of 91.413, by contrast, applies whenever the transponder is used, VFR or IFR.

stem: A private pilot flies VFR at 3,500 feet MSL, 20 nautical miles from the primary airport of a Class B area, beneath the Class B shelf and outside Class B airspace. The airplane has an engine driven electrical system. What equipment is required?
options: No transponder, because the airplane is outside Class B airspace.
An operable Mode C transponder and ADS-B Out.
A two way radio only, because the airplane remains below the shelf.
explanation: Within 30 nautical miles of a Class B primary airport, from the surface to 10,000 feet MSL (the Mode C veil), both a Mode C transponder and ADS-B Out are required, whether or not the airplane is inside Class B. Only aircraft not certificated with an engine driven electrical system, balloons, and gliders get relief. A radio is not required by the veil rule itself.

stem: In the 48 contiguous states, a pilot flies VFR at 11,000 feet MSL in Class E airspace over terrain 9,000 feet MSL, so the airplane is 2,000 feet above the surface. The area is outside any Mode C veil and outside Class B and C airspace. Is ADS-B Out required by 91.225?
options: Yes, because the airplane is at or above 10,000 feet MSL.
No, because airspace at and below 2,500 feet above the surface is excluded.
Yes, because ADS-B Out is required in all Class E airspace.
explanation: The Class E rule requires ADS-B Out at and above 10,000 feet MSL in the 48 contiguous states, but it excludes airspace at and below 2,500 feet above the surface.
