explanation: VFR flight plans go to Flight Service, reachable at 1 800 WX BRIEF, through the online Flight Service portal, or through EFB apps that file to it. Towers and approach controls do not accept or open VFR flight plans.

stem: After takeoff, how does a pilot activate a filed VFR flight plan?
options: The tower activates it automatically on takeoff
Contact Flight Service, usually by radio, and give the actual departure time
It activates automatically at the proposed departure time
explanation: A filed VFR flight plan stays proposed until the pilot asks Flight Service to activate it. The tower does not open it, and it does not activate on its own.

stem: A pilot on a VFR flight plan lands at a towered airport. Who closes the flight plan?
options: The tower closes it automatically on landing
The pilot must close it with Flight Service
ATC closes it when the transponder is turned off
explanation: Control towers do not automatically close VFR flight plans because they do not know which VFR aircraft are on one. The pilot closes it with Flight Service by radio, phone, or app.

stem: If a pilot on a VFR flight plan does not close it or report, when does search and rescue begin?
options: 30 minutes after the estimated time of arrival
1 hour after the estimated time of arrival
Immediately at the estimated time of arrival
explanation: Flight Service starts search procedures when the flight is 30 minutes overdue. Extend the ETA by radio if you will be late, and always close the plan to avoid an unneeded search.

stem: An intercepting military aircraft rocks its wings from a position slightly above and ahead, normally to the left, then makes a slow level turn. What does this mean?
options: You may proceed
Land at this airport
You have been intercepted; follow me
explanation: Rocking wings and then a slow level turn means follow me. Acknowledge by rocking your wings and following. An abrupt breakaway climbing turn of 90° or more means you may proceed.

stem: If intercepted, what should a pilot do with the radio and transponder, unless otherwise instructed?
options: Switch to 122.75 MHz and squawk 7600
Stay on the current frequency and squawk 1200
Try to contact the interceptor or ATC on 121.5 MHz and squawk 7700
explanation: An intercepted pilot follows the interceptor's signals, notifies ATC if possible, calls on the emergency frequency 121.5, and selects 7700 unless ATC directs otherwise. 7600 is the lost communications code.

stem: A pilot is unsure of position over unfamiliar terrain. Which sequence reflects the recommended lost procedure?
options: Descend to read town names, then call Flight Service
Climb, communicate, confess, comply, and conserve fuel
Circle until a landmark is found, then resume the planned heading
explanation: Climbing improves radio range, radar coverage, and the view. Then call for help on the frequency in use or 121.5, admit the problem, follow ATC instructions, and reduce power to save fuel. Descending low over unknown terrain adds obstacle risk.

stem: A lost pilot can identify the airplane's position with two VOR receivers by
options: tuning two different VORs and finding where the two radials cross on the chart
tuning one VOR on both receivers and averaging the radials
noting where the TO/FROM flag changes on a single VOR
explanation: Center each CDI with a FROM flag to read the radial you are on, then draw both radials from their stations. Their intersection is your position. One station gives only a line, not a point.

stem: A pilot is lost, fuel is getting low, and the weather is lowering. What is the appropriate step?
options: Declare an emergency with ATC or on 121.5 and squawk 7700 to get immediate help
Avoid contacting ATC to prevent enforcement action
Keep searching for a landmark until fuel reaches the reserve
explanation: Being lost with decreasing fuel and weather is a developing emergency. Declaring early gives priority handling and radar help while there are still options. Fear of paperwork is a hazardous attitude that has ended many flights badly.

stem: Clouds ahead are lowering toward the planned route. When should a diversion be started?
options: After the airplane enters reduced visibility, to be sure diverting is necessary
Only after asking Flight Service for permission
As soon as continuing looks doubtful, while weather and fuel still allow a safe turn
explanation: The best diversions are early and decisive. Waiting until visibility is already poor removes options and invites continued VFR into IMC. A pilot in command does not need permission to divert.

stem: When diverting, what should the pilot do first?
options: Plot the new course precisely with a plotter before turning
Turn promptly toward the new destination using an estimated heading, then refine heading, distance, time, and fuel
Close the VFR flight plan before changing direction
explanation: Fly the airplane first. Turn toward the alternate with an estimated heading, then work out the details with the chart, a rule of thumb, or GPS. Heads down plotting while holding the old course wastes time and distance.

stem: How should a pilot state an altitude of 12,500 feet MSL in a radio transmission?
options: Twelve thousand five hundred.
One two five zero zero.
One two thousand five hundred.
explanation: Below 18,000 feet, altitudes are stated by saying the thousands digits separately followed by the word thousand and then the hundreds, so 12,500 is one two thousand five hundred. Saying twelve thousand is conversational and invites a misheard digit. Reading every digit as one two five zero zero is the format for frequencies or squawk codes, not altitudes.

stem: A controller assigns a heading of 080 degrees. How is this correctly read back?
options: Heading eight zero.
Heading eighty.
Heading zero eight zero.
explanation: Headings are always spoken as three separate digits, including a leading zero, followed by nothing else, so 080 becomes zero eight zero. Dropping the leading zero (eight zero) is the common slip and could be heard as 800 or as part of another number. Saying eighty is never standard for headings.

stem: Which pair of ICAO phonetic words represents the letters G and K?
options: George, King.
Golf, Kilo.
Gulf, Kilowatt.
explanation: The ICAO phonetic alphabet used in the United States is Alfa, Bravo, Charlie, Delta, Echo, Foxtrot, Golf, Hotel, India, Juliett, Kilo, and so on. George and King come from the older World War II era alphabet that some pilots still hear in movies. Gulf and Kilowatt are invented variants.

stem: Which initial call to a Class D tower, made about 10 miles out, contains the information the controller needs in the expected order?
options: "Cessna 6413Q is ten miles north of Centerville for landing, over."
"Centerville Tower, Cessna 6413Q, ten miles north, two thousand five hundred, landing, with information Bravo."
"Centerville Tower, Cessna 6413Q, request landing instructions."
explanation: A good initial call follows who you are calling, who you are, where you are (position and altitude), what you want, and the ATIS code you have. The first choice omits the facility being called and the ATIS, and adds the outdated word over. The third choice gives no position or altitude, so the controller has to ask, wasting frequency time.

stem: You call a Class D tower while 6 miles outside its airspace. The controller responds, "Aircraft calling Centerville Tower, stand by." What may you do?
options: Remain outside the Class D airspace, because two way communication has not been established.
Enter the Class D airspace, because the controller acknowledged the call.
Enter the Class D airspace if you squawk 1200 and stay at or below 2,500 feet AGL.
explanation: Two way radio communication for Class D entry is established only when the controller responds using your call sign. A reply to an unidentified aircraft calling, even one telling you to stand by, does not count, so you must stay out. The most tempting error is treating any acknowledgment as permission.

stem: Approaching Class C airspace, you call approach control and hear, "Cessna 6413Q, stand by." Which statement is correct?
options: Two way communication is established and you may enter the Class C airspace unless told to remain outside.
You must remain outside until the controller says you are cleared into the Class C airspace.
You may enter only after the controller also says radar contact.
explanation: For Class C, as for Class D, entry requires two way radio communication, which exists once the controller responds with your call sign. A stand by that includes your call sign establishes it, so you may enter unless told to remain outside. A specific clearance into the airspace is a Class B requirement, which is the trap in the first wrong choice.

stem: Approach control tells you, "Cessna 6413Q, radar contact, eight miles southwest of the airport, maintain VFR." You are just outside the Class B boundary. May you enter the Class B airspace?
options: Yes; radar contact means communications are established.
No; you need an explicit clearance to enter Class B airspace.
Yes; the instruction to maintain VFR authorizes entry.
explanation: Class B requires an ATC clearance, normally phrased cleared into the Class Bravo airspace. Radar contact only means the controller has identified you, and maintain VFR is not a clearance. Treating established communication as sufficient is correct for Class C and D, which is exactly why it is the tempting wrong answer here.

stem: Inbound to a nontowered airport, when does the AIM recommend that you make your first self announce call on the CTAF?
options: About 5 miles from the airport.
About 10 miles from the airport.
When entering the downwind leg.
explanation: The AIM recommends the first inbound report on the CTAF about 10 miles out, followed by reports entering downwind, base, final, and leaving the runway. Five miles is the distance many pilots remember from Class D airspace, which is the trap. Waiting until downwind gives other traffic too little warning.

stem: Which ATIS elements may be omitted from the broadcast when the ceiling is above 5,000 feet and the visibility is more than 5 miles?
options: The ceiling or sky condition, visibility, and obstructions to vision.
The altimeter setting and wind.
The runway in use and the approach in use.
explanation: The AIM allows ATIS to omit sky condition, visibility, and obstructions to vision when the ceiling is above 5,000 feet and visibility exceeds 5 miles, often stated as a remark that conditions are better than 5000 and 5. Wind, altimeter, and runway in use are always included because pilots need them for every arrival and departure.

stem: Ground control instructs, "Cessna 6413Q, Runway 31, taxi via Alpha." Your route on Alpha crosses Runway 4. What does this instruction authorize?
options: Taxi on Alpha toward Runway 31, but hold short of Runway 4 unless you receive an explicit clearance to cross it.
Taxi on Alpha and cross Runway 4, since it lies on the assigned route.
Taxi on Alpha and cross Runway 4 only if no traffic is in sight.
explanation: Current procedures require an explicit crossing clearance for every runway along a taxi route, so a clearance to a runway does not include permission to cross other runways. Under the old rule a taxi to clearance did allow crossing, which is why the first wrong choice still appears in older material. Visually clearing a runway never substitutes for a crossing clearance at a towered airport.

stem: (Refer to Figure 79.) At 0500Z in January, a pilot is inbound to land at Sioux Gateway/Col Bud Day Field. How should the pilot communicate?
options: Contact Sioux City Tower on 118.7 for landing clearance.
Contact Sioux City Approach on 124.6 for sequencing.
Self announce position and intentions on the CTAF, 118.7.
explanation: The tower operates 1200 to 0330Z, and in January standard time applies, so at 0500Z the tower is closed. The entry lists CTAF 118.7, so the pilot self announces on that frequency, and the airspace reverts to Class E. Approach on 124.6 is also only available 1200 to 0330Z; at night Minneapolis Center on 124.1 provides approach service.

stem: (Refer to Figure 79 and Legend 14.) A pilot wants to talk to Fort Dodge Radio through the Sioux City RCO listed as 122.1R. How is this done?
options: Transmit and listen on 122.1 MHz.
Transmit on 122.1 MHz and listen on the Sioux City VORTAC frequency, 116.5 MHz.
Transmit on 116.5 MHz and listen on 122.1 MHz.
explanation: The legend states that a frequency followed by R is receive only for the facility, and one followed by T is transmit only. Fort Dodge Radio receives on 122.1 and transmits on 116.5T, the VORTAC, so the pilot transmits on 122.1 and listens on 116.5 with the VOR receiver volume up. Assuming two way use of 122.1 is the common mistake.

stem: While in flight, a pilot receives a steady green light signal from the tower. This means
options: return for landing.
cleared for takeoff.
cleared to land.
explanation: A steady green directed at an aircraft in flight means cleared to land. A flashing green in flight means return for landing, which is the closest trap. Cleared for takeoff is the meaning of steady green for an aircraft on the ground.

stem: A flashing green light signal directed at an aircraft in flight means
options: cleared to land.
cleared to taxi.
return for landing, to be followed by a steady green at the proper time.
explanation: In flight, a flashing green tells the pilot to return for landing and expect a steady green later as the landing clearance. Cleared to land is the meaning of a steady green. Cleared to taxi is what a flashing green means on the ground, so pilots who memorize only one column mix them up.

stem: While circling a towered airport with a failed radio, a pilot receives a steady red light. The pilot should
options: not land because the airport is unsafe.
give way to other aircraft and continue circling.
stop and hold position.
explanation: A steady red in flight means give way to other aircraft and continue circling. The airport unsafe, do not land message is a flashing red. Stop is the ground meaning of steady red.

stem: On short final with a failed radio, you see a flashing red light from the tower. What should you do?
options: Go around and do not land, because the airport is unsafe.
Continue and land, then taxi clear of the runway.
Continue circling and expect a steady green.
explanation: A flashing red to an aircraft in flight means airport unsafe, do not land. Taxi clear of the runway in use is the ground meaning of flashing red, which is the tempting mix up. Give way and continue circling is a steady red.

stem: After landing with a failed radio, you are still on the runway when the tower directs a flashing red light at you. You should
options: taxi clear of the runway in use.
stop immediately and hold position.
return to the starting point on the airport.
explanation: For aircraft on the surface, a flashing red means taxi clear of the runway in use. A steady red means stop, and a flashing white means return to the starting point on the airport. Stopping on the runway would be the worst choice because it leaves you in the path of other traffic.

stem: A flashing white light from the tower directed at an airplane on the ground means
options: cleared to taxi.
return to the starting point on the airport.
exercise extreme caution.
explanation: Flashing white is used only for aircraft on the ground and means return to the starting point on the airport; it has no meaning in flight. Cleared to taxi is a flashing green. Exercise extreme caution is alternating red and green.

stem: An alternating red and green light signal from the tower means
options: exercise extreme caution, whether on the ground or in flight.
the airport is unsafe; do not land.
taxi clear of the runway in use.
explanation: Alternating red and green is a general warning that means exercise extreme caution, and it applies both on the ground and in the air. Airport unsafe is the in flight meaning of flashing red, and taxi clear of the runway is the ground meaning of flashing red.

stem: At night, how should a pilot in flight acknowledge a light signal from the tower?
options: By rocking the wings.
By flashing the landing light or navigation lights.
By moving the ailerons or rudder.
explanation: The AIM says that in flight at night a pilot acknowledges by flashing the landing or navigation lights, because wing rocking is hard for the tower to see in the dark. Rocking the wings is the daytime acknowledgment in flight. Moving ailerons or rudder is the daytime acknowledgment on the ground.

stem: During a VFR flight your transmitter fails, but you can still hear the tower. You must land at a towered airport inside Class D airspace. What is the recommended procedure?
options: Squawk 7600, remain outside or above the Class D airspace until you determine the direction and flow of traffic, then join the pattern, monitor tower frequency, and watch for light signals.
Squawk 7700, enter the Class D airspace immediately, and land on the longest runway.
Squawk 7600 and fly a straight in approach to the active runway without waiting for any signal.
explanation: The AIM procedure for a VFR radio failure is to set 7600, stay outside or above the Class D area until you know the traffic flow, enter the pattern, and look for light signals; you acknowledge by rocking the wings in daylight. A receiver that still works lets you hear instructions, which makes the arrival easier. Squawking 7700 is for a declared emergency, and a straight in approach without a signal ignores other traffic.

stem: When may the operational test of an emergency locator transmitter be conducted?
options: During the first 5 minutes after the hour, for no more than three audio sweeps.
At any time, provided 121.5 MHz is monitored during the test.
During the last 5 minutes of the hour, for no more than 30 seconds.
explanation: The AIM limits ELT testing to the first 5 minutes after any hour and to no more than three audio sweeps, so that search facilities can tell a test from a real distress signal. Testing at any time, even while monitoring, can trigger a false alert. The last 5 minutes is a reversal of the actual window.

stem: The battery of an emergency locator transmitter must be replaced or recharged after
options: more than one cumulative hour of use, or after 50 percent of its useful life has expired.
one cumulative hour of use, or once every 12 calendar months.
two cumulative hours of use, or after 75 percent of its useful life has expired.
explanation: Under 14 CFR 91.207, ELT batteries are replaced or recharged when the transmitter has been in use for more than one cumulative hour or when 50 percent of the battery's useful life (or charge, for rechargeable batteries) has expired. The 12 calendar month figure is the ELT inspection interval, which is the trap in the first wrong choice.

stem: Unless otherwise indicated, which traffic pattern turns are made at an airport without an operating control tower?
options: Right turns.
Left turns.
Turns toward the side of the runway with the wind sock.
explanation: 14 CFR 91.126 requires airplanes approaching to land at an airport without an operating tower to make all turns to the left unless markings or light signals indicate right turns. Right traffic must be published, for example as Rgt tfc in the Chart Supplement or by traffic pattern indicators. The location of the wind sock has nothing to do with pattern direction.

stem: Where no pattern altitude is published, the AIM recommends that propeller driven airplanes fly the traffic pattern at
options: 1,500 feet above the airport elevation.
1,000 feet above the airport elevation.
800 feet above the airport elevation.
explanation: The AIM recommends 1,000 feet AGL as the traffic pattern altitude for propeller driven aircraft unless the airport establishes something else. About 1,500 feet AGL is the recommendation for large and turbine powered aircraft, which is the trap. Always convert to MSL by adding the field elevation.

stem: What is the recommended way to enter the traffic pattern at a nontowered airport?
options: On a 45 degree angle to the downwind leg, abeam the midpoint of the runway, at pattern altitude.
On a 45 degree angle to the base leg, descending to pattern altitude.
Directly onto the base leg from any direction, at 500 feet AGL.
explanation: The AIM shows the standard entry as a 45 degree intercept of the downwind leg, joined abeam midfield in level flight at pattern altitude. Entering on base, or joining base low from any direction, cuts in front of aircraft already on downwind and puts you where other pilots are not looking.

stem: (Refer to Figure 49.) The tetrahedron indicates that the wind is from the
options: northeast.
southeast.
southwest.
explanation: The small, pointed end of a tetrahedron points into the wind, like the nose of an airplane weathervaning. In Figure 49 the point aims toward the lower left, so the wind is from the southwest. Reading the wide end as the upwind end reverses the answer to northeast. A tetrahedron may be free swinging or set manually, so confirm the wind with a wind cone or a weather report when possible.

stem: (Refer to Figure 49.) Runway 22 is the runway most nearly aligned with the wind shown by the tetrahedron. Why should a pilot land on Runway 18 instead?
options: Runway 4-22 is closed, as shown by the X at each end.
Runway 22 is reserved for takeoffs, as shown by the arrows on the runway.
Runway 22 has right traffic, which conflicts with the segmented circle.
explanation: An X at each end of a runway means it is closed, so Runway 4-22 cannot be used even though it points into the southwest wind. Runway 18 is the open runway that gives a headwind component. The arrows and triangles on Runways 18 and 36 mark displaced thresholds, not a takeoff restriction on Runway 22.

stem: (Refer to Figure 50.) The wind cone indicates that the wind is from the
options: southeast.
northeast.
northwest.
explanation: A wind cone fills and its open tail streams downwind, so the wind comes from the end attached to the pole. The cone streams toward the southeast, so the wind is from the northwest. Reading the direction the tail points as the wind direction gives southeast, the classic reversal.

stem: (Refer to Figure 50.) The segmented circle serves a north and south runway and an east and west runway. A pilot landing toward the north will have a
options: right quartering headwind.
left quartering headwind.
left quartering tailwind.
explanation: The wind cone shows wind from the northwest. A northbound airplane has that wind ahead and to its left, so it is a left quartering headwind. Choosing right reverses the side, and choosing tailwind comes from reading the cone backward.

stem: (Refer to Figure 50.) According to the traffic pattern indicators, which landing direction uses a right hand traffic pattern?
options: Landing toward the east.
Landing toward the west.
Landing toward the north.
explanation: Each traffic pattern indicator shows the final approach leg with the base leg drawn as an arm at its outer end. The indicator east of the circle serves landings toward the west, and its base arm extends north; a westbound airplane on final has north to its right, so the pattern uses right turns. The indicators for landings toward the east and toward the north have their base arms on the pilot's left, which means standard left traffic.

stem: (Refer to Figure 9, area B.) You are taxiing a tricycle gear airplane and the wind is blowing from the direction shown by arrow B. How should the controls be held?
options: Right aileron up and elevator neutral.
Right aileron down and elevator down.
Left aileron up and elevator up.
explanation: Arrow B is a right quartering headwind. Turning the control wheel toward the wind raises the right aileron and keeps the upwind wing from lifting, and the elevator is held neutral in a nosewheel airplane so the nose gear keeps normal weight. Aileron down with elevator down is the setting for a quartering tailwind. Left aileron up would aid the wind in lifting the right wing.

stem: (Refer to Figure 9, area C.) Which control positions should be used while taxiing with a wind from the direction of arrow C?
options: Left aileron up and elevator neutral.
Left aileron down and elevator down.
Right aileron down and elevator up.
explanation: Arrow C is a left quartering tailwind. The rule is dive away from the wind: elevator down so the tailwind cannot get under the tail, and the control wheel turned away from the wind, which lowers the left (upwind) aileron. Left aileron up with elevator neutral is the setting for a left quartering headwind, the most common reversal.

stem: (Refer to Figure 81.) A pilot plans to depart Mineral County Memorial toward the northeast. Which procedure applies?
options: Turn right immediately after takeoff to remain clear of the glider area.
Climb to 1,000 feet AGL over the airport before departing on course.
Climb to 200 feet AGL on the extended runway centerline before turning, avoiding overflight of the trailers and homes, and stay to the right of the valley.
explanation: The remarks for Mineral Co Mem ask aircraft departing to the northeast to avoid overflying trailers and resident homes by climbing to 200 feet AGL on the extended centerline before turning, and to stay to the right of the valley on approach and departure. These are local noise abatement and terrain procedures, so pilots must read the remarks section before flying to an unfamiliar airport.

stem: (Refer to Figure 81 and Legend 5.) Winds require a landing on Runway 25 at Crawford. Which traffic pattern should be flown?
options: A left hand pattern at 7,470 feet MSL.
A right hand pattern at 7,470 feet MSL.
A right hand pattern at 1,000 feet MSL.
explanation: The Runway 25 line shows Rgt tfc, so turns are to the right. The TPA entry 7470(1000) gives the pattern altitude as 7,470 feet MSL, which is 1,000 feet above the 6,470 foot field elevation. The figure in parentheses is height above the airport, not an MSL altitude.

stem: (Refer to Figure 52.) With the tower closed and the wind calm at Lincoln, which runway and traffic pattern direction should a pilot expect?
options: Runway 36, with left traffic.
Runway 18, with right traffic.
Runway 18, with left traffic.
explanation: The airport remarks state Rwy 18 designated calm wind rwy, so Runway 18 is used when the wind is calm. The Runway 18 line includes Rgt tfc, so turns are to the right. Assuming the default left pattern is the trap, since right traffic is published for this runway end.

stem: (Refer to Figure 31.) No traffic pattern altitude is published for Coeur d'Alene. What pattern and altitude should a pilot of a light airplane use for Runway 01?
options: Left traffic at about 3,300 feet MSL.
Right traffic at about 1,000 feet MSL.
Right traffic at about 3,300 feet MSL.
explanation: Runway 01 is annotated Rgt tfc, so the pattern uses right turns. With no TPA listed, the AIM recommendation of 1,000 feet AGL applies, and the field elevation is 2,320 feet, so the pattern is flown at about 3,320 feet MSL. Flying 1,000 feet MSL would put the airplane below the airport elevation.

stem: (Refer to Figure 64.) The yellow marking at D is painted across a runway just before it intersects another runway. It shows
options: where taxiing airplanes stop before entering the runway from a taxiway.
the beginning of a displaced threshold on the intersecting runway.
where an airplane on that runway must stop when told to hold short of the intersecting runway, for example during LAHSO.
explanation: Two solid and two dashed yellow lines painted across a runway form a holding position marking on a runway, placed before an intersecting runway. An airplane on the solid side, landing or taxiing on that runway, stops there when ATC issues a hold short instruction such as a LAHSO clearance. The same pattern on a taxiway marks a taxiway entry to a runway, but D is on runway pavement, and displaced thresholds are marked in white.

stem: (Refer to Figure 64.) The single dashed yellow line across the taxiway at E indicates a
options: runway holding position, because the runway is close by.
holding position for a taxiway and taxiway intersection, used when ATC instructs you to hold there.
boundary of the ILS critical area.
explanation: A single dashed yellow line across a taxiway is the holding position marking for a taxiway intersection; you stop there when ATC tells you to hold short of the crossing taxiway. A runway holding position uses four lines, and the ILS critical area boundary looks like a ladder of two solid lines joined by short cross bars.

stem: (Refer to Figure 64.) The ladder shaped marking near B, made of two solid yellow lines connected by pairs of short lines, is a
options: runway holding position marking.
taxiway shoulder marking.
ILS critical area holding position marking.
explanation: Two solid yellow lines joined by pairs of short perpendicular lines across the taxiway mark the ILS critical area holding position. When instructed to hold short of the ILS critical area, stop before this marking so the airplane does not distort the localizer or glide slope signal. A runway holding position marking has two solid and two dashed lines instead.

stem: (Refer to Figure 64.) The continuous double yellow line at F marks the
options: edge of the taxiway, beyond which the surface is not intended for aircraft.
taxiway centerline.
boundary between the movement and nonmovement areas.
explanation: A continuous double yellow line along the side of a taxiway is the taxiway edge marking, separating the taxiway from shoulder or other surface not meant for aircraft. The centerline is a single continuous yellow line. The movement area boundary uses one solid and one dashed yellow line.

stem: (Refer to Figure 65.) Sign A, white 4-22 on a red background, located beside a taxiway, means
options: you are on Runway 4-22.
you are approaching the intersection with Runway 4-22 and must hold short unless cleared.
the route to Runway 4-22 is in the direction of the sign.
explanation: Red signs with white numbers are mandatory instruction signs; a runway number pair identifies a runway holding position, with the left number on the left. At a towered airport you stop at the associated hold line unless cleared to enter or cross. A sign telling you that you are on a runway is black with yellow numbers, and a route to a runway is a yellow destination sign.

stem: (Refer to Figure 65.) Sign F, a yellow 22 on a black background with a yellow border, indicates that the airplane is
options: located on Runway 22.
approaching the holding position for Runway 22.
on the route that leads to Runway 22.
explanation: Black signs with yellow characters are location signs and tell you where you are; with a runway number, the sign is a runway location sign. A holding position would be shown by a red mandatory sign, and a route to Runway 22 is a yellow sign with black numbers and an arrow, such as sign J.

stem: (Refer to Figure 65.) Sign L, a white 4 on a black background beside the runway, tells the pilot that
options: the airplane is on taxiway 4.
the intersection with Runway 4 is ahead.
about 4,000 feet of runway remain.
explanation: A white number on a black background beside a runway is a runway distance remaining sign, showing remaining distance in thousands of feet. Location signs use yellow characters on black, and taxiways are designated by letters, not numbers. An intersecting runway would be marked by a red mandatory sign.

stem: (Refer to Figure 65.) Sign G is seen by a pilot taxiing off the runway. What is its purpose?
options: It is a holding position sign; stop until cleared to exit.
It is a runway boundary sign; once the entire airplane is past it, the airplane is clear of the runway.
It marks the ILS critical area boundary for aircraft leaving that area.
explanation: Sign G shows a picture of the holding position marking on a yellow background and faces the runway. It is the runway boundary sign, which helps an exiting pilot judge when the airplane is clear of the runway. The ILS critical area boundary sign shows the ladder pattern instead, as on sign H.

stem: (Refer to Figure 65.) Which sign is a direction sign showing the way to another taxiway?
options: Sign J.
Sign E.
Sign K.
explanation: Direction signs are yellow with black letters and arrows naming taxiways at an intersection, so B with an arrow (sign K) shows the route to taxiway B. Sign J has a runway number with an arrow, which makes it a destination sign. Sign E is a black location sign telling you that you are on taxiway B.

stem: (Refer to Figure 48.) The area marked with yellow chevrons at E is
options: a displaced threshold area, usable for taxiing and takeoff but not for landing.
a holding apron, usable for engine run ups before departure.
a blast pad or stopway, not to be used for taxiing, takeoff, or landing.
explanation: Yellow chevrons mark a blast pad or stopway. A stopway may be used to decelerate during an aborted takeoff, but these areas are not for taxiing, takeoff, or landing. The area that can be used for taxi and takeoff but not touchdown is the white arrow area before a displaced threshold, which is the trap here.

stem: (Refer to Figure 48.) A pilot considers using the runway segment marked C for a departure. Based on its markings, the segment
options: is closed and may not be used.
may be used for takeoff only, not landing.
may be used for landing in daylight only.
explanation: The X markings on the segment at C mean the runway is closed. A closed runway may not be used for takeoff or landing at any time of day. Takeoff only use applies to pavement before a displaced threshold, which is marked with white arrows, not an X.

stem: After landing at a towered airport, ATC gives you no further taxi instructions. Where does the AIM expect you to stop?
options: As soon as the nosewheel has crossed the runway edge line.
As soon as the airplane has turned onto the taxiway, even if the tail is still short of the hold line.
Once every part of the airplane has crossed the runway holding position marking for the landing runway.
explanation: The AIM considers an airplane clear of the runway once all parts are past the runway edge, and without other instructions it expects the pilot to keep taxiing until every part of the airplane has crossed the holding position marking for the landing runway, then hold. Stopping when only the nosewheel has crossed the edge line leaves most of the airplane on the runway. Stopping short of the hold line after the turn is the tempting choice, but it leaves the tail inside the area protected for runway traffic.

stem: Which pilots should not accept a land and hold short (LAHSO) clearance?
options: Student pilots and pilots who are not familiar with LAHSO.
Only pilots flying airplanes heavier than 12,500 pounds.
Any pilot landing at night, regardless of experience.
explanation: The AIM states that student pilots and pilots not familiar with LAHSO should not participate. Any pilot in command may decline a LAHSO clearance, and should do so if the available landing distance is not adequate. Weight and night conditions are not what excludes a pilot.

stem: (Refer to Figure 79 and Legend 9.) A pilot is offered a LAHSO clearance to land on Runway 13 and hold short of Runway 17-35. What landing distance is available?
options: 5,650 feet.
9,002 feet.
5,400 feet.
explanation: The land and hold short operations table lists Runway 13 with hold short point 17-35 and a distance available of 5,400 feet. The 5,650 foot figure applies to landing on Runway 17 and holding short of 13-31. The full 9,002 foot length is not available when holding short of the intersecting runway.

stem: You normally depart Runway 27 at your home airport. Today ground control says, "Taxi to Runway 9 via Bravo." Which practice best guards against an expectation bias error?
options: Read back the clearance, then follow it on the airport diagram and confirm each sign before turning.
Start toward Runway 27 and correct if the controller objects.
Ask the controller to repeat the clearance after reaching the hold line.
explanation: Expectation bias is hearing what you expected rather than what was said, and it is a known cause of runway incursions. A full readback catches mishearing early, and tracing the route on the diagram while checking signs keeps you on the assigned path. Letting the controller catch the error, or asking after reaching the hold line, leaves the risk in place.

stem: A rotating beacon that flashes alternating white and green identifies a
options: lighted civil land airport.
military airport.
lighted water airport.
explanation: Civil land airports show alternating white and green flashes. Military airports show two quick white flashes between green flashes, and seaplane bases show white and yellow. Heliports show green, yellow, and white.

stem: Which beacon pattern identifies a military airport?
options: White and yellow flashes.
Dual peaked white flashes alternating with green.
Green, yellow, and white flashes.
explanation: A military airfield beacon shows two quick white flashes between green flashes, which distinguishes it from the single white flash of a civil airport. White and yellow identifies a water airport, and green, yellow, and white identifies a heliport.

stem: In daylight, the rotating beacon at an airport within Class D airspace is operating. This often indicates that
options: the tower is closed and the airspace has reverted to Class G.
the ceiling is less than 1,000 feet and/or the ground visibility is less than 3 miles.
the beacon has failed in the on position and should be reported.
explanation: In Class B, C, D, and E surface areas, daytime operation of the beacon often means weather is below basic VFR minimums of a 1,000 foot ceiling and 3 miles visibility, so an ATC clearance is needed to take off, land, or fly in the pattern. Pilots must not rely on the beacon alone; they should check the actual weather. The beacon is not an indicator of tower status.

stem: (Refer to Figure 47.) On final approach to a runway with a standard two bar VASI, which illustration shows the airplane on the glide path?
options: Illustration C.
Illustration A.
Illustration B.
explanation: On a two bar VASI the far bar appears above the near bar; on the glide path the far bar is red and the near bar is white, so you see red over white, as in A. Illustration C, white over white, means above the glide path. Illustration B, white over red, is not a valid two bar VASI indication.

stem: On final approach, a four light PAPI shows three white lights and one red light. The airplane is
options: slightly below the glide path.
slightly above the glide path.
on the glide path.
explanation: A PAPI shows two white and two red on the glide path. Each additional white light means you are higher, so three white and one red is slightly high, and four white is well above. Three red and one white is slightly low, which is the reversal trap.

stem: (Refer to Legend 9.) To make sure all pilot controlled lights come on at full brightness, a pilot should key the microphone on the specified frequency
options: five times within 5 seconds.
seven times within 5 seconds.
three times within 3 seconds.
explanation: The legend shows seven clicks within 5 seconds for the highest intensity, five for medium, and three for lowest. The AIM recommends always starting with seven clicks to be sure every controlled system turns on, then adjusting down if desired. Five clicks gives only medium intensity.

stem: What color are taxiway edge lights?
options: Green.
Yellow.
Blue.
explanation: Taxiway edge lights are blue, and taxiway centerline lights are green. Yellow appears on runway edge lights in the caution zone of instrument runways and in runway guard lights at holding positions.

stem: On an instrument runway, the runway edge lights change from white to yellow
options: on the last 1,000 feet of runway, to warn of the runway end.
on the last 2,000 feet of runway, or half the length if shorter, to form a caution zone.
at the touchdown zone, to show the aiming point.
explanation: High and medium intensity edge lights on instrument runways show yellow instead of white on the last 2,000 feet or half the runway, whichever is less, forming a caution zone for landings. The last 1,000 feet value belongs to runway centerline lights, which turn all red there. Touchdown zone lighting is a separate system of white bars in the pavement.

stem: (Refer to Figure 77.) A pilot plans to land at Pine Ridge at 0600Z in December. What must the pilot do to have runway and PAPI lights?
options: Activate the lights by keying the microphone on the CTAF, 122.9.
Nothing; the lights operate dusk to dawn.
Call Denver Center on 127.95 and request the lights.
explanation: The remarks say the MIRL and PAPI operate from dusk until 0530Z, and after 0530Z the pilot must activate them on the CTAF, 122.9. December is standard time, so the 0530Z cutoff applies as printed, and 0600Z is after it. The ATC center frequency cannot turn on airport lighting.

stem: (Refer to Figure 77 and Legend 3.) In the Pierre Regional sketch, the approach light symbol near Runway 31 is shown in negative form, a white A5 inside a black circle. This indicates
options: a MALSR approach light system that is pilot controlled.
a MALSR approach light system that is out of service.
a simplified short approach light system with sequenced flashers.
explanation: The sketch legend shows that A5 is a medium intensity approach light system with runway alignment indicator lights (MALSR), and that negative symbology indicates pilot controlled lighting. The Pierre remarks confirm that the MALSR for Runway 31 is activated on the CTAF. An out of service system would be reported by NOTAM, not by the symbol color.

stem: Wake turbulence is greatest behind an aircraft that is
options: heavy, clean, and slow.
light, in the landing configuration, and fast.
heavy, with flaps extended, and fast.
explanation: Wingtip vortices are strongest when the wing works hardest to make lift: high weight, gear and flaps up, and slow speed, which means high angle of attack. Extended flaps and higher speed both reduce vortex strength. This is why departing heavy aircraft just after rotation are a serious hazard.

stem: Near the ground in calm wind, wingtip vortices from a large airplane tend to
options: rise and dissipate within a few seconds.
remain stationary over the runway centerline until they dissipate.
sink to the surface and move outward from the runway at about 2 or 3 knots.
explanation: Vortices sink below the generating aircraft and, when close to the ground, spread laterally outward at roughly 2 to 3 knots. That is why a light crosswind can stall the upwind vortex over the runway. They do not rise, and in calm air they do not stay centered on the runway but move away from it.

stem: Which wind condition requires the most caution when landing behind a large aircraft?
options: A light quartering tailwind.
A strong direct headwind.
A strong direct crosswind.
explanation: A light quartering tailwind can move the preceding aircraft's vortices forward into the touchdown zone and hold one there, so it calls for maximum caution. Strong winds break up vortices quickly, and a strong crosswind carries them off the runway. Light winds are more dangerous than strong ones for wake turbulence.

stem: When landing behind a large aircraft that has just landed on the same runway, the pilot should
options: stay below the large aircraft's approach path and land before its touchdown point.
fly a wider pattern and land at least 3 minutes behind it at any point on the runway.
stay at or above the large aircraft's final approach path and touch down beyond its touchdown point.
explanation: Vortices sink below the flight path and end where the large aircraft touched down. Staying at or above its path and landing past its touchdown point keeps you out of them. Staying low and landing short puts you directly in the sinking vortices, which is the core trap.

stem: A large jet has just taken off from the runway you will use for departure. To avoid its wake, you should
options: lift off beyond the jet's rotation point and stay below its flight path.
begin the takeoff roll immediately to use the jet's wake as a tailwind.
lift off before the jet's rotation point and climb above or upwind of its flight path.
explanation: Vortices begin when the jet's wing starts producing lift at rotation, so lifting off earlier and staying above its climb path avoids them. Lifting off later and staying low places you in the descending vortices. Waiting a few minutes after a large aircraft departs is also a sound practice.

stem: What is the most effective technique for scanning for traffic in daylight?
options: A slow, continuous sweep of the horizon without stopping.
Staring at the center of the windshield and relying on peripheral vision to detect motion.
A series of short, regularly spaced eye movements, each about 10 degrees, pausing about 1 second on each area.
explanation: The eyes can only focus and detect small targets when they stop, so the AIM recommends brief stops on sectors no wider than about 10 degrees, each viewed at least 1 second. A continuous sweep never lets the eye focus. Peripheral vision is good at detecting motion, but a target on a collision course shows no relative motion.

stem: Another aircraft is on a collision course with yours. How will it most likely appear?
options: It will show little or no movement across the windshield while growing larger.
It will move rapidly across the windshield.
It will appear to drift steadily toward the horizon.
explanation: An aircraft on a collision course stays at a constant bearing, so it seems motionless in the windshield and then blossoms in size just before impact. That lack of movement is why it is so hard to see. Traffic that moves across the windshield is not on a collision course.

stem: You are holding short of the runway, ready for departure at a nontowered airport, and see an airplane on short final. What should you do?
options: Take the runway, because aircraft on the surface have the right of way.
Depart immediately if you can be airborne before the other airplane touches down.
Wait for the landing airplane, because aircraft landing have the right of way over aircraft on the surface.
explanation: Aircraft on final approach and landing have the right of way over other aircraft in flight or on the surface. Pulling onto the runway or racing the landing airplane creates a runway incursion risk. Announce your intentions on the CTAF and take the runway only after the landing traffic is clear.

stem: ATC reports traffic at 12 o'clock. You are holding a 20 degree crab to the right to correct for a crosswind. Where should you look?
options: Slightly left of the nose, because traffic calls are based on the ground track.
Directly over the nose.
Slightly right of the nose, toward the crab direction.
explanation: Controllers give traffic positions in clock terms relative to the aircraft's ground track as seen on radar, not its heading. With the nose crabbed 20 degrees right of the track, a target at 12 o'clock on the track appears about 20 degrees left of the nose. Looking straight ahead or to the right misses it.

stem: (Refer to Figure 77.) Which remark at Pierre Regional most directly affects how a pilot should manage collision avoidance in the pattern?
options: Numerous nonradio aircraft operate in the area, and there is no line of sight between the ends of Runway 07-25.
Runway 07-25 has a 0.6 percent upward slope to the west.
Taxiway C is restricted to aircraft of 75,000 pounds or less.
explanation: Nonradio aircraft will not announce themselves on the CTAF, so radio calls cannot be relied on to build a traffic picture, and the lack of line of sight means an aircraft at the far end of Runway 07-25 may be hidden. Both demand a vigorous visual scan. The runway slope and the taxiway weight limit matter for performance and ground operations, not for seeing traffic.

stem: (Refer to Figure 31 and Legend 5.) Which grade of aviation gasoline is listed at Coeur d'Alene?
options: Grade 100LL, which is dyed blue.
Grade 80, which is dyed red.
Grade 100, which is dyed green.
explanation: The fuel entry reads 100, JET A. The legend shows that 100 is grade 100 gasoline, colored green, while 100LL is the low lead blue grade. Read the code carefully rather than assuming 100LL is available.

stem: (Refer to Figure 31 and Legend 4.) In July, during what local time is Coeur d'Alene attended on weekdays?
options: 0800 to 1800 local.
0600 to 1600 local.
0700 to 1700 local.
explanation: The remarks list Attended Mon to Fri 1500 to 0100Z with the double dagger. The double dagger means hours are one hour earlier during daylight saving time, so in July the hours are 1400 to 0000Z. Local daylight time is UTC minus 7, giving 0700 to 1700. Forgetting the double dagger adjustment gives 0800 to 1800.

stem: (Refer to Figure 31 and Legend 9.) What visual glide slope indicator serves Runway 23 at Coeur d'Alene?
options: A four box VASI on the left side of the runway, set to a 3.0 degree glide path.
A two light PAPI on the left side of the runway, set to a 3.0 degree glide path.
A four light PAPI on the right side of the runway, set to a 3.0 degree glide path.
explanation: The Runway 23 line reads PAPI(P4R), GA 3.0 degrees, TCH 50 feet. The legend defines P4R as four identical light units on the right side of the runway. A two light PAPI on the left (P2L) serves Runways 01 and 19, which is the tempting mix up.

stem: (Refer to Figure 52 and Legend 9.) What is the landing distance available on Runway 14 at Lincoln, and why does it differ from the takeoff run available?
options: 8,649 feet, because displaced thresholds do not affect landing distance.
7,816 feet, because the Runway 32 threshold is displaced 470 feet.
8,286 feet, because the Runway 14 threshold is displaced 363 feet.
explanation: The declared distances list Runway 14 LDA as 8,286 feet against a TORA of 8,649 feet. The difference, 8,649 minus 8,286, equals 363 feet, the displaced threshold on Runway 14, since touchdown is not allowed before a displaced threshold. The 7,816 foot figure is the LDA for Runway 32, not Runway 14.

stem: (Refer to Figure 52 and Legend 15.) At 0700Z in February, what class of airspace surrounds Lincoln at the surface?
options: Class E.
Class C.
Class D.
explanation: The entry reads Class C svc 1130 to 0600Z with the double dagger, contact approach, other times Class E. In February, standard time applies, so Class C ends at 0600Z and the airspace is Class E at 0700Z. The tower also closes at 0600Z, so Class D is not an option.

stem: (Refer to Figure 63 and Legend 6.) The LRA in the Toledo Express entry means that pilots arriving from outside the United States must
options: give at least one hour advance notice, but need no permission to land.
apply in advance to U.S. Customs for permission to land and give at least one hour advance notice of arrival.
have prior permission from the airport manager because the airport is private.
explanation: LRA means landing rights airport, where permission to land must be requested in advance from U.S. Customs, with at least one hour advance notice of arrival. An airport of entry (AOE) requires only the advance notice, not permission, which is the tempting confusion. LRA has nothing to do with private ownership.

stem: (Refer to Figure 79 and Legend 4.) During daylight saving time, what are the operating hours of Sioux City Tower in UTC?
explanation: The tower is listed as 1200 to 0330Z with a double dagger. The legend says the double dagger means effective hours are one hour earlier during daylight saving time, so the tower operates 1100 to 0230Z in summer. Reading the printed times without the adjustment is the trap, and adding an hour moves the wrong way.

stem: (Refer to Figure 79.) What does the Sioux Gateway entry say about the portion of Taxiway A southeast of Taxiway B?
options: It is unlit and marked with retroreflective markers.
It is not visible from the tower and is designated a nonmovement area.
It is closed to aircraft over 75,000 pounds.
explanation: The remarks state that portions of Twy A southeast of Twy B are not visible from the tower and are designated a nonmovement area, so the tower does not control traffic there and pilots must watch carefully for other aircraft and vehicles. The unlit taxiway with retroreflective markers is Taxiway F. The weight limit belongs to a different airport.

stem: (Refer to Figure 81.) What does the Crawford entry say about fuel?
options: 100LL and Jet A are available during attended hours.
100LL is available for emergency use only.
No fuel of any kind is available.
explanation: The remarks state 100LL fuel avbl for emergency use only, and no fuel line appears in the header data. A pilot should not plan to refuel at Crawford except in an emergency. Read the remarks as well as the header line, since key limitations often appear only there.

stem: (Refer to Figure 52.) A pilot is inbound to Loup City Municipal. What radio procedure applies?
options: Request an airport advisory from Loup City UNICOM on 122.9.
Contact Lincoln Approach on 124.0 for landing clearance.
Self announce position and intentions on 122.9, since no tower, FSS, or UNICOM serves the airport.
explanation: Loup City is unattended and lists only CTAF 122.9, which is the MULTICOM frequency used when an airport has no tower, no FSS, and no UNICOM. Pilots self announce, and no ground station will answer. Calling UNICOM on 122.9 assumes a service that is not listed, and no landing clearance exists at a nontowered airport.

stem: (Refer to Figure 52.) Near Lincoln, a pilot has an emergency and plans to call for help. What does the Lincoln entry imply about 121.5 MHz?
options: Lincoln Tower does not have 121.5, so the pilot should call the tower or approach control on a published frequency such as 118.5 or 124.0.
Lincoln Tower guards 121.5 continuously, so the pilot should transmit there first.
121.5 is unavailable in the Lincoln area, so the pilot should squawk 7600 instead.
explanation: The Comm/Nav/Weather remarks say Emerg frequency 121.5 not available at twr, so a call to Lincoln Tower on 121.5 will not be heard. The fastest help comes from a frequency the facility actually monitors, such as tower 118.5 or approach 124.0, while squawking 7700. Code 7600 signals radio failure, not an emergency, and other facilities may still monitor 121.5.

stem: (Refer to Figure 31 and Legend 9.) Arriving at Coeur d'Alene at night with no one on duty, how does a pilot turn on the HIRL for Runway 05-23 and the MALSR for Runway 05?
options: Key the microphone seven times within 5 seconds on the CTAF, 122.8.
Key the microphone seven times within 5 seconds on the AWOS frequency, 135.075.
Ask Spokane Approach on 132.1 to turn them on.
explanation: The airport remarks say ACTIVATE MIRL Rwy 01-19, HIRL Rwy 05-23, REIL Rwy 01 and Rwy 23, MALSR Rwy 05 on the CTAF, which is 122.8, and the PAPIs operate continuously. Seven clicks in 5 seconds gives the highest intensity. The AWOS frequency only broadcasts weather, and approach control has no means to switch the lights.

stem: (Refer to Figure 65.) Sign D, a white circle with a horizontal bar on a red background, means
options: stop and hold for a clearance before continuing.
aircraft entry into the area is prohibited.
the area beyond is a nonmovement area where ATC clearance is not required.
explanation: The no entry sign is a mandatory instruction sign that prohibits aircraft from entering an area, often a one way taxiway or a road leading off the airfield. It is not a hold position you may cross with a clearance, which is the meaning of the runway holding position signs. Nonmovement areas are marked with a painted boundary, not this sign.

stem: A pilot breathing carbon monoxide from a cracked heater muff is suffering mainly from which type of hypoxia?
options: Hypemic hypoxia.
Histotoxic hypoxia.
Hypoxic hypoxia.
explanation: Carbon monoxide attaches to hemoglobin far more readily than oxygen does, so the blood cannot carry enough oxygen even though the air itself is normal. A shortage of oxygen carrying capacity in the blood is hypemic (anemic) hypoxia. Histotoxic hypoxia is the cells failing to use oxygen, and hypoxic hypoxia is low oxygen pressure at altitude.

stem: Which type of hypoxia results when alcohol or certain drugs keep the body's cells from using the oxygen that the blood delivers?
options: Stagnant hypoxia.
Hypoxic hypoxia.
Histotoxic hypoxia.
explanation: Histotoxic means poisoned tissue: the blood may be fully loaded with oxygen, but the cells cannot use it, and alcohol and some drugs cause exactly that. Stagnant hypoxia is a circulation problem, not a cell problem. Hypoxic hypoxia comes from reduced oxygen pressure at altitude.

stem: During aggressive maneuvering a pilot pulls several G, blood pools in the lower body, and the brain is briefly starved of oxygen. This is an example of
options: hypemic hypoxia.
stagnant hypoxia.
hypoxic hypoxia.
explanation: Stagnant hypoxia occurs when the blood is not flowing well enough to deliver oxygen, as with excessive G loads, shock, or very cold extremities. The blood itself is normal, so it is not hypemic hypoxia, which is a reduced carrying capacity such as from carbon monoxide or recent blood donation.

stem: According to the AIM, for the best protection against hypoxia pilots are encouraged to use supplemental oxygen above which cabin pressure altitudes?
options: 12,500 feet during the day and 10,000 feet at night.
14,000 feet during the day and 12,500 feet at night.
10,000 feet during the day and 5,000 feet at night.
explanation: The AIM recommends supplemental oxygen above 10,000 feet in the daytime and above 5,000 feet at night, because night vision begins to deteriorate at altitudes as low as 5,000 feet. The 12,500 foot figure is the regulatory threshold in 14 CFR 91.211 for required crew oxygen, which is a legal minimum, not the AIM recommendation.

stem: At 16,000 feet MSL using supplemental oxygen, you feel lightheaded and notice tingling in your fingers while dealing with a stressful situation. What should you do first?
options: Assume it is hyperventilation and breathe into a paper bag before checking anything else.
Verify that the oxygen system is working and delivering oxygen, then deliberately slow your rate and depth of breathing.
Remove the oxygen mask so you can breathe more freely and restore carbon dioxide.
explanation: The early symptoms of hyperventilation and hypoxia are similar and the two can happen together, so the AIM says a pilot on oxygen should first make sure the oxygen system is working before turning attention to breathing rate. The paper bag answer is the trap: treating only hyperventilation could leave a real hypoxia problem unsolved at 16,000 feet.

stem: Why are middle ear problems more likely during a descent than during a climb?
options: The Eustachian tube lets air escape from the middle ear easily but resists air flowing back in as outside pressure increases.
Pressure in the middle ear rises during descent and pushes the eardrum outward.
The sinuses drain into the middle ear only when outside pressure is decreasing.
explanation: In a climb, higher pressure air in the middle ear vents out through the Eustachian tube without effort. In a descent, outside pressure rises and air must flow back in, which the tube resists, especially if swollen by a cold, so the eardrum is pushed inward and painful. The second option reverses the pressure difference. Swallowing, yawning, or the Valsalva maneuver helps equalize.

stem: You made a scuba dive this morning that required a controlled ascent with decompression stops. Per the AIM, how long should you wait before flying a local flight planned at 3,500 feet MSL?
options: 12 hours, because the flight will stay below 8,000 feet MSL.
4 hours, as long as no symptoms appear.
24 hours, regardless of the planned altitude.
explanation: The AIM recommends waiting at least 24 hours after any dive that required a controlled ascent, no matter how low the flight will be. The 12 hour figure applies only to dives that did not require a controlled ascent and flights up to 8,000 feet MSL, which is the trap here.

stem: Your passenger made a recreational dive that did not require a controlled ascent, surfacing at 1600 yesterday. You plan to depart at 1000 today and cruise at 9,500 feet MSL. Following the AIM guidance, what should you do?
options: Take her as planned, because more than 12 hours have passed since the dive.
Delay until at least 1600 today, 24 hours after the dive, or plan a cruise altitude at or below 8,000 feet MSL.
Take her as planned only if the airplane carries supplemental oxygen for her.
explanation: Only 18 hours will have passed by 1000. For dives without a controlled ascent, the AIM calls for 12 hours before flying up to 8,000 feet MSL but 24 hours before flying above 8,000 feet. A 9,500 foot cruise therefore needs a 1600 departure, or the flight can stay at or below 8,000 feet. Supplemental oxygen does not prevent decompression sickness from the nitrogen already dissolved in her blood.

stem: On a winter flight with the cabin heater on, you develop a headache and become drowsy and dizzy. What is the best course of action?
options: Turn off the cabin heat, open the fresh air vents, use supplemental oxygen if available, and land as soon as practical.
Increase cabin heat, since being cold is the most likely cause of drowsiness.
Climb to a higher altitude where the outside air is cleaner.
explanation: Headache, drowsiness, and dizziness with the heater on point to carbon monoxide leaking through the heater muff. AIM 8-1-4 says to suspect carbon monoxide, immediately shut off the heater, and open the air vents; using supplemental oxygen if it is available and landing as soon as practical complete the response. Climbing makes it worse, because susceptibility to carbon monoxide increases with altitude. Increasing the heat increases the exposure.

stem: A pilot took an over the counter antihistamine for allergies this morning and plans to fly this afternoon. Which statement best reflects FAA guidance?
options: Over the counter medications are acceptable because they do not need a prescription.
Many over the counter medications, including antihistamines, can cause drowsiness and impair judgment; the safest rule is not to fly while taking a medication unless the FAA has approved it.
Antihistamines are acceptable as long as eight hours pass between the dose and the flight.
explanation: The AIM warns that both prescription and over the counter drugs, and the conditions they treat, can seriously degrade pilot performance; antihistamines and cold remedies commonly cause drowsiness. The safest rule is not to fly on any medication unless approved by the FAA. The eight hour option borrows the alcohol rule of 14 CFR 91.17, which does not make a sedating drug safe.

stem: Which statement best describes chronic stress?
options: The immediate fight or flight response to a sudden threat, such as an engine running rough.
The normal alertness a pilot feels before a checkride.
A level of ongoing stress that exceeds a person's ability to cope, which should keep the pilot from flying until it is resolved.
explanation: Chronic stress builds from continuing pressures such as work, finances, or family problems and overwhelms a person's coping ability, causing performance to fall off sharply. A pilot under chronic stress should not fly. The first option describes acute stress, which is a short term reaction to an immediate threat.

stem: After a week of poor sleep and long workdays, a pilot feels a constant tiredness that one good night of sleep did not fix. This is best described as
options: chronic fatigue, which usually needs prolonged rest, may need medical attention, and is a reason not to fly.
acute fatigue, which a short nap before the flight will cure.
mild hypoxia, which supplemental oxygen will correct.
explanation: Fatigue that accumulates over days and is not relieved by normal rest is chronic fatigue. It degrades judgment and reaction time and needs prolonged rest to resolve. Acute fatigue is the short term tiredness from a single long day or flight and is normally relieved by adequate sleep.

stem: On a long summer cross country a pilot who has not been drinking water begins to feel tired and develops a headache and leg cramps. These are early signs of
options: hypothermia.
hyperventilation.
dehydration.
explanation: Fatigue is usually the first noticeable effect of dehydration, followed by headache, cramps, sleepiness, and dizziness. Hot cockpits and dry air at altitude speed fluid loss, so pilots should drink water regularly rather than waiting to feel thirsty.

stem: A passenger becomes airsick in moderate turbulence. Which action is most appropriate?
options: Open the fresh air vents, have the passenger look at a point on the outside horizon, avoid unnecessary head movement, and land if the symptoms persist.
Have the passenger look down at a chart or phone to take their mind off the motion.
Close the vents and turn up the cabin heat to keep the passenger comfortable.
explanation: Motion sickness comes from conflicting signals between the inner ear and the eyes. Fresh air, an outside visual reference, minimal head movement, and getting on the ground help. Looking down at a chart or a phone removes the outside reference and usually makes it worse, and a warm, stuffy cabin aggravates nausea.

stem: After a forced landing in cold, wet, windy mountain terrain, which threat to survival usually needs attention first?
options: Dehydration, so all effort should go to finding water before anything else.
Loss of body heat leading to hypothermia, so shelter, dry insulating clothing, and protection from wind come first.
Hunger, so finding food should be the first task.
explanation: In cold, wet, windy conditions the body loses heat quickly, and hypothermia causes shivering, confusion, and poor judgment within hours. Shelter and dry insulation come first. People can survive days without water and much longer without food, which is why the ACS asks pilots to carry gear such as water, clothing, and shelter for 48 to 72 hours.

stem: Before a planned flight, a pilot is getting over a stomach virus, slept five hours, and is upset after an argument at home. Using the IMSAFE checklist, what is the best conclusion?
options: Only the illness item matters, and since the fever has passed the pilot is fit to fly.
IMSAFE applies only to alcohol and medications, so the pilot is fit to fly.
Several IMSAFE items are compromised at once, and together they are a strong reason not to fly as pilot in command today.
explanation: IMSAFE covers Illness, Medication, Stress, Alcohol, Fatigue, and Emotion. This pilot has recent illness, poor sleep, and emotional upset, and the effects add up. The trap is checking each item alone and deciding none is bad enough; the honest self assessment looks at the combined picture.

stem: Climbing through 12,000 feet MSL on a night flight without oxygen, a pilot feels unusually relaxed and confident and notices the instruments seem dim. What is most likely happening?
options: Hyperventilation from anxiety, which slower breathing will correct.
Early hypoxia; euphoria and reduced night vision are classic early signs, so descend or use oxygen.
Normal dark adaptation, which will improve with more time.
explanation: A false sense of well being and degraded vision are early hypoxia symptoms, and night vision begins to suffer at altitudes as low as 5,000 feet. Hypoxia is dangerous because the person affected rarely recognizes it. Hyperventilation is unlikely in a relaxed, confident pilot, and dark adaptation does not make instruments look dimmer.

stem: In the clouds, a pilot slowly drifts into a gentle left bank without noticing. Seeing the attitude indicator, the pilot abruptly levels the wings and now feels banked to the right. This illusion is
options: the leans.
the Coriolis illusion.
the inversion illusion.
explanation: A bank entered too slowly to stimulate the inner ear goes unnoticed, so an abrupt correction to level feels like a bank in the opposite direction. That is the leans, and the pilot may roll back into the original bank or lean in the seat. Coriolis needs an abrupt head movement during a prolonged turn.

stem: Which illusion is caused by an abrupt head movement, such as looking down for a chart, during a prolonged constant rate turn, and produces a strong sense of rotation in an entirely different axis?
options: The graveyard spiral.
The Coriolis illusion.
The elevator illusion.
explanation: Once the fluid in a semicircular canal stops moving in a prolonged turn, an abrupt head movement sets fluid moving in a different canal and creates a strong sensation of rotation in an entirely different axis. The graveyard spiral is also a prolonged turn problem, but it involves noticing altitude loss and pulling back, not a head movement.

stem: In a prolonged, coordinated, constant rate turn in IMC, the pilot's inner ear stops sensing the turn and the pilot feels wings level. Noticing the altitude loss, the pilot pulls back on the yoke without leveling the wings. What is the result?
options: The airplane returns to level flight, because back pressure always stops a descent.
The airplane pitches down because of the inversion illusion.
The turn tightens and the descent rate increases, which is the graveyard spiral.
explanation: In a bank, back pressure mostly tightens the turn rather than raising the nose, so the airplane spirals down faster and the pilot pulls harder. The fix is to level the wings first using the attitude indicator, then raise the nose. The first option is the trap: back pressure only stops a descent when the wings are level.

stem: On a night takeoff over a dark area, rapid acceleration gives the pilot a strong feeling that the nose is pitching up. What is the danger if the pilot pushes the nose down in response?
options: Flying into the ground, because this is the somatogravic illusion and the airplane is not actually nose high.
A stall, because the nose really is too high.
The leans, because acceleration affects only the sense of roll.
explanation: Rapid forward acceleration pushes the inner ear's otolith organs the same way a nose up tilt does, creating the somatogravic illusion. With no visual horizon, a pilot who pushes over can fly into the terrain. The defense is to hold the climb attitude shown on the attitude indicator.

stem: An abrupt upward vertical acceleration, as from a strong updraft, can create the illusion of
options: being in a descent, so the pilot tends to pull the nose up.
being in a climb, so the pilot tends to push the nose down.
turning, so the pilot tends to roll the opposite way.
explanation: This is the elevator illusion: an updraft feels like a climb and invites a nose low correction, while a downdraft feels like a descent and invites a nose up correction. Holding the attitude shown on the instruments, rather than chasing altitude with pitch, avoids the problem.

stem: An abrupt change from a climb to straight and level flight can create the illusion of
options: banking to the left.
descending with the wings level.
tumbling backward.
explanation: This is the inversion illusion. The sudden change from climb to level stimulates the otolith organs and produces a sensation of tumbling backward, and the pilot may push the nose down abruptly, which can make the illusion worse.

stem: You normally fly from a 150 foot wide runway. Arriving at an unfamiliar airport whose runway is only 60 feet wide, which tendency should you guard against?
options: Flying a higher than normal approach, because the narrow runway makes you feel lower than you are.
Flying a lower than normal approach, because the narrow runway makes you feel higher than you are.
Flaring too high, because the narrow runway makes you feel closer to the ground than you are.
explanation: A runway narrower than the one you are used to looks like a normal runway seen from farther up, so you feel high and tend to descend too low on approach. The first option describes the effect of a runway wider than you are used to. A VASI or PAPI, if available, gives an objective glidepath check.

stem: An upsloping runway, upsloping terrain, or both, can create the illusion that the airplane is
options: lower than it actually is, so the pilot tends to fly a higher approach.
closer to the runway than it actually is, so the pilot tends to land long.
higher than it actually is, so the pilot tends to fly a lower approach.
explanation: An upsloping runway shows more of its surface, which looks like the view from a steeper, higher approach, so the pilot feels high and descends too low. A downsloping runway has the opposite effect and tends to produce a high approach.

stem: Which pair of conditions both tend to make you feel lower than you are, and so lead you to fly a higher than normal approach?
options: A runway wider than you are used to, and a downsloping runway.
Rain on the windshield, and an approach over featureless water.
Atmospheric haze, and a runway narrower than you are used to.
explanation: A wide runway and a downsloping runway both make you feel lower than you are, which leads to a high approach and possibly leveling off high or overshooting. Every other condition listed (rain on the windshield, featureless terrain or water, haze, a narrow runway) makes you feel higher than you are and leads to a dangerously low approach.

stem: Atmospheric haze on approach tends to make the runway appear
options: closer, so the pilot may fly a higher approach.
brighter and wider, so the pilot may flare early.
farther away, so the pilot may fly a lower approach.
explanation: Haze makes the runway seem farther away and the airplane higher than it really is, so the pilot tends to fly a low approach. Rain on the windshield and featureless terrain push you the same way, which is why low approaches are the common danger in poor visibility.

stem: Why is off center viewing recommended when looking for a dim object at night?
options: The center of the retina is made up of cones, which work poorly in dim light, while the rods that see in dim light lie away from the center.
The rods are concentrated in the center of the retina, so looking slightly away sharpens color vision.
Off center viewing reduces glare from the panel lights reflecting in the windshield.
explanation: The fovea at the center of the retina contains only cones, which need good light, so there is a night blind spot straight ahead. Rods, which are sensitive in dim light, are concentrated around the fovea. Looking about 5 to 10 degrees to one side of the object puts the image on the rods.

stem: You are about to depart at night from a brightly lit ramp. Which statement about dark adaptation is correct?
options: Full dark adaptation takes about 5 minutes, and only red light can undo it.
Full dark adaptation takes about 30 minutes, and even a brief look at a bright light can largely undo it.
Full dark adaptation takes about 2 hours, but once achieved it cannot be lost during the flight.
explanation: It takes about 30 minutes in darkness for the eyes to adapt fully, and the AIM notes that any degree of dark adaptation is lost within a few seconds of viewing a bright light. Closing one eye when exposed to a bright light preserves some night vision in that eye. Smoking, altitude above 5,000 feet, and poor diet also impair it.

stem: On a dark night with nothing to look at outside, a pilot's eyes relax and focus only a short distance ahead, so distant traffic may go unseen. What is this condition?
options: Autokinesis.
Empty field myopia.
Hypoxia from the cabin altitude.
explanation: With no features to focus on, as at night, in haze, or above a cloud deck, the eyes tend to focus at a short distance; this is empty field myopia. The countermeasure is to deliberately focus on a distant object, such as a ground light or a star, and keep scanning. Autokinesis is the apparent motion of a stationary light that is stared at.

stem: Staring at a single stationary light against a dark background for several seconds can make the light appear to move. This illusion is
options: the false horizon.
the elevator illusion.
autokinesis.
explanation: Autokinesis makes a fixed light appear to drift after a few seconds of staring, and a pilot may try to align the airplane with it and lose control. The remedy is to keep the eyes moving with a normal scan and cross check the instruments rather than fixating on one light.

stem: On a dark night over sparsely lit terrain, a pilot sees a line of lights along a sloping shoreline and unconsciously banks to align the wings with it. Which illusion is this, and what is the best defense?
options: The false horizon; cross check the attitude indicator to confirm the real horizon.
The leans; lean in the seat until the sensation passes.
Water refraction; fly a slightly steeper approach.
explanation: Sloping clouds, an obscured horizon, ground lights mixed with stars, and geometric patterns of lights can all be mistaken for the horizon. The false horizon illusion leads the pilot to bank or pitch to match it. The attitude indicator gives the true reference. The leans is a vestibular illusion, not a visual one.

stem: Under 14 CFR 91.205, which items are required for VFR flight at night in addition to the day VFR equipment, for an airplane not operated for hire?
options: A landing light, a heated pitot tube, and an attitude indicator.
Approved position lights, an approved anticollision light system, an adequate source of electrical energy, and a set of spare fuses accessible in flight if fuses are used.
Approved position lights and a landing light, with no anticollision light needed for airplanes certificated before 1996.
explanation: Night VFR adds position lights, an anticollision light system, an adequate electrical source, and spare fuses (one spare set, or three of each kind) if the airplane uses fuses. A landing light is required only when the airplane is operated for hire. The 1996 date applies to the day VFR anticollision light rule, not to night flight.

stem: At night you see an airplane ahead and to your right at about your altitude. It shows a steady red light and a flashing white strobe, and its position on your windshield is not changing. What does this mean?
options: It is crossing from your right toward your left on a collision course; it is on your right, so it has the right of way and you must give way.
It is flying directly away from you, so no action is needed.
It is crossing from left to right, so you have the right of way and should hold your course.
explanation: The red light is on the left wingtip, so seeing only red means you are looking at its left side: it is moving from your right toward your left. A constant relative bearing means a collision course. Under 14 CFR 91.113(d), the aircraft on the right has the right of way, so you give way, normally by turning right behind it. An airplane flying away from you would show its white tail light.

stem: In the preceding 90 days your only night landings were three touch and go landings in your club's airplane, made about two hours after sunset. May you carry passengers in that airplane tonight two hours after sunset?
