stem: In the Northern Hemisphere, a magnetic compass will normally indicate initially a turn toward the east if
options: an aircraft is decelerated while on a south heading.
an aircraft is accelerated while on a north heading.
a left turn is entered from a north heading.
explanation: Turning error makes the compass lag on a north heading, so a left turn from north first shows a turn to the right, toward the east. Acceleration and deceleration errors appear only on east and west headings, so they produce no false turn on a north or south heading.

stem: In the Northern Hemisphere, a magnetic compass will normally indicate a turn toward the north if
options: a left turn is entered from a west heading.
an aircraft is decelerated while on an east or west heading.
an aircraft is accelerated while on an east or west heading.
explanation: Acceleration error on east or west headings follows ANDS: accelerate north, decelerate south. Accelerating on an east or west heading therefore indicates a turn toward north. Decelerating shows a turn toward south, and a left turn from a west heading actually turns the airplane toward south, not north.

stem: In the Northern Hemisphere, the magnetic compass will normally indicate a turn toward the south when
options: a left turn is entered from an east heading.
a right turn is entered from a west heading.
the aircraft is decelerated while on a west heading.
explanation: By ANDS, decelerating on an east or west heading makes the compass show a turn toward south, so decelerating on a west heading fits. Turns entered from east or west headings produce little turning error and the compass tracks the turn, so a left turn from east shows north and a right turn from west shows north as well.

stem: In the Northern Hemisphere, if an aircraft is accelerated or decelerated, the magnetic compass will normally indicate
options: a turn momentarily.
correctly when on a north or south heading.
a turn toward the south.
explanation: Acceleration error appears only on east and west headings. On north or south headings the compass reads correctly while speed changes. It is not always a momentary turn, and the direction of any error depends on accelerating versus decelerating, so it is not always toward south.

stem: During flight, when are the indications of a magnetic compass accurate?
options: Only in straight-and-level unaccelerated flight.
As long as the airspeed is constant.
During turns if the bank does not exceed 18°.
explanation: The compass card is pulled by the dip of the earth's field whenever the airplane turns, accelerates, or decelerates, so it is reliable only in straight and level, unaccelerated flight. Constant airspeed alone does not prevent turning error, and the 18 degree figure has no meaning here.

stem: If a pilot changes the altimeter setting from 30.11 to 29.96, what is the approximate change in indication?
options: Altimeter will indicate .15 inches Hg higher.
Altimeter will indicate 150 feet higher.
Altimeter will indicate 150 feet lower.
explanation: Lowering the setting from 30.11 to 29.96 is a change of 0.15 inch, and at about 1,000 feet per inch the needle drops roughly 150 feet. The window itself moved 0.15 inch, but the question asks about the altitude indication, so 150 feet lower is right and 150 feet higher reverses the direction.

stem: If a flight is made from an area of low pressure into an area of high pressure without the altimeter setting being adjusted, the altimeter will indicate
options: the actual altitude above sea level.
higher than the actual altitude above sea level.
lower than the actual altitude above sea level.
explanation: Flying into higher pressure with the old setting, the altimeter senses more pressure and thinks the airplane descended, so it reads lower than the actual altitude. The error is on the safe side, since the airplane is higher than shown. The dangerous case is high to low, where the airplane is lower than indicated.

stem: If a flight is made from an area of high pressure into an area of lower pressure without the altimeter setting being adjusted, the altimeter will indicate
options: lower than the actual altitude above sea level.
higher than the actual altitude above sea level.
the actual altitude above sea level.
explanation: Moving into lower pressure with the old setting, the altimeter sees less pressure and reads higher than the airplane really is. This is the classic "high to low, look out below" trap where the airplane may be closer to terrain than indicated.

stem: Under what condition will true altitude be lower than indicated altitude?
options: In colder than standard air temperature.
In warmer than standard air temperature.
When density altitude is higher than indicated altitude.
explanation: Cold air is denser, so pressure levels sit lower than in standard air. An altimeter calibrated for standard temperature then reads high, so true altitude is lower than indicated. Warm air does the opposite, and density altitude has nothing to do with true versus indicated altitude.

stem: Which condition would cause the altimeter to indicate a lower altitude than true altitude?
options: Air temperature lower than standard.
Atmospheric pressure lower than standard.
Air temperature warmer than standard.
explanation: In warmer than standard air the pressure levels are raised, so the airplane is higher than the altimeter shows; the indication is lower than true altitude. Cold air makes the altimeter read higher than true. Lower than standard pressure is corrected by the altimeter setting, not a temperature error.

stem: What should be the indication on the magnetic compass as you roll into a standard rate turn to the right from a south heading in the Northern Hemisphere?
options: The compass will initially indicate a turn to the left.
The compass will indicate a turn to the right, but at a faster rate than is actually occurring.
The compass will remain on south for a short time, then gradually catch up to the magnetic heading of the airplane.
explanation: On a south heading the compass leads the turn, so rolling into a right turn it swings in the correct direction but faster than the airplane is actually turning. Lagging, or remaining on the heading before catching up, describes turns from a north heading.

stem: What is an advantage of an attitude indicator that is displayed digitally?
options: It is more sensitive than the analog instrument.
The indicator can be moved to any place around the PFD.
The horizon line extends all the way to the edges of the PFD.
explanation: On a primary flight display the artificial horizon fills the whole screen, so the horizon line runs to the edges and gives a large, easy picture of pitch and bank. It is not inherently more sensitive than an analog gyro, and it stays fixed in the center of the PFD rather than being movable.
ref: FAA Advanced Avionics Handbook Ch. 2; PHAK Ch. 8

stem: The Air Data Computer or ADC
options: gathers pressure information from spinning gyros.
combines data from the pitot-static sensors and temperature sensors.
receives input from the airspeed and altitude indicators.
explanation: An air data computer takes pitot pressure, static pressure, and outside air temperature from sensors and computes airspeed, altitude, vertical speed, and true airspeed for the displays. It does not use spinning gyros, which feed attitude information, and it replaces the mechanical airspeed indicator and altimeter rather than receiving input from them.
ref: PHAK Ch. 8; FAA Advanced Avionics Handbook Ch. 2

stem: Glass cockpit aircraft refer to
options: those with GPS with moving map display and an autopilot.
generally an aircraft with digital instrumentation exclusively.
aircraft with both digital and limited number of analog instruments.
explanation: The FAA describes glass cockpit aircraft as having electronic primary displays, typically a PFD and MFD, while still carrying a small number of backup analog instruments such as an airspeed indicator, altimeter, and attitude indicator. A moving map GPS and autopilot alone do not make a glass cockpit. Saying the aircraft is exclusively digital is the tempting choice; some newer panels do use an electronic standby, so usage varies, but the answer the FAA scores is the mixed panel.
ref: FAA Advanced Avionics Handbook Ch. 1; PHAK Ch. 8

stem: A certified aircraft mechanic must inspect and adjust some aircraft instruments periodically. Which flight instrument can the pilot adjust?
options: Airspeed indicator.
Mechanical VSI.
Wet compass.
explanation: Many mechanical vertical speed indicators have a zero adjustment screw that lets the pilot set the needle to zero on the ground, which is the answer the FAA scores. Airspeed indicators and the wet compass are adjusted or swung only by maintenance personnel. Some argue that even the VSI screw is maintenance, so check your airplane's procedures before touching it.

stem: (Refer to Figure 20, area 3.) Determine the approximate latitude and longitude of Currituck County Airport.
explanation: Currituck County Regional (ONX) sits just south of the 36 degree 30 minute latitude tick line on the chart, about 6 minutes below it, giving 36 degrees 24 minutes N and about 76 degrees 01 minute W. The 36 degrees 48 minutes choice would put it up near Norfolk, just south of the 37 degree line, and 47 degrees N is nowhere on this chart.
ref: PHAK Ch. 16; Aeronautical Chart User's Guide; Figure 20

stem: (Refer to Figure 21, area 2.) Which airport is located at approximately 47°34'30"N latitude and 100°44'00"W longitude?
options: Turtle Lake.
Makeeff.
Johnson.
explanation: Measuring from the 48 degree and 101 degree grid lines, a point 25.5 minutes south of 48 N and 16 minutes east of 101 W lands on the Makeeff private strip in area 2. Turtle Lake is near 47 degrees 31 minutes N and 100 degrees 53 minutes W, too far south and west, and Johnson lies farther south and west still.
ref: PHAK Ch. 16; Aeronautical Chart User's Guide; Figure 21

stem: (Refer to Figure 21, area 3.) Which airport is located at approximately 47°21'N latitude and 101°01'W longitude?
options: Underwood.
Evenson.
Washburn.
explanation: Washburn (5C8), just north of the town of Washburn in area 3, lies about 39 minutes south of the 48 degree line and about a minute west of the 101 degree meridian, which matches 47 degrees 21 minutes N, 101 degrees 01 minute W. Underwood is a town farther north, not an airport at those coordinates.
ref: PHAK Ch. 16; Aeronautical Chart User's Guide; Figure 21

stem: (Refer to Figure 22, area 3.) Determine the approximate latitude and longitude of Shoshone County Airport.
explanation: Shoshone County (S83) near Kellogg in area 3 sits just north of the 47 degree 30 minute line at about 47 degrees 33 minutes N and about 116 degrees 11 minutes W. The 47 degrees 32 minutes N, 116 degrees 41 minutes W choice lies 30 minutes farther west, near Coeur d'Alene, and 47 degrees 02 minutes is far too far south.
ref: PHAK Ch. 16; Aeronautical Chart User's Guide; Figure 22

stem: (Refer to Figure 26, area 2.) What is the approximate latitude and longitude of Cooperstown Airport?
explanation: Cooperstown (S32) in area 2 is about 25 minutes north of the 47 degree line shown near Jamestown, and about 98 degrees 06 minutes W. The 99 degrees 54 minutes W choice puts it west of the 99 degree meridian, far past Jamestown, and 47 degrees 55 minutes N would lie north of the top edge of this excerpt.
ref: PHAK Ch. 16; Aeronautical Chart User's Guide; Figure 26

stem: (Refer to Figure 27.) An aircraft departs an airport in the eastern daylight time zone at 0945 EDT for a 2-hour flight to an airport located in the central daylight time zone. The landing should be at what coordinated universal time?
explanation: Departure 0945 EDT plus 2 hours is 1145 EDT. EDT converts to UTC by adding 4 hours, so 1145 + 4 = 1545Z. The destination time zone does not matter once you work in UTC. Adding the offset to the departure time and forgetting the 2 hour flight gives the 1345Z and 1445Z traps.

stem: (Refer to Figure 27.) An aircraft departs an airport in the central standard time zone at 0930 CST for a 2-hour flight to an airport located in the mountain standard time zone. The landing should be at what time?
explanation: Departure 0930 CST plus 2 hours is 1130 CST. Mountain time is one hour behind central, so landing is 1030 MST. Forgetting the zone change gives 1130, and 0930 simply repeats the departure clock time.

stem: (Refer to Figure 27.) An aircraft departs an airport in the central standard time zone at 0845 CST for a 2-hour flight to an airport located in the mountain standard time zone. The landing should be at what coordinated universal time?
explanation: Departure 0845 CST plus 2 hours is 1045 CST, and CST plus 6 hours is 1645Z. The 1445Z answer adds the 6 hour offset to departure without the flight time, and 1345Z adds the eastern standard offset of 5 hours to the departure time.

stem: (Refer to Figure 27.) An aircraft departs an airport in the mountain standard time zone at 1615 MST for a 2-hour 15-minute flight to an airport located in the Pacific standard time zone. The estimated time of arrival at the destination airport should be
explanation: Departure 1615 MST plus 2 hours 15 minutes is 1830 MST. Pacific time is one hour behind mountain time, so arrival is 1730 PST. The 1830 choice forgets the time zone change.

stem: (Refer to Figure 27.) An aircraft departs an airport in the Pacific standard time zone at 1030 PST for a 4-hour flight to an airport located in the central standard time zone. The landing should be at what coordinated universal time?
explanation: Departure 1030 PST plus 4 hours is 1430 PST, and PST plus 8 hours is 2230Z. The landing zone does not matter in UTC; using the central offset of 6 hours on 1430 would give 2030Z, the main trap.

stem: (Refer to Figure 27.) An aircraft departs an airport in the mountain standard time zone at 1515 MST for a 2-hour 30-minute flight to an airport located in the Pacific standard time zone. What is the estimated time of arrival at the destination airport?
explanation: Departure 1515 MST plus 2 hours 30 minutes is 1745 MST, which is 1645 PST because Pacific time is one hour behind. The 1745 choice forgets to change zones, and 1845 moves the clock the wrong way.

stem: (Refer to Figure 20, area 5.) The CAUTION box denotes what hazard to aircraft?
options: Unmarked balloon on cable to 3,008 feet MSL.
Unmarked balloon on cable to 3,008 feet AGL.
Unmarked blimp hangars at 300 feet MSL.
explanation: The caution box near area 5 reads UNMARKED BALLOON ON CABLE TO 3008' MSL. Like other heights in chart notes, the figure is above mean sea level unless shown in parentheses or marked AGL, so the AGL choice and the blimp hangar choice misread the note.
ref: PHAK Ch. 16; Aeronautical Chart User's Guide; Figure 20

stem: (Refer to Figure 20, area 2.) The flag symbol at Lake Drummond represents a
options: compulsory reporting point for Norfolk Class C airspace.
compulsory reporting point for Hampton Roads Airport.
visual checkpoint used to identify position for initial callup to Norfolk Approach Control.
explanation: A magenta flag marks a VFR visual checkpoint. Lake Drummond sits under the Norfolk approach area, and the flag is a place pilots report position on initial callup to Norfolk Approach. Flags are not compulsory reporting points; those are IFR symbols shown as triangles.
ref: PHAK Ch. 16; Aeronautical Chart User's Guide; Figure 20

stem: (Refer to Figure 20, area 2.) The elevation of the Chesapeake Regional Airport is
options: 19 feet.
36 feet.
360 feet.
explanation: The airport data for Chesapeake Regional (CPK) read 19 *L 55 123.075, and the first number is field elevation in feet MSL, so 19 feet. The 55 is the longest runway length in hundreds of feet, so 5,500 feet, and 36 or 360 come from misreading nearby numbers.
ref: PHAK Ch. 16; Aeronautical Chart User's Guide; Figure 20

stem: (Refer to Figure 21.) The terrain elevation of the light tan area between Minot (area 1) and Audubon Lake (area 2) varies from
options: sea level to 2,000 feet MSL.
2,000 feet to 2,500 feet MSL.
2,000 feet to 2,700 feet MSL.
explanation: The tint legend shows terrain from 2,000 to 3,000 feet in light tan, and the contour interval is 500 feet. No 2,500 foot contour appears in the tan area between Minot and Audubon Lake, and the ground under obstacles there (for example 2,507 MSL with 340 AGL) is around 2,100 to 2,200 feet. So the tan terrain is between 2,000 and 2,500 feet MSL. Sea level is clearly wrong, and 2,700 has no contour to support it.
ref: PHAK Ch. 16; Aeronautical Chart User's Guide; Figure 21 legend

stem: (Refer to Figure 21.) Which public use airport(s) depicted are indicated as having fuel?
options: Minot Intl. (area 1).
Minot Intl. (area 1) and Garrison (area 2).
Mercer County Regional Airport (area 3) and Garrison (area 2).
explanation: Small tick marks around the outside of an airport symbol mean services, including fuel, are available. Minot International's blue towered symbol in area 1 shows these ticks, while the Garrison and Mercer County symbols are plain circles with no ticks. Assuming any public airport with a beacon has fuel is the trap.
ref: PHAK Ch. 16; Aeronautical Chart User's Guide; Figure 21

stem: (Refer to Figure 23.) The flag symbols at Statesboro Bulloch County Airport, Claxton-Evans County Airport, and Ridgeland Airport are
options: outer boundaries of Savannah Class C airspace.
airports with special traffic patterns.
visual checkpoints to identify position for initial callup prior to entering Savannah Class C airspace.
explanation: The magenta flags at Statesboro Bulloch County, Claxton Evans County, and Ridgeland mark VFR visual checkpoints that pilots use to give their position when first calling Savannah Approach before entering Class C. They are not airspace boundaries, and special traffic patterns are shown in the Chart Supplement, not with flags.
ref: PHAK Ch. 16; Aeronautical Chart User's Guide; Figure 23

stem: (Refer to Figure 23, area 3.) What is the height of the lighted obstacle approximately 6 nautical miles southwest of Savannah International?
options: 1,534 feet AGL.
1,549 feet MSL.
1,500 feet MSL.
explanation: About 6 NM southwest of Savannah International the lighted obstacle is labeled 1548 with (1534) below it. The bold number is the top in feet MSL and the number in parentheses is its height above ground, so it is 1,534 feet AGL. The MSL choices do not match the printed 1548.
ref: PHAK Ch. 16; Aeronautical Chart User's Guide; Figure 23

stem: (Refer to Figure 23, area 3.) The top of the group obstruction approximately 11 nautical miles from the Savannah VORTAC on the 007° radial is
options: 253 feet AGL.
454 feet MSL.
417 feet MSL.
explanation: About 11 NM north of the Savannah VORTAC on the 007 radial, the group obstruction symbol is labeled 454 with the note stacks. A number without parentheses is the top in feet MSL, so 454 feet MSL. The 253 figure is the AGL height of a different obstacle (266 MSL), and 417 is the MSL top of another nearby obstruction.
ref: PHAK Ch. 16; Aeronautical Chart User's Guide; Figure 23

stem: (Refer to Figure 24, area 1.) What minimum altitude is necessary to vertically clear the obstacle on the northeast side of Airpark East Airport by 500 feet?
options: 1,010 feet MSL.
1,273 feet MSL.
1,283 feet MSL.
explanation: The obstacle just northeast of Airpark East (1F7) is labeled 773, its top in feet MSL. Clearing it by 500 feet requires 773 + 500 = 1,273 feet MSL. The 1,010 choice adds 500 to field elevation, and 1,283 uses the wrong obstacle height.
ref: PHAK Ch. 16; Aeronautical Chart User's Guide; Figure 24

stem: (Refer to Figure 24, area 2.) What minimum altitude is necessary to vertically clear the obstacle on the southeast side of Winnsboro Airport by 500 feet?
options: 823 feet MSL.
1,013 feet MSL.
1,403 feet MSL.
explanation: The obstacle southeast of Winnsboro is labeled 903 with (323) AGL. Clearing it by 500 feet needs 903 + 500 = 1,403 feet MSL. The 823 choice adds 500 to the AGL height, a classic mistake, since altitudes for clearance must be in MSL.
ref: PHAK Ch. 16; Aeronautical Chart User's Guide; Figure 24

stem: (Refer to Figure 25, area 2.) The control tower frequency for Addison Airport is
explanation: Addison's airport data in area 2 read CT 126.0, so the tower frequency is 126.0 MHz. The 133.4 figure is the ATIS, and 122.95 is UNICOM, the italic number at the end of the elevation line.
ref: PHAK Ch. 16; Aeronautical Chart User's Guide; Figure 25

stem: (Refer to Figure 25, area 8.) What minimum altitude is required to fly over the Cedar Hill TV towers in the congested area south of NAS Dallas?
options: 2,555 feet MSL.
3,549 feet MSL.
3,349 feet MSL.
explanation: Over a congested area 14 CFR 91.119(b) requires 1,000 feet above the highest obstacle within 2,000 feet horizontally. The tallest Cedar Hill tower is labeled 2549 MSL (1731 AGL), so the minimum is 2,549 + 1,000 = 3,549 feet MSL. The 3,349 choice clears the top by only 800 feet, and 2,555 barely clears it at all.

stem: A military air station can be identified by a rotating beacon that emits
options: white and green alternating flashes.
two quick, white flashes between green flashes.
green, yellow, and white flashes.
explanation: A military airport beacon is distinguished by two quick white flashes between each green flash. A civilian land airport beacon alternates single white and green flashes, and green, yellow, and white marks a heliport.
ref: AIM Ch. 2 Sec. 1, Airport and Heliport Beacons

stem: Which is true concerning the blue and magenta colors used to depict airports on Sectional Aeronautical Charts?
options: Airports with control towers underlying Class A, B, and C airspace are shown in blue; Class D and E airspace are magenta.
Airports with control towers underlying Class C, D, and E airspace are shown in magenta.
Airports with control towers underlying Class B, C, D, and E airspace are shown in blue.
explanation: On sectionals, airports with an operating control tower are printed in blue and nontowered airports in magenta, regardless of whether the overlying airspace is Class B, C, D, or E. The other options tie the color to the airspace class, which is not how the legend works.
ref: PHAK Ch. 16; Aeronautical Chart User's Guide

stem: Which statement about longitude and latitude is true?
options: Lines of longitude are parallel to the Equator.
Lines of longitude cross the Equator at right angles.
The 0° line of latitude passes through Greenwich, England.
explanation: Meridians of longitude run from pole to pole and cross the Equator at right angles. Lines of latitude are the ones parallel to the Equator, and it is the 0 degree meridian of longitude, not latitude, that passes through Greenwich.
ref: PHAK Ch. 16; Aeronautical Chart User's Guide

stem: The width of a Federal Airway from either side of the centerline is
options: 4 nautical miles.
6 nautical miles.
8 nautical miles.
explanation: A Federal airway includes the airspace 4 nautical miles on each side of the centerline, 8 NM wide in total. The 8 NM option is the total width, not the distance from either side of the centerline.

stem: Unless otherwise specified, Federal Airways include that Class E airspace extending upward from
options: 700 feet above the surface up to and including 17,999 feet MSL.
1,200 feet above the surface up to and including 17,999 feet MSL.
the surface up to and including 18,000 feet MSL.
explanation: Federal airways are Class E airspace that normally begins at 1,200 feet AGL and extends up to but not including 18,000 feet MSL, where Class A starts. Some segments start at 700 feet, which is why the stem says unless otherwise specified, and nothing at or above 18,000 is part of a Victor airway.

stem: Normal VFR operations in Class D airspace with an operating control tower require the ceiling and visibility to be at least
options: 1,000 feet and 1 mile.
1,000 feet and 3 miles.
2,500 feet and 3 miles.
explanation: Basic VFR in controlled airspace near an airport requires a ceiling of at least 1,000 feet and 3 statute miles visibility under 14 CFR 91.155(c) and (d). One mile is the Class G day minimum, and 2,500 feet is not a basic VFR ceiling.

stem: A blue segmented circle on a Sectional Chart depicts which class airspace?
options: Class B.
Class C.
Class D.
explanation: A dashed or segmented blue line marks Class D airspace on a sectional. Class B is a solid blue line, and Class C is a solid magenta line.
ref: PHAK Ch. 16; Aeronautical Chart User's Guide

stem: Airspace at an airport with a part-time control tower is classified as Class D airspace only
options: when the weather minimums are below basic VFR.
when the associated control tower is in operation.
when the associated Flight Service Station is in operation.
explanation: At an airport with a part time tower, the surface area is Class D only while the tower is operating; when it closes the airspace reverts to Class E or Class G as noted in the Chart Supplement. The weather and FSS options have no bearing on airspace class.

stem: What minimum radio equipment is required for operation within Class C airspace?
options: Two-way radio communications equipment and a 4096-code transponder.
Two-way radio communications equipment, a 4096-code transponder, and DME.
Two-way radio communications equipment, a 4096-code transponder, and an encoding altimeter.
explanation: Class C requires two way radio communication with ATC and an operable 4096 code transponder with Mode C altitude reporting from an encoding altimeter, per 14 CFR 91.215. Today ADS-B Out is also required under 91.225. DME has never been required for Class C, and a transponder without altitude reporting is not enough.

stem: What minimum pilot certification is required for operation within Class B airspace?
options: Recreational Pilot Certificate.
Private Pilot Certificate or Student Pilot Certificate with appropriate logbook endorsements.
Private Pilot Certificate with an instrument rating.
explanation: To operate in Class B a pilot must hold at least a private pilot certificate, or be a student, sport, or recreational pilot with the required training and logbook endorsement under 61.95 or 61.101. An instrument rating is not needed for VFR flight in Class B, and a recreational certificate alone, without the endorsement, does not qualify.

stem: What minimum radio equipment is required for VFR operation within Class B airspace?
options: Two-way radio communications equipment and a 4096-code transponder.
Two-way radio communications equipment, a 4096-code transponder, and an encoding altimeter.
Two-way radio communications equipment, a 4096-code transponder, an encoding altimeter, and a VOR or TACAN receiver.
explanation: VFR in Class B needs two way radio communication and an operable 4096 code transponder with Mode C from an encoding altimeter, and today ADS-B Out as well. A VOR or TACAN receiver is required only for IFR operations in Class B, which is the trap in the longest option.

stem: An operable 4096-code transponder and Mode C encoding altimeter are required in
options: Class B airspace and within 30 miles of the Class B primary airport.
Class D airspace.
Class E airspace below 10,000 feet MSL.
explanation: An operable Mode C transponder is required in Class B and within the 30 NM veil around the primary airport, from the surface to 10,000 feet MSL (and ADS-B Out is now required there too). Class D has no transponder requirement, and Class E needs Mode C only at or above 10,000 feet MSL, excluding the airspace at and below 2,500 feet AGL.

stem: In which type of airspace are VFR flights prohibited?
options: Class A.
Class B.
Class C.
explanation: Class A, from 18,000 feet MSL up to FL600, requires all operations to be under IFR, so VFR flight is prohibited unless otherwise authorized. VFR is allowed in Class B and Class C with the proper clearance or communication.

stem: During operations within controlled airspace at altitudes of less than 1,200 feet AGL, the minimum horizontal distance from clouds requirement for VFR flight is
options: 1,000 feet.
1,500 feet.
2,000 feet.
explanation: In controlled airspace below 10,000 feet MSL, the cloud clearance is 500 feet below, 1,000 feet above, and 2,000 feet horizontal, regardless of being under 1,200 feet AGL. The 1,000 foot figure is the vertical distance above clouds, not the horizontal one.

stem: What minimum visibility and clearance from clouds are required for VFR operations in Class G airspace at 700 feet AGL or below during daylight hours?
options: 1 mile visibility and clear of clouds.
1 mile visibility, 500 feet below, 1,000 feet above, and 2,000 feet horizontal clearance from clouds.
3 miles visibility and clear of clouds.
explanation: In Class G at or below 1,200 feet AGL during the day, VFR requires only 1 statute mile visibility and remaining clear of clouds. The 500, 1,000, 2,000 cloud clearance is the night or higher altitude rule, and 3 miles is the controlled airspace minimum.

stem: What minimum flight visibility is required for VFR flight operations on an airway below 10,000 feet MSL?
options: 1 mile.
3 miles.
4 miles.
explanation: Federal airways are Class E airspace, and below 10,000 feet MSL Class E requires 3 statute miles flight visibility. One mile is the Class G day minimum below 1,200 feet AGL, and 5 miles applies at or above 10,000 feet MSL.

stem: The minimum distance from clouds required for VFR operations on an airway below 10,000 feet MSL is
options: remain clear of clouds.
500 feet below, 1,000 feet above, and 2,000 feet horizontally.
500 feet above, 1,000 feet below, and 2,000 feet horizontally.
explanation: On an airway below 10,000 feet MSL you are in Class E, so the cloud clearance is 500 feet below, 1,000 feet above, and 2,000 feet horizontally. The last option swaps above and below, and clear of clouds applies only in some Class G and Class B situations.

stem: During operations within controlled airspace at altitudes of more than 1,200 feet AGL, but less than 10,000 feet MSL, the minimum distance above clouds requirement for VFR flight is
options: 500 feet.
1,000 feet.
1,500 feet.
explanation: In controlled airspace below 10,000 feet MSL you must stay 1,000 feet above clouds, 500 feet below, and 2,000 feet horizontally. Picking 500 feet confuses the above and below values.

stem: VFR flight in controlled airspace above 1,200 feet AGL and below 10,000 feet MSL requires a minimum visibility and vertical cloud clearance of
options: 3 miles, and 500 feet below or 1,000 feet above the clouds in controlled airspace.
5 miles, and 1,000 feet below or 1,000 feet above the clouds at all altitudes.
5 miles, and 1,000 feet below or 1,000 feet above the clouds only in Class A airspace.
explanation: Class E below 10,000 feet MSL requires 3 statute miles visibility with 500 feet below and 1,000 feet above clouds (plus 2,000 feet horizontal). Five miles and 1,000 feet below are the at or above 10,000 feet MSL values, and VFR is not allowed in Class A at all.

stem: Outside controlled airspace, the minimum flight visibility requirement for VFR flight above 1,200 feet AGL and below 10,000 feet MSL during daylight hours is
options: 1 mile.
3 miles.
5 miles.
explanation: In Class G airspace above 1,200 feet AGL but below 10,000 feet MSL, the daytime minimum is 1 statute mile flight visibility with 500 below, 1,000 above and 2,000 horizontal cloud clearance. The 3 mile value is what applies at night in that same band, and 5 miles only applies at or above 10,000 feet MSL.

stem: The minimum flight visibility required for VFR flights above 10,000 feet MSL and more than 1,200 feet AGL in controlled airspace is
options: 1 mile.
3 miles.
5 miles.
explanation: At or above 10,000 feet MSL and more than 1,200 feet AGL, VFR requires 5 statute miles of flight visibility in both Class E and Class G airspace. The 3 mile figure is the minimum below 10,000 feet MSL in controlled airspace, which is the common trap.

stem: For VFR flight operations above 10,000 feet MSL and more than 1,200 feet AGL, the minimum horizontal distance from clouds required is
options: 1,000 feet.
2,000 feet.
1 mile.
explanation: At or above 10,000 feet MSL (and more than 1,200 feet AGL) the cloud clearance becomes 1,000 feet below, 1,000 feet above and 1 statute mile horizontally. The 2,000 foot horizontal value belongs to the lower altitude band below 10,000 feet MSL.

stem: During operations at altitudes of more than 1,200 feet AGL and at or above 10,000 feet MSL, the minimum distance above clouds requirement for VFR flight is
options: 500 feet.
1,000 feet.
1,500 feet.
explanation: In the high altitude band, at or above 10,000 feet MSL, a VFR aircraft must stay 1,000 feet above clouds, 1,000 feet below and 1 statute mile horizontally. The 500 foot figure is the below cloud distance used under 10,000 feet MSL, not an above cloud value here.

stem: No person may take off or land an aircraft under basic VFR at an airport that lies within Class D airspace unless the
options: flight visibility at that airport is at least 1 mile.
ground visibility at that airport is at least 1 mile.
ground visibility at that airport is at least 3 miles.
explanation: Under basic VFR, no one may take off, land, or enter the traffic pattern in a surface area of Class B, C, D or E airspace unless ground visibility is at least 3 statute miles (flight visibility is used only if ground visibility is not reported). The 1 mile options describe special VFR, not basic VFR.

stem: The basic VFR weather minimums for operating an aircraft within Class D airspace are
options: 500-foot ceiling and 1 mile visibility.
1,000-foot ceiling and 3 miles visibility.
clear of clouds and 2 miles visibility.
explanation: Basic VFR in a Class D surface area requires a ceiling of at least 1,000 feet and 3 statute miles visibility, plus the normal 500 below, 1,000 above, 2,000 horizontal cloud clearance. A 500 foot ceiling with 1 mile is not a basic VFR standard, and clear of clouds with 2 miles matches neither basic VFR nor special VFR.

stem: A special VFR clearance authorizes the pilot of an aircraft to operate VFR while within Class D airspace when the visibility is
options: less than 1 mile and the ceiling is less than 1,000 feet.
at least 1 mile and the aircraft can remain clear of clouds.
at least 3 miles and the aircraft can remain clear of clouds.
explanation: A special VFR clearance lets an airplane operate in a surface area below basic VFR minimums as long as visibility is at least 1 statute mile and the aircraft remains clear of clouds. Less than 1 mile is never acceptable for fixed wing SVFR, and 3 miles with clear of clouds would not need special VFR at all.

stem: What is the minimum weather condition required for airplanes operating under special VFR in Class D airspace?
options: 1 mile flight visibility.
1 mile flight visibility and 1,000-foot ceiling.
3 miles flight visibility and 1,000-foot ceiling.
explanation: Special VFR for airplanes requires 1 statute mile flight visibility and remaining clear of clouds; there is no ceiling requirement. Adding a 1,000 foot ceiling turns the answer into the basic VFR rule. For takeoff or landing under SVFR, ground visibility must also be at least 1 mile when it is reported.

stem: What are the minimum requirements for airplane operations under special VFR in Class D airspace at night?
options: The airplane must be under radar surveillance at all times while in Class D airspace.
The airplane must be equipped for IFR with an altitude reporting transponder.
The pilot must be instrument rated, and the airplane must be IFR equipped.
explanation: Special VFR at night (sunset to sunrise) is only allowed when the pilot holds an instrument rating and the airplane is equipped for instrument flight. Radar surveillance and an altitude reporting transponder are not the stated conditions in the rule.

stem: No person may operate an airplane within Class D airspace at night under special VFR unless the
options: flight can be conducted 500 feet below the clouds.
airplane is equipped for instrument flight.
flight visibility is at least 3 miles.
explanation: Between sunset and sunrise a special VFR clearance is valid only if the pilot is instrument rated and current and the airplane is equipped for instrument flight. A 3 mile visibility requirement would be basic VFR, and staying 500 feet below clouds is not part of the SVFR rule.

stem: With certain exceptions, all aircraft within 30 miles of a Class B primary airport from the surface upward to 10,000 feet MSL must be equipped with
options: an operable VOR or TACAN receiver and an ADF receiver.
instruments and equipment required for IFR operations.
an operable transponder having either Mode S or 4096-code capability with Mode C automatic altitude reporting capability.
explanation: Inside the Mode C veil, within 30 NM of a Class B primary airport from the surface to 10,000 feet MSL, aircraft need an operable 4096 code or Mode S transponder with Mode C altitude reporting. Today ADS-B Out is also required in that same area under 91.225, but IFR equipment and VOR or ADF receivers are not.

stem: (Refer to Figure 25, area 4.) The floor of Class B airspace overlying Hicks Airport (T67) north-northwest of Fort Worth Meacham Field is
options: at the surface.
3,200 feet MSL.
4,000 feet MSL.
explanation: Hicks (T67) lies in the Class B area whose floor is 4,000 feet MSL and ceiling 11,000 feet MSL (110 over 40), outside the 3,000 foot shelf that surrounds Fort Worth to the east and inside the 5,000 foot shelf labeled 110 over 50 near Boyd to the west. The 3,200 figure is the bracketed Class D ceiling at nearby Meacham, an easy number to grab by mistake.
ref: Figure 25; FAA Aeronautical Chart User's Guide, Class B

stem: (Refer to Figure 25, area 2.) The floor of Class B airspace at Air Park-Dallas Airport is
options: at the surface.
3,000 feet MSL.
3,100 feet MSL.
explanation: Air Park Dallas (F69) lies in the Class B shelf labeled 110 over 30, meaning Class B starts at 3,000 feet MSL and tops out at 11,000 feet MSL. Below 3,000 feet MSL the airport is outside Class B, so the surface option is wrong.
ref: Figure 25; FAA Aeronautical Chart User's Guide, Class B

stem: (Refer to Figure 20 area 4.) What hazards to aircraft may exist in restricted areas such as R-5302B?
options: Unusual, often invisible, hazards such as aerial gunnery or guided missiles.
Military training activities that necessitate acrobatic or abrupt flight maneuvers.
High volume of pilot training or an unusual type of aerial activity.
explanation: Restricted areas contain unusual and often invisible hazards to aircraft, such as artillery firing, aerial gunnery or guided missiles. Acrobatic military training describes a MOA, and high volumes of pilot training describe an alert area.

stem: (Refer to Figure 26, area 2.) What hazards to aircraft may exist in areas such as Devils Lake East MOA?
options: High volume of pilot training or an unusual type of aerial activity.
Military training activities that necessitate acrobatic or abrupt flight maneuvers.
Unusual, often invisible, hazards to aircraft such as artillery firing, aerial gunnery, or guided missiles.
explanation: A Military Operations Area separates military training such as air combat tactics and acrobatic or abrupt maneuvers from IFR traffic. The invisible hazards option describes a restricted area, and heavy pilot training describes an alert area.

stem: (Refer to Figure 21, area 3.) What type military flight operations should a pilot expect along IR 644?
options: IFR training flights above 1,500 feet AGL at speeds in excess of 250 knots.
VFR training flights above 1,500 feet AGL at speeds less than 250 knots.
Instrument training flights below 1,500 feet AGL at speeds in excess of 150 knots.
explanation: IR means the route is flown under IFR, and a three digit route number such as 644 means at least one segment is above 1,500 feet AGL; four digit numbers are at or below 1,500 feet AGL. Military training routes are used for speeds above 250 knots, so the slower or lower options do not fit.

stem: (Refer to Figure 26, area 3.) When flying over Arrowwood National Wildlife Refuge, a pilot should fly no lower than
options: 2,000 feet AGL.
2,500 feet AGL.
3,000 feet AGL.
explanation: Pilots are requested to maintain at least 2,000 feet above the surface over national wildlife refuges, parks and similar noise sensitive areas, which includes Arrowwood National Wildlife Refuge. This is a request rather than a regulation, and the 2,500 and 3,000 values are not the published figure.

stem: (Refer to Figure 22, area 1.) The visibility and cloud clearance requirements to operate VFR during daylight hours over Sandpoint Airport at 1,200 feet AGL are
options: 3 miles and 1,000 feet above, 500 feet below, and 2,000 feet horizontally from each cloud.
1 mile and clear of clouds.
1 mile and 1,000 feet above, 500 feet below, and 2,000 feet horizontally from each cloud.
explanation: Sandpoint is inside a magenta vignette, so Class E begins at 700 feet AGL, and at 1,200 feet AGL the aircraft is in Class E below 10,000 feet MSL. That requires 3 statute miles and 500 below, 1,000 above, 2,000 horizontal. The 1 mile options apply to Class G by day.

stem: (Refer to Figure 26, area 2.) The visibility and cloud clearance requirements to operate VFR during daylight hours over the town of Cooperstown between 1,200 feet AGL and 10,000 feet MSL are
options: 1 mile and 1,000 feet above, 500 feet below, and 2,000 feet horizontally from clouds.
1 mile and clear of clouds.
3 miles and 1,000 feet above, 500 feet below, and 2,000 feet horizontally from clouds.
explanation: Between 1,200 feet AGL and 10,000 feet MSL over Cooperstown the airspace is Class E, which requires 3 statute miles visibility and 500 feet below, 1,000 feet above, 2,000 feet horizontally from clouds. The 1 mile choices are Class G daytime values.

stem: (Refer to Figure 26, area 1.) Identify the airspace over Tomlinson Airport (8J7).
options: Class G airspace - surface up to but not including 1,200 feet AGL, Class E airspace - 1,200 feet AGL up to but not including 18,000 feet MSL.
Class G airspace - surface up to but not including 18,000 feet MSL.
Class G airspace - surface up to but not including 700 feet MSL, Class E airspace - 700 feet to 14,500 feet MSL.
explanation: Tomlinson has no magenta vignette around it, so Class G runs from the surface up to but not including 1,200 feet AGL, with Class E above that up to but not including 18,000 feet MSL. Class G all the way to 18,000 feet only occurs where the chart shows it, and the 700 foot figures confuse the magenta vignette with MSL values.

stem: (Refer to Figure 26, area 5.) The airspace overlying and within 5 miles of Barnes County Airport is
options: Class D airspace from the surface to the floor of the overlying Class E airspace.
Class E airspace from the surface to 1,200 feet MSL.
Class G airspace from the surface to 700 feet AGL.
explanation: Barnes County is surrounded by a magenta vignette, so Class E begins at 700 feet AGL and the airspace from the surface up to 700 feet AGL is Class G. There is no dashed blue or dashed magenta line, so the airport has neither Class D nor a Class E surface area.
ref: Figure 26; FAA Aeronautical Chart User's Guide

stem: (Refer to Figure 25, area 7.) The airspace overlying McKinney (TKI) is controlled from the surface to
options: 2,900 feet MSL.
2,500 feet MSL.
700 feet AGL.
explanation: McKinney (TKI) sits inside a dashed blue Class D boundary with the number 29 in a bracket, meaning controlled Class D airspace extends from the surface to 2,900 feet MSL. The 700 feet AGL option describes a magenta vignette, which does not apply to a towered surface area.
ref: Figure 25; FAA Aeronautical Chart User's Guide, Class D

stem: (Refer to Figure 25, area 4.) The airspace directly overlying Fort Worth Meacham is
options: Class B airspace to 10,000 feet MSL.
Class C airspace to 5,000 feet MSL.
Class D airspace to 3,200 feet MSL.
explanation: Fort Worth Meacham is enclosed by a dashed blue line with a bracketed 32, so it is Class D airspace from the surface up to 3,200 feet MSL. Class B overlies it at higher altitudes, but the airspace directly over the field is Class D, and there is no Class C at Meacham.
ref: Figure 25; FAA Aeronautical Chart User's Guide, Class D

stem: (Refer to Figure 23, area 3.) What is the floor of the Savannah Class C airspace at the shelf area (outer circle)?
options: 1,300 feet AGL.
1,300 feet MSL.
1,700 feet MSL.
explanation: The Savannah outer shelf is labeled 41 over 13, so Class C extends from 1,300 feet MSL up to 4,100 feet MSL. Chart altitudes in Class C labels are always MSL in hundreds of feet, so 1,300 feet AGL is the trap.

stem: (Refer to Figure 20, area 1.) What minimum radio equipment is required to land and take off at Norfolk International?
options: Mode C transponder and omnireceiver.
Mode C transponder and two-way radio.
Mode C transponder, omnireceiver, and DME.
explanation: Norfolk International is a Class C primary airport, and Class C requires two way radio communication with ATC and an operable Mode C transponder (plus ADS-B Out today). No VOR receiver or DME is required to operate there.

stem: (Refer to Figure 25.) At which airports is fixed-wing Special VFR not authorized?
options: Fort Worth Meacham and Fort Worth Spinks.
Dallas-Fort Worth International and Dallas Love Field.
Addison and Redbird.
explanation: Airports where fixed wing special VFR is prohibited are marked NO SVFR above the airport name on the sectional, and in Figure 25 that note appears at Dallas Fort Worth International and Dallas Love Field. Meacham, Spinks, Addison and Redbird carry no such note.
ref: Figure 25; 14 CFR Part 91 Appendix D, Section 3

stem: (Refer to Figure 22, area 3.) The vertical limits of that portion of Class E airspace designated as a Federal Airway over Magee Airport are
options: 700 feet MSL to 12,500 feet MSL.
7,500 feet MSL to 17,999 feet MSL.
1,200 feet AGL to 17,999 feet MSL.
explanation: Federal Airways are Class E airspace that normally begin at 1,200 feet AGL and extend up to but not including 18,000 feet MSL. Magee is otherwise in Class G near the surface, and the 700 foot and 7,500 foot values are not airway limits.

stem: An airport's rotating beacon operated during daylight hours indicates
options: there are obstructions on the airport.
that weather at the airport located in Class D airspace is below basic VFR weather minimums.
the Air Traffic Control tower is not in operation.
explanation: In Class B, C, D and E surface areas, a rotating beacon on during daylight hours often means the ceiling is below 1,000 feet or the ground visibility is below 3 miles, which is below basic VFR. Pilots should not rely on this alone, since beacon operation is not standardized everywhere. It does not indicate obstructions or the tower being closed.

stem: The vertical limit of Class C airspace above the primary airport is normally
options: 1,200 feet AGL.
3,000 feet AGL.
4,000 feet AGL.
explanation: Class C airspace normally extends from the surface to 4,000 feet above the primary airport elevation, charted as an MSL value. The 1,200 feet value is an outer shelf floor idea and 3,000 feet is not a standard Class C dimension.

stem: The normal radius of the procedural Outer Area of Class C airspace is normally
options: 10 nautical miles.
30 nautical miles.
20 nautical miles.
explanation: The procedural Outer Area of Class C airspace normally extends out to 20 NM from the primary airport, where approach control provides services to participating aircraft. The 10 NM figure is the radius of the outer shelf of Class C itself, which is the usual confusion.

stem: All operations within Class C airspace must be in
options: accordance with instrument flight rules.
compliance with ATC clearances and instructions.
an aircraft equipped with a 4096-code transponder with Mode C encoding capability.
explanation: Every aircraft in Class C airspace must have an operable 4096 code transponder with Mode C altitude reporting, and today ADS-B Out as well. VFR operations are allowed, and no clearance is needed, only two way radio communication with ATC, so the IFR and ATC clearance options are wrong.

stem: Under what condition may an aircraft operate from a satellite airport within Class C airspace?
options: The pilot must file a flight plan prior to departure.
The pilot must monitor ATC until clear of the Class C airspace.
The pilot must contact ATC as soon as practicable after takeoff.
explanation: When departing a satellite airport without an operating tower inside Class C, the pilot must establish two way radio communication with the ATC facility having jurisdiction as soon as practicable after takeoff. No flight plan is required, and merely monitoring the frequency does not satisfy the communication requirement.

stem: Under what condition, if any, may pilots fly through a restricted area?
options: When flying on airways with an ATC clearance.
With the controlling agency's authorization.
Regulations do not allow this.
explanation: Flight within a restricted area is prohibited unless the pilot has permission from the using or controlling agency, which ATC can relay when the area is not active. An airway clearance does not by itself authorize entry, and it is not true that regulations ban all such flights.

stem: Responsibility for collision avoidance in an alert area rests with
options: the controlling agency.
all pilots.
Air Traffic Control.
explanation: Alert areas contain a high volume of pilot training or unusual activity, and every pilot flying in them, participating or not, is responsible for collision avoidance. No agency or ATC unit separates traffic there.

stem: The lateral dimensions of Class D airspace are based on
options: the number of airports that lie within the Class D airspace.
5 statute miles from the geographical center of the primary airport.
the instrument procedures for which the controlled airspace is established.
explanation: Class D airspace is individually tailored, and its lateral dimensions are built around the instrument procedures for which the controlled airspace is established. A fixed 5 mile radius is a common rule of thumb but is not the regulatory basis.

stem: A non-tower satellite airport, within the same Class D airspace as that designated for the primary airport, requires radio communications be established and maintained with the
options: satellite airport's UNICOM.
associated Flight Service Station.
primary airport's control tower.
explanation: In Class D, a pilot operating to or from a nontowered satellite airport must establish and maintain two way radio communication with the ATC facility providing services, which is the primary airport's control tower. UNICOM and Flight Service do not provide that control service.

stem: Which initial action should a pilot take prior to entering Class C airspace?
options: Contact approach control on the appropriate frequency.
Contact the tower and request permission to enter.
Contact the FSS for traffic advisories.
explanation: Class C airspace is controlled by approach control, so the pilot should establish two way radio communication with approach on the appropriate frequency before entering. Calling the tower is only correct when approach control is not available or for the inner core near the airport after handoff.

stem: What ATC facility should the pilot contact to receive a special VFR departure clearance in Class D airspace?
options: Automated Flight Service Station.
Air Traffic Control Tower.
Air Route Traffic Control Center.
explanation: A special VFR clearance is obtained from the ATC facility controlling the surface area, which for a Class D airport is the control tower. Flight Service can relay but does not issue the clearance, and the ARTCC is not the normal source for an SVFR departure.

stem: Pilots flying over a national wildlife refuge are requested to fly no lower than
options: 1,000 feet AGL.
2,000 feet AGL.
3,000 feet AGL.
explanation: Pilots are asked to stay at least 2,000 feet above the surface of national wildlife refuges, parks and other noise sensitive areas. This is a voluntary request, and the 1,000 and 3,000 foot values are not the published number.

stem: (Refer to Figure 22, area 1.) The visibility and cloud clearance requirements to operate over Sandpoint Airport at night at less than 700 feet AGL are
options: 3 miles and 1,000 feet above, 500 feet below, and 2,000 feet horizontally from each cloud.
1 mile and 1,000 feet above, 500 feet below, and 2,000 feet horizontally from each cloud.
3 miles and clear of clouds.
explanation: Below 700 feet AGL at Sandpoint the airspace is Class G, and at night in Class G below 1,200 feet AGL the minimum is 3 statute miles with 500 below, 1,000 above and 2,000 horizontal. The only relief is 1 mile and clear of clouds when in the traffic pattern within one half mile of the runway, which the question does not state.

stem: (Refer to Figure 26, area 2.) The day VFR visibility and cloud clearance requirements to operate over the town of Cooperstown, after departing and climbing out of the Cooperstown Airport at or below 700 feet AGL are
options: 3 miles and clear of clouds.
1 mile and 1,000 feet above, 500 feet below, and 2,000 feet horizontally from clouds.
1 mile and clear of clouds.
explanation: At or below 700 feet AGL near Cooperstown, under the magenta vignette, the airspace is Class G, and by day Class G below 1,200 feet AGL requires 1 statute mile visibility and clear of clouds. The 3 mile and standard clearance option applies once in the Class E airspace above 700 feet AGL.

stem: One of the purposes for issuing a Temporary Flight restriction (TFR) is to
options: announce Parachute Jump Areas.
protect public figures.
identify Airport Advisory Areas.
explanation: TFRs are issued for reasons such as protecting the President, Vice President and other public figures, disaster areas, space operations and major sporting events. Parachute jump areas and airport advisory areas are published elsewhere and are not created by TFR.

stem: Flight through a restricted area should not be accomplished unless the pilot has
options: filed an IFR flight plan.
received prior authorization from the controlling agency.
received prior permission from the commanding officer of the nearest military base.
explanation: Flight through an active restricted area requires prior authorization from the controlling agency, often obtained through ATC. Filing an IFR flight plan does not authorize entry, and the nearest base commander is not necessarily the controlling agency.

stem: When a control tower, located on an airport within Class D airspace, ceases operation for the day, what happens to the airspace designation?
options: The airspace designation normally will not change.
The airspace remains Class D airspace as long as a weather observer or automated weather system is available.
The airspace reverts to Class E or a combination of Class E and G airspace during the hours the tower is not in operation.
explanation: When a Class D tower closes, the surface area normally reverts to Class E, or to Class G with Class E above, for the hours the tower is closed, as listed in the Chart Supplement. The airspace does not stay Class D just because weather reporting continues.

stem: With certain exceptions, Class E airspace extends upward from either 700 feet or 1,200 feet AGL to, but does not include,
options: 10,000 feet MSL.
14,500 feet MSL.
18,000 feet MSL.
explanation: Class E airspace generally begins at 700 or 1,200 feet AGL and extends up to, but not including, 18,000 feet MSL, where Class A begins. Above Class A, Class E resumes at FL600. The 14,500 foot value is the base of Class E where it is not lower.

stem: The VFR pilot flying in Class G airspace
options: has tighter cloud and visibility restrictions because IFR aircraft flying in Class G airspace do not have air traffic control service.
has no cloud and visibility restrictions because IFR operations are prohibited in Class G airspace.
has reduced cloud and visibility restrictions because it's unlikely that IFR traffic will be operating in Class G airspace.
explanation: Class G is uncontrolled airspace where IFR traffic is uncommon, so VFR visibility and cloud clearance minimums are relaxed, for example 1 mile and clear of clouds near the surface by day. IFR operations are not prohibited in Class G, so the no restrictions option is wrong.

stem: You know when looking at a chart that the floor of Class E airspace is 700 feet AGL when it's within
options: the fuzzy side of the blue vignette.
the fuzzy side of the magenta vignette.
the magenta dashed line.
explanation: A magenta vignette marks where Class E begins at 700 feet AGL on the fuzzy, shaded side. A blue vignette marks Class E starting at 1,200 feet AGL, and a magenta dashed line marks a Class E surface area.
ref: FAA Aeronautical Chart User's Guide; AIM 3-2-6

stem: The purpose of Military Training Routes, charted as VFR Military Training Routes (VR) and IFR Military Training Routes (IR) on sectional charts, is to ensure the greatest practical level of safety for all flight operations and to allow the military to conduct
options: low altitude, high-speed training.
radar instrument training.
air-to-air refueling training.
explanation: Military Training Routes are established so the military can conduct low altitude, high speed training, generally below 10,000 feet MSL at more than 250 knots, while keeping all users as safe as practicable. Radar training and refueling tracks are separate airspace uses.

stem: (Refer to Figure 71, area 8.) What is the minimum visibility required under VFR for takeoff from the Auburn Airport at sunrise?
options: 3 Statute Miles.
5 Statute Miles.
1 Statute Mile.
explanation: Auburn sits inside a magenta vignette with no dashed surface area line, so the airspace below 700 feet AGL is Class G. Night under 14 CFR 1.1 ends at the beginning of morning civil twilight, which comes before sunrise, so a sunrise takeoff is a day operation, and day VFR in Class G below 1,200 feet AGL needs only 1 statute mile and clear of clouds. The 3 mile value applies at night or in controlled airspace.

stem: Under which conditions may a pilot fly under VFR within 60 nautical miles of the DCA VOR in Washington, D.C.?
options: None.
Only if the pilot has completed special awareness training and filed a flight plan.
As long as the pilot has completed special awareness training and remains clear of the SFRA.
explanation: Any pilot flying VFR within 60 NM of the DCA VOR must have completed the FAA special awareness training, and it is then permitted as long as the pilot stays clear of the SFRA. Flying inside the SFRA has additional requirements such as a flight plan, a discrete code and two way communication, so the flight plan option describes only that case.

stem: The airspace system designations used throughout the United States
options: makes our airspace system more complex than it is in other countries.
standardizes airspace classifications with other countries.
separates all IFR and VFR operations.
explanation: The United States adopted the ICAO airspace classes A through G so that its airspace classifications are standardized with other countries. The system does not separate all IFR and VFR traffic, and it simplified rather than complicated the earlier designations.

stem: Uncontrolled airspace is
options: Class G airspace.
for flying VFR only.
primarily for instrument flight operations.
explanation: Class G is the only uncontrolled airspace in the United States. IFR flight is permitted in Class G, so describing it as VFR only or primarily for instrument operations is wrong.

stem: The basic VFR minimum visibility at night for Class G, E, D, and C airspace below 10,000 feet MSL is 3 statute miles. An exception to that minimum is when below 1,200 feet above the surface and the visibility is at least 1 but less than 3 statute miles
options: in Class C and D airspace clear of clouds if communications are established with the control tower.
in Class G airspace clear of clouds when operating in an airport traffic pattern within 1/2 mile of the runway.
in Class E airspace clear of clouds when operating in an airport traffic pattern within 1/2 mile of the runway.
explanation: The only exception to the 3 mile night minimum below 1,200 feet AGL is in Class G, where an airplane may operate with at least 1 mile and clear of clouds when in an airport traffic pattern within one half mile of the runway. Class C, D and E have no such relief.

stem: (Refer to Figure 22.) What are the visibility and cloud clearance requirements in an airplane at night when conducting takeoffs and landings at Shoshone County Airport (Area 3) if the pattern altitude is 1,000 feet AGL?
options: 3 SM visibility and clear of clouds.
1 SM visibility and clear of clouds if remaining within one-half mile of the airport.
Remain clear of clouds and operate at a speed that allows adequate opportunity to see other traffic and obstructions in time to avoid a collision.
explanation: Shoshone County has no magenta vignette, so the pattern at 1,000 feet AGL is in Class G below 1,200 feet AGL. At night the rule normally requires 3 statute miles and standard cloud clearance, but an airplane in the traffic pattern within one half mile of the runway may operate with 1 statute mile and clear of clouds.

stem: The ceiling of Class D airspace is
options: listed in the Chart Supplement in feet MSL and AGL.
shown on the sectional chart in feet AGL.
shown on the sectional chart in feet MSL.
explanation: The ceiling of Class D is printed on the sectional as a bracketed number in hundreds of feet MSL, for example a bracketed 32 for 3,200 feet MSL. Chart airspace altitudes are MSL, so the AGL option is wrong, and the Chart Supplement is not the primary place it is shown.
ref: FAA Aeronautical Chart User's Guide, Class D

stem: (Refer to FAA-CT-8080-2G, Figure 75, west of area 6.) During preflight planning, your course is plotted to fly through R-2305. Where would you find additional information regarding this airspace?
options: In the Aeronautical Information Manual.
In the Chart Supplements U.S. (formerly Airport Facility Directory).
On the Sectional Chart in the Special Use Airspace area.
explanation: Each sectional chart has a Special Use Airspace table in its margin listing the number, altitudes, times of use, controlling agency and contact facility for areas such as R-2305. The AIM explains SUA in general but does not list individual areas.
ref: Figure 75; FAA Aeronautical Chart User's Guide, Special Use Airspace

stem: (Refer to Figure 20, area 3.) What is the recommended communications procedure for a landing at Currituck County Airport?
options: Transmit intentions on 122.9 MHz when 10 miles out and give position reports in the traffic pattern.
Contact Elizabeth City FSS for airport advisory service.
Contact New Bern FSS for area traffic information.
explanation: Currituck County shows 122.9 followed by a C, marking it as the CTAF, and the recommended practice is to self announce about 10 miles out and give position reports in the pattern. Flight Service no longer provides local airport advisory at airports like this, so the FSS options do not apply.

stem: (Refer to Figure 21, area 2.) The CTAF/MULTICOM frequency for Garrison Airport is
explanation: The frequency next to the circled C after the Garrison airport data is the CTAF, and it reads 122.9 MHz, the MULTICOM frequency used at airports without a tower or UNICOM. 122.8 is a common UNICOM frequency and does not appear for this field.

stem: (Refer to Figure 22, area 2; and Figure 31.) At Coeur d'Alene, which frequency should be used as a Common Traffic Advisory Frequency (CTAF) to self-announce position and intentions?
explanation: The Chart Supplement entry for Coeur d'Alene lists CTAF/UNICOM 122.8, and the sectional shows 122.8 with the circled C. 122.05 is the RCO for Flight Service and 108.8 is the VOR used to receive Flight Service on a duplex setup.

stem: (Refer to Figure 22, area 2; and Figure 31.) At Coeur d'Alene, which frequency should be used as a Common Traffic Advisory Frequency (CTAF) to monitor airport traffic?
explanation: Coeur d'Alene has no tower, and its CTAF is 122.8, the frequency to monitor and use for traffic announcements. 135.075 is the AWOS weather broadcast and 122.05 is the Flight Service RCO, neither of which carries traffic calls.

stem: (Refer to Figure 22, area 2; and Figure 31.) What is the correct UNICOM frequency to be used at Coeur d'Alene to request fuel?
explanation: At Coeur d'Alene the CTAF and UNICOM share 122.8, so fuel requests go on 122.8. 135.075 is the AWOS, and 122.1 transmit with 108.8 receive is a Flight Service duplex pairing.

stem: (Refer to Figure 25, area 3.) If Dallas Executive (RBD) Tower is not in operation, which frequency should be used as a Common Traffic Advisory Frequency (CTAF) to monitor airport traffic?
explanation: For Dallas Executive the tower frequency is 127.25 with a star and a circled C, meaning the tower is part time and that frequency becomes the CTAF when the tower is closed. 126.35 is the ATIS and 122.95 is the UNICOM.
ref: Figure 25; FAA Aeronautical Chart User's Guide

stem: (Refer to Figure 26, area 2.) What is the recommended communication procedure when inbound to land at Cooperstown Airport?
options: Broadcast intentions when 10 miles out on the CTAF/MULTICOM frequency, 122.9 MHz.
Contact UNICOM when 10 miles out on 122.8 MHz.
Circle the airport in a left turn prior to entering traffic.
explanation: Cooperstown lists 122.9 with the circled C, so the CTAF is the MULTICOM frequency 122.9, and pilots should announce intentions about 10 miles out. There is no UNICOM on 122.8 listed, and circling the field in a left turn is not a standard entry procedure.

stem: (Refer to Figure 26, area 4.) The CTAF/UNICOM frequency at Jamestown Airport is
explanation: Jamestown Regional shows 123.0 with a circled C, so 123.0 is the CTAF and UNICOM. 123.6 appears on the nearby navaid box and is not the airport's frequency.
ref: Figure 26; FAA Aeronautical Chart User's Guide

stem: (Refer to Figure 26, area 5.) What is the CTAF/UNICOM frequency at Barnes County Airport?
explanation: Barnes County lists 122.8 with the circled C, so 122.8 MHz is the CTAF and UNICOM. 118.725 is the AWOS, and 122.0 and 123.6 do not apply to this airport.
ref: Figure 26; FAA Aeronautical Chart User's Guide

stem: When flying HAWK N666CB, the proper phraseology for initial contact with McAlester AFSS is
options: "MC ALESTER RADIO, HAWK SIX SIX SIX CHARLIE BRAVO, RECEIVING ARDMORE VORTAC, OVER."
"MC ALESTER STATION, HAWK SIX SIX SIX CEE BEE, RECEIVING ARDMORE VORTAC, OVER."
"MC ALESTER FLIGHT SERVICE STATION, HAWK NOVEMBER SIX CHARLIE BRAVO, RECEIVING ARDMORE VORTAC, OVER."
explanation: Flight Service facilities are called by name followed by RADIO, the full aircraft type and registration are given using the phonetic alphabet, and the pilot states the frequency or navaid on which a reply is expected. Calling the facility STATION or FLIGHT SERVICE STATION, or using CEE BEE, is not standard.

stem: The correct method of stating 4,500 feet MSL to ATC is
options: "FOUR THOUSAND FIVE HUNDRED."
"FOUR POINT FIVE."
"FORTY-FIVE HUNDRED FEET MSL."
explanation: Altitudes below 18,000 feet are spoken by stating the thousands and hundreds separately, so 4,500 is FOUR THOUSAND FIVE HUNDRED. Point notation is not used, and saying forty five hundred feet MSL is nonstandard.

stem: The correct method of stating 10,500 feet MSL to ATC is
options: "TEN THOUSAND, FIVE HUNDRED FEET."
"TEN POINT FIVE."
"ONE ZERO THOUSAND, FIVE HUNDRED."
explanation: For altitudes of 10,000 feet and above, the thousands are spoken digit by digit, so 10,500 becomes ONE ZERO THOUSAND, FIVE HUNDRED. Saying TEN THOUSAND can be misheard, which is exactly why the digit form is required.

stem: Prior to entering an Airport Advisory Area, a pilot should
options: monitor ATIS for weather and traffic advisories.
contact approach control for vectors to the traffic pattern.
contact the local FSS for airport and traffic advisories.
explanation: The FAA keyed answer is to contact the local FSS for airport and traffic advisories, since airport advisory areas were served by an FSS on the field. Today Local Airport Advisory exists only at a few Alaska FSS sites, so in practice pilots at nontowered airports self announce on the CTAF.
note: Airport Advisory Areas and Local Airport Advisory remain only at a few Alaska FSS locations.

stem: Automatic Terminal Information Service (ATIS) is the continuous broadcast of recorded information concerning
options: pilots of radar-identified aircraft whose aircraft is in dangerous proximity to terrain or to an obstruction.
nonessential information to reduce frequency congestion.
noncontrol information in selected high-activity terminal areas.
explanation: ATIS is a continuous recorded broadcast of noncontrol information, such as weather, runway in use and NOTAMs, in selected high activity terminal areas. Its purpose is to reduce frequency congestion by relieving controllers of repeating essential, not nonessential, information. Terrain proximity warnings are safety alerts, not ATIS.

stem: An ATC radar facility issues the following advisory to a pilot flying on a heading of 090°: "TRAFFIC 3 O'CLOCK, 2 MILES, WESTBOUND..." Where should the pilot look for this traffic?
options: East.
South.
West.
explanation: Traffic calls use clock positions relative to the aircraft's track, with 12 o'clock straight ahead. On a heading of 090, 3 o'clock is 90 degrees to the right, which is 090 plus 90 or 180, so the pilot looks south. Westbound only tells you the other aircraft's direction of travel, not where it is.

stem: An ATC radar facility issues the following advisory to a pilot flying on a heading of 360°: "TRAFFIC 10 O'CLOCK, 2 MILES, SOUTHBOUND..." Where should the pilot look for this traffic?
options: Northwest.
Northeast.
Southwest.
explanation: 10 o'clock is 60 degrees left of the nose, so on a heading of 360 the traffic bears 360 minus 60, or 300 degrees, which is northwest. Southbound describes the traffic's direction of movement, which tempts the southwest choice.

stem: An ATC radar facility issues the following advisory to a pilot during a local flight: "TRAFFIC 2 O'CLOCK, 5 MILES, NORTHBOUND..." Where should the pilot look for this traffic?
options: Between directly ahead and 90° to the left.
Between directly behind and 90° to the right.
Between directly ahead and 90° to the right.
explanation: 2 o'clock is 60 degrees to the right of the nose, which lies between straight ahead and 90 degrees right. The pilot's heading does not matter for this question, and northbound only describes the traffic's direction of movement.

stem: An ATC radar facility issues the following advisory to a pilot flying north in a calm wind: "TRAFFIC 9 O'CLOCK, 2 MILES, SOUTHBOUND..." Where should the pilot look for this traffic?
options: South.
North.
West.
explanation: With calm wind, heading equals track, so flying north the 9 o'clock position is 90 degrees left, or west. Southbound is the traffic's direction of travel, which is the trap behind the south option.

stem: Basic radar service in the terminal radar program is best described as
options: safety alerts, traffic advisories, and limited vectoring to VFR aircraft.
mandatory radar service provided by the Automated Radar Terminal System (ARTS) program.
wind-shear warning at participating airports.
explanation: Basic radar service for VFR aircraft provides safety alerts, traffic advisories and limited vectoring on a workload permitting basis. It is not mandatory, and wind shear warnings are not what defines the service.

stem: From whom should a departing VFR aircraft request radar traffic information during ground operations?
options: Clearance delivery.
Tower, just before takeoff.
Ground control, on initial contact.
explanation: A departing VFR pilot who wants radar traffic information should request it from ground control on initial contact, along with the direction of flight. Waiting until calling the tower just before takeoff is too late to coordinate the service.

stem: TRSA Service in the terminal radar program provides
options: IFR separation (1,000 feet vertical and 3 miles lateral) between all aircraft.
warning to pilots when their aircraft are in unsafe proximity to terrain, obstructions, or other aircraft.
sequencing and separation for participating VFR aircraft.
explanation: In a Terminal Radar Service Area, TRSA service provides sequencing and separation for participating VFR aircraft, in addition to basic radar services. IFR style separation between all aircraft is not provided, and participation is voluntary.

stem: When operating under VFR below 18,000 feet MSL, unless otherwise authorized, what transponder code should be selected?
explanation: Unless ATC assigns another code, VFR aircraft below 18,000 feet MSL squawk 1200. 7600 indicates lost communications and 7700 indicates an emergency.

stem: If Air Traffic Control advises that radar service is terminated when the pilot is departing Class C airspace, the transponder should be set to code
explanation: When radar service is terminated, the pilot returns the transponder to the VFR code 1200 unless told otherwise. 0000 is not a code a pilot should select, and 4096 is the number of available codes, not a code.

stem: As standard operating practice, all inbound traffic to an airport without a control tower should continuously monitor the appropriate facility from a distance of
options: 25 miles.
20 miles.
10 miles.
explanation: The AIM recommends that inbound traffic at a nontowered airport monitor and communicate on the CTAF from 10 miles out. The 20 and 25 mile figures are not in the guidance; 10 miles gives enough time to hear the pattern picture before you arrive.

stem: When an air traffic controller issues radar traffic information in relation to the 12-hour clock, the reference the controller uses is the aircraft's
options: true course.
ground track.
magnetic heading.
explanation: Radar shows where the airplane is actually moving over the ground, so controllers give clock positions relative to your ground track. With a crosswind your nose points somewhere else, so you may need to look a little upwind of the called position. Magnetic heading is the trap; the controller cannot see your heading, only your track.

stem: Absence of the sky condition and visibility on an ATIS broadcast indicates that
options: weather conditions are at or above VFR minimums.
the sky condition is clear and visibility is unrestricted.
the ceiling is at least 5,000 feet and visibility is 5 miles or more.
explanation: When the ATIS leaves out sky condition and visibility, the ceiling is at least 5,000 feet and visibility is 5 miles or more. It does not mean clear skies with unlimited visibility, and it promises more than basic VFR minimums of 1,000 and 3.

stem: When operating under VFR below 18,000 feet MSL, unless otherwise authorized, what transponder code should be selected?
options: Mode 3/A code 1200.
Mode F code 1200.
Mode 3/A code 7700.
explanation: The VFR code is 1200 in Mode 3/A, the civil identity mode. There is no Mode F for this purpose, and 7700 is the emergency code, not a routine VFR setting.

stem: When making routine transponder code changes, pilots should avoid inadvertent selection of which code?
explanation: While you change codes, avoid passing through 7500, 7600 and 7700, because each one sets off an alarm at ATC facilities. Of the choices, only 7600 (lost communications) is a special code; 7200 and 7400 are ordinary discrete codes.

stem: When making routine transponder code changes, pilots should avoid inadvertent selection of which code?
explanation: Code 7500 means unlawful interference (hijack) and triggers an immediate alert, so do not dial through it during routine changes. 7200 and 4000 are ordinary codes with no special meaning to the pilot.

stem: In what controlled airspace are you not required to contact ATC when flying in VMC?
options: TRSA.
Class C.
Class D.
explanation: TRSA service is voluntary for VFR pilots, so you may fly through a TRSA without contacting ATC, although participation is encouraged. Class C requires two way radio communication before entry, and so does Class D, so neither is optional.

stem: Which transponder code should be used when in DISTRESS or for a general EMERGENCY?
explanation: 7700 is the general emergency and distress code. 7600 means lost radio communications and 7500 means unlawful interference, so neither describes a general emergency.

stem: ADS-B-Out equipment is required
options: below the shelf of Class C airspace.
At an airport with a control tower.
In Class E airspace at and above 10,000 feet MSL, excluding airspace at and below 2,500 feet AGL.
explanation: 14 CFR 91.225 requires ADS-B Out in Class E airspace at and above 10,000 feet MSL, excluding the airspace at and below 2,500 feet AGL. Below the shelf of Class C it is required only if you are also inside a Mode C veil, and a towered airport alone creates no requirement.

stem: ADS-B-Out equipment is not required
options: within a Terminal Radar Service Area.
in Class A airspace.
at 9,500 MSL within the lateral confines of Class C airspace.
explanation: A TRSA is not listed in 14 CFR 91.225, so its airspace carries no ADS-B Out requirement of its own. Class A requires it, and so does the airspace above the ceiling and within the lateral boundaries of Class C up to 10,000 feet MSL, which includes 9,500 MSL over a Class C.

stem: Unless otherwise authorized by ATC, which airspace requires the appropriate Automatic Dependent Surveillance-Broadcast (ADS-B) Out equipment installed?
options: Within Class E airspace below the upper shelf of Class C Airspace.
Above the ceiling and within the lateral boundaries of Class D airspace up to 10,000 feet MSL.
Within Class G airspace 25 nautical miles from a Class B airport.
explanation: The Mode C veil extends 30 NM around the primary Class B airport, from the surface to 10,000 feet MSL, and the ADS-B rule applies there whatever the airspace class, so Class G within 25 NM is covered. The above the ceiling rule is for Class C, not Class D, and Class E under a Class C shelf needs it only if a veil also covers it.

stem: (Refer to Figure 20.) What is your approximate position on low altitude airway Victor 1, southwest of Norfolk (area 1), if the VOR receiver indicates you are on the 340° radial of Elizabeth City VOR (area 3)?
options: 15 nautical miles from Norfolk VORTAC.
18 nautical miles from Norfolk VORTAC.
23 nautical miles from Norfolk VORTAC.
explanation: Draw the 340 radial north from the Elizabeth City VOR using its compass rose, and follow V1 southwest from the Norfolk VORTAC (about the 233 radial). The two lines cross about 17 NM from Norfolk on the chart's nautical mile scale, so 18 NM is the best answer. 15 NM and 23 NM put the fix too close to and too far from Norfolk along the airway.

stem: (Refer to Figure 20, area 3; and Figure 28.) The VOR is tuned to Elizabeth City VOR, and the aircraft is positioned over Shawboro. Which VOR indication is correct?
explanation: Shawboro bears about 030 magnetic from the Elizabeth City VOR, so the airplane is on the 030 radial. Illustration 9 shows 030 set, a FROM flag and a centered needle, which is exactly that radial.
