Illustration 8 has 030 with TO, which would place you on the 210 radial on the opposite side of the station.

stem: (Refer to Figure 21.) What course should be selected on the omnibearing selector (OBS) to make a direct flight from Mercer County Regional Airport (area 3) to the Minot VORTAC (area 1) with a TO indication?
explanation: Lay a line from Mercer County Regional to the Minot VORTAC and read it against the Minot compass rose, which is already aligned to magnetic north: the line runs about 359. Set 359 and you get a TO flag while flying to the station. 179 is the reciprocal and would show FROM, and 001 comes from applying the variation wrongly.

stem: (Refer to Figure 23.) What is the approximate position of the aircraft if the VOR receivers indicate the 320° radial of Savannah VORTAC (area 3) and the 191° radial of Allendale VOR (area 1)?
options: Briggs private airfield.
Town of Guyton.
3 miles east of Blirchton.
explanation: Plot each radial off its own compass rose: the 320 radial runs northwest from Savannah, and the 191 radial runs south from Allendale. They cross about 1 NM from the Briggs private airfield. The town of Guyton is about 2 NM northeast of the fix, so it is the near miss.

stem: (Refer to Figure 23.) On what course should the VOR receiver (OBS) be set to navigate direct from Hampton Varnville Airport (area 1) to Savannah VORTAC (area 3)?
explanation: A line from Hampton Varnville to the Savannah VORTAC, read against the Savannah compass rose, runs about 194 magnetic, so 196 is the closest choice. Set 196 for a TO indication. 016 is the reciprocal and would show FROM, and 200 is too far west of the measured line.

stem: (Refer to Figure 24.) What is the approximate position of the aircraft if the VOR receivers indicate the 245° radial of Sulphur Springs VOR-DME (area 5) and the 145° radial of Bonham VORTAC (area 3)?
options: Meadowview Airport.
Glenmar Airport.
Majors Airport.
explanation: With about 5 to 6 degrees east variation, the 145 radial of Bonham and the 245 radial of Sulphur Springs cross about 1 NM from the Glenmar private airport, east of Greenville. Majors Airport is about 6 NM west of the fix, so it is the tempting but wrong pick.

stem: (Refer to Figure 24.) On what course should the VOR receiver (OBS) be set in order to navigate direct from Majors Airport (area 1) to Quitman VORTAC (area 2)?
explanation: The true course from Majors to Quitman VORTAC measures about 105, and the Quitman rose shows about 6 degrees east variation, so the magnetic course is about 099, which rounds to 100. Set 100 with a TO flag. 280 is the reciprocal and would read FROM.

stem: (Refer to Figures 24 and 28.) The VOR is tuned to Bonham VORTAC (area 3), and the aircraft is positioned over the town of Sulphur Springs (area 5). Which VOR indication is correct?
explanation: The town of Sulphur Springs lies on about the 120 radial of Bonham. With 030 set the airplane is abeam the station, so the flag goes blank, and because the airplane is southeast of the 030 course line the needle deflects left. That is illustration 7. Illustration 8 (030 TO, centered) would put you on the 210 radial.

stem: (Refer to Figure 25, area 5.) The VOR is tuned to the Maverick VOR/DME. The omnibearing selector (OBS) is set on 253°, with a TO indication, and a right course deviation indicator (CDI) deflection. What is the aircraft's position from the VORTAC?
options: East-northeast.
North-northeast.
West-southwest.
explanation: A TO indication with 253 set means the station lies roughly 253 from you, so you are on the 073 side, east northeast of the VOR. The right deflection only says you are slightly off that radial, not on another side of the station. West southwest would produce a FROM flag with 253 set.

stem: (Refer to Figure 26, areas 4 and 2; and Figure 28.) The VOR is tuned to Jamestown VOR, and the aircraft is positioned over the town of Cooperstown. Which VOR indication is correct?
explanation: Measured against the Jamestown compass rose, Cooperstown lies on about the 027 radial. With 210 set and a TO flag, a centered needle would mean the 030 radial; being 3 degrees counterclockwise of it puts the course line to your left, so the needle sits a little over one dot left (2 degrees per dot). That is illustration 4. Illustration 5 is the near miss because it is centered on 030, and illustration 1 deflects the wrong way.

stem: (Refer to Figure 28, illustration 4.) The VOR receiver has the indications shown. What is the aircraft's position relative to the station?
options: North.
East.
South.
explanation: Illustration 4 shows 210 set with a TO flag, so you are on the northeast side of the station, and the needle is deflected left. Flying 210, the course line is then to your left (southeast), which puts you northwest of the 030 radial, north of the station. South would give a FROM flag with 210 set.

stem: (Refer to Figure 28, illustration 7.) The VOR receiver has the indications shown. What is the aircraft's position relative to the station?
options: East.
Southeast.
West.
explanation: Illustration 7 shows 030 set with no TO or FROM flag, so the airplane is abeam the station on the 120 or 300 radial. The needle is deflected left, so the 030 course lies to the northwest and you are on the southeast side. West would need the needle deflected right.

stem: (Refer to Figure 28, illustration 5.) The VOR receiver has the indications shown. What radial is the aircraft crossing?
explanation: Illustration 5 shows 210 set, a TO flag and a centered needle, so flying 210 takes you to the station and you are on the reciprocal, the 030 radial. 210 would require a FROM flag.

stem: (Refer to Figure 25, area 5.) The navigation facility at Dallas-Ft. Worth International (DFW) is a
options: VOR.
VOR/DME.
VORTAC.
explanation: The symbol beside the DFW runways is a hexagon with a dot inside a square, the chart symbol for a VOR/DME. A VORTAC would show the hexagon with three tabs, and a plain VOR is the hexagon alone.

stem: How many satellites make up the Global Positioning System (GPS)?
explanation: The GPS baseline constellation is 24 satellites in six orbital planes, which is the number the FAA wants. The US normally keeps about 31 operating satellites today, but the design baseline the question asks about is still 24.

stem: What is the minimum number of Global Positioning System (GPS) satellites that are observable by a user anywhere on earth?
explanation: The constellation is arranged so that at least five satellites are in view from any point on earth. Four is the minimum needed for a three dimensional fix, which makes it the tempting trap, and five allows RAIM fault detection.

stem: How many Global Positioning System (GPS) satellites are required to yield a three dimensional position (latitude, longitude, and altitude) and time solution?
explanation: A receiver solves for four unknowns (latitude, longitude, altitude and receiver clock error), so it needs four satellites. Five lets the receiver run RAIM integrity checks, but is not required just for the position solution.

stem: What symbol would indicate a VORTAC location on an airport?
options: A hexagon with a dot in the middle.
A runway configuration with a dot.
A circle with a dot in the center.
explanation: Per the sectional legend, a dot within a hard surfaced runway configuration marks the approximate location of a VOR, VOR DME or VORTAC on the airport. A hexagon with a dot is the standalone VOR symbol, and a plain circle with a dot is not how a VORTAC is charted.

stem: Which of the symbols depicted with a hexagon represents a VOR-DME?
options: A hexagon with a dot in the center and enclosed within a square.
A hexagon with a dot in the middle.
The airport symbol with runway configurations and a dot.
explanation: The VOR-DME symbol is the VOR hexagon with its center dot enclosed in a square. A hexagon with a dot alone is a plain VOR, and the runway outline with a dot only marks a navaid located on an airport.

stem: A VORTAC station is represented by
options: A single dot inside a square.
A single dot inside a hexagon.
A single dot inside a hexagon with tabs on three of the sides.
explanation: A VORTAC is drawn as the VOR hexagon with a dot and solid tabs on three alternating sides. A dot inside a hexagon alone is just a VOR, and the square around a dot belongs to the VOR-DME symbol.

stem: A GPS with an expired database may be used
options: under no circumstances.
only on the ground for taxi.
under VFR flight for situational awareness.
explanation: Under VFR, a GPS with an expired database can still be used, but only as an aid to situational awareness. You must confirm waypoints and frequencies against current charts. Under no circumstances is too strict for VFR, while IFR navigation generally does require a current database.

stem: (Refer to Figure 25, area 5.) The VOR is tuned to the Ranger VORTAC. The omnibearing selector (OBS) is set on 256°, with a TO indication, and a left course deviation indicator (CDI) deflection. What is the aircraft's position from the VORTAC?
options: East-Northeast.
East-Southeast.
West-Northwest.
explanation: With 256 set and a TO flag, the station is ahead on 256, so you are on the 076 side, east of Ranger. A left deflection means the course line is south of you, so you are slightly north of that radial: east northeast. East southeast would need the needle deflected right.

stem: Can a GPS be used as an altimeter?
options: No, there can be too many errors in the vertical height computations of the GPS to rely on it as an altimeter.
Yes, but only if a barometric altimeter is available as a backup.
Yes.
explanation: GPS vertical accuracy is worse than horizontal, and the geometric height it computes is not barometric altitude, which is what ATC, separation and terrain clearance rely on. So a GPS cannot replace the altimeter. Yes with a barometric backup is the trap; the barometric altimeter is primary, not a backup.

stem: When using a VOT to make a VOR receiver check, the CDI should be centered and the OBS should indicate that the aircraft is on the
options: 090 degree radial with a FROM indication.
180 degree radial with a FROM indication.
360 degree radial with a FROM indication.
explanation: A VOT radiates the same 360 radial everywhere, so with the CDI centered the OBS should read 360 FROM (or 180 TO). Readings within plus or minus 4 degrees are acceptable. 090 and 180 FROM are not what a VOT transmits.

stem: While operating in Class D airspace, each pilot of an aircraft approaching to land on a runway served by a visual approach slope indicator (VASI) shall
options: maintain a 3° glide until approximately 1/2 mile to the runway before going below the VASI.
maintain an altitude at or above the glide slope until a lower altitude is necessary for a safe landing.
stay high until the runway can be reached in a power-off landing.
explanation: 14 CFR 91.129(e) requires a pilot approaching a runway served by a visual approach slope indicator to stay at or above the glide slope until a lower altitude is necessary for a safe landing. There is no half mile rule, and staying high enough for a power off landing is not required.

stem: When approaching to land on a runway served by a visual approach slope indicator (VASI), the pilot shall
options: maintain an altitude that captures the glide slope at least 2 miles downwind from the runway threshold.
maintain an altitude at or above the glide slope.
remain on the glide slope and land between the two-light bar.
explanation: The rule is to stay at or above the VASI glide slope until a lower altitude is needed for a safe landing. Nothing requires capturing it 2 miles out, and touching down between the light bars is not the regulatory standard.

stem: Excessively high engine temperatures will
options: cause damage to heat-conducting hoses and warping of the cylinder cooling fins.
cause loss of power, excessive oil consumption, and possible permanent internal engine damage.
not appreciably affect an aircraft engine.
explanation: Excessive engine heat breaks down the oil and can cause detonation. The result is loss of power, high oil consumption and possible permanent internal damage such as scored cylinders. Damage to hoses and fins is not the primary concern, and high temperatures certainly affect the engine.

stem: If the engine oil temperature and cylinder head temperature gauges have exceeded their normal operating range, the pilot may have been operating with
options: the mixture set too rich.
higher-than-normal oil pressure.
too much power and with the mixture set too lean.
explanation: High power settings make more heat, and a lean mixture removes the cooling effect of extra fuel, so both push oil and cylinder head temperatures up. A rich mixture does the opposite and cools the engine, and higher oil pressure is not a cause of overheating.

stem: One purpose of the dual ignition system on an aircraft engine is to provide for
options: improved engine performance.
uniform heat distribution.
balanced cylinder head pressure.
explanation: Two magnetos, each firing its own spark plug in every cylinder, give redundancy and a more complete, even burn that improves engine performance. Dual ignition does not distribute heat or balance cylinder pressure.

stem: On aircraft equipped with fuel pumps, when is the auxiliary electric driven pump used?
options: In the event engine-driven fuel pump fails.
All the time to aid the engine-driven fuel pump.
Constantly except in starting the engine.
explanation: The auxiliary electric pump is a backup in case the engine driven pump fails, and many POHs also call for it during takeoff and landing. It is not meant to run all the time alongside the engine driven pump.

stem: The operating principle of float-type carburetors is based on the
options: automatic metering of air at the venturi as the aircraft gains altitude.
difference in air pressure at the venturi throat and the air inlet.
increase in air velocity in the throat of a venturi causing an increase in air pressure.
explanation: Air speeding up through the venturi drops in pressure, and the difference between that low pressure and the higher pressure at the air inlet draws fuel from the float bowl. The trap says velocity raises pressure; Bernoulli says it lowers it. A float type carburetor does not automatically meter for altitude, which is why there is a mixture control.

stem: The basic purpose of adjusting the fuel/air mixture at altitude is to
options: decrease the amount of fuel in the mixture in order to compensate for increased air density.
decrease the fuel flow in order to compensate for decreased air density.
increase the amount of fuel in the mixture to compensate for the decrease in pressure and density of the air.
explanation: As you climb, air density drops while the carburetor keeps sending the same fuel, so the mixture gets richer. Leaning reduces fuel flow to match the thinner air. Density does not increase with altitude, and adding fuel would make the over rich condition worse.

stem: During the run-up at a high-elevation airport, a pilot notes a slight engine roughness that is not affected by the magneto check but grows worse during the carburetor heat check. Under these circumstances, what would be the most logical initial action?
options: Check the results obtained with a leaner setting of the mixture.
Taxi back to the flight line for a maintenance check.
Reduce manifold pressure to control detonation.
explanation: At a high elevation airport the mixture is already rich because the air is thin, and carburetor heat adds warmer, thinner air, which makes it richer still and worse. Roughness that grows with carb heat but not with the magneto check points to an over rich mixture, so try leaning first. Detonation is not the issue here.

stem: While cruising at 9,500 feet MSL, the fuel/air mixture is properly adjusted. What will occur if a descent to 4,500 feet MSL is made without readjusting the mixture?
options: The fuel/air mixture may become excessively lean.
There will be more fuel in the cylinders than is needed for normal combustion, and the excess fuel will absorb heat and cool the engine.
The excessively rich mixture will create higher cylinder head temperatures and may cause detonation.
explanation: In a descent the air gets denser while the fuel flow stays where you set it, so a mixture leaned for 9,500 feet becomes too lean lower down. Enrich as you descend. The other options assume the mixture gets richer, which is backwards.

stem: Which condition is most favorable to the development of carburetor icing?
options: Any temperature below freezing and a relative humidity of less than 50 percent.
Temperature between 32 and 50 °F and low humidity.
Temperature between 20 and 70 °F and high humidity.
explanation: Carburetor ice is most likely between about 20 and 70 °F with high humidity. Fuel vaporization and the venturi pressure drop can cool the air by as much as 60 °F in a fraction of a second, which freezes the moisture. Low humidity removes the water needed for ice, so the other choices fail.

stem: Applying carburetor heat will
options: result in more air going through the carburetor.
enrich the fuel/air mixture.
not affect the fuel/air mixture.
explanation: Heated air is less dense, but the carburetor meters fuel by volume of airflow, so the same fuel goes into less air mass and the mixture becomes richer. Carb heat does not increase airflow, and it clearly does affect the mixture.

stem: What change occurs in the fuel/air mixture when carburetor heat is applied?
options: A decrease in RPM results from the lean mixture.
The fuel/air mixture becomes richer.
The fuel/air mixture becomes leaner.
explanation: Carb heat brings in warmer, less dense air while fuel flow stays about the same, so the mixture becomes richer. The RPM drop you see comes from the lower air density and the rich mixture, not from leaning.

stem: Generally speaking, the use of carburetor heat tends to
options: decrease engine performance.
increase engine performance.
have no effect on engine performance.
explanation: Warm air is less dense, so applying carb heat cuts the mass of air reaching the cylinders and richens the mixture, both of which reduce power. That is why carb heat is not used for takeoff unless the POH says otherwise.

stem: The presence of carburetor ice in an aircraft equipped with a fixed-pitch propeller can be verified by applying carburetor heat and noting
options: an increase in RPM and then a gradual decrease in RPM.
a decrease in RPM and then a constant RPM indication.
a decrease in RPM and then a gradual increase in RPM.
explanation: With a fixed pitch propeller, applying carb heat first drops RPM because of the less dense air. If ice is present, the RPM then rises gradually as the ice melts. A drop and then steady RPM means there was no ice, and an initial rise is not what carb heat does.

stem: If the grade of fuel used in an aircraft engine is lower than specified for the engine, it will most likely cause
options: a mixture of fuel and air that is not uniform in all cylinders.
lower cylinder head temperatures.
detonation.
explanation: Lower grade fuel has less resistance to knock, so the charge can explode in the cylinder instead of burning smoothly, which is detonation. It also raises, not lowers, cylinder head temperatures.

stem: Detonation occurs in a reciprocating aircraft engine when
options: the spark plugs are fouled or shorted out or the wiring is defective.
hot spots in the combustion chamber ignite the fuel/air mixture in advance of normal ignition.
the unburned charge in the cylinders explodes instead of burning normally.
explanation: Detonation is the unburned charge exploding instead of burning progressively after the spark. Hot spots igniting the mixture before the spark describe preignition, the main trap, and fouled plugs cause misfiring, not detonation.

stem: If a pilot suspects that the engine (with a fixed-pitch propeller) is detonating during climb-out after takeoff, the initial corrective action to take would be to
options: lean the mixture.
lower the nose slightly to increase airspeed.
apply carburetor heat.
explanation: Lowering the nose slightly increases airspeed and cooling airflow, which reduces cylinder temperatures and pressures; enriching the mixture and reducing power also help. Leaning makes detonation worse, and carburetor heat adds hot air and makes it worse too.

stem: The uncontrolled firing of the fuel/air charge in advance of normal spark ignition is known as
options: combustion.
pre-ignition.
detonation.
explanation: Preignition is uncontrolled ignition of the charge before the normal spark, usually from a hot spot such as carbon deposits or an overheated plug. Detonation is the explosive burning that happens after ignition, so it is the near miss.

stem: Which would most likely cause the cylinder head temperature and engine oil temperature gauges to exceed their normal operating ranges?
options: Using fuel that has a lower-than-specified fuel rating.
Using fuel that has a higher-than-specified fuel rating.
Operating with higher-than-normal oil pressure.
explanation: Fuel with a lower than specified rating burns hotter and is prone to detonation, which drives cylinder head and oil temperatures up. Higher grade fuel will not cause overheating, and higher oil pressure is not a cause of high temperatures.

stem: Filling the fuel tanks after the last flight of the day is considered a good operating procedure because this will
options: force any existing water to the top of the tank away from the fuel lines to the engine.
prevent expansion of the fuel by eliminating airspace in the tanks.
prevent moisture condensation by eliminating airspace in the tanks.
explanation: A full tank leaves little airspace, so less moist air can condense into water overnight as it cools. Water is heavier than fuel and sinks rather than rising, and full tanks can actually overflow when the fuel expands.

stem: For internal cooling, reciprocating aircraft engines are especially dependent on
options: a properly functioning thermostat.
air flowing over the exhaust manifold.
the circulation of lubricating oil.
explanation: Besides lubricating, the oil carries heat away from internal parts the cooling air cannot reach, such as pistons and bearings. Air cooled aircraft engines have no thermostat like a car, and airflow over the exhaust does not cool the inside of the engine.

stem: An abnormally high engine oil temperature indication may be caused by
options: the oil level being too low.
operating with a too high viscosity oil.
operating with an excessively rich mixture.
explanation: With too little oil there is less volume to absorb and carry away heat, so oil temperature climbs. A high viscosity oil is not the usual cause, and a rich mixture tends to cool the engine.

stem: When taxiing with strong quartering tailwinds, which aileron positions should be used?
options: Aileron down on the downwind side.
Ailerons neutral.
Aileron down on the side from which the wind is blowing.
explanation: With a quartering tailwind, "dive away from the wind": elevator down, and the aileron on the upwind side down, so the yoke turns away from the wind. That keeps the wind from lifting the upwind wing from behind. Neutral ailerons give no protection, and aileron down on the downwind side is the quartering headwind position.

stem: Which aileron positions should a pilot generally use when taxiing in strong quartering headwinds?
options: Aileron up on the side from which the wind is blowing.
Aileron down on the side from which the wind is blowing.
Ailerons neutral.
explanation: In a quartering headwind, turn the yoke into the wind so the aileron on the upwind side is up, which keeps that wing from lifting. Aileron down on the windward side would help the wind raise that wing.

stem: Which wind condition would be most critical when taxiing a nosewheel equipped high-wing airplane?
options: Quartering tailwind.
Direct crosswind.
Quartering headwind.
explanation: A quartering tailwind is the most critical for a high wing tricycle gear airplane, because the wind can get under the upwind wing and tail from behind and tip the airplane over on its nose and wing. A headwind or direct crosswind is easier to counter with controls.

stem: (Refer to Figure 9, area A.) How should the flight controls be held while taxiing a tricycle-gear equipped airplane into a left quartering headwind?
options: Left aileron up, elevator neutral.
Left aileron down, elevator neutral.
Left aileron up, elevator down.
explanation: For a left quartering headwind in a tricycle gear airplane, turn the yoke left so the left aileron is up and hold the elevator neutral. Area A of the figure shows this. A tailwheel airplane would hold elevator up, and elevator down applies only to tailwinds.

stem: (Refer to Figure 9, area B.) How should the flight controls be held while taxiing a tailwheel airplane into a right quartering headwind?
options: Right aileron up, elevator up.
Right aileron down, elevator neutral.
Right aileron up, elevator down.
explanation: In a tailwheel airplane taxiing into a right quartering headwind, turn the yoke right so the right aileron is up, and hold the elevator up to keep the tail down. Elevator neutral is the tricycle gear technique, and elevator down is for tailwinds.

stem: (Refer to Figure 9, area C.) How should the flight controls be held while taxiing a tailwheel airplane with a left quartering tailwind?
options: Left aileron up, elevator neutral.
Left aileron down, elevator neutral.
Left aileron down, elevator down.
explanation: With a left quartering tailwind, dive away from the wind: turn the yoke right so the left (upwind) aileron is down, and push the elevator down so the wind cannot get under the tail. Tailwheel and tricycle airplanes use the same tailwind technique. Aileron up on the windward side is the headwind setting.

stem: (Refer to Figure 9, area C.) How should the flight controls be held while taxiing a tricycle-gear equipped airplane with a left quartering tailwind?
options: Left aileron up, elevator neutral.
Left aileron down, elevator down.
Left aileron up, elevator down.
explanation: For a quartering tailwind from the left, put the left aileron down (yoke turned away from the wind) and the elevator down, which keeps the wind from lifting the left wing and tail. Left aileron up is for a left headwind, and the third option mixes the two.

stem: (Refer to Figure 24, area 1.) For information about the parachute jumping at Caddo Mills Airport, refer to
options: notes on the border of the chart.
the Chart Supplement.
the Notices to Airmen (NOTAM) publication.
explanation: The parachute symbol on the sectional only flags a jump area; details such as times and altitudes are in the Chart Supplement, which used to be the Airport/Facility Directory. The chart border notes do not cover jump operations, and NOTAMs carry only temporary changes.

stem: What action can a pilot take to aid in cooling an engine that is overheating during a climb?
options: Reduce rate of climb and increase airspeed.
Reduce climb speed and increase RPM.
Increase climb speed and increase RPM.
explanation: Climbing at a shallower angle with more airspeed sends more cooling air through the cowling and lowers cylinder temperatures. Reducing climb speed cuts cooling airflow, and increasing RPM adds heat, so both make overheating worse.

stem: What is one procedure to aid in cooling an engine that is overheating?
options: Enrichen the fuel mixture.
Increase the RPM.
Reduce the airspeed.
explanation: Enriching the mixture adds fuel that absorbs heat as it evaporates, which helps cool the cylinders. Raising RPM makes more heat, and lowering airspeed cuts cooling airflow.

stem: How is engine operation controlled on an engine equipped with a constant-speed propeller?
options: The throttle controls power output as registered on the manifold pressure gauge and the propeller control regulates engine RPM.
The throttle controls power output as registered on the manifold pressure gauge and the propeller control regulates a constant blade angle.
The throttle controls engine RPM as registered on the tachometer and the mixture control regulates the power output.
explanation: With a constant speed propeller, the throttle sets power, read on the manifold pressure gauge, and the propeller control sets the RPM, which the governor holds by changing blade angle automatically. The propeller control does not fix a blade angle, and the mixture does not set power output.

stem: What is an advantage of a constant-speed propeller?
options: Permits the pilot to select and maintain a desired cruising speed.
Permits the pilot to select the blade angle for the most efficient performance.
Provides a smoother operation with stable RPM and eliminates vibrations.
explanation: A constant speed propeller lets the pilot choose the blade angle, through the RPM setting, that is most efficient for each phase of flight, such as fine pitch for takeoff and coarser pitch for cruise. It does not directly select airspeed, and smoothness is a side benefit, not the main advantage.

stem: A precaution for the operation of an engine equipped with a constant-speed propeller is to
options: avoid high RPM settings with high manifold pressure.
avoid high manifold pressure settings with low RPM.
always use a rich mixture with high RPM settings.
explanation: High manifold pressure combined with low RPM can overstress the cylinders and promote detonation. Generally reduce manifold pressure before RPM, and increase RPM before manifold pressure. High RPM with high manifold pressure is normal takeoff power, and the mixture rule offered is not the precaution.

stem: What should be the first action after starting an aircraft engine?
options: Adjust for proper RPM and check for desired indications on the engine gauges.
Place the magneto or ignition switch momentarily in the OFF position to check for proper grounding.
Test each brake and the parking brake.
explanation: Right after start, set the recommended RPM and check the engine gauges, especially oil pressure, which should rise within about 30 seconds. A magneto grounding check is done just before shutdown, and brakes are tested as you begin to taxi.

stem: Should it become necessary to handprop an airplane engine, it is extremely important that a competent pilot
options: call "contact" before touching the propeller.
be at the controls in the cockpit.
be in the cockpit and call out all commands.
explanation: Hand propping needs a competent pilot at the controls in the cockpit to hold the brakes, manage the throttle and respond to the person at the propeller. Calling "contact" before touching the propeller is backwards; the person at the propeller gives the commands, so calling out all commands from the cockpit is also wrong.

stem: During the preflight inspection who is responsible for determining the aircraft is safe for flight?
options: The owner or operator.
The pilot in command.
The certificated mechanic who performed the annual inspection.
explanation: Under 14 CFR 91.7 the pilot in command is responsible for determining whether the aircraft is in condition for safe flight. The owner or operator is responsible for maintaining airworthiness, and the mechanic who signed the annual is responsible for that inspection, not for today's flight.

stem: How should an aircraft preflight inspection be accomplished for the first flight of the day?
options: Thorough and systematic means recommended by the manufacturer.
Quick walk around with a check of gas and oil.
Any sequence as determined by the pilot-in-command.
explanation: The first flight of the day calls for a thorough, systematic inspection following the manufacturer's checklist. A quick walk around misses problems, and an arbitrary sequence invites skipped items.

stem: FAA advisory circulars (some free, others at cost) are available to all pilots and are obtained by
options: distribution from the nearest FAA district office.
ordering those desired from the Government Printing Office.
subscribing to the Federal Register.
explanation: The FAA intended answer is ordering from the Government Printing Office. Today every current advisory circular is free to view and download from the FAA's online advisory circular library, so you no longer need to order them. They were never distributed by FAA district offices or carried in the Federal Register.
note: ACs are now free online from faa.gov; GPO ordering is obsolete.

stem: The most important rule to remember in the event of a power failure after becoming airborne is to
options: immediately establish the proper gliding attitude and airspeed.
quickly check the fuel supply for possible fuel exhaustion.
determine the wind direction to plan for the forced landing.
explanation: First fly the airplane: immediately pitch for best glide speed so you keep your energy and buy time. Checking fuel and judging the wind come right after, but delaying the glide attitude can cost altitude or lead to a stall.

stem: What is the most effective way to use the eyes during night flight?
options: Look only at far away, dim lights.
Scan slowly to permit offcenter viewing.
Concentrate directly on each object for a few seconds.
explanation: At night the cones in the center of the retina are poor at low light, so an object looked at directly can disappear. Looking about 10 degrees off center puts the image on the rod cells, and a slow scan with short stops gives the rods time to register it. Staring straight at an object for several seconds is the trap: it uses the night blind spot and invites the object to fade.

stem: The best method to use when looking for other traffic at night is to
options: look to the side of the object and scan slowly.
scan the visual field very rapidly.
look to the side of the object and scan rapidly.
explanation: Rods, which do the work at night, sit around the edge of the retina, so traffic is seen best by looking slightly to the side of where it is. The scan must be slow because rods need a moment to detect a dim light. Scanning rapidly, even while looking off center, sweeps past lights before the eye can pick them up.

stem: The most effective method of scanning for other aircraft for collision avoidance during nighttime hours is to use
options: regularly spaced concentration on the 3-, 9-, and 12-o'clock positions.
a series of short, regularly spaced eye movements to search each 30-degree sector.
peripheral vision by scanning small sectors and utilizing off-center viewing.
explanation: Night scanning relies on peripheral, off center viewing, moving through small sectors so the rods can detect dim lights. The short, regularly spaced eye movements through 10 degree sectors are the daytime technique built around central vision, and this option even misstates the sector size as 30 degrees. Fixing on a few clock positions leaves most of the sky unchecked.

stem: Airport taxiway edge lights are identified at night by
options: white directional lights.
blue omnidirectional lights.
alternate red and green lights.
explanation: Taxiway edge lights are blue and omnidirectional, outlining the edges of taxiways at night and in low visibility. White lights mark runway edges, and green taxiway centerline lights are a different system. Alternating red and green does not describe any taxiway edge lighting.

stem: VFR approaches to land at night should be accomplished
options: at a higher airspeed.
with a steeper descent.
the same as during daytime.
explanation: A night approach and landing should be flown with the same pattern, airspeeds and descent path used in daylight. Fewer visual cues make it tempting to change technique, but a higher speed only lengthens the float and the landing, and a steeper descent removes the margin above unlit obstacles. Consistency, plus use of any visual glide slope lighting, is the safe method.
ref: Airplane Flying Handbook, Night Operations chapter

stem: A slightly high glide slope indication from a precision approach path indicator is
options: four white lights.
three white lights and one red light.
two white lights and two red lights.
explanation: A four light PAPI shows two white and two red when on the glide path. Each additional white light means higher, so three white and one red is slightly high and four white is well above the path. The two white and two red option is the on path picture, not slightly high.

stem: A below glide slope indication from a pulsating approach slope indicator is a
options: pulsating white light.
steady white light.
pulsating red light.
explanation: A pulsating visual approach slope indicator shows a steady white light (or alternating red and white) on the glide path and a pulsating white light above it. Slightly below the path the light turns steady red, and further below it begins to pulsate red, so pulsating red is the below glide slope signal among these options. The pulse rate increases the further the aircraft is from the path. A steady white light is the on path signal, so it is the most common wrong pick.

stem: (Refer to Figure 47.) Illustration A indicates that the aircraft is
options: below the glide slope.
on the glide slope.
above the glide slope.
explanation: Illustration A shows red over white on each side of a two bar VASI: the far bar red and the near bar white. That combination means the aircraft is on the glide path. Below the path both bars would show red, and above it both would show white.

stem: (Refer to Figure 47.) VASI lights as shown by illustration C indicate that the airplane is
options: off course to the left.
above the glide slope.
below the glide slope.
explanation: In illustration C both bars of the two bar VASI show white, which means the airplane is above the glide path. A VASI gives vertical guidance only, so it cannot show being off course left or right. Both bars red would mean below the path.

stem: (Refer to Figure 47.) While on final approach to a runway equipped with a standard 2-bar VASI, the lights appear as shown by illustration D. This means that the aircraft is
options: above the glide slope.
below the glide slope.
on the glide slope.
explanation: Illustration D shows all red on both bars of the two bar VASI, the below glide path indication, often remembered as red over red, you are dead. On the glide path the far bar is red and the near bar white. All white would mean above the path.

stem: To set the high intensity runway lights on medium intensity, the pilot should click the microphone seven times, and then click it
options: one time within 4 seconds.
three times within 3 seconds.
five times within 5 seconds.
explanation: With pilot controlled lighting, keying the microphone seven times within 5 seconds selects the highest intensity, five times within 5 seconds selects medium, and three times within 5 seconds selects low. So after the seven clicks, five clicks within 5 seconds sets medium intensity. Three clicks is the trap: it would set the lights to low.

stem: (Refer to Figure 48.) According to the airport diagram, which statement is true?
options: Runway 30 is equipped at position E with emergency arresting gear to provide a means of stopping military aircraft.
Takeoffs may be started at position A on Runway 12, and the landing portion of this runway begins at position B.
The takeoff and landing portion of Runway 12 begins at position B.
explanation: Position A is marked with arrows leading to a threshold bar, which identifies a displaced threshold. The pavement before the displaced threshold may be used for taxi, takeoff and rollout in the opposite direction, so a takeoff may begin at A, while landings on Runway 12 begin at the threshold at position B. The chevrons at E mark a blast pad or stopway, not arresting gear.

stem: (Refer to Figure 48.) What is the difference between area A and area E on the airport depicted?
options: "A" may be used for taxi and takeoff; "E" may be used only as an overrun.
"A" may be used for all operations except heavy aircraft landings; "E" may be used only as an overrun.
"A" may be used only for taxiing; "E" may be used for all operations except landings.
explanation: Area A is the displaced threshold portion of the runway, usable for taxi and takeoff but not for landing in that direction. Area E carries yellow chevrons, marking a blast pad or stopway that is not usable for taxi, takeoff or landing and serves only as an overrun. Treating A as a taxi only area, or giving E landing privileges, misreads the markings.

stem: (Refer to Figure 48.) Area C on the airport depicted is classified as a
options: stabilized area.
multiple heliport.
closed runway.
explanation: Area C carries large X markings at its ends, the standard marking for a closed runway or taxiway. A stabilized area would carry yellow chevrons, and a heliport is marked with an H. Closed pavement should not be used for any operation.

stem: (Refer to Figure 49.) The arrows that appear on the end of the north/south runway indicate that the area
options: may be used only for taxiing.
is usable for taxiing, takeoff, and landing.
cannot be used for landing, but may be used for taxiing and takeoff.
explanation: The arrows leading to a threshold bar on each end of Runway 18 and 36 mark displaced thresholds. That pavement may be used for taxiing and takeoff, and for rollout from the other direction, but not for landing. Calling it taxi only is the common trap; takeoffs from the displaced area are permitted.

stem: The numbers 9 and 27 on a runway indicate that the runway is oriented approximately
options: 009° and 027° true.
090° and 270° true.
090° and 270° magnetic.
explanation: Runway numbers are the magnetic direction of the runway rounded to the nearest 10 degrees with the last zero dropped. Runway 9 is about 090 degrees magnetic and Runway 27 about 270 degrees magnetic. They are not true headings, because pilots compare them with the magnetic compass and heading indicator.

stem: (Refer to Figure 49.) Select the proper traffic pattern and runway for landing.
options: Left-hand traffic and Runway 18.
Right-hand traffic and Runway 18.
Left-hand traffic and Runway 22.
explanation: Runway 22 is closed, shown by the X at each end, so the choice is between 18 and 36. The tetrahedron points into a southwest wind (about 224 degrees measured from the figure), which is 44 degrees off Runway 18 and gives it a headwind, while 36 would have a tailwind. The traffic pattern indicator at the north end of the segmented circle shows the base leg to the west, which is right hand traffic for Runway 18. Runway 22 looks ideal for the wind, but it is closed.

stem: (Refer to Figure 49.) If the wind is as shown by the landing direction indicator, the pilot should land on
options: Runway 18 and expect a crosswind from the right.
Runway 22 directly into the wind.
Runway 36 and expect a crosswind from the right.
explanation: The tetrahedron points into the wind, here toward the southwest at about 224 degrees. Runway 22 would be into the wind but it is marked closed, so Runway 18 is the usable choice. Landing on a heading of 180 with wind from about 224, the wind comes 44 degrees from the right, giving a right crosswind with a headwind component. Runway 36 would mean a tailwind.

stem: (Refer to Figure 50.) The segmented circle indicates that the airport traffic is
options: left-hand for Runway 36 and right-hand for Runway 18.
left-hand for Runway 18 and right-hand for Runway 36.
right-hand for Runway 9 and left-hand for Runway 27.
explanation: Each L shaped traffic pattern indicator shows the base and final legs for one runway end. The indicators for both ends of Runway 18 and 36 put the base leg on the west side: landing north on 36 that is a left turn, and landing south on 18 that is a right turn. So traffic is left hand for 36 and right hand for 18; the reversed option is the trap.

stem: (Refer to Figure 50.) The traffic patterns indicated in the segmented circle have been arranged to avoid flights over an area to the
options: south of the airport.
north of the airport.
southeast of the airport.
explanation: Working through all four indicators: Runway 36 is left hand, 18 right hand, 9 left hand and 27 right hand. Every one of those patterns lies on the north or west side of the field. The patterns therefore avoid the area to the southeast of the airport.

stem: (Refer to Figure 50.) The segmented circle indicates that a landing on Runway 27 will be with a
options: right-quartering headwind.
left-quartering headwind.
right-quartering tailwind.
explanation: The wind cone streams toward the southeast, so the wind blows from the northwest at about 300 degrees. Landing on Runway 27 means a heading of about 270, so the wind is 30 degrees to the right of the nose, a right quartering headwind (headwind component cos 30 = 0.87 of the wind). A left quartering headwind would need wind from the southwest.

stem: (Refer to Figure 50.) Which runway and traffic pattern should be used as indicated by the wind cone in the segmented circle?
options: Right-hand traffic on Runway 9.
Right-hand traffic on Runway 18.
Left-hand traffic on Runway 36.
explanation: The wind cone shows wind from about 300 degrees. Of the runways offered, Runway 36 is 60 degrees off the wind with a headwind component, while Runways 9 and 18 would have tailwinds. The segmented circle shows left hand traffic for Runway 36. Runway 27 fits the wind even better but is not among the options.

stem: How should a VFR flight plan be closed at the completion of the flight at a controlled airport?
options: The tower will automatically close the flight plan when the aircraft turns off the runway.
The pilot must close the flight plan with the nearest FSS outlet or other FAA facility upon landing.
The tower will relay the instructions to the nearest FSS outlet when the aircraft contacts the tower for landing.
explanation: A VFR flight plan stays open until the pilot closes it, even at a towered airport; the tower does not close it on landing or relay it automatically. The pilot must close it with Flight Service or another FAA facility, by radio, phone or approved electronic means. If it is not closed, search and rescue procedures begin about 30 minutes after the estimated arrival time.

stem: Large accumulations of carbon monoxide in the human body result in
options: tightness across the forehead.
loss of muscular power.
an increased sense of well-being.
explanation: Carbon monoxide binds to hemoglobin far more readily than oxygen, so large accumulations starve the body of oxygen and produce loss of muscular power, along with headache, drowsiness and eventually unconsciousness. Tightness across the forehead is an early, mild symptom rather than the result of a large accumulation. An increased sense of well being is associated with hypoxia, not CO buildup.

stem: What effect does haze have on the ability to see traffic or terrain features during flight?
options: Haze causes the eyes to focus at infinity.
The eyes tend to overwork in haze and do not detect relative movement easily.
All traffic or terrain features appear to be farther away than their actual distance.
explanation: Haze reduces contrast, which the brain reads as distance, so traffic and terrain appear farther away than they really are. That illusion can lead a pilot to underestimate how close a hazard is, and on approach it can cause a low approach. The focus option is a trap: in a featureless sky or haze layer the eyes relax to a comfortable focus of only about 10 to 30 feet (empty field myopia), not infinity.

stem: The most effective method of scanning for other aircraft for collision avoidance during daylight hours is to use
options: regularly spaced concentration on the 3-, 9-, and 12-o'clock positions.
a series of short, regularly spaced eye movements to search each 10-degree sector.
peripheral vision by scanning small sectors and utilizing off-center viewing.
explanation: In daylight the most effective scan is a series of short, regularly spaced eye movements that bring successive areas of the sky into the central visual field, each movement covering no more than about 10 degrees with a pause of about a second. Central vision is sharpest in daylight. Off center peripheral viewing is the night technique, which makes it the tempting wrong choice.

stem: Which technique should a pilot use to scan for traffic to the right and left during straight-and-level flight?
options: Systematically focus on different segments of the sky for short intervals.
Concentrate on relative movement detected in the peripheral vision area.
Continuous sweeping of the windshield from right to left.
explanation: Because the eye only detects detail when it pauses, the pilot should systematically focus on successive segments of the sky for short intervals. A continuous sweep across the windshield never lets the eye stop, so small or distant targets are missed. Waiting for movement in peripheral vision fails for a collision course target, which shows little relative motion.

stem: How can you determine if another aircraft is on a collision course with your aircraft?
options: The other aircraft will always appear to get larger and closer at a rapid rate.
The nose of each aircraft is pointed at the same point in space.
There will be no apparent relative motion between your aircraft and the other aircraft.
explanation: An aircraft on a collision course stays in the same spot on the windshield, with no apparent relative motion. It often seems to grow only slowly at first and then very rapidly just before impact, so waiting for it to get obviously larger is a dangerous test. Nose direction says nothing about whether the paths actually meet.

stem: (Refer to Figure 52.) Which type radar service is provided to VFR aircraft at Lincoln Municipal?
options: Sequencing to the primary Class C airport and standard separation.
Sequencing to the primary Class C airport and conflict resolution so that radar targets do not touch, or 1,000 feet vertical separation.
Sequencing to the primary Class C airport, traffic advisories, conflict resolution, and safety alerts.
explanation: The Chart Supplement shows Lincoln in Class C airspace during tower hours. Class C service to VFR aircraft includes sequencing to the primary airport, traffic advisories, conflict resolution between IFR and VFR aircraft, and safety alerts. Standard separation is an IFR to IFR service, and the conflict resolution standard is radar targets not touching or 500 feet vertical, not 1,000 feet.

stem: (Refer to Figure 52.) Traffic patterns in effect at Lincoln Municipal are
options: to the right on Runway 17 and Runway 35; to the left on Runway 18 and Runway 35.
to the left on Runway 17 and Runway 36; to the right on Runway 18 and Runway 35.
to the right on Runways 14 - 32.
explanation: The runway data in the Lincoln entry lists Rgt tfc only for Runway 18 and Runway 35. Every other runway end, including 17 and 36, uses the standard left hand pattern. The first option is self contradictory, putting Runway 35 in both directions.

stem: Which statement best defines hypoxia?
options: A state of oxygen deficiency in the body.
An abnormal increase in the volume of air breathed.
A condition of gas bubble formation around the joints or muscles.
explanation: Hypoxia is a state of oxygen deficiency in the body, enough to impair the brain and other organs. An abnormal increase in the volume of air breathed describes hyperventilation. Gas bubbles around the joints are decompression sickness.

stem: Rapid or extra deep breathing while using oxygen can cause a condition known as
options: hyperventilation.
aerosinusitis.
aerotitis.
explanation: Breathing rapidly or too deeply, even while using oxygen, blows off too much carbon dioxide and causes hyperventilation. Symptoms include tingling, dizziness and lightheadedness that can resemble hypoxia. Aerosinusitis and aerotitis are pressure blocks in the sinuses and middle ear, unrelated to breathing rate.

stem: Which would most likely result in hyperventilation?
options: Emotional tension, anxiety, or fear.
The excessive consumption of alcohol.
An extremely slow rate of breathing and insufficient oxygen.
explanation: Hyperventilation is most often triggered by emotional tension, anxiety or fear, which speed up breathing and reduce carbon dioxide in the blood. A slow breathing rate with insufficient oxygen describes the conditions for hypoxia, the opposite problem. Alcohol impairs judgment but is not a typical cause.

stem: A pilot should be able to overcome the symptoms or avoid future occurrences of hyperventilation by
options: closely monitoring the flight instruments to control the airplane.
slowing the breathing rate, breathing into a bag, or talking aloud.
increasing the breathing rate in order to increase lung ventilation.
explanation: The cure for hyperventilation is to restore carbon dioxide by slowing the breathing rate, breathing into a paper bag, or talking aloud, which naturally slows breathing. Increasing the breathing rate would make it worse. Watching the instruments helps keep control of the airplane but does not treat the condition.

stem: Susceptibility to carbon monoxide poisoning increases as
options: altitude increases.
altitude decreases.
air pressure increases.
explanation: At higher altitude there is less oxygen available, so the hypoxia caused by carbon monoxide is added to altitude hypoxia and the effects appear sooner. Susceptibility therefore increases as altitude increases. Higher air pressure means more oxygen and less susceptibility, the reverse of the trap options.

stem: What preparation should a pilot make to adapt the eyes for night flying?
options: Wear sunglasses after sunset until ready for flight.
Avoid red lights at least 30 minutes before the flight.
Avoid bright white lights at least 30 minutes before the flight.
explanation: The rods need about 30 minutes in darkness to fully adapt, and bright white light destroys that adaptation quickly. A pilot should therefore avoid bright white lights for at least 30 minutes before a night flight. Red light preserves night vision, so avoiding red lights is backwards, and sunglasses after sunset add nothing.

stem: The danger of spatial disorientation during flight in poor visual conditions may be reduced by
options: shifting the eyes quickly between the exterior visual field and the instrument panel.
having faith in the instruments rather than taking a chance on the sensory organs.
leaning the body in the opposite direction of the motion of the aircraft.
explanation: In poor visibility the inner ear and body sensations give false attitude information, so the pilot must trust the flight instruments over those feelings. Rapidly shifting the eyes between outside and inside, or moving the head and body, can worsen the confusion. Instrument training builds the habit of believing the instruments.

stem: A state of temporary confusion resulting from misleading information being sent to the brain by various sensory organs is defined as
options: spatial disorientation.
hyperventilation.
hypoxia.
explanation: Spatial disorientation is the temporary confusion that results when the eyes, inner ear and body sensors send the brain conflicting or misleading information about the aircraft's attitude. Hyperventilation is excessive breathing, and hypoxia is oxygen deficiency. Neither describes a sensory mismatch.

stem: Pilots are more subject to spatial disorientation if
options: they ignore the sensations of muscles and inner ear.
visual cues are taken away, as they are in instrument meteorological conditions (IMC).
eyes are moved often in the process of cross-checking the flight instruments.
explanation: Vision normally overrides false inner ear sensations, so when visual references are removed, as in instrument meteorological conditions, disorientation becomes far more likely. Ignoring body sensations and cross checking the instruments are exactly what prevent it. The cross check option is a trap because frequent eye movement over the instruments is good technique.

stem: If a pilot experiences spatial disorientation during flight in a restricted visibility condition, the best way to overcome the effect is to
options: rely upon the aircraft instrument indications.
concentrate on yaw, pitch, and roll sensations.
consciously slow the breathing rate until symptoms clear and then resume normal breathing rate.
explanation: The way out of spatial disorientation is to rely on the flight instrument indications and fly the airplane by them. Concentrating on yaw, pitch and roll sensations feeds the very illusion causing the problem. Slowing the breathing rate is the remedy for hyperventilation, not disorientation.

stem: FAA advisory circulars containing subject matter specifically related to Airmen are issued under which subject number?
explanation: FAA advisory circulars are numbered by subject to match the related part of the regulations. Subject 60 covers Airmen, matching Part 61, while 70 is Airspace and 90 is Air Traffic Control and General Operations. Mixing up 60 and 90 is common because Part 91 is the rule most pilots use.

stem: FAA advisory circulars containing subject matter specifically related to Airspace are issued under which subject number?
explanation: Advisory circulars use subject numbers that mirror the regulation parts. Subject 70 covers Airspace, matching Parts 71 through 77. Subject 60 is Airmen and 90 is Air Traffic Control and General Operations.

stem: FAA advisory circulars containing subject matter specifically related to Air Traffic Control and General Operations are issued under which subject number?
explanation: Subject 90 advisory circulars cover Air Traffic Control and General Operations, matching Part 91 and nearby parts; AC 90-66 on nontowered airport operations is an example. Subject 70 is Airspace and 60 is Airmen. Remembering that the AC subject follows the CFR part number avoids the confusion.

stem: What is it often called when a pilot pushes his or her capabilities and the aircraft's limits by trying to maintain visual contact with the terrain in low visibility and ceiling?
options: Scud running.
Mind set.
Peer pressure.
explanation: Scud running is pushing pilot and aircraft limits by trying to stay visual under a low ceiling and in poor visibility, ducking under clouds to keep sight of the ground. It is one of the classic operational pitfalls and often ends in controlled flight into terrain. Mind set and peer pressure are separate pitfalls.

stem: What is the antidote when a pilot has a hazardous attitude, such as "Antiauthority"?
options: Rules do not apply in this situation.
I know what I am doing.
Follow the rules.
explanation: The antiauthority attitude says do not tell me, and its antidote is follow the rules, because they are usually right. The other two options are expressions of hazardous thinking themselves, antiauthority and macho in tone. Recognizing the thought and replacing it with the antidote is the ADM method.

stem: What is the antidote when a pilot has a hazardous attitude, such as "Impulsivity"?
options: It could happen to me.
Do it quickly to get it over with.
Not so fast, think first.
explanation: Impulsivity is the urge to do something, anything, quickly. Its antidote is not so fast, think first. Do it quickly to get it over with is the hazardous thought itself, and it could happen to me is the antidote for invulnerability.

stem: What is the antidote when a pilot has a hazardous attitude, such as "Invulnerability"?
options: It will not happen to me.
It can not be that bad.
It could happen to me.
explanation: Invulnerability is the belief that it will not happen to me. The antidote is it could happen to me, which keeps a pilot taking risks seriously. The first option is the hazardous thought itself and the second is a minimizing statement, not an antidote.

stem: What is the antidote when a pilot has a hazardous attitude, such as "Macho"?
options: I can do it.
Taking chances is foolish.
Nothing will happen.
explanation: The macho attitude says I can do it and tries to prove something by taking risks. Its antidote is taking chances is foolish. I can do it is the hazardous thought, and nothing will happen is invulnerability talking.

stem: What is the antidote when a pilot has a hazardous attitude, such as "Resignation"?
options: What is the use.
Someone else is responsible.
I am not helpless.
explanation: Resignation is the feeling of what is the use, that the pilot cannot make a difference. The antidote is I am not helpless, I can make a difference. Someone else is responsible is a shifting of responsibility, not a cure, and what is the use is the hazardous thought itself.

stem: Who is responsible for determining whether a pilot is fit to fly for a particular flight, even though he or she holds a current medical certificate?
options: The FAA.
The medical examiner.
The pilot.
explanation: A medical certificate shows fitness at the time of the exam, but before each flight the pilot alone must decide whether he or she is fit to fly. 14 CFR 61.53 prohibits acting as a required crewmember with a known or suspected medical condition that makes the pilot unable to meet the medical standards. The medical examiner and the FAA are not present to make that call before each flight.

stem: What is the one common factor which affects most preventable accidents?
options: Structural failure.
Mechanical malfunction.
Human error.
explanation: Human error is the common factor in most preventable accidents; studies attribute roughly 80 percent of aviation accidents to it. Structural failure and mechanical malfunction account for a much smaller share. That is why ADM and risk management training target the pilot's decisions.

stem: What often leads to spatial disorientation or collision with ground/obstacles when flying under Visual Flight Rules (VFR)?
options: Continual flight into instrument conditions.
Getting behind the aircraft.
Duck-under syndrome.
explanation: Continuing VFR flight into instrument conditions is the operational pitfall that most often leads to spatial disorientation or collision with the ground or obstacles. Getting behind the aircraft is a separate pitfall about falling behind events. Duck under syndrome is descending below minimums on an instrument approach, not a VFR pitfall.

stem: What is one of the neglected items when a pilot relies on short and long term memory for repetitive tasks?
options: Checklists.
Situation awareness.
Flying outside the envelope.
explanation: When a pilot relies on short and long term memory for repetitive tasks, checklists are among the items that get neglected, along with flight planning and preflight inspection. Memory fails under distraction or fatigue, which is why written checklists exist. Situation awareness is a broader skill, and flying outside the envelope is a separate pitfall.

stem: Who should not participate in the Land and Hold Short Operations (LAHSO) program?
options: Recreational pilots only.
Military pilots.
Student pilots.
explanation: The AIM says student pilots, and pilots not familiar with LAHSO, should not participate in the program. A hold short clearance demands precise landing performance and quick judgment in a busy environment. Recreational and military pilots are not excluded by that guidance.

stem: Who has final authority to accept or decline any land and hold short (LAHSO) clearance?
options: Pilot-in-command.
Owner/operator.
Second-in-command.
explanation: The pilot in command has final authority to accept or decline any land and hold short clearance, consistent with 14 CFR 91.3. The owner or operator may set policy but is not in the cockpit making the call. A second in command assists but does not hold final authority.

stem: When should pilots decline a land and hold short (LAHSO) clearance?
options: When it will compromise safety.
Only when the tower operator concurs.
Pilots can not decline clearance.
explanation: Pilots should decline a LAHSO clearance whenever accepting it would compromise safety, for example when the available landing distance is not adequate for the conditions. No concurrence from the tower is needed; the pilot simply says unable. Pilots can always decline, so the last option is false.

stem: Where is the "Available Landing Distance" (ALD) data published for an airport that utilizes Land and Hold Short Operations (LAHSO)?
options: Chart Supplement.
14 CFR Part 91, General Operating and Flight Rules.
Aeronautical Information Manual (AIM).
explanation: Available Landing Distance data for LAHSO runways is published in the Chart Supplement, and also in the Terminal Procedures Publication. The AIM explains the procedures but does not list airport by airport distances. Part 91 contains rules, not airport data.

stem: What is the minimum visibility for a pilot to receive a land and hold short (LAHSO) clearance?
options: 3 nautical miles.
3 statute miles.
1 statute mile.
explanation: A pilot may receive a land and hold short clearance only when the weather is at least a 1,000 foot ceiling and 3 statute miles visibility. Visibility in the United States is reported in statute miles, which rules out the nautical mile choice. One statute mile is the Class G day minimum, not a LAHSO limit.

stem: Detonation may occur at high-power settings when
options: The fuel mixture ignites instantaneously instead of burning progressively and evenly.
an excessively rich fuel mixture causes an explosive gain in power.
the fuel mixture is ignited too early by hot carbon deposits in the cylinder.
explanation: Detonation occurs when the fuel and air mixture explodes instantaneously in the cylinder instead of burning progressively and evenly, sharply raising cylinder temperatures and pressures. Common causes are fuel of too low a grade, high power with too lean a mixture, and overheating. Ignition too early by hot carbon deposits is preignition, the tempting look alike; a rich mixture actually helps prevent detonation.

stem: Select the four flight fundamentals involved in maneuvering an aircraft.
options: Aircraft power, pitch, bank, and trim.
Starting, taxiing, takeoff, and landing.
Straight-and-level flight, turns, climbs, and descents.
explanation: Every flight maneuver is built from four fundamentals: straight and level flight, turns, climbs and descents. Mastering these and their combinations is the basis of all flying. Starting, taxiing, takeoff and landing are phases of flight, and power, pitch, bank and trim are control inputs, not the fundamentals.

stem: (Refer to Figure 66.) While practicing S-turns, a consistently smaller half-circle is made on one side of the road than on the other, and this turn is not completed before crossing the road or reference line. This would most likely occur in turn
options: 1-2-3 because the bank is decreased too rapidly during the latter part of the turn.
4-5-6 because the bank is increased too rapidly during the early part of the turn.
4-5-6 because the bank is increased too slowly during the latter part of the turn.
explanation: The wind is from the south, so the 4 5 6 half circle is flown on the upwind side and begins heading into the wind at the lowest groundspeed; the bank should start shallow and steepen gradually as the airplane turns downwind. Steepening too quickly early on tightens the turn, producing a smaller half circle, and the south wind then drifts the airplane north back to the road before the turn is finished. On the 1 2 3 side the turn starts heading downwind, where the bank is steepest at the start and shallows later, so the described error does not fit it.

stem: Excessively high engine temperatures, either in the air or on the ground, will
options: increase fuel consumption and may increase power due to the increased heat.
result in damage to heat-conducting hoses and warping of cylinder cooling fans.
cause loss of power, excessive oil consumption, and possible permanent internal engine damage.
explanation: Excessive engine temperatures cause loss of power, excessive oil consumption, detonation, and possible permanent internal engine damage. Heat never adds power in a piston engine. Air cooled aircraft engines use cooling fins on the cylinders, not cooling fans, which makes the second option wrong.

stem: When approaching taxiway holding lines from the side with the continuous lines, the pilot
options: may continue taxiing.
should not cross the lines without ATC clearance.
should continue taxiing until all parts of the aircraft have crossed the lines.
explanation: Holding position markings have two solid and two dashed yellow lines, and the solid lines face the side where the aircraft must hold. Approaching from the solid side, the pilot must not cross without an ATC clearance at a towered airport. From the dashed side the pilot may continue and cross until clear of the markings, which is the trap answer.

stem: The numbers 8 and 26 on the approach ends of the runway indicate that the runway is orientated approximately
options: 008° and 026° true.
080° and 260° true.
080° and 260° magnetic.
explanation: Runway numbers are the magnetic heading of the runway rounded to the nearest 10 degrees with the last zero dropped. Runway 8 is about 080 degrees magnetic and Runway 26 about 260 degrees magnetic. They are not true directions.

stem: The recommended entry position to an airport traffic pattern is
options: 45° to the base leg just below traffic pattern altitude.
to enter 45° at the midpoint of the downwind leg at traffic pattern altitude.
to cross directly over the airport at traffic pattern altitude and join the downwind leg.
explanation: The recommended traffic pattern entry is a 45 degree entry to the midpoint of the downwind leg, at traffic pattern altitude. Entering on base leg is not recommended. AC 90-66C describes a midfield crossing only as an alternative when it can be done safely, so it is not the recommended standard entry.

stem: To minimize the side loads placed on the landing gear during touchdown, the pilot should keep the
options: direction of motion of the aircraft parallel to the runway.
longitudinal axis of the aircraft parallel to the direction of its motion.
downwind wing lowered sufficiently to eliminate the tendency for the aircraft to drift.
explanation: To avoid side loads on the gear, touchdown must occur with the longitudinal axis of the airplane aligned with its direction of motion, meaning no crab and no drift. Keeping the motion parallel to the runway is only half the job, because the airplane could still be crabbed. Lowering the upwind wing, not the downwind wing, is the correct crosswind technique.
ref: Airplane Flying Handbook, Approaches and Landings chapter

stem: (Refer to Figure 62.) In flying the rectangular course, when would the aircraft be turned less than 90°?
options: Corners 1 and 4.
Corners 1 and 2.
Corners 2 and 4.
explanation: The wind is from the north and the course is flown counterclockwise: north on the east leg, west on the north leg, south on the west leg and east on the south leg. Both east and west legs need a crab toward the north, so at corner 1 the turn is from 360 to about 277 degrees and at corner 4 from about 083 to 360 degrees, both less than 90 degrees, while corners 2 and 3 need about 97 degrees (assuming, for example, a 10 knot wind at 80 knots, a 7 degree wind correction). The short turns are the two that join the headwind leg, because the airplane is already crabbed toward the wind on the legs on either side of it.

stem: Most midair collision accidents occur during
options: hazy days.
clear days.
cloudy nights.
explanation: Most midair collisions happen in good weather, in daylight, on clear days, often near airports. Good visibility brings more traffic and leads pilots to relax their scan. Hazy days and cloudy nights are less common settings for midair collisions.

stem: Hazardous attitudes occur to every pilot to some degree at some time. What are some of these hazardous attitudes?
options: Poor risk management and lack of stress management.
Antiauthority, impulsivity, macho, resignation, and invulnerability.
Poor situational awareness, snap judgments, and lack of a decision making process.
explanation: The FAA identifies five hazardous attitudes: antiauthority, impulsivity, invulnerability, macho and resignation. Poor risk or stress management and poor situational awareness are outcomes or skill gaps, not the named attitudes. Each attitude has a specific antidote.

stem: In the aeronautical decision making (ADM) process, what is the first step in neutralizing a hazardous attitude?
options: Making a rational judgment.
Recognizing hazardous thoughts.
Recognizing the invulnerability of the situation.
explanation: Neutralizing a hazardous attitude starts with recognizing the hazardous thought. Only then can the pilot label it and replace it with the matching antidote. Making a rational judgment comes later in the process, and invulnerability is itself one of the hazardous attitudes.

stem: Risk management, as part of the aeronautical decision making (ADM) process, relies on which features to reduce the risks associated with each flight?
options: Application of stress management and risk element procedures.
Situational awareness, problem recognition, and good judgment.
The mental process of analyzing all information in a particular situation and making a timely decision on what action to take.
explanation: Risk management relies on situational awareness, problem recognition and good judgment to reduce the risks of each flight. The third option describes judgment or decision making in general rather than the features risk management relies on. Stress management is a related but separate skill.

stem: An electrical system failure (battery and alternator) occurs during flight. In this situation, you would
options: experience avionics equipment failure.
probably experience failure of the engine ignition system, fuel gauges, aircraft lighting system, and avionics equipment.
probably experience engine failure due to the loss of the engine-driven fuel pump and also experience failure of the radio equipment, lights, and all instruments that require alternating.
explanation: The engine's ignition comes from magnetos, which generate their own current and run independently of the battery and alternator. With a complete electrical failure the engine keeps running, but electrically powered avionics, lights and electric gauges stop working. The ignition failure and engine driven fuel pump options are traps, since neither depends on the electrical system.

stem: What is the purpose of the runway/runway hold position sign
options: Denotes entrance to runway from a taxiway.
Denotes area protected for an aircraft approaching or departing a runway.
Denotes intersecting runways.
explanation: A runway and runway holding position sign, such as 4 22 on a red sign, is installed on a runway at the point where it intersects another runway. It denotes intersecting runways, and a pilot told to hold short must stop there. The entrance to a runway from a taxiway is marked by a taxiway and runway holding position sign.

stem: To properly purge water from the fuel system of an aircraft equipped with fuel tank sumps and a fuel strainer quick drain, it is necessary to drain fuel from the
options: fuel strainer drain.
lowest point in the fuel system.
fuel strainer drain and the fuel tank sumps.
explanation: Water is heavier than fuel and settles at the low points of the system, which include both the tank sumps and the fuel strainer. To purge it properly the pilot must drain both the fuel strainer and each fuel tank sump. Draining only the strainer can leave water in the tanks, and lowest point alone is vague when there are several low points.

stem: If an emergency situation requires a downwind landing, pilots should expect a faster
options: airspeed at touchdown, a longer ground roll, and better control throughout the landing roll.
groundspeed at touchdown, a longer ground roll, and the likelihood of overshooting the desired touchdown point.
groundspeed at touchdown, a shorter ground roll, and the likelihood of undershooting the desired touchdown point.
explanation: In a downwind landing the airspeed is normal, but the tailwind adds to it, giving a higher groundspeed at touchdown, a longer ground roll, and a tendency to overshoot the touchdown point. Control is not better, since the airplane is moving faster over the ground. A shorter roll and undershooting are the reverse of what a tailwind does.
ref: Airplane Flying Handbook, Emergency Procedures chapter

stem: Information concerning parachute jumping sites may be found in the
options: NOTAMs.
Chart Supplement.
Graphic Notices and Supplemental Data.
explanation: Parachute jumping areas are listed in the Chart Supplement, and frequently used sites are also shown on sectional charts. NOTAMs are used for temporary or specific jump activity, not as the standing reference for jump sites. Graphic Notices and Supplemental Data is no longer the source for this information.

stem: When turning onto a taxiway from another taxiway, the "taxiway directional sign" indicates
options: direction to the take-off runway.
designation and direction of taxiway leading out of an intersection.
designation and direction of exit taxiway from runway.
explanation: A direction sign, black letters and an arrow on yellow, identifies the designation and direction of taxiways leading out of an intersection. A destination sign points the way to a takeoff runway. The exit from a runway is identified by a runway exit sign, which is also a direction sign but located on the runway.

stem: The "runway hold position" sign denotes
options: intersecting runways.
an entrance to runway from a taxiway.
an area protected for an aircraft approaching a runway.
explanation: The runway holding position sign, white numbers on red, is located on a taxiway at the entrance to a runway, so it denotes an entrance to a runway from a taxiway. Do not cross it without clearance at a towered airport. The protected area for an approaching aircraft is marked by an ILS critical area or runway approach area sign.

stem: (Refer to Figure 65.) The red symbol at sign D would most likely be found
options: upon exiting all runways prior to calling ground control.
near the approach end of ILS runways.
at an intersection where a roadway may be mistaken as a taxiway.
explanation: Sign D is the No Entry sign, a white circle with a horizontal bar on red. It is placed on taxiways intended for one way traffic or where a vehicle roadway meets a movement area and might be mistaken for a taxiway. ILS runways use the ILS critical area sign, and runway exits use yellow and black direction signs.

stem: "Runway hold position" markings on the taxiway
options: identifies where aircraft hold short of the runway.
identifies area where aircraft are prohibited.
allows an aircraft permission onto the runway.
explanation: Runway holding position markings are four yellow lines, two solid and two dashed, painted across a taxiway where it meets a runway. With the solid lines on your side you must stop short of them unless cleared onto or across the runway. They do not prohibit an area and they never grant permission to enter; only an ATC clearance (or, at a nontowered field, your own clearing of the runway) does that.

stem: (Refer to Figure 65.) The pilot generally calls ground control after landing when the aircraft is completely clear of the runway. This is when the aircraft
options: passes sign D.
is on the dashed-line side of sign G.
is past the solid-line side of sign G.
