explanation: Sign G is the runway boundary sign, which shows the hold marking as it looks to a pilot leaving the runway: dashed lines toward the runway, solid lines toward the taxiway. You are clear of the runway only when the entire airplane has crossed past the solid line side of that marking, and that is when you call ground. Being on the dashed side means you are still inside the runway safety area, and sign D is a no entry sign that has nothing to do with exiting.

stem: The "taxiway ending" marker
options: indicates taxiway does not continue.
identifies area where aircraft are prohibited.
provides general taxiing direction to named taxiway.
explanation: The taxiway ending marker is a yellow and black striped sign or marking placed where a taxiway physically ends, telling the pilot the taxiway does not continue beyond it. A no entry sign or other mandatory sign is what marks prohibited areas, and direction signs (yellow with black arrows) give taxi direction to a named taxiway.
ref: PHAK Ch. 14 (airport signs); Figure 65 sign N

stem: When should pilots state their position on the airport when calling the tower for takeoff?
options: When visibility is less than 1 mile.
When parallel runways are in use.
When departing from a runway intersection.
explanation: When you plan to take off from a point other than the full length runway end, tell the tower which intersection you are at so the controller does not assume you are at the threshold. Low visibility or parallel runway operations do not by themselves trigger this report; the trigger is the intersection departure.

stem: When a stressful situation is encountered in flight, an abnormal increase in the volume of air breathed in and out can cause a condition known as
options: hyperventilation.
aerosinusitis.
aerotitis.
explanation: Breathing too fast or too deeply, which is common under stress or anxiety, blows off too much carbon dioxide and produces hyperventilation, with tingling, dizziness and lightheadedness. Aerosinusitis and aerotitis are pressure injuries of the sinuses and middle ear caused by altitude changes, not by breathing rate.

stem: If the ground wire between the magneto and the ignition switch becomes disconnected, the most noticeable result will be that the engine
options: will run very rough.
cannot be started with the switch in the ON position.
cannot be shut down by turning the switch to the OFF position.
explanation: Turning the ignition switch OFF works by grounding the magneto primary circuit through the P lead. If that ground wire is broken the magneto stays hot, so the engine keeps running when you select OFF. The engine still starts and runs normally, which is why the fault can go unnoticed until shutdown or a mag check.

stem: How can a military airport be identified at night?
options: Alternate green and white flashes.
Dual peaked (two quick) white flashes between green flashes.
White flashing lights with steady green at the same location.
explanation: A civil land airport beacon alternates white and green, while a military airport beacon shows two quick white flashes between each green flash. Alternating white and green alone is the civil pattern, which is the tempting wrong answer.

stem: What does the outbound destination sign identify?
options: Identifies entrance to the runway from a taxiway.
Identifies runway on which an aircraft is located.
Identifies direction to take-off runways.
explanation: Destination signs are yellow with black text and an arrow, and an outbound destination sign points the way to the takeoff runways. A runway location sign (black with yellow text) tells you which runway you are on, and a holding position sign (red with white numerals) marks the entrance to a runway from a taxiway.

stem: If the ground wire between the magneto and the ignition switch becomes disconnected, the engine
options: will not operate on one magneto.
cannot be started with the switch in the on position.
could accidentally start if the propeller is moved with fuel in the cylinder.
explanation: A disconnected P lead leaves the magneto ungrounded, or hot, even with the switch OFF. Anyone moving the propeller by hand with fuel in a cylinder could make the engine fire and start, which is why every propeller must be treated as live. The magneto itself still works, so the engine runs fine on it and starts normally.

stem: (Refer to Figure 64.) Which marking indicates a vehicle lane?
options: Letter A.
Letter C.
Letter E.
explanation: Letter C points to the white markings on the ramp next to the terminal: solid white edge lines and a dashed or zipper style center line, which define a vehicle roadway. Letter A is a holding position sign and letter E marks a yellow dashed line on the taxiway, so neither is a vehicle lane; aircraft markings are yellow, roadway markings are white.

stem: The 'yellow demarcation bar' marking indicates
options: runway with a displaced threshold that precedes the runway.
a hold line from a taxiway to a runway.
the beginning of available runway for landing on the approach side.
explanation: A yellow demarcation bar is a wide yellow bar across the full pavement width that separates a runway with a displaced threshold from a blast pad, stopway or taxiway that precedes the runway. It is not a hold line, and the beginning of the runway available for landing is shown by the white threshold bar, not the yellow demarcation bar.

stem: This sign is a visual clue that
options: confirms the aircraft's location to be on taxiway "B."
warns the pilot of approaching taxiway "B."
indicates "B" holding area is ahead.
explanation: The sign shown in the FAA source is a taxiway location sign: a black background with a yellow letter and yellow border. Location signs tell you which taxiway you are on right now, so it confirms you are on taxiway B. A sign warning of an approaching taxiway would be a yellow direction sign with a black letter and arrow.

stem: A lack of orientation with regard to the position, attitude, or movement of the aircraft in space is defined as
options: spatial disorientation.
hyperventilation.
hypoxia.
explanation: Spatial disorientation is the loss of correct orientation regarding the position, attitude or movement of the aircraft relative to the earth, usually when outside visual references are lost. Hyperventilation and hypoxia are physiological conditions about breathing and oxygen, not definitions of orientation.

stem: Which approach and landing objective is assured when the pilot remains on the proper glidepath of the VASI?
options: Runway identification and course guidance.
Safe obstruction clearance in the approach area.
Lateral course guidance to the runway.
explanation: Staying on the VASI glidepath guarantees safe obstruction clearance within about 10 degrees of the extended centerline out to 4 NM from the threshold. The VASI gives vertical guidance only; it does not identify the runway or provide lateral course guidance, so you still have to line up yourself.

stem: Who is responsible for filing a Near Midair Collision (NMAC) Report?
options: A passenger aboard the involved aircraft.
Local law enforcement.
Pilot and/or flight crew of aircraft involved in the incident.
explanation: The FAA asks the pilot and/or flight crew of the involved aircraft to file a Near Midair Collision report, since they are the ones who saw the event and can describe it. Passengers and police have no role in the NMAC reporting program.

stem: Pilots and/or flight crewmembers involved in NMAC occurrences are urged to report each incident immediately:
options: By cell phone to the nearest Flight Standards District Office (FSDO) as this is an emergency.
To local law enforcement.
By radio or telephone to the nearest FAA ATC Facility or FSS.
explanation: An NMAC should be reported right away by radio or telephone to the nearest FAA ATC facility or FSS, which can capture the details while they are fresh. It is not an emergency call to a FSDO, and local law enforcement is not part of the process.

stem: Pilot fatigue is
options: easily overcome by using stimulants such as caffeine or engaging in limited physical exercise.
hazardous because it leads to a decrease in the ability to carry out tasks.
is negated by the normal adrenalin generated in flight.
explanation: Fatigue degrades judgment, reaction time and the ability to carry out tasks, which makes it a real hazard in flight. Caffeine or exercise only mask it briefly, and adrenaline in flight does not cancel it; the cure is adequate rest.

stem: During which phase of flight is a pilot at increased odds of experiencing a somatogravic illusion?
options: Landing.
Takeoff.
Steep turns.
explanation: A somatogravic illusion comes from rapid acceleration, which the inner ear reads as a nose up attitude and tempts the pilot to push the nose down. That acceleration is greatest on takeoff and during a go around, especially at night or in low visibility. Steep turns produce other vestibular illusions, and landing involves deceleration.

stem: It is the responsibility of the pilot and crew to report a near midair collision as a result of proximity of at least
options: 50 feet or less to another aircraft.
500 feet or less to another aircraft.
1,000 feet or less to another aircraft.
explanation: An NMAC is an incident in which there was a possibility of collision because the aircraft came within less than 500 feet of each other, or a crewmember reports a collision hazard. 50 feet is far too tight and 1,000 feet is not the defined threshold.

stem: A left turn at this intersection would place the aircraft
options: ready for a runway 26 intersection takeoff.
on the taxiway leading to runway 26.
ready for a runway 8 intersection takeoff.
explanation: This red and white sign is a runway holding position sign at the point where a taxiway meets runway 8/26, and the numbers are arranged to match the thresholds: 26 on the left means the runway 26 threshold lies to your left. Turning left therefore points you toward the 26 end, which means you are heading east, lined up for a runway 8 departure from the intersection. The tempting runway 26 choice reverses the logic, and the turn puts you on the runway itself, not on a taxiway leading to it.

stem: What antidotal phrase can help reverse the hazardous attitude of impulsivity?
options: Do it quickly to get it over with.
It could happen to me.
Not so fast, think first.
explanation: The antidote for impulsivity is Not so fast, think first. It could happen to me answers invulnerability, and Do it quickly to get it over with is the impulsive attitude itself, not its antidote.

stem: When you adjust the fuel/air ratio with the mixture control for a change of altitude, the ratio you are changing is the
options: volume of fuel to the volume of air.
weight of fuel to the weight of air.
weight of fuel to the volume of air.
explanation: The fuel/air ratio is a ratio by weight: the weight of fuel compared to the weight of air entering the cylinders. As you climb the air becomes less dense, so the same volume of air weighs less and the mixture gets richer, which is why you lean. Comparing volumes misses the density change that the mixture control is correcting.

stem: When departing a non-towered airport traffic pattern (left-hand traffic), you continue straight out or
options: make a 45° turn to the left.
make a 45° turn to the right.
make a 180° turn to the left.
explanation: When departing a nontowered airport pattern you either continue straight out or exit with a 45 degree turn in the direction of the pattern, which is to the left for left traffic, once past the departure end and at pattern altitude. A right turn would cut across traffic flow, and a 180 turn would bring you back against arriving traffic.

stem: While on approach for landing on runway 9 at an uncontrolled airport, you notice ripples on the southeast corner of a small lake located 3/4 miles east of the airport. What is the correct course of action?
options: Continue to land on runway 9.
Change approach to land on runway 27.
Observe the airport's windsock to determine wind direction.
explanation: Wind blowing across water leaves the upwind shore calm and builds ripples toward the downwind shore, so ripples in the southeast corner suggest a northwest wind, which would be a quartering tailwind for runway 9. That is a good reason to question runway 9, but the lake is 3/4 mile away and the cue is easy to misread, so confirm with the airport windsock, which shows the wind at the runway, before deciding. Switching to runway 27 on the lake alone acts on unverified evidence, and continuing ignores a warning sign.

stem: What is an effective way to mitigate a collision hazard in the traffic pattern
options: Enter a traffic pattern leg during a descent
Maintain the proper traffic pattern altitude and continually scan the area
Rely on radio reports from other aircraft in the pattern
explanation: Flying the published pattern altitude puts you where other pilots expect to see you, and a continuous scan is the primary way to see and avoid traffic. Descending into a pattern leg hides you below and behind others, and radio reports help but cannot be relied on since not every aircraft has or uses a radio.

stem: Pilots should develop an instrument cross-check technique that avoids excessive and abrupt movements to avoid
options: Spatial disorientation.
Losing critical information.
Reliance on primary instrumentation.
explanation: Large, abrupt head and eye movements while cross checking can stimulate the semicircular canals and trigger spatial disorientation, so a smooth, efficient scan is taught. Losing information and reliance on primary instruments are not what abrupt movement causes.
ref: PHAK Ch. 17; Instrument Flying Handbook Ch. 3

stem: On final approach to the landing runway, the pilot adjusts
options: pitch attitude, power, and trim to maintain a constant angle glidepath towards a predetermined aiming point on the landing runway in the landing configuration.
power to maintain a constant glideslope.
pitch to maintain a constant airspeed.
explanation: On final the pilot uses pitch attitude, power and trim together, in the landing configuration, to hold a constant angle glidepath to a chosen aiming point. The other options each name only one control, and in practice pitch and power are coordinated rather than used in isolation.

stem: Your nose wheel has a tire pressure of 35 PSI. If you were to land on a runway with standing water, what speed do you expect dynamic hydroplaning could occur?
options: 51 knots.
30 knots.
17 knots.
explanation: Minimum dynamic hydroplaning speed is roughly 8.6 to 9 times the square root of tire pressure in psi. With 35 psi: 8.6 x 5.92 = 50.9 knots, about 51 knots. 30 and 17 knots come from using the wrong multiplier or the pressure itself.

stem: Hydroplaning can occur to
options: only lightweight airplanes landing at less than 3,500 pounds.
any airplane.
when a propeller is placed in the Beta pitch position.
explanation: Hydroplaning depends on tire pressure, speed and water depth, not on airplane weight, so any airplane can hydroplane. Beta propeller pitch is a turboprop reverse thrust feature and has nothing to do with whether hydroplaning occurs.

stem: You’re flying to airport where there’s reports of standing water on the runway, your best option to avoid hydroplaning is to
options: decrease tire pressures by 10 PSI.
apply brakes heavily as soon as possible after touchdown.
land at the slowest speed possible.
explanation: The best defense is to touch down as slowly as safely possible, since hydroplaning risk rises sharply with ground speed. Lower tire pressure actually lowers the hydroplaning speed, and heavy early braking on a wet runway invites skidding; braking should be firm but moderate once the weight is on the wheels.

stem: The runway you’re attempting to land on is contaminated with a thin layer of oil, what type of hydroplaning is this?
options: Dynamic.
Viscous.
Reverted.
explanation: Viscous hydroplaning happens when a very thin film of fluid, such as oil, rubber deposits or a light layer of water on smooth pavement, acts as a lubricant between tire and surface. Dynamic hydroplaning requires standing water deep enough to lift the tire, and reverted hydroplaning involves a locked wheel generating steam.

stem: What type of hydroplaning causes steam to build up under the tire?
options: Reverted.
Dynamic.
Viscous.
explanation: Reverted rubber hydroplaning occurs when a locked, skidding tire generates enough friction heat to turn the water into steam, which supports the tire and melts the rubber. Dynamic hydroplaning is lift from standing water, and viscous hydroplaning comes from a thin slippery film.

stem: For landing in turbulent conditions, the approach should be flown at what airspeed?
options: Slightly above normal approach speed.
Below normal approach speed.
Normal approach speed.
explanation: In turbulent or gusty conditions fly the approach slightly faster than normal, commonly normal approach speed plus one half the gust factor, to keep a margin above the stall and better control authority. Flying slower risks a stall in a lull or downdraft, and normal speed gives no margin for gusts.

stem: During a emergency approach, what is the first action after engine failure?
options: Turn into the wind.
Lower flaps.
Establish best glide speed.
explanation: After an engine failure the first priority is to pitch for best glide speed, which preserves altitude and maximizes the distance you can reach. Turning into the wind and lowering flaps come later, once you have picked a field and know you can make it.

stem: A runway VASI system provides:
options: Illumination to better see the landing area.
Left and right descent guidance to the runway.
Visual descent information to the runway.
explanation: A VASI is a set of light bars that shows the pilot whether the airplane is above, on or below the visual glidepath, giving visual descent information to the runway. It does not light the landing area and it gives no left or right course guidance.

stem: According to FAA guidance and industry best practices, what is the primary benefit of consistently flying a stabilized approach?
options: Reduces pilot workload
Eliminates the need to use a checklist
Requires less flaps to be used during landing
explanation: Holding a steady speed, descent rate and configuration means fewer corrections are needed, which frees attention for traffic, wind and the landing itself. A stabilized approach never replaces the checklist and has nothing to do with using less flap.

stem: In the context of FAA-recommended approach and landing techniques for light general aviation aircraft, which description most accurately defines the execution of a stabilized approach?
options: Keeps adjusting the speed to maintain a constant pitch attitude toward the runway.
Keeps adjusting the pitch attitude to maintain a constant speed to the runway.
Maintains a constant descent angle to a fixed point on the runway.
explanation: The FAA defines a stabilized approach as one in which the pilot establishes and maintains a constant angle glidepath toward a predetermined point on the landing runway. The other two options describe chasing speed or pitch alone, which is the opposite of a stable, coordinated approach.

stem: What is the standard glide path angle recommended for a stabilized approaches in most general aviation operations?
options: 3 degrees
4 degrees
2 degrees
explanation: The standard visual and electronic glidepath is about 3 degrees, which most VASI and PAPI installations provide. A 2 degree path is flat and low over obstacles, and 4 degrees is steeper than normal.

stem: What is the objective of flying a stabilized approach from the key point to the landing flare?
options: To maintain an airspeed +/- 20 knots and a descent rate of around 1,000 fpm.
The airplane should be on speed, in trim, configured for landing, tracking the extended centerline of the runway, and established in a constant angle of descent toward an aiming point on the runway.
To be positioned and fully configured on the final approach leg at no less than 3 NM from the runway threshold.
explanation: From the key point to the flare the airplane should be on speed, in trim, configured for landing, tracking the extended centerline and descending at a constant angle toward the aiming point. A plus or minus 20 knot band and a 1,000 fpm sink are far outside a stabilized approach, and no fixed 3 NM rule applies to light airplane visual approaches.

stem: In accordance with most Pilot’s Operating Handbooks (POH) or Airplane Flight Manuals (AFM), what target airspeed, including tolerances, should be maintained throughout a stabilized final approach segment?
options: The speed at the bottom of the green arc on the airspeed indicator, +/- 10 KIAS.
1.5 times Vso, plus the gust factor.
The landing speed specified in the POH or AFM, +10/-5 KIAS.
explanation: Fly the approach speed the POH or AFM specifies, held within plus 10 and minus 5 knots, which matches the ACS tolerance. The bottom of the green arc is a stall speed reference, not an approach target, and 1.5 Vso is not the standard; absent a published speed the guidance is no more than 1.3 Vso.

stem: If you land without the use of flaps, the approach will be:
options: Slower and shallower.
Faster and shallower.
Slower and steeper.
explanation: Without flaps the airplane must fly a higher approach speed and a flatter, shallower descent, then floats farther in the flare. Flaps are what allow a slower and steeper approach, so that option describes a full flap landing instead.

stem: A go-around or rejected landing is a normal maneuver and may be an appropriate reaction to a number of contributing factors. Which of the following would NOT normally be considered a likely contributing factor?
options: Wind-shear and/or turbulence.
Unexpected appearance of hazards on the runway.
Lack of experience or skill.
explanation: The AFH lists ATC requirements, unexpected hazards on the runway, overtaking another airplane, wind shear, wake turbulence, mechanical failure and an unstable approach as reasons to go around. It specifically calls the belief that a go around always results from insufficient experience or skill a fallacy, so lack of experience is the factor that does not belong. Windshear and runway hazards are both named reasons.

stem: When performing an approach and landing to a soft field, what is the proper approach angle?
options: Shallow approach angle.
Normal approach angle.
Steep approach angle.
explanation: The soft field approach is flown much like a normal approach; the difference comes in the flare, where the airplane is held just off the surface and touched down as slowly and softly as possible, often with some power. A steep approach risks a hard touchdown, and a shallow one is not called for.

stem: How should the ailerons be positioned when landing in a crosswind?
options: Neutral ailerons
Up aileron into the wind
Down aileron into the wind
explanation: In a crosswind landing hold aileron into the wind, which raises the aileron on the upwind wing and lowers that wing to stop drift. Neutral ailerons let the airplane drift, and down aileron into the wind would raise the upwind wing and make the drift worse.

stem: What can happen when a pilot experiences an illusion while approaching to land on a runway that is narrower than the typical runway width?
options: The tendency to fly slower than the planned final approach speed.
Risk of the pilot leveling out the aircraft high and landing hard or overshooting the runway.
The pilot will fly a lower approach, with the risk of striking objects along the approach path or possibly landing short.
explanation: A runway narrower than usual looks like a normal runway seen from higher up, so the pilot thinks he is high and descends too low, risking obstacles and a short landing. Flaring high and landing hard or long is the wide runway illusion, the mirror image of this one.

stem: (Refer to figure 48) ATC instructs you to line up and wait for takeoff on Runway 12, while another heavy airplane lands on Runway 17R. While waiting on Runway 12, you observe the heavy airplane touchdown past the runway intersection. How will the vortices affect your takeoff? The winds are from 120° at 5 knots.
options: The vortices will be pushed into your takeoff path
The vortices will rise and stay clear of your path
The vortices will dissipate in the light wind
explanation: In Figure 48 the heavy crossed over the 12/17R intersection while still airborne and touched down beyond it, so its vortices settled at the intersection on your takeoff path. A 5 knot wind from 120 blows straight down runway 12 from the southeast and carries those vortices toward you and along the runway, and a light wind keeps them in place rather than breaking them up. Vortices sink, they do not rise.

stem: When landing, you spot another airplane halfway down the runway. How should you proceed?
options: Continue for landing
Go-around
Complete a 360 turn on the final approach leg
explanation: An airplane still on the runway is an unexpected hazard on the runway, which the AFH lists as a reason to go around. Continuing to land risks a collision or forces you to land long, and a 360 on final creates a collision hazard for traffic behind you.

stem: What is the difference between a normal landing and a crosswind landing?
options: Aileron down on the upwind wing
Aileron up on the downwind wing
Aileron up on the upwind wing
explanation: With the wing low method the pilot holds aileron into the wind, so the aileron on the upwind wing is up and that wing is lowered into the wind. A normal landing uses no such deflection. Down aileron on the upwind wing would raise it, and up aileron on the downwind wing would bank the wrong way.

stem: If you observe a dust devil crossing the runway while approaching to land, what action should you take?
options: Go around
Land past the dust devil
Continue landing as normal
explanation: A dust devil is a strong, small whirlwind that can cause sudden roll and loss of control near the ground, so the safe response is to go around and let it pass. Landing past it or continuing as normal puts the airplane in that rotating flow at low speed and low altitude.

stem: While operating in regions known for dust devils, such as the Southwest US, what is the recommended action a pilot should take when one is detected during flight operations at low altitudes?
options: Continue on the planned flight path, as dust devils are harmless and pose no risk to aircraft.
Recognize and avoid the dust devil and be prepared to take evasive action if necessary.
Immediately divert to the nearest airport and land as soon as possible to avoid the dust devil.
explanation: Dust devils can contain strong rotating winds that upset a light airplane at low altitude, so recognize them and steer clear, ready for evasive action. They are not harmless, but they are also local and brief, so diverting to land is unnecessary in most cases.
ref: Aviation Weather Handbook (dust devils); AFH Ch. 9

stem: While approaching to land on Runway 17 at an uncontrolled airport, you spot a lake on the east side of the airport which has ripples in the water at the southeastern edge. How should you proceed?
options: Check the windsock on the airfield to make the correct determination with runway choice.
Continue with your approach and land on runway 17.
Change your approach and land on runway 35.
explanation: Ripples form toward the downwind shore of a lake while the upwind shore stays calm, so ripples at the southeastern edge suggest a northwest wind, a tailwind for runway 17. That should make you doubt runway 17, but a lake off the field is an indirect cue that is easy to misread, so check the windsock, which shows the wind at the runway, before choosing between 17 and 35. Switching to 35 on the lake alone skips that check, and continuing ignores the warning.

stem: What is the primary purpose of the brakes on an airplane during the after-landing roll?
options: To increase lift.
To change direction.
To reduce speed on the ground.
explanation: Wheel brakes exist to slow the airplane on the ground after touchdown, and differential braking can assist steering at low speed. They have no effect on lift, and steering is primarily done with the rudder and nosewheel.

stem: During the touchdown phase of a normal landing, the airplane should touch down on which gear first?
options: Main gear.
All gear simultaneously.
Nose gear.
explanation: In a normal landing the airplane touches down on the main gear first, nose held off, at about the power off stall attitude. Touching down on the nosewheel or all wheels at once risks wheelbarrowing, porpoising and nosewheel damage.

stem: What action should be taken if wheelbarrowing occurs during the landing roll?
options: Apply brakes heavily.
Apply forward pressure on the elevator.
Apply back-elevator pressure.
explanation: Wheelbarrowing happens when too much weight rests on the nosewheel and the mains lose traction. Relieve it with back elevator pressure to shift weight back to the main wheels, or go around if conditions allow. Forward elevator or heavy braking adds weight to the nose and makes it worse.

stem: In a go-around, what is the first cardinal principle?
options: Power.
Attitude.
Configuration.
explanation: The three cardinal principles of a go around are power, attitude and configuration, in that order. Full power comes first to stop the descent, then pitch for climb, then clean up; retracting flaps before power is applied can cause a sink.

stem: What is the purpose of an intentional forward slip?
options: To reduce descent rate.
To increase airspeed.
To dissipate altitude without increasing airspeed.
explanation: A forward slip increases drag so the airplane can lose altitude quickly without picking up airspeed, useful when high on final or in airplanes without flaps. It increases, not reduces, the descent rate, and its whole point is to avoid building speed.

stem: During a crosswind landing using the wing-low method, which wheel touches down first?
options: Upwind main wheel.
Nose wheel.
Downwind main wheel.
explanation: With the upwind wing lowered in the wing low method, the upwind main wheel contacts the runway first, followed by the downwind main and then the nosewheel. Touching down on the downwind wheel first would mean the bank is the wrong way.

stem: The demonstrated crosswind velocity for an airplane is typically equal to what value?
options: 0.1 Vso.
0.3 Vso.
0.2 Vso.
explanation: Certification rules for small airplanes required a demonstrated 90 degree crosswind component of at least 0.2 Vso, so the demonstrated value is typically about 0.2 Vso. For a 50 knot Vso that is 10 knots. 0.1 and 0.3 Vso are not the certification standard.

stem: In a short-field landing, touchdown should occur at what airspeed?
options: Best glide speed.
Normal approach speed.
Minimum controllable airspeed.
explanation: A short field landing aims for touchdown at minimum controllable airspeed, near the power off stall attitude, to minimize ground roll. Best glide and normal approach speed would both float the airplane and lengthen the landing.

stem: For a soft-field landing, the airplane should touch down in what attitude?
options: Nose-high.
Level.
Nose-low.
explanation: On a soft field the airplane touches down nose high at the lowest possible speed, and the nosewheel is held off as long as possible to keep weight off it. A level or nose low touchdown would dig the nosewheel into the soft surface.

stem: If a wing rises during the after-landing roll in a crosswind, what should the pilot do?
options: Apply aileron toward the high wing.
Apply brakes on the low wing.
Apply rudder toward the high wing.
explanation: If a wing rises on the rollout, the crosswind is lifting the upwind wing, so increase aileron toward that high wing to hold it down. Rudder controls direction, not bank, and braking the low wing side does nothing to lower the rising wing.

stem: In a go-around, after applying power, what is the next step?
options: Retract flaps.
Retract gear.
Establish positive climb attitude.
explanation: After power, the next cardinal principle is attitude: establish a positive climb pitch attitude. Flaps are retracted in stages and the gear raised only after a positive rate of climb is established.

stem: What is the effect of ground effect during a low go-around?
options: Reduces induced drag, giving false performance.
Increases drag.
Increases lift excessively.
explanation: In ground effect induced drag drops, so the airplane may seem to climb or accelerate better than it really will. Once it climbs out of ground effect the drag returns and the climb can stall out, which is the trap during a low go around. Ground effect reduces drag rather than increasing it.

stem: When using forward slip for landing, flaps are usually
options: Fully extended.
Partially extended.
Retracted.
explanation: The AFH describes the forward slip to a landing with flaps usually retracted, since the slip itself supplies the drag that flaps would otherwise provide, which is why this item expects retracted. Some airplanes do allow slips with flaps, while others restrict them because of tail stall or airflow concerns, so always follow the POH. Full or partial flaps are not the standard configuration described for the maneuver.
ref: AFH Ch. 9 (Forward Slip to a Landing)

stem: In crosswind, the crab method requires removing crab just before
options: Touchdown.
Flare.
Round out.
explanation: With the crab method the airplane is held in a crab until just before touchdown, then rudder aligns the longitudinal axis with the runway and aileron stops the drift. Removing the crab early at the flare or round out lets the airplane drift before contact.

stem: During crosswind touchdown with wing-low, which wheel touches down first?
options: Downwind main wheel.
Nose wheel.
Upwind main wheel.
explanation: In the wing low method the upwind wing is lowered, so the upwind main wheel touches down first, then the downwind main, then the nose. Touching down on the downwind wheel first means the bank is the wrong way.

stem: The weathervaning tendency during after-landing roll is due to
options: Greater side area behind main gear.
Brakes.
Ailerons.
explanation: Weathervaning on the ground comes from the larger side area behind the main gear, mainly the tail and vertical fin, which the crosswind pushes so the nose turns into the wind. Brakes and ailerons are tools to counter it, not the cause.

stem: In turbulent landing, use
options: Partial flaps.
No flaps.
Full flaps.
explanation: In turbulent or gusty conditions a partial flap setting is recommended, giving better control and a speed margin while avoiding the large lift and drag changes full flaps cause in gusts. No flaps can give an excessively long landing, and full flaps make the airplane more sensitive to gusts.

stem: For short-field, approach speed is
options: 1.4 Vso.
Best glide.
1.3 Vso.
explanation: Use the POH short field approach speed, or, if none is published, no more than 1.3 Vso. Best glide is a cruise descent speed, and 1.4 Vso is faster than the short field target.

stem: In soft-field landing, power is used to
options: Cushion touchdown.
Increase speed.
Reduce descent.
explanation: In a soft field landing a little power during the flare helps cushion the touchdown and lets the airplane settle at minimum speed with a low sink rate. Power is not used to increase speed, and the descent is reduced only in the sense of softening contact.

stem: Ballooning is caused by
options: Low AO
High speed.
Rapid increase in AOA.
explanation: Ballooning happens when the pilot raises the nose too quickly in the round out, so a rapid increase in angle of attack makes the airplane climb. Excess speed can make it worse, but the cause is the abrupt pitch change, not speed alone.

stem: To correct porpoising
options: Go-around if severe.
Apply brakes.
Lower nose.
explanation: A severe porpoise can quickly build into a nosewheel collapse or prop strike, so apply power and go around rather than trying to fix it with pitch inputs. Lowering the nose aggravates the oscillation, and braking does nothing while bouncing.

stem: Unlike an automobile, your airplane can only be loaded to a certain weight. If it is loaded beyond the maximum allowable weight it will experience:
options: Lower rate of climb and longer landing roll.
Higher stall speeds and longer takeoff distances.
The other two statements are both correct.
explanation: An overweight airplane needs more lift, so it has higher stall speeds, longer takeoff runs, lower climb rates and a longer landing roll because of its greater momentum. Both listed statements are true, so the combined answer is correct.

stem: If you are on approach and picking up ½ in. of rime ice on the leading edge of your wings, you should consider:
options: A faster than normal approach and landing speed.
Approaching and landing at your normal speed since the ice is not thick enough to have any noticeable effect.
Flying your approach slower than normal to lessen the “wind chill” effect and break up the ice.
explanation: Even a thin layer of ice changes the airfoil shape, cutting lift and raising stall speed, so fly a faster than normal approach and landing. Flying slower actually reduces the stall margin, and ice is not broken up by speed or wind chill.

stem: Every physical process of weather is accompanied by, or is the result of, a
options: movement of air.
pressure differential.
heat exchange.
explanation: Every physical weather process involves, or results from, a heat exchange, because uneven heating drives pressure differences, air movement and moisture changes. Movement of air and pressure differences are effects of that heat exchange rather than the underlying cause.

stem: What causes variations in altimeter settings between weather reporting points?
options: Unequal heating of the Earth's surface.
Variation of terrain elevation.
Coriolis force.
explanation: The sun heats the Earth unevenly, so air over some areas warms, expands and lowers the surface pressure while air elsewhere stays cooler and denser. Those pressure differences are what show up as different altimeter settings from station to station. Terrain elevation is the tempting trap, but altimeter settings are already corrected to sea level, so elevation is removed from the number.

stem: The most frequent type of ground or surface-based temperature inversion is that which is produced by
options: terrestrial radiation on a clear, relatively still night.
warm air being lifted rapidly aloft in the vicinity of mountainous terrain.
the movement of colder air under warm air, or the movement of warm air over cold air.
explanation: On a clear, nearly calm night the ground radiates heat to space and chills the air in contact with it, leaving cooler air at the surface under warmer air above. This radiation inversion is the most common surface based inversion. Frontal overrunning (cold air under warm air) also creates inversions, but those are aloft along the frontal surface and are less frequent at ground level.

stem: Which weather conditions should be expected beneath a low-level temperature inversion layer when the relative humidity is high?
options: Smooth air, poor visibility, fog, haze, or low clouds.
Light wind shear, poor visibility, haze, and light rain.
Turbulent air, poor visibility, fog, low stratus type clouds, and showery precipitation.
explanation: An inversion is a very stable layer that blocks vertical mixing, so the air beneath it is smooth while moisture, haze and smoke are trapped near the ground. With high humidity that gives fog, haze and low clouds with poor visibility. Turbulence and showery precipitation are signs of unstable air, which is the opposite of what an inversion produces.

stem: What are the standard temperature and pressure values for sea level?
options: 15 °C and 29.92 inches Hg.
59 °C and 1013.2 millibars.
59 °F and 29.92 millibars.
explanation: The International Standard Atmosphere at sea level is 15 °C (59 °F) and 29.92 inches of mercury (1013.2 millibars). The wrong options mix units: 59 is Fahrenheit, not Celsius, and 29.92 is inches of mercury, not millibars.

stem: What is meant by the term "dewpoint"?
options: The temperature at which condensation and evaporation are equal.
The temperature at which dew will always form.
The temperature to which air must be cooled to become saturated.
explanation: Dewpoint is the temperature the air must be cooled to, at constant pressure and moisture content, for it to become saturated. Dew does not always form at that temperature, because a surface below freezing produces frost instead. Equal condensation and evaporation describes the saturated state, not the definition of dewpoint.

stem: The amount of water vapor which air can hold depends on the
options: dewpoint.
air temperature.
stability of the air.
explanation: The maximum amount of water vapor air can hold rises with temperature: warm air can hold far more than cold air. Dewpoint describes how much vapor is actually present, not how much the air could hold, which makes it the tempting but wrong choice.

stem: Clouds, fog, or dew will always form when
options: water vapor condenses.
water vapor is present.
relative humidity reaches 100 percent.
explanation: Clouds, fog and dew are all visible water produced when water vapor condenses into liquid. Relative humidity reaching 100 percent does not guarantee it, since condensation also needs nuclei or a surface, and air can briefly become supersaturated. Vapor being present alone is never enough; it is invisible until it condenses.

stem: What are the processes by which moisture is added to unsaturated air?
options: Evaporation and sublimation.
Heating and condensation.
Supersaturation and evaporation.
explanation: Water vapor is added to air by evaporation (liquid to vapor) and sublimation (ice directly to vapor). Condensation removes vapor from the air, so any option that lists condensation or supersaturation as a source of added moisture is wrong.

stem: Which conditions result in the formation of frost?
options: The temperature of the collecting surface is at or below freezing when small droplets of moisture fall on the surface.
The temperature of the collecting surface is at or below the dewpoint of the adjacent air and the dewpoint is below freezing.
The temperature of the surrounding air is at or below freezing when small drops of moisture fall on the collecting surface.
explanation: Frost forms when the collecting surface cools to or below the dewpoint of the air next to it and that dewpoint is below freezing, so vapor deposits directly as ice crystals. Frost is not frozen droplets falling onto a surface; droplets freezing on contact would be freezing rain or drizzle, which is the trap in the other two options.

stem: The presence of ice pellets at the surface is evidence that there
options: are thunderstorms in the area.
has been cold frontal passage.
is a temperature inversion with freezing rain at a higher altitude.
explanation: Ice pellets begin as rain falling from a warm layer aloft that then freezes while dropping through colder air near the surface. Their presence therefore shows a temperature inversion with above freezing air, and freezing rain, at a higher altitude. They are not a reliable sign of thunderstorms or a cold front.

stem: What measurement can be used to determine the stability of the atmosphere?
options: Atmospheric pressure.
Actual lapse rate.
Surface temperature.
explanation: Stability is judged by comparing the actual (environmental) lapse rate with the adiabatic rate of rising air. A steep actual lapse rate means a lifted parcel stays warmer than its surroundings and keeps rising, so the air is unstable. Surface temperature or pressure alone says nothing about how temperature changes with height.

stem: What would decrease the stability of an air mass?
options: Warming from below.
Cooling from below.
Decrease in water vapor.
explanation: Warming air from below steepens the lapse rate, which makes the air mass less stable. Cooling from below does the opposite and creates stability or an inversion. Removing water vapor also tends to increase stability, so that option is wrong as well.

stem: What is a characteristic of stable air?
options: Stratiform clouds.
Unlimited visibility.
Cumulus clouds.
explanation: Stable air resists vertical motion, so any clouds that form spread out in flat layers called stratiform clouds. Visibility in stable air is usually reduced because haze and smoke are trapped, not unlimited, and cumulus clouds are the signature of unstable air.

stem: If an unstable air mass is forced upward, what type clouds can be expected?
options: Stratus clouds with little vertical development.
Stratus clouds with considerable associated turbulence.
Clouds with considerable vertical development and associated turbulence.
explanation: Unstable air that is lifted keeps accelerating upward, producing cumuliform clouds with considerable vertical development and turbulence. Stratus clouds with little vertical growth are the product of lifting stable air, so both stratus options are wrong.

stem: What feature is associated with a temperature inversion?
options: A stable layer of air.
An unstable layer of air.
Chinook winds on mountain slopes.
explanation: In an inversion temperature increases with altitude, which is the most stable lapse rate possible, so an inversion is a stable layer. It cannot be unstable by definition, and chinook winds are a downslope wind effect, not a defining feature of an inversion.

stem: What is the approximate base of the cumulus clouds if the surface air temperature at 1,000 feet MSL is 70 °F and the dewpoint is 48 °F?
options: 4,000 feet MSL.
5,000 feet MSL.
6,000 feet MSL.
explanation: Cumulus base is about 1,000 feet above the surface for every 4.4 °F of temperature and dewpoint spread. Spread is 70 minus 48 = 22 °F, and 22 ÷ 4.4 = 5, so the base is about 5,000 feet above the surface. The surface here is 1,000 feet MSL, so the base is 6,000 feet MSL; the trap is answering 5,000 and forgetting to add the field elevation.

stem: At approximately what altitude above the surface would the pilot expect the base of cumuliform clouds if the surface air temperature is 82 °F and the dewpoint is 38 °F?
options: 9,000 feet AGL.
10,000 feet AGL.
11,000 feet AGL.
explanation: Using 4.4 °F of spread per 1,000 feet: 82 minus 38 = 44 °F, and 44 ÷ 4.4 = 10, so the base is about 10,000 feet AGL. The question asks for height above the surface, so no elevation is added.

stem: What are characteristics of a moist, unstable air mass?
options: Cumuliform clouds and showery precipitation.
Poor visibility and smooth air.
Stratiform clouds and showery precipitation.
explanation: Moist, unstable air rises freely and builds cumuliform clouds that produce showery precipitation. Stratiform clouds and smooth air with poor visibility belong to stable air, so the option pairing stratiform clouds with showers mixes the two types.

stem: What are characteristics of unstable air?
options: Turbulence and good surface visibility.
Turbulence and poor surface visibility.
Nimbostratus clouds and good surface visibility.
explanation: Vertical currents in unstable air make it turbulent, and the same mixing carries haze and pollutants upward, so surface visibility is good outside of showers. Poor surface visibility goes with stable air, and nimbostratus is a stable layer cloud.

stem: A stable air mass is most likely to have which characteristic?
options: Showery precipitation.
Turbulent air.
Smooth air.
explanation: Stable air suppresses vertical motion, so the ride is smooth. Showery precipitation and turbulent air are characteristics of unstable air.

stem: The suffix "nimbus," used in naming clouds, means
options: a cloud with extensive vertical development.
a rain cloud.
a middle cloud containing ice pellets.
explanation: Nimbus means a rain cloud, as in nimbostratus and cumulonimbus. Extensive vertical development is described by the word cumulus or the prefix towering, not by nimbus.

stem: Clouds are divided into four families according to their
options: outward shape.
height range.
composition.
explanation: Clouds are grouped by the height of their bases into low, middle and high clouds, plus clouds with extensive vertical development. Shape (stratus, cumulus, cirrus) is used inside those families to name the cloud, not to define the four families.

stem: An almond or lens-shaped cloud which appears stationary, but which may contain very strong winds, is referred to as
options: an inactive frontal cloud.
a funnel cloud.
a lenticular cloud.
explanation: Lenticular clouds are lens or almond shaped clouds that form in the crests of mountain waves. They look stationary because air flows through them while the cloud keeps reforming at the crest, yet winds inside can be very strong. A funnel cloud is a tornado vortex, not a lens shaped cloud.

stem: Crests of standing mountain waves may be marked by stationary, lens-shaped clouds known as
options: mammatocumulus clouds.
standing lenticular clouds.
roll clouds.
explanation: The crests of standing mountain waves are marked by standing lenticular clouds. Roll (rotor) clouds sit lower, beneath the crests, where the worst turbulence is, and mammatus clouds hang from thunderstorm anvils.

stem: What clouds have the greatest turbulence?
options: Towering cumulus.
Cumulonimbus.
Nimbostratus.
explanation: Cumulonimbus clouds contain the strongest updrafts and downdrafts in the atmosphere and therefore the greatest turbulence. Towering cumulus indicate convective turbulence too, but they are an earlier, weaker stage, and nimbostratus is a stable layer cloud.

stem: What cloud types would indicate convective turbulence?
options: Cirrus clouds.
Nimbostratus clouds.
Towering cumulus clouds.
explanation: Towering cumulus are built by strong rising currents, so they indicate convective turbulence. Cirrus are high ice clouds and nimbostratus is a stable rain layer, neither of which signals convection.

stem: The boundary between two different air masses is referred to as a
options: frontolysis.
frontogenesis.
front.
explanation: The boundary between two air masses of different properties is a front. Frontogenesis is the birth or strengthening of a front and frontolysis is its dissipation, so those terms describe processes, not the boundary itself.

stem: One of the most easily recognized discontinuities across a front is
options: a change in temperature.
an increase in cloud coverage.
an increase in relative humidity.
explanation: Air masses differ most noticeably in temperature, so a temperature change is one of the easiest discontinuities to recognize when crossing a front. Cloud cover and humidity may or may not change, depending on the moisture in each air mass.

stem: One weather phenomenon which will always occur when flying across a front is a change in the
options: wind direction.
type of precipitation.
stability of the air mass.
explanation: A front always lies in a pressure trough, so the wind direction always shifts across it. Precipitation type and stability may change, but neither is guaranteed; a dry front can pass with no precipitation at all.

stem: Steady precipitation preceding a front is an indication of
options: stratiform clouds with moderate turbulence.
cumuliform clouds with little or no turbulence.
stratiform clouds with little or no turbulence.
explanation: Steady precipitation comes from stratiform clouds forming in stable air, typically ahead of a warm front, and stable air means little or no turbulence. Showery precipitation would point to cumuliform clouds and turbulence instead.

stem: Possible mountain wave turbulence could be anticipated when winds of 40 knots or greater blow
options: across a mountain ridge, and the air is stable.
down a mountain valley, and the air is unstable.
parallel to a mountain peak, and the air is stable.
explanation: Mountain wave forms when strong wind (40 knots or more) blows roughly perpendicular across a ridge and the air is stable, so it oscillates downstream like water over a rock. Wind parallel to a ridge or flowing down a valley does not set up the wave.

stem: Where does wind shear occur?
options: Only at higher altitudes.
Only at lower altitudes.
At all altitudes, in all directions.
explanation: Wind shear is any change in wind speed or direction over a short distance, and it can occur at any altitude and in both the horizontal and vertical directions. It is most dangerous near the ground, but it is not limited to low altitudes.

stem: When may hazardous wind shear be expected?
options: When stable air crosses a mountain barrier where it tends to flow in layers forming lenticular clouds.
In areas of low-level temperature inversion, frontal zones, and clear air turbulence.
Following frontal passage when stratocumulus clouds form indicating mechanical mixing.
explanation: Hazardous wind shear is found in low level temperature inversions, frontal zones, and areas of clear air turbulence, along with thunderstorms. The mountain lenticular option describes mountain wave, which can be turbulent but is not the general answer the question asks for.

stem: A pilot can expect a wind-shear zone in a temperature inversion whenever the windspeed at 2,000 to 4,000 feet above the surface is at least
options: 10 knots.
15 knots.
25 knots.
explanation: With a low level inversion the surface air can be calm while the air just above the inversion moves fast. A shear zone should be expected whenever the wind 2,000 to 4,000 feet above the surface is 25 knots or more, which matters most on climbout and approach.
ref: PHAK Ch. 12 (wind shear and inversions); Aviation Weather Handbook (FAA-H-8083-28)

stem: One in-flight condition necessary for structural icing to form is
options: small temperature/dewpoint spread.
stratiform clouds.
visible moisture.
explanation: Structural icing requires visible moisture, such as cloud or rain, plus an aircraft surface at or below freezing. A small temperature and dewpoint spread only suggests moisture may form, and stratiform clouds are just one place visible moisture can exist.

stem: In which environment is aircraft structural ice most likely to have the highest accumulation rate?
options: Cumulus clouds with below freezing temperatures.
Freezing drizzle.
Freezing rain.
explanation: Freezing rain consists of large supercooled drops that spread back before freezing and build clear ice very quickly, giving the highest accumulation rate. Freezing drizzle has smaller drops, and supercooled cumulus clouds can ice heavily but generally not as fast as freezing rain.

stem: The conditions necessary for the formation of cumulonimbus clouds are a lifting action and
options: unstable air containing an excess of condensation nuclei.
unstable, moist air.
either stable or unstable air.
explanation: A cumulonimbus needs a lifting action plus unstable, moist air. Stable air resists lifting and will not build a towering cloud, and an excess of condensation nuclei is not a requirement.

stem: What feature is normally associated with the cumulus stage of a thunderstorm?
options: Roll cloud.
Continuous updraft.
Frequent lightning.
explanation: The cumulus stage is the building stage, dominated by continuous updrafts. Frequent lightning and the roll cloud along the gust front come later, in the mature stage, when downdrafts reach the ground.

stem: Which weather phenomenon signals the beginning of the mature stage of a thunderstorm?
options: The appearance of an anvil top.
Precipitation beginning to fall.
Maximum growth rate of the clouds.
explanation: The mature stage begins when precipitation starts falling from the base of the cloud, dragging air down into a downdraft alongside the updraft. The anvil top is typical of a mature or dissipating cell, but it is not the event that marks the start of the stage.

stem: What conditions are necessary for the formation of thunderstorms?
options: High humidity, lifting force, and unstable conditions.
High humidity, high temperature, and cumulus clouds.
Lifting force, moist air, and extensive cloud cover.
explanation: Thunderstorms require sufficient water vapor (high humidity), an unstable lapse rate, and an initial lifting force. High temperature or existing cloud cover is not on that list, so the other options replace one essential ingredient with something optional.

stem: During the life cycle of a thunderstorm, which stage is characterized predominately by downdrafts?
options: Cumulus.
Dissipating.
Mature.
explanation: In the dissipating stage the downdrafts spread through the whole cell and cut off the updrafts, so downdrafts predominate. The mature stage has both updrafts and downdrafts, and the cumulus stage is mostly updrafts.

stem: Thunderstorms reach their greatest intensity during the
options: mature stage.
downdraft stage.
cumulus stage.
explanation: The mature stage has updrafts and downdrafts side by side, heavy precipitation, lightning and hail, so it is the most intense period. There is no official downdraft stage; the stages are cumulus, mature and dissipating.

stem: Thunderstorms which generally produce the most intense hazard to aircraft are
options: squall line thunderstorms.
steady-state thunderstorms.
warm front thunderstorms.
explanation: Squall line thunderstorms generally produce the most intense hazards, including severe turbulence, hail, heavy rain and tornadoes, and a line can be too long to fly around. Steady state cells are long lived, but the squall line is the classic answer for the most severe hazard.

stem: A nonfrontal, narrow band of active thunderstorms that often develop ahead of a cold front is a known as a
options: prefrontal system.
squall line.
dry line.
explanation: A squall line is a nonfrontal, narrow band of active thunderstorms, often forming 50 to 300 miles ahead of a fast moving cold front. A dry line is a moisture boundary, not the band of storms itself.

stem: If there is thunderstorm activity in the vicinity of an airport at which you plan to land, which hazardous atmospheric phenomenon might be expected on the landing approach?
options: Precipitation static.
Wind-shear turbulence.
Steady rain.
explanation: Thunderstorm outflow and microbursts can spread many miles from the cell and cause sudden wind shear on approach, which can rob the airplane of airspeed close to the ground. Precipitation static is only a radio nuisance, and steady rain is not the hazard.

stem: What situation is most conducive to the formation of radiation fog?
options: Warm, moist air over low, flatland areas on clear, calm nights.
Moist, tropical air moving over cold, offshore water.
The movement of cold air over much warmer water.
explanation: Radiation fog forms over low, flat land on clear, calm nights when the ground cools by radiation and chills moist air down to its dewpoint. Moist air moving over cold water is advection fog, and cold air over much warmer water is steam fog.

stem: If the temperature/dewpoint spread is small and decreasing, and the temperature is 62 °F, what type weather is most likely to develop?
options: Freezing precipitation.
Thunderstorms.
Fog or low clouds.
explanation: A small and shrinking temperature and dewpoint spread means the air is nearing saturation, so fog or low clouds are likely. At 62 °F there is no freezing precipitation, and a small spread by itself says nothing about the instability and lift that thunderstorms need.

stem: In which situation is advection fog most likely to form?
options: A warm, moist air mass on the windward side of mountains.
An air mass moving inland from the coast in winter.
A light breeze blowing colder air out to sea.
explanation: Advection fog forms when moist air moves over a colder surface, such as coastal air moving inland over cold ground in winter. Moist air rising up the windward side of mountains produces upslope fog, and colder air blown out over warmer water gives steam fog.

stem: What types of fog depend upon wind in order to exist?
options: Radiation fog and ice fog.
Steam fog and ground fog.
Advection fog and upslope fog.
explanation: Advection fog needs wind to carry moist air over a cold surface, and upslope fog needs wind to push moist air up rising terrain where it cools. Radiation fog and ground fog form in calm conditions and wind tends to lift or disperse them.

stem: Low-level turbulence can occur and icing can become hazardous in which type of fog?
options: Rain-induced fog.
Upslope fog.
Steam fog.
explanation: Steam fog forms when cold air moves over much warmer water; the water heats the air from below, so the layer is unstable and can be turbulent, and supercooled droplets can make icing hazardous. Rain induced and upslope fog form in stable air and lack the convection that causes the turbulence.
ref: PHAK Ch. 12 (steam fog); Aviation Weather Handbook (FAA-H-8083-28)

stem: Which weather phenomenon is always associated with a thunderstorm?
options: Lightning.
Heavy rain.
Hail.
explanation: Lightning, and the thunder it produces, is always present in a thunderstorm; that is what makes it a thunderstorm. Heavy rain and hail are common but not guaranteed.

stem: When telephoning a weather briefing facility for preflight weather information, pilots should state
options: the aircraft identification or the pilot's name.
true airspeed.
fuel on board.
explanation: When requesting a briefing, the pilot identifies as a pilot and gives the aircraft identification or the pilot's name, then aircraft type, route, altitude and departure time. True airspeed and fuel on board are not part of the information the briefer needs to start the briefing.

stem: To get a complete weather briefing for the planned flight, the pilot should request
options: a general briefing.
an abbreviated briefing.
a standard briefing.
explanation: A standard briefing is the complete package for a planned flight: adverse conditions, synopsis, current and forecast weather, winds aloft and NOTAMs. An abbreviated briefing only updates or supplements information already received, and general briefing is not a briefing type.

stem: Which type weather briefing should a pilot request, when departing within the hour, if no preliminary weather information has been received?
options: Outlook briefing.
Abbreviated briefing.
Standard briefing.
explanation: With no weather already in hand and a departure within the hour, the pilot needs the full picture, which is a standard briefing. An abbreviated briefing assumes earlier information exists, and an outlook briefing is for departures 6 or more hours away.

stem: Which type of weather briefing should a pilot request to supplement mass disseminated data?
options: An outlook briefing.
A supplemental briefing.
An abbreviated briefing.
explanation: An abbreviated briefing is requested to supplement mass disseminated data, update a previous briefing, or get one or two specific items. Supplemental briefing is not an official briefing type.

stem: To update a previous weather briefing, a pilot should request
options: an abbreviated briefing.
a standard briefing.
an outlook briefing.
explanation: To update a previous briefing the pilot asks for an abbreviated briefing and tells the briefer the time and source of the earlier information so only the changes are covered. A second standard briefing would repeat everything.

stem: A weather briefing that is provided when the information requested is 6 or more hours in advance of the proposed departure time is
options: an outlook briefing.
a forecast briefing.
a prognostic briefing.
explanation: An outlook briefing is given when the proposed departure is 6 or more hours away and focuses on forecast conditions for planning. Forecast briefing and prognostic briefing are not briefing types.

stem: When requesting weather information for the following morning, a pilot should request
options: an outlook briefing.
a standard briefing.
an abbreviated briefing.
explanation: Weather for the following morning is normally requested 6 or more hours before departure, which calls for an outlook briefing. A standard briefing should then be obtained closer to departure time.

stem: (Refer to Figure 12.) Which of the reporting stations have VFR weather?
options: All.
KINK, KBOI, and KJFK.
KINK, KBOI, and KLAX.
explanation: In the reporting categories of AIM 7-1-7, VFR means a ceiling greater than 3,000 feet (or no ceiling) and visibility greater than 5 SM. KINK (15SM SKC), KBOI (30SM SCT150) and KLAX (6SM with only SCT007 and SCT250, so no ceiling) all qualify. KMDW (1 1/2SM OVC007) is IFR and KJFK (1/2SM FG OVC005) is LIFR, which rules out the options that include them.

stem: For aviation purposes, ceiling is defined as the height above the Earth's surface of the
options: lowest reported obscuration and the highest layer of clouds reported as overcast.
lowest broken or overcast layer or vertical visibility into an obscuration.
lowest layer of clouds reported as scattered, broken, or thin.
explanation: Ceiling is the height above the surface of the lowest layer reported as broken or overcast, or the vertical visibility into an obscuration. Scattered and thin layers never form a ceiling, and the ceiling is the lowest qualifying layer, not the highest overcast.

stem: (Refer to Figure 12.) The wind direction and velocity at KJFK is from
options: 180° true at 4 knots.
180° magnetic at 4 knots.
040° true at 18 knots.
explanation: KJFK reports 18004KT: wind from 180° at 4 knots. METAR winds are referenced to true north; only winds broadcast by ATC and ATIS are magnetic. The 040 option misreads R04/2200, which is the runway visual range group for runway 04 (2,200 feet), not a wind.

stem: (Refer to Figure 12.) What are the wind conditions at Wink, Texas (KINK)?
options: Calm.
110° at 12 knots, gusts 18 knots.
111° at 2 knots, gusts 18 knots.
explanation: KINK reports 11012G18KT: the first three digits are direction, the next two are speed, and G18 is the gust value, so 110° at 12 knots gusting 18 knots. Reading 111 as the direction breaks the fixed three digit direction format.

stem: (Refer to Figure 12.) The remarks section for KMDW has RAB35 listed. This entry means
options: blowing mist has reduced the visibility to 1-1/2 SM.
rain began at 1835Z.
the barometer has risen .35 inches Hg.
explanation: RAB35 in remarks means rain began at 35 minutes past the hour. The report is issued at 1856Z, so the hour is 18 and rain began at 1835Z. Pressure tendency and blowing obstructions are coded differently.

stem: (Refer to Figure 12.) What are the current conditions depicted for Chicago Midway Airport (KMDW)?
options: Sky 700 feet overcast, visibility 1-1/2SM, rain.
Sky 7000 feet overcast, visibility 1-1/2SM, heavy rain.
Sky 700 feet overcast, visibility 11, occasionally 2SM, with rain.
explanation: SPECI KMDW shows 1 1/2SM RA OVC007: visibility 1 1/2 statute miles, moderate rain (no plus sign, so not heavy), and an overcast layer at 700 feet, since cloud heights are coded in hundreds of feet. Reading 007 as 7,000 feet is the common trap.

stem: (Refer to Figure 14.) The base and tops of the overcast layer reported by a pilot are
options: 1,800 feet MSL and 5,500 feet MSL.
5,500 feet AGL and 7,200 feet MSL.
7,200 feet MSL and 8,900 feet MSL.
explanation: The sky group is BKN018 TOP055 / OVC072 TOP089, and PIREP heights are MSL. The overcast layer has its base at 7,200 feet MSL and tops at 8,900 feet MSL. The 1,800 and 5,500 values belong to the lower broken layer.

stem: (Refer to Figure 14.) The wind and temperature at 12,000 feet MSL as reported by a pilot are
options: 090° at 21 knots and -9 °C.
090° at 21 MPH and -9 °F.
080° at 21 knots and -7 °C.
explanation: The report is at FL120 with /WV 08021, wind from 080° at 21 knots, and /TA M7, temperature minus 7 °C. PIREP winds are in knots and temperatures in Celsius, so the MPH and Fahrenheit option is wrong.

stem: (Refer to Figure 14.) If the terrain elevation is 1,295 feet MSL, what is the height above ground level of the base of the ceiling?
options: 505 feet AGL.
1,295 feet AGL.
6,586 feet AGL.
explanation: The lowest broken or overcast layer is BKN018, a base of 1,800 feet MSL because PIREP heights are MSL. Height above ground is 1,800 minus 1,295 = 505 feet AGL. The other options use the terrain elevation itself or an unrelated sum.

stem: (Refer to Figure 14.) The intensity of the turbulence reported at a specific altitude is
options: moderate at 5,500 feet and at 7,200 feet.
light from 5,500 feet to 7,200 feet.
moderate from 5,500 feet to 7,200 feet.
explanation: /TB LGT 055-072 reports light turbulence from 5,500 to 7,200 feet MSL, the layer between the broken tops and the overcast base. Moderate is the icing intensity (LGT MOD) and is not part of the turbulence group.

stem: (Refer to Figure 14.) The intensity and type of icing reported by a pilot is
options: light to moderate.
light to moderate rime.
light to moderate clear.
explanation: /IC LGT-MOD RIME 072-089 reports light to moderate rime ice from 7,200 to 8,900 feet, inside the overcast layer. The type is stated as rime, so the answer that leaves out the type is incomplete and the clear ice option is wrong.

stem: (Refer to Figure 15.) What is the valid period for the TAF for KMEM?
explanation: The valid period group 1218/1324 runs from the 12th at 1800Z to the 13th at 2400Z, a 30 hour TAF. The 121720Z group is the issuance time, not the start of validity. In clock terms the period is 1800Z to 2400Z.

stem: (Refer to Figure 15.) In the TAF for KMEM, what does "SHRA" stand for?
options: Rain showers.
A shift in wind direction is expected.
A significant change in precipitation is possible.
explanation: SH is the descriptor for showers and RA is rain, so SHRA means rain showers. A wind shift would show up as a change group with a new wind, not as a weather code.

stem: (Refer to Figure 15.) Between 1000Z and 1200Z the visibility at KMEM is forecast to be?
options: 1/2 statute mile.
3 statute miles.
6 statute miles.
explanation: BECMG 1310/1312 00000KT 3SM BR SKC forecasts conditions becoming calm with 3 SM visibility in mist and sky clear between 1000Z and 1200Z on the 13th. The 1/2SM FG value is in a TEMPO group for 1200Z to 1400Z, which is outside the asked window.

stem: (Refer to Figure 15.) What is the forecast wind for KMEM from 1600Z until the end of the forecast?
options: Variable in direction at 4 knots.
No significant wind.
Variable in direction at 6 knots.
explanation: The last group is FM131600 VRB06KT P6SM SKC: from 1600Z on the 13th until the end of the forecast the wind is variable in direction at 6 knots. Reading the speed as 4 knots is a misread of the 06.

stem: (Refer to Figure 15.) In the TAF from KOKC, the "FM (FROM) Group" is forecast for the hours from 1600Z to 2200Z with the wind from
options: 180° at 10 knots.
180° at 10 knots, becoming 200° at 13 knots.
160° at 10 knots.
explanation: FM051600 18010KT sets the wind from 180° at 10 knots from 1600Z. The change to 200° at 13 gusting 20 is in BECMG 0522/0524, which starts at 2200Z, so for 1600Z to 2200Z the wind is simply 180° at 10 knots.

stem: (Refer to Figure 15.) In the TAF from KOKC, the clear sky becomes
options: overcast at 2,000 feet during the forecast period between 2200Z and 2400Z.
overcast at 200 feet with a 40 percent probability of becoming overcast at 600 feet during the forecast period between 2200Z and 2400Z.
overcast at 200 feet with the probability of becoming overcast at 400 feet during the forecast period between 2200Z and 2400Z.
explanation: FM051600 forecasts SKC, then BECMG 0522/0524 brings OVC020: the clear sky becomes overcast at 2,000 feet between 2200Z and 2400Z. Heights are in hundreds of feet, so 020 is 2,000, not 200.

stem: (Refer to Figure 15.) During the time period from 0600Z to 0800Z, what visibility is forecast for KOKC?
options: Possibly 6 statute miles.
Not forecasted.
Greater than 6 statute miles.
explanation: BECMG 0606/0608 21015KT P6SM SCT040 covers 0600Z to 0800Z, and P6SM means visibility greater than 6 statute miles. The PROB40 2SM TSRA group applies only to 0000Z to 0600Z.

stem: (Refer to Figure 15.) The only cloud type forecast in TAF reports is
options: Nimbostratus.
Cumulonimbus.
Scattered cumulus.
explanation: Cumulonimbus (CB) is the only cloud type ever included in a TAF, as in OVC008CB in Figure 15. Other clouds are reported only by coverage and height.

stem: To determine the freezing level and areas of probable icing aloft, the pilot should refer to the
options: Weather Depiction Chart.
Area Forecast.
Inflight Aviation Weather Advisories.
explanation: Inflight aviation weather advisories include AIRMET Zulu, which describes moderate icing and gives freezing level heights, and SIGMETs for severe icing. A weather depiction chart shows only ceilings, visibility and fronts, with no icing. The Area Forecast was replaced by the Graphical Forecasts for Aviation, which also displays G AIRMET icing and freezing levels.

stem: What is indicated when a current CONVECTIVE SIGMET forecasts thunderstorms?
options: Moderate thunderstorms covering 30 percent of the area.
Moderate or severe turbulence.
Thunderstorms obscured by massive cloud layers.
explanation: Embedded thunderstorms, meaning storms hidden inside widespread cloud layers, are one of the criteria for issuing a convective SIGMET, so a convective SIGMET that forecasts thunderstorms can be describing storms you will not see until you are in them. The turbulence choice is tempting, but every convective SIGMET implies severe or greater turbulence, not moderate or severe, and that is implied rather than forecast. Thirty percent coverage of moderate storms is below the issuance criteria.

stem: What information is contained in a CONVECTIVE SIGMET?
options: Tornadoes, embedded thunderstorms, and hail 3/4 inch or greater in diameter.
Severe icing, severe turbulence, or widespread dust storms lowering visibility to less than 3 miles.
Surface winds greater than 40 knots or thunderstorms equal to or greater than video integrator processor (VIP) level 4.
explanation: A Convective SIGMET covers convective hazards: tornadoes, lines or areas of thunderstorms (including embedded ones), and hail of 3/4 inch or larger, plus surface winds of 50 knots or more. Severe icing, severe turbulence and widespread dust storms are the content of a regular (non convective) SIGMET, which is the trap in the second option.

stem: SIGMET's are issued as a warning of weather conditions hazardous to which aircraft?
options: Small aircraft only.
Large aircraft only.
All aircraft.
explanation: SIGMETs warn of weather that is potentially hazardous to all aircraft, such as severe icing, severe or extreme turbulence, volcanic ash and widespread dust or sand storms. It is the AIRMET that is aimed mainly at light aircraft with limited capability, so do not confuse the two.

stem: Which in-flight advisory would contain information on severe icing not associated with thunderstorms?
options: Convective SIGMET.
SIGMET.
AIRMET.
explanation: Severe icing that is not associated with thunderstorms is issued as a (non convective) SIGMET. A Convective SIGMET covers thunderstorm related hazards, and icing in a thunderstorm is already implied there; an AIRMET (Zulu) only covers moderate icing.

stem: AIRMETs are advisories of significant weather phenomena but of lower intensities than SIGMETs and are intended for dissemination to
options: All pilots.
only IFR pilots.
only VFR pilots.
explanation: AIRMETs describe weather of lower intensity than SIGMETs, such as moderate icing, moderate turbulence, IFR and mountain obscuration, and they are intended for dissemination to all pilots in preflight and en route planning. They are of particular concern to light aircraft, but they are not restricted to IFR or VFR pilots.

stem: (Refer to Figure 17.) What wind is forecast for STL at 9,000 feet?
options: 230° magnetic at 25 knots.
230° true at 32 knots.
230° true at 25 knots.
explanation: The STL 9,000 foot group is 2332+02: direction 230 degrees true, speed 32 knots, temperature plus 2 C. Winds aloft forecasts are always referenced to true north and given in knots, so the magnetic option is wrong, and 25 knots belongs to the 6,000 foot group (2325+07).
ref: Aviation Weather Handbook 27.2.1 (FB Winds and Temperatures Aloft); Figure 17

stem: (Refer to Figure 17.) What wind is forecast for STL at 12,000 feet?
options: 230° true at 39 knots.
230° magnetic at 56 knots.
230° true at 56 knots.
explanation: The STL 12,000 foot group is 2339-04: 230 degrees true at 39 knots, temperature minus 4 C. The 56 knot figure comes from the 18,000 foot group (2356-16), and directions in this product are never magnetic.
ref: Aviation Weather Handbook 27.2.1 (FB Winds and Temperatures Aloft); Figure 17

stem: (Refer to Figure 17.) Determine the wind and temperature aloft forecast for DEN at 9,000 feet.
options: 230° magnetic at 53 knots, temperature 47 °C.
230° true at 21 knots, temperature -4 °C.
230° true at 53 knots, temperature -47 °C.
explanation: DEN at 9,000 feet reads 2321-04: 230 degrees true, 21 knots, minus 4 C. The 53 knot and minus 47 options come from misreading the higher altitude groups (for example 235347 at 30,000 feet, where temperatures are implied negative), and the direction is true, not magnetic.
ref: Aviation Weather Handbook 27.2.1 (FB Winds and Temperatures Aloft); Figure 17

stem: (Refer to Figure 17.) Determine the wind and temperature aloft forecast for MKC at 6,000 feet.
options: 200° true at 6 knots, temperature +3 °C.
050° true at 7 knots, temperature missing.
200° magnetic at 6 knots, temperature +3 °C.
explanation: MKC at 6,000 feet is 2006+03: 200 degrees true at 6 knots with a temperature of plus 3 C. The 0507 group is the 3,000 foot level, where no temperature is forecast, and wind direction in this forecast is always true.
ref: Aviation Weather Handbook 27.2.1 (FB Winds and Temperatures Aloft); Figure 17

stem: (Refer to Figure 17.) What wind is forecast for STL at 12,000 feet?
options: 230° true at 106 knots.
230° magnetic at 39 knots.
230° true at 39 knots.
explanation: The STL 12,000 foot group 2339-04 decodes to 230 degrees true at 39 knots. The 106 knot option is a misread of a 7xxx coded group at higher levels (where 50 is added to the direction code and 100 to the speed), and the magnetic option is wrong because this forecast uses true direction.
ref: Aviation Weather Handbook 27.2.1 (FB Winds and Temperatures Aloft); Figure 17

stem: What values are used for Winds Aloft Forecasts?
options: Magnetic direction and knots.
Magnetic direction and miles per hour.
True direction and knots.
explanation: Winds and Temperatures Aloft forecasts give direction relative to true north and speed in knots, with temperature in degrees Celsius. Only the winds reported by ATC and ATIS for runway use are magnetic, which is the source of the magnetic trap.
ref: Aviation Weather Handbook 27.2.1 (FB Winds and Temperatures Aloft)

stem: When the term "light and variable" is used in reference to a Winds Aloft Forecast, the coded group and windspeed is
options: 0000 and less than 7 knots.
9900 and less than 5 knots.
9999 and less than 10 knots.
explanation: A wind group coded 9900 means light and variable, which is used when the forecast speed is less than 5 knots. A group of 0000 is not used for this, and 9999 is not a valid code.
ref: Aviation Weather Handbook 27.2.1 (FB Winds and Temperatures Aloft)
