stem: Radar weather reports are of special interest to pilots because they indicate
options: location of precipitation along with type, intensity, and trend.
location of precipitation along with type, intensity, and cell movement of precipitation.
large areas of low ceilings and fog.
explanation: The textual Radar Weather Report (SD) gave the location of precipitation echoes along with their type, intensity and the movement of the cells, which is the FAA key. Intensity trend is not the focus, and low ceilings and fog are invisible to weather radar. Today the same information comes from NEXRAD mosaic imagery rather than the old SD text product.
ref: Aviation Weather Handbook 24.6 (Radar Observations); Ch. 15 (Weather Radar)
note: The text Radar Weather Report (SD) is no longer issued; radar data is now used through NEXRAD mosaics.

stem: (Refer to Figure 19.) How are Significant Weather Prognostic Charts best used by a pilot?
options: For overall planning at all altitudes.
For determining areas to avoid (freezing levels and turbulence).
For analyzing current frontal activity and cloud coverage.
explanation: The low level Significant Weather prog is a forecast planning tool that highlights areas to avoid: IFR and MVFR areas, moderate or greater turbulence and freezing levels. It does not show current fronts or observed cloud cover, and it only covers the surface to 400 mb (about FL240), not all altitudes.
ref: Aviation Weather Handbook 27.8.1 (Low Level SIGWX Charts); Figure 19

stem: (Refer to Figure 19.) Interpret the weather symbol depicted in Utah on the 12-hour Significant Weather Prognostic Chart.
options: Moderate turbulence, surface to 18,000 feet.
Base of clear air turbulence, 18,000 feet.
Thunderstorm tops at 18,000 feet.
explanation: Over Utah the 12 hour chart shows the moderate turbulence symbol with 180/ and nothing below the slash. The number above is the top in hundreds of feet MSL and a missing base means the turbulence extends from the surface, so it is moderate turbulence from the surface to 18,000 feet. The symbol is not a thunderstorm marker, and the value is a top, not a base.
ref: Figure 19 legend; Aviation Weather Handbook 27.8.1 (Low Level SIGWX Charts)

stem: What should pilots state when telephoning a weather briefing facility for preflight weather information?
options: The intended route of flight radio frequencies.
The intended route of flight and destination.
The address of the pilot in command.
explanation: The briefer needs your intended route of flight and destination, along with type of flight, aircraft identification or pilot name, aircraft type, departure point, altitude and time information. Radio frequencies and the pilot's address have nothing to do with tailoring the weather briefing.

stem: When telephoning a weather briefing facility for preflight weather information, pilots should state
options: the full name and address of the formation commander.
that they possess a current pilot certificate.
whether they intend to fly VFR only.
explanation: Stating whether you intend to fly VFR only or IFR lets the briefer tailor the briefing, for example by adding the statement that VFR flight is not recommended when appropriate. You do not have to prove you hold a current certificate, and formation commander details are irrelevant.

stem: What weather information can a pilot get from a Flight Service Station when enroute?
options: Actual weather information and thunderstorm activity along the route.
Preferential routing and radar vectoring to circumnavigate severe weather.
Clearance into Class B airspace to avoid severe weather.
explanation: En route, Flight Service can give you actual weather and information on thunderstorm activity along your route. Radar vectors and Class B clearances come from ATC radar facilities, not from Flight Service. The former Flight Watch (EFAS) frequency is gone, but you still reach Flight Service on its published frequencies for en route weather.

stem: The destination airport has one runway, "08-26", and the wind is calm. The normal approach in calm wind is a left hand pattern to runway 08. There is no other traffic at the airport. A thunderstorm about 6 miles west is beginning its mature stage, and rain is starting to reach the ground. The pilot decides to
options: fly the pattern to runway 08 since the storm is too far away to affect the wind at the airport.
fly the normal pattern to runway 08 since the storm is west and moving north and any unexpected wind will be from the east or southeast toward the storm.
fly an approach to runway 26 since any unexpected wind due to the storm will be westerly.
explanation: A thunderstorm in its mature stage has strong downdrafts that spread out at the surface as a gust front, and with the storm 6 miles west any sudden wind at the airport will blow from the west. Landing on runway 26 puts that wind on the nose instead of on the tail. Gust fronts can run well beyond 6 miles from the cell, so the storm is not too far away to matter.
ref: PHAK Ch. 12; Aviation Weather Handbook Ch. 22 (Thunderstorms)

stem: When speaking to an AFSS weather briefer you should state
options: the pilot in command's full name and address.
a summary of your qualifications.
whether the flight is VFR or IFR.
explanation: Tell the briefer whether the flight will be VFR or IFR, since that decides which hazards and products are emphasized. Your name and address or a summary of your qualifications are not part of the request. Automated Flight Service Stations are now simply called Flight Service, but the briefing request items are unchanged.

stem: Cumulonimbus Mamma clouds are associated with
options: the dissipating stage of a thunderstorm.
violent thunderstorms and tornadoes.
the cumulus state of a thunderstorm.
explanation: Mammatus (pouch shaped bulges hanging under the anvil) mark extremely turbulent air and are associated with violent, severe thunderstorms that can produce tornadoes. They are not a sign of the gentle dissipating stage, and they do not appear in the early cumulus stage before an anvil exists.
ref: Aviation Weather Handbook Ch. 22 (Thunderstorms); Appendix A (Cloud Types)

stem: The Low-Level Significant Weather Prognostic Chart depicts weather conditions
options: that are forecast to exist at a valid time shown on the chart.
as they existed at the time the chart was prepared.
that existed at the time shown on the chart which is about 3 hours before the chart is received.
explanation: A prognostic chart is a forecast, so it shows conditions expected to exist at the valid time printed on the chart (for example VT 18Z). Charts that show what existed when they were prepared are analyses such as the surface analysis or weather depiction chart.

stem: Graphical Forecasts for Aviation (GFA) are weather charts best used to
options: plan a flight within 5 miles of your home airport.
learn the forecast weather along your proposed route of flight as well as at your destination if it has no terminal forecast.
learn the reported surface conditions of the airports along your route of flight.
explanation: The Graphical Forecasts for Aviation give forecast clouds, visibility, weather, winds, icing and turbulence over a wide area, so they are best for seeing conditions along your route and at a destination that has no TAF. Reported surface conditions come from METARs, and the product is not limited to a 5 mile radius.

stem: (Refer to Figure 260, area A.) What is the predominant visibility around the letter A on the Washington and Oregon coast?
options: VFR – visibility greater than 5 statute miles.
MVFR – visibility 3 to 5 statute miles.
IFR – visibility 1 to 3 statute miles.
explanation: Around Circle A on the Washington and Oregon coast the shading is mostly the light blue that the legend assigns to MVFR, visibility 3 to 5 statute miles, with only small patches of pink IFR to the north. White would be VFR, and IFR is not the predominant color at A.
ref: Figure 260 legend; Aviation Weather Handbook 28.2.1 (GFA Static Images)

stem: (Refer to Figure 262, area C.) The wind at Circle C is forecast to blow from which direction and at what velocity?
options: South at 10 knots.
Northwest at 5 knots.
Northwest at 10 knots.
explanation: The staff of a wind barb runs from the station toward the direction the wind comes from, and the feathers sit on the far end; a full feather is 10 knots and a half feather 5 knots. The barb at Circle C starts just north of the circle, its staff runs south behind the circle, and its single full feather sticks out just below it, so the wind comes from the south at 10 knots. The column of barbs just east of C is drawn the same way and confirms the reading. The barb just southwest of C points southeast; reading it, or the C barb, from the feathered end back toward the station gives a northwesterly or northerly wind, which is the trap in both northwest options.
ref: Figure 262 legend; Aviation Weather Handbook 28.2.1 (GFA Static Images)

stem: (Refer to Figure 260, area D.) The visibility in central New York just west of Circle D is mostly
options: LIFR – visibility 0 to 1 statute mile.
IFR – visibility 0 to 1 statute mile.
MVFR – visibility 3 to 5 statute miles.
explanation: Just west of Circle D over central New York the shading is purple, which the legend defines as LIFR with visibility 0 to 1 statute mile. The second option pairs the correct visibility with the wrong category, since IFR is the pink band from 1 to 3 miles.
ref: Figure 260 legend; Aviation Weather Handbook 28.2.1 (GFA Static Images)

stem: (Refer to Figure 260, area D.) Immediately to the left of the letter D in western New York, what are the surface winds?
options: Wind 25 gusting to 35 kts.
Wind 20 gusting to 30 kts.
Steady wind at 20 kts.
explanation: The barb immediately left of D has two full black feathers (20 knots) and a red gust barb showing one additional feather, so the forecast is 20 knots gusting to 30. A steady 20 knots ignores the red gust overlay, and 25 gusting 35 would need a half feather that is not there.
ref: Figure 260 legend; Aviation Weather Handbook 28.2.1 (GFA Static Images)

stem: (Refer to Figure 269, area A.) Just southwest of Circle A what cloud layer is forecast to be over Lake Michigan?
options: Bases of 5,500 feet MSL and tops at 6,000 feet MSL.
Bases of 550 feet MSL and tops at 600 feet MSL.
Bases of 5,500 feet AGL and tops 6,000 feet AGL.
explanation: Southwest of Circle A over Lake Michigan the label reads OVC055 TOP 060: overcast with bases at 5,500 feet and tops at 6,000 feet. The GFA cloud legend states that layers are given in MSL and the numbers are in hundreds of feet, so neither 550 feet nor AGL is correct.
ref: Figure 269 legend; Aviation Weather Handbook 28.2.1 (GFA Static Images)

stem: (Refer to Figure 269, area A.) What is the forecast ceiling at Delta County Airport (Field Elevation 609 feet MSL) in the Upper Peninsula of Michigan southwest of letter A?
options: 609 feet MSL.
4,891 feet AGL.
5,391 feet AGL.
explanation: The station southwest of A near Delta County shows OVC055, an overcast ceiling at 5,500 feet MSL. Subtracting field elevation gives 5,500 minus 609 = 4,891 feet AGL. Using the 6,000 foot top instead of the base gives the 5,391 trap, and 609 MSL is only the field elevation.
ref: Figure 269 legend; Aviation Weather Handbook 28.2.1 (GFA Static Images)

stem: (Refer to Figure 269, area B.) You're starting your trip in northeast Indiana. What kind of cloud coverage can you expect in this area?
options: Scattered at 6,000 feet MSL with tops at 7,000 feet MSL.
Few at 600 feet AGL.
Overcast at 6,000 feet MSL with tops at 7,000 feet MSL.
explanation: Around Circle B in northeast Indiana the stations read OVC060 TOP 070, an overcast layer based at 6,000 feet MSL with tops at 7,000 feet MSL, and the dark blue shading confirms overcast coverage. Scattered coverage would be light grey on this chart, and there is no FEW006 label.
ref: Figure 269 legend; Aviation Weather Handbook 28.2.1 (GFA Static Images)

stem: (Refer to Figure 269, area C.) What cloud layers are forecast in central New York?
options: Sky clear, few at 11,000 feet MSL and clear above.
Few at 11,000 feet MSL and scattered at 15,000 feet MSL.
Scattered layer at 15,000 feet MSL.
explanation: The station label beside Circle C reads FEW110 SCT150 CI ABV: few clouds at 11,000 feet MSL, scattered at 15,000 feet MSL, and cirrus above. The SKC station just east of C is clear, but the label belonging to the central New York area includes both layers, so the scattered only option leaves out the 11,000 foot layer.
ref: Figure 269 legend; Aviation Weather Handbook 28.2.1 (GFA Static Images)

stem: Given the following; Airport Elevation: 500 feet MSL Temperature: 23 °C Dewpoint: 15 °C Lapse Rate: 2 °C per 1,000 feet Find the approximate base of the cumulus clouds.
options: 4,000 feet MSL.
4,500 feet MSL.
2,300 feet MSL.
explanation: The temperature and dewpoint spread is 23 minus 15 = 8 C. The stem calls it a lapse rate, but the 2 C per 1,000 feet it gives is really the rate at which temperature and dewpoint converge, so the cloud base is 8 / 2 x 1,000 = 4,000 feet above the airport. Adding the 500 foot elevation gives about 4,500 feet MSL. Choosing 4,000 feet MSL forgets that the calculation gives height above ground. Outside this question use the standard convergence of 2.5 C (or 4.4 F) per 1,000 feet: here that gives 3,200 feet AGL, about 3,700 feet MSL, which is why you must use the rate the question supplies.

stem: You're flying on a cross country and your weather briefer tells you of an approaching warm front with steady precipitation. What can you expect:
options: Cumuliform clouds with little to no turbulence.
Stratiform clouds with moderate turbulence.
Stratiform clouds with little to no turbulence.
explanation: An approaching warm front with steady precipitation indicates stable air being lifted gently over cooler air, which produces stratiform clouds and generally smooth air. Cumuliform clouds and turbulence go with unstable air and showery precipitation, so the turbulence options do not fit.

stem: Dynamic hydroplaning is related to what factor?
options: Tire inflation pressure.
Weight.
Airspeed.
explanation: Dynamic hydroplaning occurs when standing water lifts the tire off the runway, and the minimum speed at which it begins is about 9 times the square root of tire pressure in psi. Speed is what sets it off, but the speed at which it starts is fixed by tire inflation pressure, so the factor the FAA tests is tire pressure: a properly inflated tire resists hydroplaning to a higher speed, and an underinflated one starts hydroplaning sooner. Aircraft weight is not part of the relationship.
ref: Airplane Flying Handbook Ch. 9; PHAK Ch. 14

stem: What causes reverted rubber hydroplaning?
options: Viscous water.
Water film.
Prolonged locked-wheel skid.
explanation: Reverted rubber hydroplaning results from a prolonged locked wheel skid: friction heat turns trapped water to steam and reverts the rubber, which then rides on the steam. Viscous hydroplaning is the one caused by a thin water film on a smooth or contaminated surface, which is the tempting distractor.
ref: Airplane Flying Handbook Ch. 9; PHAK Ch. 14

stem: With respect to the certification of airmen, which is a class of aircraft?
options: Airplane, rotorcraft, glider, lighter-than-air.
Single-engine land and sea, multiengine land and sea.
Lighter-than-air, airship, hot air balloon, gas balloon.
explanation: For airman certification, class means single engine land, single engine sea, multiengine land and multiengine sea (and similar groupings in other categories). Airplane, rotorcraft, glider and lighter than air are categories, and airship and balloon are classes within the lighter than air category.

stem: With respect to the certification of aircraft, which is a category of aircraft?
options: Normal, utility, acrobatic.
Airplane, rotorcraft, glider.
Landplane, seaplane.
explanation: For aircraft certification, category refers to the intended use or operating limits: normal, utility, acrobatic, limited, restricted, transport and so on. Airplane, rotorcraft and glider are categories only in the airman certification sense, and landplane or seaplane is a class.

stem: With respect to the certification of aircraft, which is a class of aircraft?
options: Normal, utility, acrobatic, limited.
Airplane, rotorcraft, glider, balloon.
Transport, restricted, provisional.
explanation: For aircraft certification, class is a broad grouping with similar characteristics of propulsion, flight or landing, such as airplane, rotorcraft, glider and balloon. Normal, utility and acrobatic, as well as transport, restricted and provisional, are categories of aircraft certification.

stem: The definition of nighttime is
options: sunset to sunrise.
1 hour after sunset to 1 hour before sunrise.
the time between the end of evening civil twilight and the beginning of morning civil twilight.
explanation: 14 CFR 1.1 defines night as the time between the end of evening civil twilight and the beginning of morning civil twilight, converted to local time. The 1 hour after sunset to 1 hour before sunrise window is the separate period used for night passenger currency, and sunset to sunrise governs position lights.

stem: Preventive maintenance has been performed on an aircraft. What paperwork is required?
options: A full, detailed description of the work done must be entered in the airframe logbook.
The date the work was completed, and the name of the person who did the work must be entered in the airframe and engine logbook.
The signature, certificate number, and kind of certificate held by the person approving the work and a description of the work must be entered in the aircraft maintenance records.
explanation: Under 14 CFR 43.9, a maintenance record entry must include a description of the work, the date completed, the name of the person who did it, and the signature, certificate number and kind of certificate of the person approving the aircraft for return to service. The other options each leave out required items.

stem: Which operation would be described as preventive maintenance?
options: Servicing landing gear wheel bearings.
Alteration of main seat support brackets.
Engine adjustments to allow automotive gas to be used.
explanation: Servicing landing gear wheel bearings, such as cleaning and greasing, is listed as preventive maintenance in Part 43 Appendix A. Altering seat support brackets is an alteration and engine adjustments for automotive fuel require approved data, so neither is preventive maintenance.

stem: Which operation would be described as preventive maintenance?
options: Repair of landing gear brace struts.
Replenishing hydraulic fluid.
Repair of portions of skin sheets by making additional seams.
explanation: Replenishing hydraulic fluid in the hydraulic reservoir is specifically listed as preventive maintenance. Repairing landing gear brace struts and making additional seams in skin sheets are structural repairs that require a certificated mechanic.

stem: What document(s) must be in your personal possession or readily accessible in the aircraft while operating as pilot in command of an aircraft?
options: A pilot certificate with an endorsement showing accomplishment of an annual flight review and a pilot logbook showing recency of experience.
Certificates showing accomplishment of a checkout in the aircraft and a current biennial flight review.
An appropriate pilot certificate and an appropriate current medical certificate if required.
explanation: 14 CFR 61.3 requires the PIC to have an appropriate pilot certificate and, when required, a current medical certificate in personal possession or readily accessible in the aircraft (along with government photo identification). A logbook and flight review endorsement are required to be current, but they do not have to be carried.

stem: When must a current certificate be in the pilot's personal possession?
options: When acting as a crew chief during launch and recovery.
Only when passengers are carried.
Anytime when acting as a pilot in command or as a required crewmember.
explanation: The pilot certificate must be in personal possession or readily accessible whenever you act as pilot in command or as a required flight crewmember, regardless of whether passengers are aboard. Ground crew roles such as a crew chief are not covered.

stem: A recreational or private pilot acting as pilot in command, or in any other capacity as a required pilot flight crewmember, must have in their personal possession while aboard the aircraft a current
options: logbook endorsement to show that a flight review has been satisfactorily accomplished.
medical certificate if required and an appropriate pilot certificate.
endorsement on the pilot certificate to show that a flight review has been satisfactorily accomplished.
explanation: When acting as PIC or required crewmember, a recreational or private pilot must have an appropriate pilot certificate and a current medical certificate if one is required. The flight review is recorded by a logbook endorsement, and neither the logbook nor such an endorsement has to be carried.

stem: Each person who holds a pilot certificate or a medical certificate shall present it for inspection upon the request of the Administrator, the National Transportation Safety Board, or any
options: authorized representative of the Department of Transportation.
person in a position of authority.
federal, state, or local law enforcement officer.
explanation: Certificates must be presented for inspection on request of the Administrator, an authorized NTSB representative, any federal, state or local law enforcement officer, or an authorized TSA representative. A generic person in a position of authority does not qualify.

stem: A Third-Class Medical Certificate is issued to a 36-year-old pilot on August 10, this year. To exercise the privileges of a Private Pilot Certificate, the medical certificate will be valid until midnight on
options: August 10, 2 years later.
August 31, 5 years later.
August 31, 2 years later.
explanation: For a pilot under 40 on the date of the exam, a third class medical is valid for private pilot privileges for 60 calendar months. Calendar months end on the last day of the month, so an August 10 exam runs to midnight August 31, 5 years later. The 2 year options apply only to pilots 40 or older.

stem: A Third-Class Medical Certificate is issued to a 51-year-old pilot on May 3, this year. To exercise the privileges of a Private Pilot Certificate, the medical certificate will be valid until midnight on
options: May 3, 1 year later.
May 31, 1 year later.
May 31, 2 years later.
explanation: A pilot who is 40 or older on the exam date gets 24 calendar months of third class privileges, so a May 3 exam is good until midnight on May 31, 2 years later. One year limits apply only to first class privileges for older pilots, and the expiration is always the end of the month.

stem: For private pilot operations, a Second-Class Medical Certificate issued to a 42-year-old pilot on July 15, this year, will expire at midnight on
options: July 15, 2 years later.
July 31, 1 year later.
July 31, 2 years later.
explanation: A second class medical reverts to third class privileges after its second class period, and for a pilot 40 or older third class privileges last 24 calendar months. So for private flying it runs until midnight July 31, 2 years later. The 1 year date only limits commercial privileges.

stem: For private pilot operations, a First-Class Medical Certificate issued to a 23-year-old pilot on October 21, this year, will expire at midnight on
options: October 21, 2 years later.
October 31, next year.
October 31, 5 years later.
explanation: For a pilot under 40, any class of medical used for private pilot privileges lasts 60 calendar months. An October 21 exam therefore expires at midnight October 31, 5 years later. The 12 month periods of a first class medical apply to airline transport and commercial privileges, not to private flying.

stem: The pilot in command is required to hold a type rating in which aircraft?
options: Aircraft operated under an authorization issued by the Administrator.
Aircraft having a gross weight of more than 12,500 pounds.
Aircraft involved in ferry flights, training flights, or test flights.
explanation: A type rating is required to act as PIC of a large aircraft (more than 12,500 pounds maximum takeoff weight), any turbojet powered airplane, and other aircraft the Administrator specifies through type certification. The other options describe operating authorizations or types of flights, not type rating triggers.

stem: What is the definition of a high-performance airplane?
options: An airplane with 180 horsepower, or retractable landing gear, flaps, and a fixed-pitch propeller.
An airplane with a normal cruise speed in excess of 200 knots.
An airplane with an engine of more than 200 horsepower.
explanation: A high performance airplane is one with an engine of more than 200 horsepower. Retractable gear, flaps and a controllable pitch propeller define a complex airplane, and cruise speed is not part of the definition.

stem: Before a person holding a private pilot certificate may act as pilot in command of a high- performance airplane, that person must have
options: passed a flight test in that airplane from an FAA inspector.
an endorsement in that person's logbook that he or she is competent to act as pilot in command.
received ground and flight instruction from an authorized flight instructor who then endorses that person's logbook.
explanation: To act as PIC of a high performance airplane you need ground and flight training from an authorized instructor in such an airplane and a one time logbook endorsement stating you are proficient. No FAA flight test is required, and a vague competence endorsement without the training does not satisfy the rule.

stem: In order to act as pilot in command of a high performance airplane, a pilot must have
options: received and logged ground and flight instruction in an airplane that has more than 200 horsepower.
made and logged three solo takeoffs and landings in a high performance airplane.
passed a flight test in a high performance airplane.
explanation: The rule requires received and logged ground and flight training in an airplane with an engine of more than 200 horsepower, plus the instructor's endorsement. There is no solo takeoff and landing requirement and no flight test for the high performance endorsement.

stem: To act as pilot in command of an aircraft carrying passengers, a pilot must show by logbook endorsement the satisfactory completion of a flight review or completion of a pilot proficiency check within the preceding
options: 6 calendar months.
12 calendar months.
24 calendar months.
explanation: To act as PIC at all, not only with passengers, a pilot must have completed a flight review within the preceding 24 calendar months, or a pilot proficiency check or other approved alternative. The 90 day rule covers passenger currency, not the flight review.

stem: If recency of experience requirements for night flight are not met and official sunset is 1830, the latest time passengers may be carried is
explanation: Without night currency you may not carry passengers during the period from 1 hour after sunset to 1 hour before sunrise. With sunset at 1830, that period begins at 1930, so the latest time with passengers is 1929. The 1829 option confuses this with the sunset to sunrise lighting rule.

stem: To act as pilot in command of an aircraft carrying passengers, the pilot must have made at least three takeoffs and three landings in an aircraft of the same category, class, and if a type rating is required, of the same type, within the preceding
options: 90 days.
12 calendar months.
24 calendar months.
explanation: Passenger carrying currency requires three takeoffs and three landings in the preceding 90 days in the same category, class and type (if a type rating is required). The 24 calendar month period is the flight review interval, not landing currency.

stem: To act as pilot in command of an aircraft carrying passengers, the pilot must have made three takeoffs and three landings within the preceding 90 days in an aircraft of the same
options: make and model.
category and class, but not type.
category, class, and type, if a type rating is required.
explanation: The three takeoffs and landings must be in an aircraft of the same category and class, and of the same type when a type rating is required. Make and model is not the regulatory standard, and type does matter for type rated aircraft.

stem: The takeoffs and landings required to meet the recency of experience requirements for carrying passengers in a tailwheel airplane
options: may be touch and go or full stop.
must be touch and go.
must be to a full stop.
explanation: For a tailwheel airplane the three takeoffs and landings for passenger currency must be made to a full stop. Touch and go landings count only for nosewheel airplanes during the day.

stem: The three takeoffs and landings that are required to act as pilot in command at night must be done during the time period from
options: sunset to sunrise.
1 hour after sunset to 1 hour before sunrise.
the end of evening civil twilight to the beginning of morning civil twilight.
explanation: Night passenger currency requires three takeoffs and landings to a full stop during the period from 1 hour after sunset to 1 hour before sunrise. The end of civil twilight definition is used for logging night time and night equipment requirements, not for this currency.

stem: To meet the recency of experience requirements to act as pilot in command carrying passengers at night, a pilot must have made at least three takeoffs and three landings to a full stop within the preceding 90 days in
options: the same category and class of aircraft to be used.
the same type of aircraft to be used.
any aircraft.
explanation: Night passenger currency requires three full stop takeoffs and landings in the preceding 90 days in the same category and class (and type, if a type rating is required) as the aircraft to be flown. Any aircraft is not enough, and type matters only for type rated aircraft.

stem: If a certificated pilot changes permanent mailing address and fails to notify the FAA Airmen Certification Branch of the new address, the pilot is entitled to exercise the privileges of the pilot certificate for a period of only
options: 30 days after the date of the move.
60 days after the date of the move.
90 days after the date of the move.
explanation: A pilot who changes permanent mailing address may not exercise certificate privileges after 30 days from the move unless the FAA Airmen Certification Branch has been notified. The 60 and 90 day options have no basis in the rule.

stem: A certificated private pilot may not act as pilot in command of an aircraft towing a glider unless there is entered in the pilot's logbook a minimum of
options: 100 hours of pilot-in-command time in the aircraft category, class, and type, if required, that the pilot is using to tow a glider.
200 hours of pilot-in-command time in the aircraft category, class, and type, if required, that the pilot is using to tow a glider.
100 hours of pilot flight time in any aircraft, that the pilot is using to tow a glider.
explanation: To tow a glider, the pilot must have logged at least 100 hours of pilot in command time in the aircraft category, class and type (if required) used for the tow. The 200 hour figure is invented, and time in any aircraft does not meet the category and class requirement.

stem: To act as pilot in command of an aircraft towing a glider, a pilot is required to have made within the preceding 12 months
options: at least three flights in a powered glider.
at least three flights as observer in a glider being towed by an aircraft.
at least three actual or simulated glider tows while accompanied by a qualified pilot.
explanation: The recent experience requirement for towing is at least three actual or simulated glider tows accompanied by a qualified pilot, or three flights as PIC of a towed glider. The current rule looks back 24 calendar months rather than the 12 months in the stem, but the content of the key is unchanged. Flights as an observer or in a powered glider do not count.
note: 14 CFR 61.69(a)(6) now uses a 24 calendar month look back, not 12 months.

stem: In regard to privileges and limitations, a private pilot may
options: not be paid in any manner for the operating expenses of a flight.
not pay less than the pro rata share of the operating expenses of a flight with passengers provided the expenses involve only fuel, oil, airport expenditures, or rental fees.
act as pilot in command of an aircraft carrying a passenger for compensation if the flight is in connection with a business or employment.
explanation: A private pilot may share operating expenses with passengers but may not pay less than the pro rata share, and only for fuel, oil, airport expenditures or rental fees. Carrying passengers for compensation is never allowed, even when the flight is incidental to business, though the pilot may act as PIC on such a flight if no passengers or property are carried for hire.

stem: According to regulations pertaining to privileges and limitations, a private pilot may
options: not pay less than the pro rata share of the operating expenses of a flight with passengers provided the expenses involve only fuel, oil, airport expenditures, or rental fees.
not be paid in any manner for the operating expenses of a flight.
be paid for the operating expenses of a flight if at least three takeoffs and three landings were made by the pilot within the preceding 90 days.
explanation: Under 61.113(c) a private pilot may not pay less than the pro rata share of fuel, oil, airport expenditures or rental fees with passengers. Expense sharing is allowed, so the never paid option is too strict, and landing currency has nothing to do with being paid.

stem: What exception, if any, permits a private pilot to act as pilot in command of an aircraft carrying passengers who pay for the flight?
options: If the passengers pay all the operating expenses.
If a donation is made to a charitable organization for the flight.
There is no exception.
explanation: Under 61.113(d) a private pilot may act as PIC of a charitable, nonprofit or community event flight where passengers make a donation to the sponsoring organization, subject to conditions in 91.146 such as at least 500 hours of flight time. Passengers paying all the operating expenses is prohibited, since the pilot must pay at least a pro rata share.

stem: The final authority as to the operation of an aircraft is the
options: Federal Aviation Administration.
pilot in command.
aircraft manufacturer.
explanation: The pilot in command is directly responsible for, and is the final authority as to, the operation of the aircraft. The FAA writes the rules and the manufacturer sets limitations, but neither has operational authority in flight.

stem: If an in-flight emergency requires immediate action, the pilot in command may
options: deviate from any rule of 14 CFR Part 91 to the extent required to meet the emergency, but must submit a written report to the Administrator within 24 hours.
deviate from any rule of 14 CFR Part 91 to the extent required to meet that emergency.
not deviate from any rule of 14 CFR Part 91 unless prior to the deviation approval is granted by the Administrator.
explanation: In an in flight emergency requiring immediate action, the PIC may deviate from any rule of Part 91 to the extent required to meet that emergency. A written report is only required if the Administrator requests one, so the 24 hour report option is a trap.

stem: When must a pilot who deviates from a regulation during an emergency send a written report of that deviation to the Administrator?
options: Within 7 days.
Within 10 days.
Upon request.
explanation: A pilot who deviates from a rule during an emergency must send a written report of the deviation only upon request of the Administrator. There is no fixed 7 or 10 day deadline in 91.3.

stem: Where may an aircraft's operating limitations be found?
options: On the Airworthiness Certificate.
In the current, FAA-approved flight manual, approved manual material, markings, and placards, or any combination thereof.
In the aircraft airframe and engine logbooks.
explanation: Operating limitations are found in the current FAA approved flight manual, approved manual materials, markings and placards, or any combination of these. The airworthiness certificate does not list them, and logbooks record maintenance, not limitations.

stem: Under what conditions may objects be dropped from an aircraft?
options: Only in an emergency.
If precautions are taken to avoid injury or damage to persons or property on the surface.
If prior permission is received from the Federal Aviation Administration.
explanation: No PIC may allow an object to be dropped that creates a hazard, but dropping is permitted if reasonable precautions are taken to avoid injury or damage to persons or property on the surface. No FAA permission is required, and it is not limited to emergencies.

stem: A person may not act as a crewmember of a civil aircraft if alcoholic beverages have been consumed by that person within the preceding
options: 8 hours.
12 hours.
24 hours.
explanation: No person may act as a crewmember within 8 hours after consuming any alcoholic beverage. The 12 and 24 hour figures are common personal or airline policies, not the 91.17 rule.

stem: Under what condition, if any, may a pilot allow a person who is obviously under the influence of drugs to be carried aboard an aircraft?
options: In an emergency or if the person is a medical patient under proper care.
Only if the person does not have access to the cockpit or pilot's compartment.
Under no condition.
explanation: Except in an emergency, a pilot may not allow a person who appears intoxicated or under the influence of drugs to be carried, with an exception for a medical patient under proper care. Restricting cockpit access does not create an exception.

stem: No person may attempt to act as a crewmember of a civil aircraft with
options: .008 percent by weight or more alcohol in the blood.
.004 percent by weight or more alcohol in the blood.
.04 percent by weight or more alcohol in the blood.
explanation: The regulatory limit is an alcohol concentration of 0.04 or greater in blood or breath. The .004 and .008 options misplace the decimal, which is the trap.

stem: Which preflight action is specifically required of the pilot prior to each flight?
options: Check the aircraft logbooks for appropriate entries.
Become familiar with all available information concerning the flight.
Review wake turbulence avoidance procedures.
explanation: Before every flight the PIC must become familiar with all available information concerning that flight. Checking logbooks and reviewing wake turbulence procedures are good practice, but they are not the specific 91.103 requirement.

stem: Preflight action, as required for all flights away from the vicinity of an airport, shall include
options: the designation of an alternate airport.
a study of arrival procedures at airports/ heliports of intended use.
an alternate course of action if the flight cannot be completed as planned.
explanation: For flights not in the vicinity of an airport, preflight action must include weather reports and forecasts, fuel requirements, and alternatives available if the planned flight cannot be completed. Designating an alternate airport is an IFR flight plan requirement, and study of arrival procedures is not specified.

stem: In addition to other preflight actions for a VFR flight away from the vicinity of the departure airport, regulations specifically require the pilot in command to
options: review traffic control light signal procedures.
check the accuracy of the navigation equipment and the emergency locator transmitter (ELT).
determine runway lengths at airports of intended use and the aircraft's takeoff and landing distance data.
explanation: The PIC must determine runway lengths at airports of intended use and the airplane's takeoff and landing distance data. Light gun signals and navigation or ELT accuracy checks are not part of the specific 91.103 list.

stem: Flight crewmembers are required to keep their safety belts and shoulder harnesses fastened during
options: takeoffs and landings.
all flight conditions.
flight in turbulent air.
explanation: Required flight crewmembers must keep safety belts fastened while at their stations, and shoulder harnesses fastened during takeoff and landing (if installed), so the regulatory answer is takeoffs and landings. Keeping them on in all conditions or in turbulence is good practice, not the stated requirement.

stem: Which best describes the flight conditions under which flight crewmembers are specifically required to keep their safety belts and shoulder harnesses fastened?
options: Safety belts during takeoff and landing; shoulder harnesses during takeoff and landing.
Safety belts during takeoff and landing; shoulder harnesses during takeoff and landing and while en route.
Safety belts during takeoff and landing and while en route; shoulder harnesses during takeoff and landing.
explanation: Under 91.105 each required flight crewmember must keep the safety belt fastened while at the crew station, which covers the whole flight including en route. The shoulder harness, if installed, is only required during takeoff and landing. The tempting trap is choice B, which reverses the two requirements.

stem: With respect to passengers, what obligation, if any, does a pilot in command have concerning the use of safety belts?
options: The pilot in command must instruct the passengers to keep their safety belts fastened for the entire flight.
The pilot in command must brief the passengers on the use of safety belts and notify them to fasten their safety belts during taxi, takeoff, and landing.
The pilot in command has no obligation in regard to passengers' use of safety belts.
explanation: 14 CFR 91.107 requires the pilot in command to brief each person on board on how to fasten and unfasten the safety belt and shoulder harness, and to notify them to fasten them before taxi, takeoff, and landing. The rule does not require belts for the entire flight, so choice A overstates it, and choice C ignores a clear PIC duty.

stem: With certain exceptions, safety belts are required to be secured about passengers during
options: taxi, takeoffs, and landings.
all flight conditions.
flight in turbulent air.
explanation: Each person on board must occupy a seat with the safety belt and any installed shoulder harness fastened during movement on the surface, takeoff, and landing. Belts are recommended but not required in all flight conditions or only in turbulence. The exceptions cover persons under two held by an adult and certain parachuting and floor seating operations.

stem: Safety belts are required to be properly secured about which persons in an aircraft and when?
options: Pilots only, during takeoffs and landings.
Passengers, during taxi, takeoffs, and landings only.
Each person on board the aircraft during the entire flight.
explanation: The passenger requirement in 91.107 is limited to taxi, takeoff, and landing. Choice C sounds safer but no rule requires belts for every occupant for the entire flight, and crew belt rules are a separate requirement under 91.105 rather than a takeoff and landing only rule for pilots.

stem: No person may operate an aircraft in formation flight
options: over a densely populated area.
in Class D airspace under special VFR.
except by prior arrangement with the pilot in command of each aircraft.
explanation: 14 CFR 91.111 prohibits formation flight except by arrangement with the pilot in command of each aircraft in the formation, and it bans carrying passengers for hire in formation. There is no specific formation prohibition tied to densely populated areas or special VFR in Class D, so choices A and B are distractors.

stem: Which aircraft has the right-of-way over all other air traffic?
options: A balloon.
An aircraft in distress.
An aircraft on final approach to land.
explanation: An aircraft in distress has the right of way over all other air traffic under 91.113(c). A balloon has the right of way over other categories only when nobody is in distress, and an aircraft on final has priority over aircraft in flight or on the surface but still yields to an emergency.

stem: What action is required when two aircraft of the same category converge, but not head-on?
options: The faster aircraft shall give way.
The aircraft on the left shall give way.
Each aircraft shall give way to the right.
explanation: When aircraft of the same category converge at about the same altitude, other than head on, the aircraft to the other's right has the right of way, so the aircraft on the left gives way. Speed does not determine right of way, and "each gives way to the right" is the head on rule, not the converging rule.

stem: Which aircraft has the right-of-way over the other aircraft listed?
options: Glider.
Airship.
Aircraft refueling other aircraft.
explanation: A glider has the right of way over an airship and over all engine driven aircraft. An aircraft refueling or towing another aircraft has the right of way only over other engine driven aircraft, so it still yields to the glider. The trap is thinking the refueling aircraft beats everything.

stem: An airplane and an airship are converging. If the airship is left of the airplane's position, which aircraft has the right-of-way?
options: The airship.
The airplane.
Each pilot should alter course to the right.
explanation: Category priority applies before the converging rule: an airship has the right of way over an airplane regardless of relative position. The "aircraft on the right" rule only decides between aircraft of the same category, which is why choice B is wrong even though the airship is on the left.

stem: Which aircraft has the right-of-way over the other aircraft listed?
options: Airship.
Aircraft towing other aircraft.
Gyroplane.
explanation: An aircraft towing or refueling other aircraft has the right of way over all other engine driven aircraft, and both an airship and a gyroplane are engine driven. An airship normally has priority over a gyroplane, but the towing exception places the towing aircraft above both.

stem: What action should the pilots of a glider and an airplane take if on a head-on collision course?
options: The airplane pilot should give way to the left.
The glider pilot should give way to the right.
Both pilots should give way to the right.
explanation: When aircraft are approaching each other head on or nearly so, each pilot alters course to the right regardless of category under 91.113(e). The glider's category priority applies to converging traffic, not to a head on encounter where both must turn right.

stem: When two or more aircraft are approaching an airport for the purpose of landing, the right-of-way belongs to the aircraft
options: that has the other to its right.
that is the least maneuverable.
at the lower altitude, but it shall not take advantage of this rule to cut in front of or to overtake another.
explanation: For aircraft approaching to land, the one at the lower altitude has the right of way, but it may not use that to cut in front of or overtake another aircraft on final. The "other to its right" logic in choice A is the converging rule for en route traffic, and maneuverability is not a factor.

stem: A seaplane and a motorboat are on crossing courses. If the motorboat is to the left of the seaplane, which has the right-of-way?
options: The motorboat.
The seaplane.
Both should alter course to the right.
explanation: On the water, the craft that has the other on its right gives way. The motorboat is on the seaplane's left, so the motorboat has the seaplane on its right and must give way, and the seaplane has the right of way. Choice C borrows the head on rule, which does not apply to crossing courses.

stem: Unless otherwise authorized, what is the maximum indicated airspeed at which a person may operate an aircraft below 10,000 feet MSL?
options: 200 knots.
250 knots.
288 knots.
explanation: Below 10,000 feet MSL the speed limit is 250 knots indicated unless otherwise authorized. 200 knots is the limit near Class C or D primary airports and beneath Class B or in VFR corridors, and 288 knots has no meaning in this rule.

stem: Unless otherwise authorized, the maximum indicated airspeed at which aircraft may be flown when at or below 2,500 feet AGL and within 4 nautical miles of the primary airport of Class C airspace is
options: 200 knots.
230 knots.
250 knots.
explanation: At or below 2,500 feet AGL within 4 NM of the primary airport of Class C or Class D airspace, the maximum is 200 knots indicated. The 250 knot figure is the general limit below 10,000 feet MSL and is the tempting wrong choice.

stem: When flying in the airspace underlying Class B airspace, the maximum speed authorized is
options: 200 knots.
230 knots.
250 knots.
explanation: In the airspace beneath the lateral limits of Class B airspace, or in a VFR corridor through it, aircraft are limited to 200 knots indicated. 230 knots appears in holding speeds and 250 knots is the general rule below 10,000 feet, neither of which applies here.

stem: When flying in a VFR corridor designated through Class B airspace, the maximum speed authorized is
options: 180 knots.
200 knots.
250 knots.
explanation: A VFR corridor through Class B airspace carries the same 200 knot limit as the airspace underlying the Class B shelf. Choice C is the general limit below 10,000 feet MSL, which is too high inside a corridor.

stem: Except when necessary for takeoff or landing, what is the minimum safe altitude for a pilot to operate an aircraft anywhere?
options: An altitude allowing, if a power unit fails, an emergency landing without undue hazard to persons or property on the surface.
An altitude of 500 feet above the surface and no closer than 500 feet to any person, vessel, vehicle, or structure.
An altitude of 500 feet above the highest obstacle within a horizontal radius of 1,000 feet.
explanation: Anywhere, 91.119(a) requires an altitude that allows an emergency landing without undue hazard to persons or property if a power unit fails. The 500 foot and 1,000 foot figures in the other choices are the additional rules for other than congested areas and for congested areas.

stem: Except when necessary for takeoff or landing, what is the minimum safe altitude required for a pilot to operate an aircraft over congested areas?
options: An altitude of 1,000 feet above any person, vessel, vehicle, or structure.
An altitude of 500 feet above the highest obstacle within a horizontal radius of 1,000 feet of the aircraft.
An altitude of 1,000 feet above the highest obstacle within a horizontal radius of 2,000 feet of the aircraft.
explanation: Over a congested area such as a city or an open air assembly of persons, you must stay 1,000 feet above the highest obstacle within a horizontal radius of 2,000 feet. Choice A mixes in the 1,000 foot figure but drops the 2,000 foot radius, and choice B uses the wrong numbers.

stem: Except when necessary for takeoff or landing, what is the minimum safe altitude required for a pilot to operate an aircraft over other than a congested area?
options: An altitude allowing, if a power unit fails, an emergency landing without undue hazard to persons or property on the surface.
An altitude of 500 feet AGL, except over open water or a sparsely populated area, which requires 500 feet from any person, vessel, vehicle, or structure.
An altitude of 500 feet above the highest obstacle within a horizontal radius of 1,000 feet.
explanation: Over other than congested areas you need 500 feet above the surface, and over open water or sparsely populated areas you may go lower but must stay at least 500 feet from any person, vessel, vehicle, or structure. Choice A is the rule for anywhere, and choice C uses the radius idea that belongs to congested areas.

stem: Except when necessary for takeoff or landing, an aircraft may not be operated closer than what distance from any person, vessel, vehicle, or structure?
options: 500 feet.
700 feet.
1,000 feet.
explanation: Over open water or sparsely populated areas the aircraft may not be operated closer than 500 feet to any person, vessel, vehicle, or structure. The 1,000 foot figure belongs to the congested area rule, which is measured above obstacles rather than as a standoff distance.

stem: If an altimeter setting is not available before flight, to which altitude should the pilot adjust the altimeter?
options: The elevation of the nearest airport corrected to mean sea level.
The elevation of the departure area.
Pressure altitude corrected for nonstandard temperature.
explanation: If no altimeter setting is available, 91.121 says to set the altimeter to the elevation of the departure airport, which the FAA words here as the departure area. With the field elevation set, the Kollsman window then shows an approximate local setting. Choices A and C describe corrections that are not part of the rule.

stem: Prior to takeoff, the altimeter should be set to which altitude or altimeter setting?
options: The current local altimeter setting, if available, or the departure airport elevation.
The corrected density altitude of the departure airport.
The corrected pressure altitude for the departure airport.
explanation: Before takeoff set the current local altimeter setting if one is available, otherwise set the departure airport elevation. Density altitude and pressure altitude are performance values, not altimeter settings, so choices B and C are traps.

stem: At what altitude shall the altimeter be set to 29.92, when climbing to cruising flight level?
options: 14,500 feet MSL.
18,000 feet MSL.
24,000 feet MSL.
explanation: In the United States the transition altitude is 18,000 feet MSL, where pilots climbing into Class A airspace set 29.92 and fly flight levels. 14,500 feet MSL is the base of Class E airspace only where no lower floor is designated, and it has nothing to do with altimeter settings. 24,000 feet is unrelated to altimeter procedure.

stem: When an ATC clearance has been obtained, no pilot in command may deviate from that clearance, unless that pilot obtains an amended clearance. The one exception to this regulation is
options: when the clearance states "at pilot's discretion."
an emergency.
if the clearance contains a restriction.
explanation: 14 CFR 91.123 allows a pilot to deviate from a clearance without an amendment only in an emergency, or when needed to respond to a TCAS resolution advisory. A clearance at pilot's discretion still has to be followed as issued, and restrictions in a clearance are part of what must be obeyed.

stem: When would a pilot be required to submit a detailed report of an emergency which caused the pilot to deviate from an ATC clearance?
options: Within 48 hours if requested by ATC.
Immediately.
Within 7 days.
explanation: A pilot who is given priority by ATC in an emergency must submit a detailed report within 48 hours to the manager of that ATC facility, but only if requested. No immediate written report or 7 day report is required by this rule; the 7 day figure is a trap from NTSB reporting.

stem: What action, if any, is appropriate if the pilot deviates from an ATC instruction during an emergency and is given priority?
options: Take no special action since you are pilot in command.
File a detailed report within 48 hours to the chief of the appropriate ATC facility, if requested.
File a report to the FAA Administrator, as soon as possible.
explanation: When ATC gives an emergency aircraft priority, the pilot must file a detailed report within 48 hours to the manager of that ATC facility if requested. Choice A ignores that obligation, and choice C names the wrong recipient and an open ended deadline.

stem: A steady green light signal directed from the control tower to an aircraft in flight is a signal that the pilot
options: is cleared to land.
should give way to other aircraft and continue circling.
should return for landing.
explanation: A steady green light to an aircraft in flight means cleared to land. Giving way and continuing to circle is steady red, and returning for landing is flashing green, which is the most common mixup.

stem: Which light signal from the control tower clears a pilot to taxi?
options: Flashing green.
Steady green.
Flashing white.
explanation: On the ground, flashing green means cleared to taxi, while steady green means cleared for takeoff. Flashing white means return to the starting point on the airport. Confusing the steady and flashing green signals is the classic trap.

stem: If the control tower uses a light signal to direct a pilot to give way to other aircraft and continue circling, the light will be
options: flashing red.
steady red.
alternating red and green.
explanation: Steady red to an aircraft in flight means give way to other aircraft and continue circling. Flashing red in flight means the airport is unsafe and do not land, and alternating red and green means exercise extreme caution.

stem: An alternating red and green light signal directed from the control tower to an aircraft in flight is a signal to
options: hold position.
exercise extreme caution.
not land; the airport is unsafe.
explanation: Alternating red and green is a general warning to exercise extreme caution, both on the ground and in the air. Hold position would be steady red on the ground, and airport unsafe, do not land is flashing red in flight.

stem: While on final approach for landing, an alternating green and red light followed by a flashing red light is received from the control tower. Under these circumstances, the pilot should
options: discontinue the approach, fly the same traffic pattern and approach again, and land.
exercise extreme caution and abandon the approach, realizing the airport is unsafe for landing.
abandon the approach, circle the airport to the right, and expect a flashing white light when the airport is safe for landing.
explanation: The alternating signal means exercise extreme caution, and a flashing red light to an aircraft in flight means the airport is unsafe, do not land. The pilot should break off the approach and not land. Choice C invents a right hand circle and a flashing white all clear, but flashing white only applies to aircraft on the ground.

stem: Which is the correct traffic pattern departure procedure to use at a noncontrolled airport?
options: Depart in any direction consistent with safety, after crossing the airport boundary.
Make all turns to the left.
Comply with any FAA traffic pattern established for the airport.
explanation: The regulations require a departing pilot to comply with any traffic pattern the FAA has established for the airport (14 CFR 91.127(b)). Where no special pattern exists, the AIM recommends departing straight out or with a 45 degree turn beyond the departure end of the runway after reaching pattern altitude. Making all turns to the left is the rule for aircraft approaching to land, not a departure procedure, and departing in any direction after crossing the airport boundary is not a recognized procedure.

stem: What is the specific fuel requirement for flight under VFR during daylight hours in an airplane?
options: Enough to complete the flight at normal cruising speed with adverse wind conditions.
Enough to fly to the first point of intended landing and to fly after that for 30 minutes at normal cruising speed.
Enough to fly to the first point of intended landing and to fly after that for 45 minutes at normal cruising speed.
explanation: Day VFR in an airplane requires fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and then for at least 30 minutes at normal cruising speed, assuming normal conditions. The 45 minute reserve is the night requirement, which is the tempting wrong pick.

stem: What is the specific fuel requirement for flight under VFR at night in an airplane?
options: Enough to complete the flight at normal cruising speed with adverse wind conditions.
Enough to fly to the first point of intended landing and to fly after that for 30 minutes at normal cruising speed.
Enough to fly to the first point of intended landing and to fly after that for 45 minutes at normal cruising speed.
explanation: At night the VFR reserve in an airplane rises to 45 minutes at normal cruising speed beyond the first point of intended landing. The 30 minute figure is the day rule, and choice A is not how the regulation is written.

stem: Which cruising altitude is appropriate for a VFR flight on a magnetic course of 135°?
options: Even thousandths.
Even thousandths plus 500 feet.
Odd thousandths plus 500 feet.
explanation: VFR cruising altitudes apply above 3,000 feet AGL and are based on magnetic course. A course of 135 degrees falls in the 0 through 179 degree range, so the pilot flies odd thousands plus 500 feet, such as 5,500. Even thousands plus 500 feet is for westbound courses, 180 through 359 degrees.

stem: Which VFR cruising altitude is acceptable for a flight on a Victor Airway with a magnetic course of 175°? The terrain is less than 1,000 feet.
options: 4,500 feet.
5,000 feet.
5,500 feet.
explanation: A magnetic course of 175 degrees is eastbound, so VFR cruise is odd thousands plus 500 feet. With terrain below 1,000 feet MSL, 5,500 feet MSL is well above 3,000 feet AGL, so the rule applies and 5,500 is correct. The trap is 4,500, an even plus 500 altitude meant for westbound courses, and 5,000 is an IFR style altitude.

stem: Which VFR cruising altitude is appropriate when flying above 3,000 feet AGL on a magnetic course of 185°?
options: 4,000 feet.
4,500 feet.
5,000 feet.
explanation: A magnetic course of 185 degrees is in the 180 through 359 range, so VFR cruise is even thousands plus 500 feet, giving 4,500 feet. 4,000 and 5,000 are whole thousands that VFR traffic should avoid because IFR aircraft use them.

stem: Each person operating an aircraft at a VFR cruising altitude shall maintain an odd- thousand plus 500-foot altitude while on a
options: magnetic heading of 0° through 179°.
magnetic course of 0° through 179°.
true course of 0° through 179°.
explanation: The hemispheric rule in 91.159 is based on magnetic course, the track over the ground referenced to magnetic north. Heading is affected by wind correction and true course ignores variation, so neither is what the regulation uses.

stem: In addition to a valid Airworthiness Certificate, what documents or records must be aboard an aircraft during flight?
options: Aircraft engine and airframe logbooks, and owner's manual.
Radio operator's permit, and repair and alteration forms.
Operating limitations and Registration Certificate.
explanation: 14 CFR 91.203 requires the airworthiness certificate and registration certificate on board, and 91.9 requires the approved flight manual, markings, or placards that contain the operating limitations. Logbooks stay on the ground with the owner, and a radio operator's permit is only needed for international flight.

stem: When must batteries in an emergency locator transmitter (ELT) be replaced or recharged, if rechargeable?
options: After any inadvertent activation of the ELT.
When the ELT has been in use for more than 1 cumulative hour.
When the ELT can no longer be heard over the airplane's communication radio receiver.
explanation: ELT batteries must be replaced, or recharged if rechargeable, when the transmitter has been in use for more than 1 cumulative hour, or when 50 percent of their useful life or useful charge has expired. A brief inadvertent activation does not by itself trigger replacement, and audibility on a com radio is not the standard.

stem: When are non-rechargeable batteries of an emergency locator transmitter (ELT) required to be replaced?
options: Every 24 months.
When 50 percent of their useful life expires.
At the time of each 100-hour or annual inspection.
explanation: Nonrechargeable ELT batteries must be replaced when 50 percent of their useful life has expired, or after more than 1 cumulative hour of use. The ELT itself is inspected every 12 calendar months, but there is no fixed 24 month battery rule and no tie to the 100 hour inspection.

stem: Except in Alaska, during what time period should lighted position lights be displayed on an aircraft?
options: End of evening civil twilight to the beginning of morning civil twilight.
1 hour after sunset to 1 hour before sunrise.
Sunset to sunrise.
explanation: 14 CFR 91.209 requires lighted position lights from sunset to sunrise, except in Alaska. The civil twilight period in choice A is the definition of night for logging and currency, and the one hour window in choice B is the night passenger currency rule in 61.57(b).

stem: When operating an aircraft at cabin pressure altitudes above 12,500 feet MSL up to and including 14,000 feet MSL, supplemental oxygen shall be used during
options: the entire flight time at those altitudes.
that flight time in excess of 10 minutes at those altitudes.
that flight time in excess of 30 minutes at those altitudes.
explanation: Above 12,500 feet MSL up to and including 14,000 feet MSL cabin altitude, the required minimum flight crew must use oxygen for the part of the flight at those altitudes lasting more than 30 minutes. Above 14,000 feet crew oxygen is required the entire time, which makes choice A the tempting trap.

stem: Unless each occupant is provided with supplemental oxygen, no person may operate a civil aircraft of U.S. registry above a maximum cabin pressure altitude of
options: 12,500 feet MSL.
14,000 feet MSL.
15,000 feet MSL.
explanation: Above a cabin pressure altitude of 15,000 feet MSL, each occupant must be provided with supplemental oxygen. 12,500 and 14,000 feet are the thresholds for crew oxygen use, not for providing oxygen to passengers.

stem: An operable 4096-code transponder with an encoding altimeter is required in which airspace?
options: Class A, Class B (and within 30 miles of the Class B primary airport), and Class C.
Class D and Class E (below 10,000 feet MSL).
Class D and Class G (below 10,000 feet MSL).
explanation: 14 CFR 91.215 requires an operable transponder with altitude encoding in Class A, Class B, within 30 NM of a Class B primary airport (the Mode C veil), and in and above Class C. Class D and Class G have no general transponder requirement, and in Class E it is only required at and above 10,000 feet MSL excluding the space at and below 2,500 feet AGL. ADS-B Out under 91.225 is now required in the same airspace.

stem: Which is normally prohibited when operating a restricted category civil aircraft?
options: Flight under instrument flight rules.
Flight over a densely populated area.
Flight within Class D airspace.
explanation: 14 CFR 91.313 says no person may operate a restricted category aircraft over a densely populated area, in a congested airway, or near a busy airport unless specifically authorized. IFR flight and Class D operations are not the general prohibition, though IFR may also be limited by the aircraft's operating limitations.

stem: Unless otherwise specifically authorized, no person may operate an aircraft that has an experimental certificate
options: beneath the floor of Class B airspace.
over a densely populated area or in a congested airway.
from the primary airport within Class D airspace.
explanation: Unless authorized in its operating limitations, an experimental aircraft may not be flown over a densely populated area or in a congested airway. Nothing in 91.319 bars flight beneath the Class B shelf or from a Class D primary airport, which makes choices A and C distractors.

stem: The responsibility for ensuring that an aircraft is maintained in an airworthy condition is primarily that of the
options: pilot in command.
owner or operator.
mechanic who performs the work.
explanation: 14 CFR 91.403 places primary responsibility for maintaining an aircraft in an airworthy condition, including AD compliance, on the owner or operator. The PIC decides whether the aircraft is safe for a particular flight, and the mechanic is responsible for the work performed, but neither carries the primary duty.

stem: The responsibility for ensuring that maintenance personnel make the appropriate entries in the aircraft maintenance records indicating the aircraft has been approved for return to service lies with the
options: owner or operator.
pilot in command.
mechanic who performed the work.
explanation: Under 91.405 the owner or operator must ensure that maintenance personnel make the required entries approving the aircraft for return to service. The mechanic actually makes the entry, which makes choice C tempting, but ensuring it happens is the owner or operator's duty.

stem: Completion of an annual inspection and the return of the aircraft to service should always be indicated by
options: the relicensing date on the Registration Certificate.
an appropriate notation in the aircraft maintenance records.
an inspection sticker placed on the instrument panel that lists the annual inspection completion date.
explanation: Completion of an annual inspection and approval for return to service is shown by an entry in the aircraft maintenance records, as required by 43.11 and 91.417. Registration certificates do not track inspections, and an inspection sticker has no regulatory standing.

stem: If an alteration or repair substantially affects an aircraft's operation in flight, that aircraft must be test flown by an appropriately-rated pilot and approved for return to service prior to being operated
options: by any private pilot.
with passengers aboard.
for compensation or hire.
explanation: After maintenance or alteration that may have appreciably changed flight characteristics, 91.407 requires a test flight by an appropriately rated pilot, holding at least a private certificate, before the aircraft carries passengers. The rule is about passengers, not about private pilots in general or flights for hire.

stem: Before passengers can be carried in an aircraft that has been altered in a manner that may have appreciably changed its flight characteristics, it must be flight tested by an appropriately-rated pilot who holds at least a
options: Commercial Pilot Certificate with an instrument rating.
Private Pilot Certificate.
Commercial Pilot Certificate and a mechanic's certificate.
explanation: The test flight required by 91.407 must be flown by an appropriately rated pilot holding at least a Private Pilot Certificate, who logs the flight and its result in the aircraft records. No commercial certificate, instrument rating, or mechanic's certificate is needed.

stem: An aircraft's annual inspection was performed on July 12, this year. The next annual inspection will be due no later than
options: July 1, next year.
July 13, next year.
July 31, next year.
explanation: An annual inspection is due within the preceding 12 calendar months, and a calendar month ends on the last day of the month. An annual done on July 12 therefore expires at the end of July 31 the following year. July 13 is the trap from counting exact days instead of calendar months.

stem: To determine the expiration date of the last annual aircraft inspection, a person should refer to the
options: Airworthiness Certificate.
Registration Certificate.
aircraft maintenance records.
explanation: The date of the last annual inspection, and therefore when it expires, is found in the aircraft maintenance records. The airworthiness certificate has no expiration date tied to inspections, and the registration certificate only shows ownership and its own expiration.

stem: How long does the Airworthiness Certificate of an aircraft remain valid?
options: As long as the aircraft has a current Registration Certificate.
Indefinitely, unless the aircraft suffers major damage.
As long as the aircraft is maintained and operated as required by Federal Aviation Regulations.
explanation: A standard airworthiness certificate stays in effect as long as maintenance, preventive maintenance, and alterations are performed in accordance with Parts 43 and 91 and the aircraft is registered in the United States. It is not simply tied to the registration, and major damage alone does not end it if the aircraft is properly repaired.

stem: What aircraft inspections are required for rental aircraft that are also used for flight instruction?
options: Annual and 100-hour inspections.
Biannual and 100-hour inspections.
Annual and 50-hour inspections.
explanation: Every aircraft needs an annual inspection, and an aircraft carrying a person for hire or used for flight instruction for hire, when provided by the person giving the instruction, also needs a 100 hour inspection. There is no biannual or 50 hour inspection requirement in Part 91.

stem: An aircraft had a 100-hour inspection when the tachometer read 1259.6. When is the next 100-hour inspection due?
options: 1349.6 hours.
1359.6 hours.
1369.6 hours.
explanation: The next 100 hour inspection is due 100 hours of time in service after the last one: 1259.6 plus 100 equals 1359.6. The 100 hour limit may be exceeded by up to 10 hours only to reach a place where the inspection can be done, which is where the 1369.6 trap comes from.

stem: No person may use an ATC transponder unless it has been tested and inspected within at least the preceding
options: 6 calendar months.
12 calendar months.
24 calendar months.
explanation: A transponder may not be used unless it has been tested and inspected within the preceding 24 calendar months under 91.413. The 12 calendar month interval applies to the ELT inspection under 91.207, which is the common mixup.

stem: Which records or documents shall the owner or operator of an aircraft keep to show compliance with an applicable Airworthiness Directive?
options: Aircraft maintenance records.
Airworthiness Certificate and Pilot's Operating Handbook.
Airworthiness and Registration Certificates.
explanation: The owner or operator must keep the current status of applicable Airworthiness Directives, including method of compliance, in the aircraft maintenance records. Certificates and the POH do not document AD compliance.

stem: If an aircraft is involved in an accident which results in substantial damage to the aircraft, the nearest NTSB field office should be notified
options: immediately.
within 48 hours.
within 7 days.
explanation: 49 CFR 830.5 requires the operator to notify the nearest NTSB office immediately, by the most expeditious means, after an aircraft accident, which includes substantial damage. The 7 day and 10 day figures relate to follow up written reports, not to the initial notification.

stem: Which incident requires an immediate notification to the nearest NTSB field office?
options: A forced landing due to engine failure.
Landing gear damage, due to a hard landing.
Flight control system malfunction or failure.
explanation: A flight control system malfunction or failure is one of the listed serious incidents that require immediate notification. A forced landing from engine failure is not on the list unless it results in an accident, and landing gear damage alone is excluded from substantial damage.

stem: Which incident would necessitate an immediate notification to the nearest NTSB field office?
options: An in-flight generator/alternator failure.
An in-flight fire.
An in-flight loss of VOR receiver capability.
explanation: An in flight fire is a listed serious incident under 830.5 that requires immediate NTSB notification. A single generator or alternator failure and loss of a VOR receiver are not reportable incidents.

stem: Which incident requires an immediate notification be made to the nearest NTSB field office?
options: An overdue aircraft that is believed to be involved in an accident.
An in-flight radio communications failure.
An in-flight generator or alternator failure.
explanation: Under 830.5 an aircraft that is overdue and believed to have been involved in an accident requires immediate notification. Radio failure and a single generator failure are not reportable; only failure of electrical systems requiring sustained use of emergency power is.

stem: May aircraft wreckage be moved prior to the time the NTSB takes custody?
options: Yes, but only if moved by a federal, state, or local law enforcement officer.
Yes, but only to protect the wreckage from further damage.
No, it may not be moved under any circumstances.
explanation: Wreckage may be disturbed before the NTSB takes custody only to remove injured or trapped persons, to protect the wreckage from further damage, or to protect the public from injury. Choice C is too absolute, and choice A invents a law enforcement exception.

stem: The pilot of an aircraft that has been involved in an accident is required to file an NTSB accident report within how many days?
explanation: The operator must file NTSB Form 6120.1 within 10 days after an accident. The 7 day figure applies when an aircraft is overdue and still missing, which makes it the most tempting wrong answer.

stem: The operator of an aircraft that has been involved in an incident is required to submit a report to the nearest field office of the NTSB
options: within 7 days.
within 10 days.
when requested.
explanation: For an incident, as opposed to an accident, the operator files a report only when requested by an authorized NTSB representative. The 10 day deadline applies to accidents and the 7 day deadline to an overdue aircraft that is still missing.

stem: Who is primarily responsible for maintaining an aircraft in airworthy condition?
options: Pilot-in-command.
Mechanic.
Owner or operator.
explanation: 14 CFR 91.403 makes the owner or operator primarily responsible for maintaining the aircraft in an airworthy condition. The PIC must determine the aircraft is safe before each flight, and mechanics answer for their own work, but the primary responsibility is not theirs.

stem: Prior to starting each maneuver, pilots should
options: check altitude, airspeed, and heading indications.
visually scan the entire area for collision avoidance.
announce their intentions on the nearest CTAF.
explanation: Before each maneuver, pilots should visually scan the whole area for other traffic, usually with clearing turns, as the Airplane Flying Handbook stresses. Checking instruments matters but does not prevent collisions, and the CTAF is used around airports, not before every practice maneuver.

stem: During a night flight, you observe a steady red light and a flashing red light ahead and at the same altitude. What is the general direction of movement of the other aircraft?
options: The other aircraft is crossing to the left.
The other aircraft is crossing to the right.
The other aircraft is approaching head-on.
explanation: The red position light is on the left wingtip, so seeing only steady red plus the flashing red beacon means you are looking at the other aircraft's left side. That aircraft is moving from your right to your left, crossing to the left. Choice B is the trap from forgetting which wing carries the red light.

stem: During a night flight, you observe a steady white light and a flashing red light ahead and at the same altitude. What is the general direction of movement of the other aircraft?
