explanation: Without baggage: 1,350 + 250 + 400 + 180 (30 gal) + 15 (oil) = 2,195 pounds and a moment of about 51.5 + 9.4 + 29.4 + 8.7 minus 0.2 = 98.8. The 2,300 pound limit leaves 105 pounds; adding it (about 10 more moment) gives about 108.8, still inside the envelope. 110 and 120 pounds would put the airplane over max weight.

stem: (Refer to Figure 34.) Calculate the moment of the airplane and determine which category is applicable. WEIGHT (LB) MOM/1000 Empty weight 1,350 51.5 Pilot and front passenger 310 --- Rear passengers 96 --- Fuel, 38 gal --- --- Oil, 8 qt --- –0.2
options: 79.2, utility category.
80.8, utility category.
81.2, normal category.
explanation: From the loading graph: 310 pounds up front is about 11.5, 96 pounds in the rear is about 7.0, and 38 gallons (228 pounds) is about 11.0. Moment = 51.5 + 11.5 + 7.0 + 11.0 minus 0.2 for oil = about 80.8, at 1,350 + 310 + 96 + 228 + 15 = 1,999 pounds. That point is at or below the 2,000 pound utility weight and just forward of the dashed aft utility line, so the airplane is in the utility category. Reading the lines generously gives 81.2, which would fall outside the utility envelope; the trap is careless chart reading near a boundary.

stem: (Refer to Figure 34.) What is the maximum amount of fuel that may be aboard the airplane on takeoff if loaded as follows? WEIGHT (LB) MOM/1000 Empty weight 1,350 51.5 Pilot and front passenger 340 --- Rear passengers 310 --- Baggage 45 --- Oil, 8 qt --- ---
options: 24 gallons.
32 gallons.
40 gallons.
explanation: Without fuel: 1,350 + 340 + 310 + 45 + 15 = 2,060 pounds, so 240 pounds of fuel brings it to the 2,300 pound limit: 240 / 6 = 40 gallons. The moment then is about 102.7, inside the envelope, so weight is the limiting factor.

stem: (Refer to Figure 34.) Determine the moment with the following data: WEIGHT (LB) MOM/1000 Empty weight 1,350 51.5 Pilot and front passenger 340 --- Fuel (std tanks) Capacity --- Oil, 8 qt --- ---
options: 69.9 pound-inches.
74.9 pound-inches.
77.6 pound-inches.
explanation: Fuel capacity in standard tanks is 38 gallons (228 pounds), about 11.0 on the fuel line. 340 pounds up front reads about 12.6 on the pilot and front passenger line. Moment = 51.5 + 12.6 + 11.0 minus 0.2 for oil = 74.9. The 77.6 option uses the 48 gallon long range tanks (about 13.7) instead of the standard tanks.

stem: (Refer to Figure 34.) Determine the aircraft loaded moment and the aircraft category. WEIGHT (LB) MOM/1000 Empty weight 1,350 51.5 Pilot and front passenger 380 --- Fuel, 48 gal 288 --- Oil, 8 qt --- ---
options: 78.2, normal category.
79.2, normal category.
80.4, utility category.
explanation: Moment = 51.5 + about 14.3 (380 pounds up front) + 13.7 (48 gal) minus 0.2 (oil) = about 79.3, so 79.2. Weight = 1,350 + 380 + 288 + 15 = 2,033 pounds, above the 2,000 pound utility limit, so the airplane is in the normal category.

stem: (Refer to Figures 32 and 33.) Upon landing, the front passenger (180 pounds) departs the airplane. A rear passenger (204 pounds) moves to the front passenger position. What effect does this have on the CG if the airplane weighed 2,690 pounds and the MOM/100 was 2,260 just prior to the passenger transfer?
options: The CG moves forward approximately 3 inches.
The weight changes, but the CG is not affected.
The CG moves forward approximately 0.1 inch.
explanation: Old CG = 226,000 / 2,690 = 84.0 inches. Removing 180 pounds at arm 85 takes off 153 (moment/100), and moving 204 pounds from arm 121 to 85 takes off another 73.4, so the new moment/100 is 2,033.6 at 2,510 pounds, a CG of 81.0 inches. The CG moves about 3 inches forward.

stem: (Refer to Figures 32 and 33.) What effect does a 35-gallon fuel burn (main tanks) have on the weight and balance if the airplane weighed 2,890 pounds and the MOM/100 was 2,452 at takeoff?
options: Weight is reduced by 210 pounds and the CG is aft of limits.
Weight is reduced by 210 pounds and the CG is unaffected.
Weight is reduced to 2,680 pounds and the CG moves forward.
explanation: 35 gallons is 210 pounds with a moment/100 of 158. New weight 2,680 pounds, new moment/100 2,452 minus 158 = 2,294, but the table maximum at 2,680 pounds is 2,287, so the CG (about 85.6 inches) is aft of limits. Fuel at arm 75 is forward of the CG, so burning it moves the CG aft, not forward.

stem: (Refer to Figures 32 and 33.) With the airplane loaded as follows, what action can be taken to balance the airplane? Front seat occupants.......................411 lb Rear seat occupants........................100 lb Main wing tanks.............................44 gal
options: Fill the auxiliary wing tanks.
Add a 100-pound weight to the baggage compartment.
Transfer 10 gallons of fuel from the main tanks to the auxiliary tanks.
explanation: As loaded: 2,790 pounds and moment/100 2,222, below the 2,243 minimum, so the CG is too far forward. Adding 100 pounds of baggage at arm 140 gives 2,890 pounds and 2,362, above the 2,354 minimum and within limits. Filling the aux tanks or moving 10 gallons to them still leaves the moment under the minimum.

stem: (Refer to Figure 61.) If 50 pounds of weight is located at point X and 100 pounds at point Z, how much weight must be located at point Y to balance the plank?
options: 30 pounds.
50 pounds.
300 pounds.
explanation: With the fulcrum as datum, X is 50 inches left, Y 25 inches left and Z 100 inches right. Balance needs 50 x 50 + Y x 25 = 100 x 100, so 25Y = 7,500 and Y = 300 pounds.

stem: (Refer to Figure 60.) How should the 500-pound weight be shifted to balance the plank on the fulcrum?
options: 1 inch to the left.
1 inch to the right.
4.5 inches to the right.
explanation: Left moment = 500 x 15 = 7,500; right moment = 250 x 20 + 200 x 15 (plank CG) = 8,000. The right side is 500 lb in heavier, so the 500 pound weight must move 500 / 500 = 1 inch farther left. Moving it right would make the imbalance worse; forgetting the plank weight leads to the wrong direction entirely.

stem: Center of gravity can be found by
options: multiplying weight times arm.
dividing total weight by total moment.
dividing total moment by total weight.
explanation: CG = total moment / total weight, the average arm of all the items. Weight times arm gives a single moment, and dividing weight by moment gives the reciprocal of what you want.

stem: In weight and balance calculations, arm is
options: the distance between items.
the distance from the datum line to the item.
weight times moment.
explanation: Arm is the horizontal distance from the reference datum to the item's CG, positive aft and negative forward. Weight times arm is moment, so the third option mixes up the terms.

stem: During operations outside controlled airspace at altitudes of more than 1,200 feet AGL, but less than 10,000 feet MSL, the minimum flight visibility for VFR flight at night is
options: 1 mile.
3 miles.
5 miles.
explanation: In Class G airspace more than 1,200 feet AGL but below 10,000 feet MSL, night VFR requires 3 statute miles flight visibility and cloud clearance of 500 feet below, 1,000 feet above and 2,000 feet horizontally. One mile is the day value for the same band, which is the trap. Five miles applies at or above 10,000 feet MSL.
